# The Evaluation Field Guide

A concept-first guide to designing, interpreting and operating evaluations of AI systems, agents and real workflows.

Coverage: Supplied coverage validated: 313 sources, 63 accepted readers; at most 5 sources per reader.

Source review and rendering limitations: https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/methodology.html

## What evaluation can establish: design, evidence and uncertainty

Teaches evaluation structure, evidence scope, uncertainty in claims and evaluation maturity; specific experimental estimators and product economics belong elsewhere. Owns control, sampling, uncertainty and causal interpretation; does not teach item-response models.

An AI evaluation is a structured way to collect evidence about a system performing specified tasks. It can inform a decision without proving that the system will succeed on every future case—or that a measured improvement caused a business outcome. The question is always: *what was measured, under which conditions, and how far does that evidence travel?*

## Build an interpretable measurement

An evaluation combines cases, a runnable system and its environment, a description of acceptable behavior, a scoring or judging method, and a way to inspect or aggregate results. A support-agent case might provide a customer request and account state, run the agent with its tools, and assess both its reply and the resulting account action. An expectation can describe an acceptable policy-consistent response rather than one exact sentence. Even a small loop and spreadsheet can make outputs inspectable; the format does not itself establish representative coverage or a reliable grader. [Source 1](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-1) [Source 2](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-2)

A benchmark is a reusable set of such tasks and scoring rules. Ask whether its tasks and standards reflect the capability of interest (**validity**), whether results are sufficiently consistent across relevant repetitions (**reliability**), and whether scores can distinguish the candidates (**discrimination**). If all systems hit the floor or ceiling, a benchmark may be unable to discriminate even if its tasks look relevant. A popular benchmark can still reward a shortcut; common use is not evidence of validity. [Source 3](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-3) [Source 4](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-4)

The result belongs to the measured population, task and outcome. One speaker describes a controlled developer experiment reporting a 55.8% speedup on a templated JavaScript HTTP-server task with twelve visible tests. That reported result does not establish the same gain across engineering work, labor removal or autonomous production delivery; the underlying study was not independently reviewed in the supplied evidence. Likewise, a percentage of AI-attributed pull requests needs its period, total population and attribution definition; participation is not the same as no-human-intervention delivery. [Source 5](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-5) [Source 6](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-6)

### Check the measuring instrument

A score can change because the grader changes, not because the agent improves. A math answer parser can lose a minus sign or mishandle a fraction. In a security demonstration, generated SQL contained the target flag but the grader checked the wrong representation; a without-skill run also produced the flag. The application still had unresolved vulnerabilities, so neither the grading difference nor the flag establishes a secure application or a reliable comparative advantage. Inspect artifacts and grader inputs before explaining a score as model ability. [Source 7](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-7) [Source 8](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-8) [Source 9](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-9)

## Evidence, assurance and maturity are different

A high aggregate score estimates performance under the evaluation conditions; it does not certify each output or prove a rule is *never* violated. For a financial value that must be correct, an independently implemented check against a trusted canonical source can withhold a value it cannot verify. That assurance remains conditional on the inputs, parser, rules and implementation being correct; deterministic does not mean infallible. A design's brand fit may resist a simple unit test, although explicit design rules can check parts of it and a human can decide whether a failed rule should be changed. [Source 10](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-10) [Source 11](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-11) [Source 12](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-12) [Source 13](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-13) [Source 14](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-14)

A maturity score answers a different question again. One proposed rubric distinguishes a capability that is absent, measurable, or tracked and analyzed over time; manual measurement can count. Its levels describe management practice, not a calibrated probability that a task succeeds. A polished results interface likewise does not by itself enable controlled comparisons or reveal production failures. [Source 15](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-15) [Source 16](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-16) [Source 17](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-17)

A working prototype is useful for demonstrating a possibility and giving colleagues something concrete to inspect, but a selected demonstration does not establish reliability over a real workload. Conversely, if the sample or measurement cannot support a consequential numerical decision, say the evidence is insufficient and gather more or defer the claim. A speaker's reluctance to report an A/B statistic for a 50-user product is an illustration, not a universal sample-size cutoff. [Source 18](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-18) [Source 19](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-19)

## Design comparisons around a decision

**Illustrative example:** A team wants to know whether conversation summarization preserves a support agent's quality while reducing context use. Run the same cases against the existing policy and the candidate, holding the model, prompt, tools and starting conditions fixed. Agree in advance on what counts as acceptable resolution and which cost and quality tradeoffs matter. Use a sensible baseline, repeated trials, and cases long enough to trigger summarization; record whether it actually ran. Otherwise a tied score could simply compare two runs in which the intervention never activated. Even with a trigger check, a handful of trials is suggestive, not a precise ranking. [Source 20](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-20) [Source 21](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-21) [Source 22](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-22)

Pre-registering cases, scoring, conditions and directional predictions makes it easier to distinguish a planned test from a result chosen afterward. A proposed historical-persona study fixes its instrument before collection and tests a hypothesis on a different figure from the one that motivated it; its predicted benefit of documentary anchoring remains a prediction, not a completed result. Pre-registration and controls constrain some biases, but neither proves a hypothesis. [Source 23](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-23) [Source 24](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-24)

Look at changes by case and criterion, not just the average: an agent may improve ordinary resolutions while regressing on sensitive refunds or becoming less clear. Those rows can change a release decision even when a headline score rises. For how to set the decision's case mix, see [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html); for investigation of individual traces, see [Tracing, failure analysis and evaluator methods](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods.html). [Source 25](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-25)

## Interpret variation and missing counterfactuals

Zero temperature chooses the highest-scoring token at each step, but underlying scores and system behavior can still vary; a perfectly repeated answer can also repeat an error. Repeated model rollouts expose variation in trajectories, whereas different task environments introduce another source of uncertainty. Running the same easy environment many times cannot substitute for sampling relevant environments. Confidence intervals should respect the task-and-environment hierarchy, and their coverage—the frequency with which the procedure contains the target across repeated samples—needs checking rather than being assumed from the nominal label. One speaker reports poor coverage for base-case-only intervals, but does not supply the simulation setup or estimator implementation. [Source 26](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-26) [Source 27](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-27) [Source 28](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-28)

More repetitions also cannot recover an unobserved counterfactual. A cafe agent inferred that existing opening hours were best because there were no sales outside them; the cafe had never opened then, so those observations say nothing direct about demand under extended hours. This is missing support for an alternative policy. A different problem is **confounding** between observed groups: an observational human-versus-agent pull-request comparison may reflect easier work assigned to agents. Checking pull-request size is useful, but equal size does not establish equal requirements, risk or review; authorship signals and reverts are proxies too. Neither example supports a causal ranking. [Source 29](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-29) [Source 30](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-30) [Source 31](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-31)

Survey percentages have their own population boundary. One presenter reports 1,048 respondents in a builder-heavy survey, without a sampling frame establishing representation of all organizations. The result describes those respondents; it cannot establish universal adoption or that the most common practice is adequate. Changing survey composition also prevents assuming a year-to-year change describes the same organizations. [Source 32](#what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish-source-32)

## From business problem to meaningful success criteria

Owns problem framing, construct selection and customer interpretation; detailed experiment design and model comparisons are separate.

A successful AI system is not defined by selecting a model or producing an impressive demo. Define the work that needs to improve, who experiences the pain and what an acceptable outcome looks like; only then decide which measurements can tell you whether a proposed solution helps.

## Frame the problem without prescribing the solution

Describe the user, current process, measurable pain and desired outcome in terms that would still make sense if no agent were built. For example, an illustrative insurance-claims problem is that reviewers take too long to process claims, delaying care. The objective might be a shorter decision cycle while retaining required human review and respecting data and model restrictions. These are hypothetical design conditions, not measured results. [Source 1](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-1)

Turn the problem into a specification before selecting models: which cases should be handled, what counts as a correct resolution, which errors or actions are unacceptable, and what operating constraints must hold? For support, the share of eligible simple queries resolved without a human can be a target, but deflection alone is not success if answers are wrong or customers need to return. An enterprise banking case describes setting handling and accuracy targets before model selection; its targets should not be read as achieved outcomes. [Source 2](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-2)

Agree on the criteria with domain, customer-facing, product and technical stakeholders. Data scientists' statistical expertise is valuable alongside operational knowledge; neither a model team alone nor a product aspiration replaces both. This is organizational guidance, not evidence that a particular staffing pattern causes better outcomes. [Source 3](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-3) [Source 4](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-4)

## Choose metrics for the actual decision

Name the thing each metric measures, its denominator, and the action it should inform. For the claims example, elapsed time from receipt to reviewed decision addresses the delay; a separately assessed decision-quality measure addresses whether the recommendation was usable. Reviewer override rate and review duration can flag investigation: long reviews might indicate confusing output, but that explanation is a hypothesis, and an override is not automatically a model error. These are workflow proxies, not accuracy itself. [Source 5](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-5)

Activity is especially easy to mistake for value. One demonstration found an agent run was reportedly 28% cheaper even though it still did not use the tool the experiment intended to assess; the speaker said cost variance needed investigation, so the number is not an established causal saving. Similarly, cursor movement is not a universal measure of useful information work: the proposed “mousepower” device was a metaphor ultimately rejected as a metric. [Source 6](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-6) [Source 7](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-7)

Choose technical metrics at the layer where they answer a real question. Precision, recall and F1 can help assess a judge against human labels, but they do not alone describe whether an agent completes the user's job. For image generation, a generic image score may not measure the text-rendering capability the product needs; the cited presentation describes larger separation on text-specific measures but supplies no uncertainty or proof of construct validity. Use complementary measures and understand what each omits. Human inspection also depends on who rates and which examples they see. [Source 8](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-8) [Source 9](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-9) [Source 10](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-10) [Source 11](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-11)

## Separate useful progress from complete delivery

A partial-credit score summarizes the fraction of criteria satisfied; a fully correct rate asks how often the *entire* deliverable meets every requirement. These are different estimands, not alternative names for the same quality number. A draft with most criteria satisfied may save a reviewer time, while the same result may be unacceptable for unreviewed client delivery. Report both if both uses matter, and measure the human correction burden for the draft workflow. There is no universal conversion from average partial credit to whole-task success. [Source 12](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-12)

## Measure policy choices, not recognition alone

Even if the underlying recognition hypotheses do not change, an assistant can act, reject or ask for confirmation. These choices change the errors and recovery effort experienced by users. In a speaker's illustrative music-assistant scenario, wrong playback takes effort to notice, interrupt and retry; rejection also delays a user, including one whose original hypothesis was correct. Confirmation has two distinct branches: a correct suggestion may receive a quick yes, while an incorrect one requires correction. [Source 13](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-13) [Source 14](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-14) [Source 15](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-15)

Compare policies using observed action outcomes and context-appropriate costs, including the burden of unnecessary confirmation as well as prevented mistakes. A simple low-confidence reject, middle-confidence confirm and high-confidence act policy can clarify the choice, but two thresholds are not a required architecture. It assumes useful calibration of confidence; the source's recovery times are illustrative, and lower estimated recovery cost is not a measured improvement in user satisfaction.

## Keep authority and outcome separate

An agent may obey every restriction and still fail its assigned job; it may also produce a useful-looking answer by taking an unauthorized action. Track authorized behavior and role success as separate dimensions rather than averaging them into a single correctness label. In an illustrative invoice workflow, a ceiling on approvals is an authority constraint; correct purchase-order matching and timely reconciliation describe the work. A conceptual scorecard can check clear rules and separately judge whether the intended outcome was achieved, without implying that the proposed governance framework has demonstrated effectiveness. [Source 16](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-16) [Source 17](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-17)

## Explain results in the customer's terms

Compare outcomes against a familiar baseline, such as the existing human review process, with the same task boundaries and required quality. A token count can explain a cost component but not by itself whether the work was worth doing. Early adopters who enjoy experimenting may tolerate workflows that ordinary customers cannot use; involve the intended population rather than treating builder enthusiasm as customer value. The familiar-baseline analogy is a communication aid, not a validated universal efficiency metric. [Source 18](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-18) [Source 19](#from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria-source-19)

Once criteria are explicit, [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html) helps determine which cases and populations the measurements must cover; [Defining agent roles, boundaries and oversight](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight.html) develops the adjacent authority and oversight design.

## Benchmarks, leaderboards and model selection

Owns benchmark transfer, rank interpretation, lifecycle and local selection; does not replace measurement of deployed-system reliability.

A leaderboard can narrow the field, but it answers a question about the tasks, candidates and scoring procedure on that board—not automatically which model will serve your users best. Use it to choose candidates for a decision, then test the relevant task and the assembled application. A higher score is evidence of performance under a particular measurement, not a general reliability guarantee. [Source 1](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-1) [Source 2](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-2)

## Read the ranking before choosing the winner

Ask what the board measures, which models and versions it includes, how examples were selected and scored, and whether its task mix resembles yours. Image editing illustrates why: object removal, background changes and text editing can have different rankings, so a team primarily removing objects should inspect that slice rather than assume the aggregate winner is best for it. The speaker describes category plots, not a complete dataset or a statistical test establishing the ranking for every application. [Source 3](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-3)

Multiple boards can disagree because they sample different tasks or participants, use different scoring methods or contain duplicate model entries. Even similar-looking Elo values need not share a scale across sites. A small rank difference is not, by itself, proof of either a meaningful advantage or equivalence. Product-specific rubric scores can be useful for improving one application while being unsuitable for ranking different products whose rubrics and tastes differ. [Source 1](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-1) [Source 4](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-4)

Disagreement about the verifier matters too. One speaker attributes a 0.3% false-positive claim to DeepSWE and a 44.9% critique to Frontier Code. The available account does not supply comparable sampling or denominators, so neither number resolves the dispute. The same speaker initially suggests averaging benchmarks but acknowledges the unresolved choice of weights. An average cannot repair incomparable audits: retain their provenance, show task composition and justify any weights against the actual decision. [Source 5](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-5) For designing that distribution, see [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html).

## Compare the model and the complete system separately

Decide which difference you are trying to estimate. To compare **models under a common setup**, hold the tasks, prompts, tools, scoring and other feasible settings constant, record necessary model-specific differences, and interpret the result as conditional on that setup. To choose a **deployable stack**, compare the candidate configurations—including their prompts, retrieval, tools and runtime—under the same user-relevant scenarios and budget. That comparison can answer which configuration worked better, but cannot attribute the entire difference to model weights when other components changed.

A hosted provider's tests do not test the application team's particular context and integrations. For example, an agent can answer benchmark questions well yet fail when a tool is unavailable or a workflow extends across multiple steps. Test capability offline, test the assembled workflow on representative scenarios, and observe it in use; these layers answer different questions. The proposed greater operational value of production telemetry is a speaker's framework, not a measured ranking of evidence sources. [Source 6](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-6) [Source 7](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-7) [Source 8](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-8)

The capability ceiling is also distinct from the failure floor: an impressive successful demonstration does not establish that the application avoids unwanted emails or destructive actions. Assess consequences alongside task success rather than assuming a better general score removes the need for controls. [Source 9](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-9) See [Defining agent roles, boundaries and oversight](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight.html) for those boundaries.

## Treat hindsight as headroom, not a shipped result

A retrieval experiment indexed the same material at several chunk sizes and, knowing the answers, chose the best size separately for each query. Comparing that hindsight oracle with one fixed size shows potential benefit from query-dependent selection; it does not provide a way to pick the right size for a new query. The reported percentage convention is unclear, so the headroom should not be converted into a precise deployable gain. A practical fusion method must be evaluated separately; its reported recall results are not final-answer quality results. [Source 10](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-10) [Source 11](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-11)

## Keep the comparison alive

A published ranking is a snapshot. Models can be replaced or withdrawn and an endpoint can change behind a familiar name. Record the model and endpoint identity as far as observable, configuration, task set, scoring and run date; retain historical artifacts and rerun the relevant comparison when candidates or the stack change. If a provider does not expose an immutable identity, record that limitation instead of claiming exact reproducibility. [Source 12](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-12) [Source 13](#benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection-source-13)

## Tracing, failure analysis and evaluator methods

Owns trace evidence, diagnostic scope and evaluator methods; execution environment design and statistical comparison are separate.

A plausible final answer does not reveal whether an agent retrieved the right information, failed a tool call or ignored a user’s constraint. A trace gives you evidence of execution; an evaluation asks a quality question about that evidence. Neither a trace nor a passing check, by itself, proves the whole task was done correctly. [Source 1](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-1)

## Trace tree and evidence boundary

A **span** represents a unit of work, such as a model call or tool invocation, and can record inputs, outputs, timing, token use and model metadata. Spans can nest: a child belongs to a parent operation; a root span has no parent and can represent the whole task. In one workshop, separate research and writing turns would otherwise have appeared as separate traces, so a parent wrapped both. The same demonstration suppressed instrumentation for judge calls to avoid mixing them into application traces; it did not measure production buffering performance. [Source 2](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-2)

Choose the observation boundary for the question:

- **Single span:** did this tool call receive and return the expected kind of data?
- **Multiple spans:** did one agent pass the needed information to another? Both sides of the handoff matter.
- **Trajectory:** what sequence of actions and intermediate results led to the outcome, including a loop or failed write?
- **Root task or session:** was the overall task completed, or were the user’s questions resolved across the conversation?

A locally acceptable call cannot establish a successful handoff or a satisfactory session. These scopes describe the evidence needed, independently of whether code, a model or a person judges it. Instrumentation may omit events, and observed behavior is not automatically a quality verdict. For the evaluator’s concrete input contract and field mapping, see [Give judges the evidence and context they need](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need.html). [Source 3](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-3) [Source 4](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-4)

## From observations to provisional failure categories

Read available traces end to end before imposing a taxonomy. Record what happened in ordinary language: the request, relevant intermediate outputs, actions and final answer. Then group recurring observations into provisional categories. For example, “wrong answer” is a symptom; possibilities include a parser dropping a constraint, retrieval returning irrelevant material, reasoning misusing good material, a plan stopping early, or self-review declaring incomplete work finished. Inspect the intermediates that could distinguish these explanations. [Source 5](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-5) [Source 6](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-6)

**Illustrative example:** a weather assistant answers for the wrong city. If the trace shows the user’s city was parsed incorrectly, the likely investigation differs from a case where the right city reached the weather tool but the final response ignored its result. Record the evidence and uncertainty rather than announcing a root cause from the final answer alone. Stage-level checks for intent, tool selection and completion can help localize a failure without implying that every valid run must use the same path. [Source 7](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-7)

Across traces, group similar observations and retain examples that challenge the grouping. Expert comments or model-assisted clustering can suggest recurring patterns, but the taxonomy remains provisional: selected examples do not establish prevalence or causation. Continue human sampling after automation to find missed categories. One workshop’s displayed category frequencies used random codes, so they are not evidence of actual failure rates. [Source 8](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-8) [Source 9](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-9)

## Match rigor to maturity and consequence

Early in development, direct inspection can produce directional feedback while the architecture and capabilities are changing rapidly. Focus expert attention on consequential failures rather than trying to enumerate everything immediately. A team reported that this unscalable exploratory phase helped it understand what to evaluate; that is experience, not a controlled comparison. [Source 10](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-10) [Source 11](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-11)

As use and consequences grow, maintain explicit tests and measurable standards for consequential decisions. Maturity is a continuum, not a requirement to wait for a particular stage before checking serious risks. Informal impressions alone are not launch evidence, and a model judge used for such decisions needs its own [independent validation against human judgments](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html). Release thresholds and promotion decisions belong to [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html). [Source 12](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-12) [Source 13](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-13)

## Distill incidents and expert rationales into candidate checks

An expert’s explanation of *why* an answer failed can yield a more reusable question than a thumbs-down alone. Review rationales and recurring incidents for a candidate property, then ask a domain owner whether it actually reflects the task. Hindsight analysis or a model can help propose cheaper repeated checks, but a plausible generated criterion is not yet a validated evaluator. [Source 14](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-14) [Source 15](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-15)

A shopping workshop deliberately seeded an over-budget result. Its proposed candidate rule was that every returned product must fall within the requested price range. That is more actionable than “shopping quality is poor,” but the workshop’s verification path was not fully executed; it is not production proof. [Source 16](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-16) A persistent agent reading many traces for patterns is another proposed discovery mechanism, not a demonstrated exhaustive detector. [Source 17](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-17)

Discovery, criterion validation and regression promotion are separate handoffs. Use [rubric design](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics.html) to make a candidate operational, [judge validation](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html) to assess alignment, and [dataset maintenance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html) to select and maintain regression cases. These quality signals complement rather than replace availability and latency monitoring.

## Use complementary evaluator layers

A useful layered evaluation keeps failures interpretable. Code can check reproducible format or inspectable state; a semantic judge can assess a meaning-dependent property; humans can examine unfamiliar failures and provide domain judgments. A model judge adds cost and can be wrong; an explanation helps inspect a verdict but does not prove it. A decision model may emit a label or probability without a comparable explanation; claimed speed and cost advantages in the workshop were not benchmarked. [Source 18](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-18) [Source 19](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-19)

Keep different properties, such as faithfulness and actionability, distinct instead of relying on one opaque overall score. A ticker appearing in a financial report, for example, is a narrow reproducible proxy—not proof that the analysis is accurate. No stack of finite checks guarantees complete coverage. For deeper architectural choices, see [Choose and combine judge methods](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/choose-and-combine-judge-methods.html). [Source 20](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-20) [Source 21](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-21)

## Make qualitative judgment teachable

Where no complete objective metric exists, an expert can explain a preference with a concrete critique and contrasting examples rather than simply saying an answer has good or bad taste. **Illustrative example:** a reviewer might prefer one explanation because it states the decision before the background, and show another that buries the decision. Colleagues can then discuss the tradeoff and learn what the reviewer values. This is conceptual guidance, not a measured improvement or a universal taste metric; other audiences may legitimately prefer a different ordering. [Source 22](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-22)

## Feedback is not acceptance

A repair loop can get a better feedback score while exploiting a weak proxy. **Illustrative example:** if the only check for a useful report is that it contains a ticker, adding the ticker makes the check pass without improving the analysis. Define the actual acceptance criterion and assess whether the verifier distinguishes genuine success from such shortcuts. More attempts cannot repair a defective acceptance test. [Source 23](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-23) [Source 24](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-24)

One architectural proposal allows adaptive revision inside a work step while an external deterministic gate controls progression. That can preserve a required boundary without prescribing every revision, but its usefulness still depends on the gate’s inputs, implementation and coverage. A deterministic pass is not comprehensive correctness, and the proposal is not a controlled production result. [Source 25](#tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods-source-25)

## Defining agent roles, boundaries and oversight

Owns contracts, responsibilities and completion claims; business goal setting and runtime implementation are adjacent but separate. Owns architecture vocabulary and system-level attribution; retrieval internals and model selection are treated elsewhere.

An agent’s task is not defined by a prompt alone, and its assertion that it is done is not proof that the work is ready for use. Define the role and its boundaries independently of the implementation; then require evidence and the appropriate approval for each consequential completion claim.

## Define the task without prescribing every move

A useful agent contract names the intended outcome and why it matters, its inputs and outputs, responsibilities and excluded jobs, required context and integrations, permissions, constraints, and examples of acceptable and unacceptable behavior. A stable task interface lets callers rely on the same input and output shape while the model, prompt, or tool strategy changes. But the signature is not the whole contract: prose conveys intent, executable checks enforce selected requirements, and examples expose aspects of quality that are hard to enumerate. Even together they do not prove that every requirement has been captured. [Source 1](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-1) [Source 2](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-2) [Source 3](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-3)

**Illustrative example:** A refund assistant’s role might be to investigate a request and prepare a resolution, using the order record and current policy; it must not issue a refund until identity has been verified. The contract can permit different search sequences to find the order. It cannot treat identity verification as an optional intermediate step merely because the final answer looks plausible. Compose the work as obligations: establish identity, assess eligibility, then obtain any required approval before a refund. Intermediate obligations can constrain a run without prescribing every tool call. A written contract still needs a harness capable of carrying it out; portable text alone does not provide missing tools or subagents. [Source 4](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-4) [Source 5](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-5) [Source 6](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-6)

A purpose-oriented instruction is not a substitute for the facts and scaffolding that make it meaningful. Plan close enough to the work to use current knowledge: preserve the problem, goal, user journey, non-negotiable boundaries and rationale, but revise the plan as discoveries change it. The case for just-in-time planning is a practitioner’s critique of exhaustive, fossilized specifications, not evidence that preparation is unnecessary. Prose also does not enforce itself. [Source 7](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-7) [Source 8](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-8) [Source 9](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-9)

For choosing the business outcome itself, see [From business problem to meaningful success criteria](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria.html).

## Completion is a set of claims, not a status flag

A completion record should distinguish the artifact and scope delivered from the evidence against the rubric, who verified it, who has authority to approve it, residual risks, and the next owner or action. These fields express claims to be checked; their presence is not proof of correctness. A pull request can exist, have passing tests and a closed issue while merge approval, deployment readiness and customer communication remain separate decisions. [Source 10](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-10)

In the illustrative refund case, an agent can report “eligibility assessment prepared,” cite the order and identity-check result, and identify an unresolved policy exception. That does not mean the refund was issued or that someone authorized it. A reviewer should inspect the evidence for the specific approval being requested, not infer it from the agent’s activity. A goal watchdog may encourage continued work, but needs real blocker and bounded-loop rules; persistence does not establish completion. [Source 11](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-11) [Source 12](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-12)

For a decision product, additional trust controls may include source receipts, clearly separated facts and estimates, checks that related numbers agree, surfaced contradictions, and a logged accountable human approval. These complement model quality; a stronger benchmark score does not itself supply them. The financial-work recommendation is a buyer’s perspective, not a validated implementation or a finding that model quality is irrelevant. [Source 13](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-13) [Source 14](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-14)

## Decide where human judgment remains

A software-factory framing describes repeated planning, building, checking and shipping. In a “lights-on” version people exercise judgment throughout; a “dark” version aims to move them toward intent and exceptions. These are conceptual operating models, not evidence that generated work is inherently safe. In one speaker’s terminology, **autonomy** concerns how much correction an agent needs to reach a suitable result, while **automation** concerns how much human review is still required before acceptance. An agent can solve a task without nudging and still need its entire result reviewed. [Source 15](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-15) [Source 16](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-16)

Before reducing review, identify the verification gap and the risks that remain. For a browser change, a recording or screenshot can show a reviewer what was exercised, but not certify unobserved paths. Labeling agent-written changes can support tracking without transferring accountability away from a human owner. See [Human Review and Agent Governance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/human-review-and-agent-governance.html) for governance decisions. [Source 17](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-17) [Source 18](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-18) [Source 19](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-19)

## Identify the system being tested

The **model** produces responses; an **agent runtime harness** surrounds it with the loop, tool registry, context management, guardrails and verification. An **evaluation harness** instead runs cases and scores results. Terminology varies, but a test runner is not a substitute for runtime controls, and an agent loop is only part of the runtime. [Source 20](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-20) [Source 21](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-21)

The **environment** is where the agent works: infrastructure, resources, incentives and guardrails. A workflow describes how work proceeds; a contract describes what is required. Changing any of these can change results even with the same model. A separate context layer can supply documents while the harness chooses searches and iterates on the results; this is an architectural framing, not proof that retrieval quality has ceased to matter. For comparisons, evaluate the actual model–harness–environment combination rather than attributing every difference to the model. [Source 22](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-22) [Source 23](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-23) See [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html).

A **skill** supplies reusable procedural knowledge and judgment; a **tool** supplies an actual capability, such as reading a service. For example, instructions about which feature flags are dangerous to remove cannot by themselves access rollout state. Typed steps are one proposed way to make guidance more inspectable, but the proposal does not establish a measured performance gain; guidance also needs maintenance when its assumptions age. [Source 24](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-24) [Source 25](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-25) [Source 26](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-26) [Source 27](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-27)

A protocol and its client are also distinct. A client that eagerly inserts every tool description and full response into model context may create overhead not required by the protocol; that does not mean protocols have no costs of their own. Diagnose the implementation before blaming the interface standard. [Source 28](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-28)

## Choose components for the actual work

Start with the simplest design that can meet the contract, evaluate it, and add agentic complexity where observed gaps justify it. A deterministic check can handle a directly observable condition while a model addresses context-dependent interpretation; simple rules are not universally sufficient. Focused, usable tools are themselves part of the capability being evaluated. [Source 29](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-29) [Source 30](#agent-contracts-completion-and-oversight-source-30)

In **code mode**, the agent uses an execution environment to compose tool calls with loops, conditionals or parallel operations and return relevant results, rather than requiring a separate model interaction for every call. A small fixed toolset may work well with ordinary calls. Code mode introduces generated-code debugging, resource and sandbox management, and recovery if a program fails midway; fewer model turns do not establish simpler or safer operation. ## Building and maintaining evaluation coverage

Owns evaluation settings, regression promotion, changing architecture and ownership; evaluator machinery is covered in the trace article.

Evaluation coverage should evolve with both the system and the evidence available about its use. Early exploration can compare candidates on repeatable tasks; deployment adds observations of real workflows and exposes behaviors that the initial test design missed. Neither a single score nor a static suite establishes that the entire product will work reliably.

## Combine controlled tests with actual use

Use benchmarks for repeatable comparisons, then add realistic scenarios that exercise the agent in an environment: a support task, for example, can require the agent to use tools and complete a workflow, not merely produce a plausible answer. The scenario can examine completion, tool use, planning and resource use. Production observations add another perspective: traces, outcomes, escalations and feedback show what occurred in the deployed system. A benchmark can measure capability without covering API outages, changing context or long workflows. [Source 1](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-1) [Source 2](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-2) [Source 3](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-3)

These settings complement rather than replace each other. A controlled comparison is easier to repeat; direct use can reveal conditions not anticipated in the test. One proposed evaluation pyramid puts production signals above scenarios and benchmarks in operational value, but that ordering is a speaker's framework, not a measured ranking. Production traffic is not automatically representative of every user or failure: sampling, missing outcomes and privacy need attention. Similarly, benchmark scores and user experience are both imperfect evidence; there is no validated universal formula for weighting them. [Source 4](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-4) [Source 5](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-5)

## Add pre-release evidence without removing runtime defenses

A pre-release scenario asks whether a candidate behaved acceptably in a known case. A runtime harness constrains or handles actions as they occur, including cases the suite did not anticipate. The two operate at different times: a passing offline test does not make a runtime control redundant, and a runtime control does not show that the agent can complete intended tasks. Neither guarantees prevention of every exploit. The source motivates this division with anecdotes rather than a controlled safety comparison. [Source 6](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-6) For the enforcement mechanisms themselves, see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html).

## Assign evaluation responsibility for customizations

A provider may evaluate a general agent harness, while a customer adds instructions or a skill that changes what the agent does. Write down which behaviors the provider's evidence actually covers and who will test the combined system in the customer's context. Define the intended behavior before implementing the customization, then test representative scenarios against it. For instance, if a skill should direct the agent to a particular documentation workflow, check that behavior rather than relying on the skill's text looking correct. [Source 7](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-7)

One speaker argued that personal coding-agent skills do not need their own evaluation because the provider owns the harness and the skill is deterministically authored. That is a position based on assumed provider coverage, not a demonstration that instructions cannot introduce failures or that agent outputs become deterministic. In the other skill demonstration, a grader checked the wrong representation and the comparison did not establish an improvement; it supports the proposed evaluation practice, not a proven effect. [Source 8](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-8) [Source 7](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-7)

## Reuse environments, not necessarily cases

An executable environment can package a task, the harness that runs an agent, its rollout and a way to verify the outcome. Build that machinery to compare candidates now, and it may later support demonstration collection, prompt optimization or training. This reduces duplicated infrastructure without requiring an early commitment to post-training. [Source 9](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-9) [Source 10](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-10)

Keep the infrastructure decision separate from data and reward decisions: reusing an environment does not justify evaluating on the same cases used for training, and an executable reward is not automatically a valid measure of success. The proposed production-to-training loop also depends on obtaining useful real-world feedback and translating it into tasks and rewards; the speaker identifies that translation as an unresolved engineering and research problem. The underlying workshop was a vendor-led architectural proposal, not an end-to-end controlled benchmark. [Source 11](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-11)

## Change coverage when the architecture changes

Preserve the durable description of desired behavior and the old tests that remain relevant, but map each new component and interaction to its own coverage needs. A product that adds cross-session memory, generated-code execution or a skill directory can fail in places a final-answer test of the old loop never exercises. For example, when adding memory, ask whether retrieval affects the intended workflow; when adding execution, consider outcomes and failures of that new surface. These are coverage prompts, not a claimed validated memory or sandbox test protocol. [Source 12](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-12) [Source 13](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-13)

Also look for failure categories the team did not already name. The source describes clustering production data as a way to surface candidates for new datasets and guardrails, not as proof that every cluster is a genuine failure or that discovery is complete. Review leads before deciding what to add; the cited vendor description gives no discovery-quality measurements. For the subsequent handling of production-derived cases, see [Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html). [Source 14](#building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage-source-14)

## Improvement loops, adaptation and overfitting

Owns optimization loops and adaptation tradeoffs; empirical comparison design and memory architecture are separate.

An agent can improve its score without improving the work people actually need. Treat the development loop itself as an optimization process: specify the desired behavior, seek evidence against it, and keep the feedback used to make changes distinct from evidence used to assess them.

## Discover the target separately from optimizing it

An outer loop learns what users need from feedback and online evidence, then revises tasks and measures. An inner loop changes the model or system to perform better against those targets. If a task is easy to score but misses the user's real problem, more inner-loop optimization may simply make the wrong target easier to hit. This separation is a described organizational framework, not proof that either loop caused a particular outcome. [Source 1](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-1)

For an automated change loop, name the target, the sensor that observes the current state, the controller choosing a change, the actuator applying it, and the feedback after the change. For an illustrative example, a code-quality sensor might detect a specified undesirable pattern, while a proposed edit must be checked against that target and other relevant constraints. If the property cannot be observed or an edit cannot be checked, repeating prompts is not a closed control loop. The control analogy does not prove stability for a stochastic agent. [Source 2](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-2)

## Optimize without teaching to the test

Changing a prompt, tool or harness after inspecting scores resembles training, even with frozen model weights: the suite guides successive choices. Repeated use can fit particular cases, or reward a shortcut that raises the verifier's score without achieving the task. This is an analogy and a risk, not evidence that every score improvement is overfitting. Inspect both outcome and traces to see what actually changed; a pass/fail result tells you much less about the failure mechanism than an execution trace can. [Source 3](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-3) [Source 4](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-4) [Source 5](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-5)

Use development feedback to formulate a change and keep independent evidence for evaluating it. Rollout trajectories can feed supervised training, rewards can support reinforcement learning, and textual feedback can guide prompt or harness revisions, but a rollout used to optimize is not thereby a held-out test. Protect independent cases from iterative tuning and investigate when a gain is confined to the familiar suite. For practical set maintenance see [Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html); for holdout protection see [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html). [Source 6](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-6)

## Make claims falsifiable

Write down a claim that could fail, then deliberately seek a counterexample rather than only demonstrating favorable cases. One answer-first strategy chooses a known expected result, constructs an input intended to require it, and checks whether the system recovers it. A tool workflow can similarly have an expected endpoint order. Sometimes the solution must be redesigned to make these checks possible, and not every task admits a known-answer construction. [Source 7](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-7) [Source 8](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-8)

A planted case tests the chosen rule, not the entire problem. A green synthetic suite is useful development evidence but not sufficient release authorization; retain real-world and independent evidence for cases the construction did not anticipate. There is no universal stopping rule in the cited challenge loop. [Source 9](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-9)

## Choose where to adapt and where to repeat

A fixed executable workflow can repeat a known procedure, but an interface change may break it; a model-driven agent can adapt to an altered interface but may make different decisions on identical runs. Choose the stable path where repeatability matters and adaptive handling where variation is unavoidable. Determinism does not guarantee correct results in a changed environment. [Source 10](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-10)

One experimental hybrid records a successful trajectory as code and tries replay on a similar request, checking intermediate state and stopping or invoking adaptive repair on a mismatch. A live demonstration needed fallback after a replay hiccup; its verification predicates and miss rate were not specified. Treat this as a design option to test, not a solved reliability or safety guarantee. [Source 11](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-11) [Source 12](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-12)

## Evaluate learning across time, not only recall

Continual learning asks whether a system can use ongoing experience efficiently while retaining still-useful knowledge and updating when facts change. A meaningful sequence includes a stable period to test retention, then a change such as renamed database columns to test whether stale knowledge is discarded without losing valid schema knowledge. Measure performance as experience accumulates, not only whether a note was saved. [Source 13](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-13) [Source 14](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-14)

Two narrated traces illustrate different failures: a forecast returned to an already rejected high value after feedback said a later forecast was too low; elsewhere, relevant cohort definitions were stored but dismissed as belonging to another study. These individual traces do not establish prevalence or prove a repair. They show why preservation and willingness to update must both be tested. [Source 15](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-15) [Source 16](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-16)

Use a simple retained-context baseline before crediting a more elaborate memory system. In initial speaker-reported medium-horizon comparisons, vanilla context led aggregate reward and the reported reward-to-cost or gain-to-cost frontiers; exact scores and uncertainty were not given, and longer horizons may change the comparison. Designing architecture and training explicitly for ongoing learning is a research hypothesis, not a demonstrated universal winner over contextual methods. [Source 17](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-17) [Source 18](#improvement-loops-adaptation-and-overfitting-source-18)

## Understanding context, memory and retrieval

Owns knowledge and context access, memory and retrieval mechanisms; screen observations and general model architecture are separate.

An agent needs more than general language ability: it needs the facts, constraints and relationships relevant to the work in front of it. **Context** is what the model sees on a particular call; **retrieval** finds potentially useful information; **memory** includes policies for writing, managing and bringing information back over time. A connected database is not the same thing as useful context.

## Begin with the decision and the evidence

Knowledge work turns information into a decision or finding. A legal research workflow, for example, may require a different organization of sources and intermediate work from a coding task. Design around the actual question and how its answer will be used, rather than assuming one search pattern suits every domain. Tools and work organization can evolve together; that is a design proposal, not evidence of a universal architecture. [Source 1](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-1) [Source 2](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-2)

Before writing a query, state what evidence would resolve the question. If the question concerns a thirty-day rule, identify whether the relevant evidence is a deadline, grace period or retention requirement: the same phrase can describe different concepts. Then choose queries for the needed evidence rather than guessing overlapping words. This ambiguity is not unique to noncoding work, nor is code always unambiguous. [Source 3](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-3) [Source 4](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-4)

A capable model may still lack an organization's current rules, relationships and expectations. Connecting a search tool does not fix a missing, stale or contradictory knowledge base. Identify and maintain authoritative, task-useful information as well as the route to it. [Source 5](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-5) [Source 6](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-6)

## Choose how to find and represent information

Lexical search matches words or identifiers; it can be useful for exact product IDs or named symbols. Semantic search can match related meaning despite different wording. Neither mechanism always wins: test both identifier-heavy and paraphrased questions. One workshop favors combining lexical and semantic search, while acknowledging that either alone may suffice and that others prefer starting lexical-first. Choose the simplest approach that meets the task's needs rather than adopting a universal ordering. [Source 7](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-7) [Source 8](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-8)

The size of the pieces indexed matters too. A small chunk can preserve a local detail but omit the context that explains it; a large chunk can carry that context while diluting the detail in its representation. Test granularity against different questions. An agent that searches iteratively still pays for poorly organized, widely dispersed evidence. For deeper design choices see [Retrieval and query optimization](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/retrieval-and-query-optimization.html) and [Evaluate and represent retrieval corpora](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora.html). [Source 9](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-9) [Source 10](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-10)

A domain map or typed knowledge graph offers a different representation: resolve aliases to a canonical entity and record relationships among people, systems or processes. This can make navigation and disambiguation explicit, but the proposed healthcare architecture did not establish entity-resolution accuracy or a general advantage over vector retrieval. [Source 11](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-11)

Do not confuse retrieved examples with a complete population. To answer a count or mean over all records, a handful of top-ranked chunks is not a reliable denominator. If a suitable structured dataset exists, execute an aggregate or relationship query over the intended population, and verify both the data and query. A travel demonstration compared this approach with a simple top-k vector workflow; it was not a comparison against every retrieval architecture. [Source 12](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-12)

## Keep the meaning, not just the flag

State should retain qualifications that change behavior. Approving a research plan while restricting it to the US and excluding California is not equivalent to a bare approval flag. Similarly, a preference for Celsius generally but Fahrenheit while cooking has a condition that a single global unit value loses. These are conceptual examples, not evidence that an unstructured memory architecture has been validated; structured fields can preserve conditions too. [Source 13](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-13) [Source 14](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-14)

## Select context and manage memory over time

A model's window is a capacity limit, not a promise that everything within it will be used. Select and rank the instructions, history and evidence relevant to the current decision. Compression can discard detail; preserving every token can also impose cost or obscure what matters. A speaker-reported study found distinctive facts easier to recover than ambiguous ones, but its incomplete follow-up protocol does not establish general long-context competence. Its recommendation against compaction by default also coexisted with an announced 30,000-token compaction policy without an explained reconciliation: the number is not a universal threshold. [Source 15](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-15) [Source 16](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-16) [Source 17](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-17)

Memory is a **write–manage–read** loop: decide what to save, maintain or revise it, and retrieve it when useful. Distinguish what is always visible in the current session from a recall block and a persistent archive across sessions. A stored item that is never selected does not help the next decision, and an old item may need correction. The layered arrangement is an organizing model, not proof that a particular backend is best. [Source 18](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-18) [Source 19](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-19) [Source 20](#context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations-source-20)

To test whether these choices work, including delayed recall and whether retrieved evidence is actually used, continue to [Evaluating retrieval, memory and learning in agent workflows](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops.html). For operational context and persistence decisions, see [Maintaining agent context, memory and knowledge](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/reliable-agent-context-and-memory.html) and [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html).

## Choosing tasks with verifiable outcomes

Owns task verifiability and training suitability, not claims of measured ROI or model superiority.

A task is not a good agent candidate merely because a model can produce an answer. The work needs boundaries, a way to tell whether the result is acceptable and an economic reason to use the system. The same properties affect learning: an available outcome check can make a task attractive for reinforcement learning, but does not by itself make the agent’s path safe.

## Separate uncertainty about steps from uncertainty about acceptance

Ask two different questions. How variable is the route to completion? And how clear are the criteria for accepting the result? Booking a flight requires recognizable information and actions, although choices can vary; creating a masterpiece has a less predictable route and a less settled standard of success. The contrast is a thought-starter for task selection, not a validated numerical measure of uncertainty. [Source 1](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-1)

When the steps are predictable, a conventional script may be preferable to an agent: flexibility has a cost and should address real variability. At the other extreme, when acceptance criteria are so unclear that a reviewer must effectively redo the work, the checking burden can consume the apparent benefit. This does not mean subjective work cannot be assisted; it means that value and review effort need to be assessed, not inferred from output volume. [Source 2](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-2) [Source 3](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-3)

A promising candidate has enough execution variability to benefit from flexible behavior but a repeatable, comparatively inexpensive way to check results. Treat this as a hypothesis to evaluate, not a guaranteed return on investment. An agent might help with checking too, but that does not automatically make its judgment reliable. Specify the system’s interfaces and limits, the observable result, and the costs of execution and review before choosing the workflow. [Source 4](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-4) [Source 5](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-5)

## Inspect what makes a result verifiable

One heuristic separates three properties: whether work can be decomposed into checkable pieces, whether people agree on correctness, and whether verified examples occur often enough to learn from. These dimensions need not move together. A task may have many examples but disputed acceptance criteria, or clear criteria but too few verified examples for the intended learning process. The framework is a way to organize investigation, not a validated prediction of which market or domain will mature first. [Source 6](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-6)

Code illustrates the affordance: parts can often be decomposed and executed, making some outcomes easier to observe than an overall judgment of design or writing. Look for observable components of a subjective task without pretending they capture the entire quality target. The claim that measurability explains differences in model capability is a conceptual argument, not an isolated causal finding. [Source 7](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-7)

## Match learning to available evidence and risk

Reinforcement learning is worth considering when tasks are available or can be generated, expert demonstrations are expensive, several action paths can reach acceptable results, and outcomes can be checked. A reward tied to the outcome can in principle recognize different successful routes rather than requiring every trajectory to imitate a small set of demonstrations. That is a task-fit argument, not evidence that reinforcement learning generally outperforms supervised fine-tuning; the cited account gives no comparative experiment. [Source 8](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-8)

A final-state reward can miss harmful intermediate actions. A browser agent might eventually complete its intended task after taking a dangerous or unauthorized action along the way; checking the final result alone would not expose that failure. The speaker therefore advocates tracking and penalizing risky actions throughout the trajectory, not just failed outcomes. The account does not specify a reward formula or quantify how well this approach prevents harm. **Illustrative example:** reaching the correct record after changing an unrelated account setting is not an acceptable route merely because the record is correct. [Source 9](#choosing-verifiable-tasks-and-learning-methods-source-9)

Before adopting a learning method, examine whether the available checks represent the desired outcome and whether unsafe routes are observable. Verifiability is a useful affordance, not a substitute for validating the evaluator or deciding what evidence an evaluation can establish. See [What evaluation can establish: design, evidence and uncertainty](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/what-an-ai-evaluation-can-and-cannot-establish.html) and [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html).

## Evaluating visual and multimodal agent capabilities

Owns modality and platform distinctions; generic agent traces and retrieval are covered elsewhere.

A visual agent needs more than the ability to name what appears on a screen. It must take in the right evidence, connect it to the user’s task, reason about details and changes, and act through an interface available on the particular platform. Each step can fail independently.

## Condition on reference media when words underspecify targets

A user may recognize a desired speaking rhythm or visual style without being able to describe it precisely. An example clip or image gives the model another conditioning channel: the request can say what to do while the reference conveys qualities that are difficult to specify in words. This is an input expressing the target, not a gold answer proving the output is correct. One vendor panel proposed this use for sound, prosody and visual aesthetics; its members disagreed on whether the apparent limitation of language is fundamental or could be addressed by better data and focused development. The account does not establish a general ceiling on text instructions. [Source 1](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-1)

## Combine partial interface observations and inspect changes

A screenshot shows rendered pixels, including visual content that may not appear in a DOM or accessibility tree. But it only shows the captured viewport; a structural representation may reveal elements below it or provide roles and labels that pixels alone leave ambiguous. Accessibility information can also omit visible elements. Choose channels according to the task and cross-check when the distinction matters, rather than assuming any one is complete. A described browser demonstration included an advertisement whose image carried information absent from the DOM; the examples do not quantify overall channel coverage. [Source 2](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-2) [Source 3](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-3)

Grounding means determining which visible or structural element actually serves the intended purpose, not merely finding a button with matching text. In the browser example, an early trajectory followed a sponsored submit button away from the intended expense workflow; later behavior distinguished it. These are selected trajectories, not a measured reliability improvement. After an action, compare the new observation with the intended change: a click arriving at a target is not evidence that the correct operation happened. Capturing a screenshot after each step provides observations, but the agent still has to interpret them. [Source 2](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-2) [Source 4](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-4)

A reported alternative architecture pairs a general reasoning model with a smaller screen recognizer, sometimes fine-tuned for that role. This makes grounding a separable component to investigate; the reported combined harness does not isolate how much the specialized recognizer contributed. Likewise, a workshop’s screen-understanding proposal should not be reconstructed from unavailable visuals or treated as a validated production capability. [Source 5](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-5) [Source 6](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-6)

## Distinguish recognition from visual reasoning

Recognizing a familiar scene is different from inspecting the particular arrangement needed for a count or localization. In a narrated failure, a model reportedly supplied the standard white-square count for a complete chessboard when shown only part of one. The source image and full protocol are unavailable, so this is a selected failure illustrating a possible shortcut, not an accuracy estimate. [Source 7](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-7)

For a detail-intensive task, evaluate intermediate decisions as well as the final answer. A narrated example counts red hotels by locating candidate hotels, filtering them by color, then counting the remainder. A wrong result can arise at localization, attribute filtering or counting; inspecting the stages makes the next investigation more specific. The example does not establish general superiority over text-based reasoning. To scope a task, the speaker suggests asking whether a human could answer after viewing the image for roughly one second: a quick recognition question may need less inspection than counting a detailed arrangement. This is a qualitative heuristic, not a formal definition of reasoning or a permanent model limit. [Source 8](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-8) [Source 9](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-9)

A visually plausible sequence also need not maintain the correct state over time or obey physical constraints. One narrated robot example described missed changes to a lid and a stove; it does not establish the cause of the error. For physical designs, programmatic checks or simulation were proposed to test specified constraints, but simulator fidelity and real-world transfer were not evaluated. Treat those as additional tests under modeled conditions, not as proof of safety or manufacturability. [Source 10](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-10) [Source 11](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-11)

## Check coherence between modalities

Good audio and good-looking video can still disagree: visible lip motion and speech are observations of the same event and must line up. Assess their timing and correspondence together, not only each stream in isolation. A vendor panel described joint audiovisual modeling as an approach to that coupling, but supplied no controlled comparison against staged generation. It is a design proposal, not evidence that joint generation always wins. [Source 12](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-12)

## Bound background action by platform

Perceiving an interface and controlling it in the background are separate capabilities. One desktop driver reportedly attempts an accessibility action first and falls back to a pixel click when necessary. Test both routes on the actual application and operating system: accessibility support differs, undocumented APIs were mentioned, and equivalent behavior across desktop platforms was not established. [Source 13](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-13)

Do not infer phone GUI control from desktop results. In an exploratory answer, the same team described Android background containerized workloads and activity-framework tool use as closer to tool use than control of the visible GUI; it did not demonstrate unrestricted mobile automation or establish an iOS capability. [Source 14](#visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities-source-14)

For simulated interaction settings, see [Building and validating simulated agent worlds](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds.html).
