## Testing specialized representations and instruction robustness

Owns distinct representations for language and biological data and anonymous-speaker labeling; does not claim cross-domain equivalence. Owns the lexical instruction-density experiment, its failure categories and relevant robustness probes; general agent failure diagnosis belongs with traces.

A model's representation and its evaluation target are choices, not interchangeable abstractions. A sentence-like sequence of gene measurements, anonymous speaker IDs, and a list of exact words may all be processed by machine learning systems, but success on one tells us little about the others. In each case, identify what the representation preserves, what counts as the same answer, and what the test leaves out.

## Source context: language interoperability and adoption

One language-tooling speaker proposed exposing functions to existing languages through bindings rather than requiring a wholesale rewrite. The demonstration included Python calls and callbacks. This is **peripheral adoption context**, not an evaluation method: lower migration friction is the speaker's rationale, not a measured result, and the demonstration is not a broad compatibility study. For evaluating executable programs, see [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html). [Source 1](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-1)

## Specialized representations and identity tasks

### Language as an intermediate representation

One panelist explains language-based intermediate reasoning as a way to use capabilities already learned in language pretraining. That is a plausible rationale for a productive current approach, not a controlled comparison proving that latent, code, or visual representations cannot work. A different representation may be preferable when the task requires information that text does not readily convey. [Source 2](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-2)

For example, a reference recording can convey prosody that a user struggles to describe in words. The panel disagreed about whether such limits are fundamental to language or reflect insufficient data and development; observed difficulties do not settle that question. Compare representations against the information and outputs the actual task requires, rather than assuming a single channel is universally best. [Source 3](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-3)

### Cells as gene-related tokens

In one described single-cell modeling approach, a cell-by-gene expression matrix is represented with cells analogous to sentences and genes to tokens. A transformer learns by predicting masked genes or expression information using bidirectional attention. Its learned representations can then be used for tasks such as cell-type prediction or perturbation-response modeling. This is a modeling analogy and training objective, not evidence that cells share the statistical properties of language. The available account does not specify the exact objectives or tokenization of the named models, and its captions need review; it does not establish clinical benefit. [Source 4](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-4)

### Anonymous identity is not a person's name

Diarization groups speech turns by speaker; it does not necessarily determine real names or know the true number of participants in advance. A meeting attendee list may help but does not establish who joined or shared a channel. Evaluation should allow a **consistent permutation** of anonymous labels. [Source 5](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-5)

**Illustrative example:** If the reference assigns three turns A, B, A and the system assigns 2, 1, 2, swapping the system's 1 and 2 yields the same grouping. Scoring literal label names as errors would be wrong. Conversely, 2, 1, 1 still incorrectly groups the final turn after any consistent swap. This scoring equivalence does not identify either person's real name.

## Testing instruction capacity and robustness

### What the word-inclusion proxy measures

A simple instruction-density experiment asks a model to write a synthetic business report containing a specified list of exact words. Vary the number of requested words and score the fraction present; this measures tracking of these simple lexical constraints, not quality of the business analysis or reliable compliance with an entire skill file. [Source 6](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-6) [Source 7](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-7)

The speaker reported sharp decline near 2,000 constraints for some tested models and up to 5,000 for the best. These are model-, version-, and task-specific observations, not safe general instruction limits; the word list was filtered for one model, the tested models varied, and the results were not independently verified in the supplied notes. Track *how* runs fail: omission, refusal, exhausted reasoning budget, or an incomplete but polished-looking response demand different remedies. A single fraction hides those differences. [Source 8](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-8) [Source 9](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-9)

If the intended application has interacting or conflicting instructions, test those separately. Adding more instructions may increase coverage but also consumes tokens and can add latency; a longer prompt is not automatically a better system. [Source 7](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-7) [Source 10](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-10)

### Probe presentation separately from capacity

Specify which variations should preserve acceptable behavior for the role, then test them: typos, paraphrases, and reordered equivalent instructions, for example. Keep the underlying requirement fixed while varying presentation so that a failure indicates sensitivity to the change rather than a different task. The reported effect of wording and order is secondhand in the source, without its full method or data; it motivates a probe, not a quantified reliability claim. [Source 11](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-11) [Source 12](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-12)

**Illustrative example:** A support agent's policy limits a discount. Compare a plainly worded request with a misspelled paraphrase and reorder the same policy instructions; record the response and whether the limit was respected. If the change alters the allowed discount, investigate the failure. Passing these finite variants cannot prove the rule will never be violated. Choose variants and their prevalence for the decision at hand, as discussed in [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html). [Source 13](#specialized-representations-and-identity-tasks-source-13)

## Item response models for evaluation

Owns IRT estimation and diagnostics, not general case-by-case experiment diffs or causal claims about model ancestry.

A benchmark's raw score says how many items a model answered correctly, but not which items were answered or how informative they were. Item response theory (IRT) offers a different description: fit a relationship between each item's probability of success and a model's position on a latent ability scale. That scale is a model of performance on the observed items, not a direct measurement of a model's general intelligence. [Source 1](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-1)

## From item curves to an ability estimate

Start with a response matrix: rows are evaluated models, columns are benchmark items, and each entry records a correct or incorrect response under a defined testing procedure. Fit item response curves from those observations. In the simple single-ability formulation, each curve plots predicted probability of correctness against latent ability. An item's **difficulty** locates the curve's midpoint on the ability scale; **discrimination** describes how sharply the probability changes around that point. A steep curve distinguishes models near its midpoint more than a flat one does. Difficulty and discrimination are fitted properties under the model and the available data, not intrinsic guarantees about every future population. [Source 1](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-1)

For an individual model, combine the likelihood contributions of its correct and incorrect answers across the fitted curves to estimate a distribution or interval for its ability. An answer's surprise at a given ability is not the same as its effect on the comparison between abilities. Item discrimination affects how sharply predicted success changes with ability, so the fitted item properties and the complete response pattern matter to that comparison. An estimate is uncertain, particularly when responses provide little information about a region of the scale. More questions can improve estimation, but only if their data and modeling assumptions support it; the source does not establish calibration for its intervals or supply estimation code. [Source 1](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-1) [Source 2](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-2)

**Illustrative example:** two systems each solve half a small test. One solves items fitted as difficult and misses several easy items; the other has the opposite pattern. Difficulty alone does not establish that their ability estimates differ. If the fitted items also differ in discrimination, their response patterns can lead to different estimates, depending on the curves and estimation method. Nor does it follow that the first system is necessarily superior: a surprising pattern can reflect sampling, item fit or a skill the single scale fails to represent.

## Investigate residuals, not just rankings

For each model–item pair, compare the observed correctness with its fitted probability. The difference is a residual: an unexpected correct answer is positive, and an unexpected miss is negative. Inspect the item, response and evaluation setup; repeat samples of the question where practical to see whether the pattern persists or behavior varies. The speaker suggests residuals may direct investigation toward inference or quantization problems, but a surprising answer alone proves neither a defect nor contamination or overfitting. [Source 3](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-3)

Residuals also make a model-level pattern visible. Correlate the vectors of residuals across items for pairs of models: systems that miss and solve the same unexpected items may cluster even when their aggregate scores differ. Such similarity is a lead for further investigation, not proof of shared ancestry or unauthorized distillation. Shared tasks, training data or measurement artifacts could also produce similar patterns; the demonstrated clusters lack validation sufficient to establish a cause. [Source 4](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-4)

## Compare groups at the same estimated ability

To look for differential item functioning, divide models into groups and fit or compare an item's curves by group on a comparable ability scale. If predicted correctness differs at the same estimated ability, that item behaves differently for the groups under the model. Examine whether related items show a similar gap, and investigate their content and measurement conditions. A group gap is not itself proof of item bias or why the difference occurred; the presented example does not disclose the flagged items or establish a cause. [Source 5](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-5)

The comparison depends on the shared scale being meaningful and the fitted curves being supported by enough data in the relevant ability range. A gap outside the range where both groups are well represented is a weaker basis for interpretation than one supported by observations in both.

## Know what the scale leaves out

A single ability dimension compresses potentially different skills into one coordinate. A model can be strong on one kind of task and weak on another, so systematic residuals or group gaps may signal that the simple model is missing structure rather than revealing a special property of an item. Multidimensional or hierarchical models and combining benchmarks are proposed ways to study separate skills and improve estimation, but they are future research directions in the cited presentation, not demonstrated results there. [Source 6](#item-response-models-for-evaluation-source-6)

IRT is therefore useful as a compact, uncertainty-aware description and an investigative tool. It does not replace a close look at the actual tasks, the response-generation procedure or independent evidence for any explanation of a surprising pattern. For broader evaluation of what a benchmark supports, see [Benchmarks, leaderboards and model selection](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/benchmarks-leaderboards-and-model-selection.html).

## Choosing and designing agent benchmarks

Covers task selection and validity, not experimental execution.

A benchmark is useful only in relation to a question. A difficult public agent task can probe a capability frontier without resembling the work for which a team is buying an agent; a private task can resemble that work without automatically representing it. Before comparing scores, state the decision, the work distribution and the capability the tasks are supposed to exercise. The question of how far findings apply beyond the studied tasks and conditions is **external validity**.

## Start with the decision and the capability thesis

For deployment selection, sample the actual requests, available tools, inputs and constraints. A curated demonstration may prove that a tool connection works while hiding how people use it: in one internal rollout, a pointed demo worked, but teammates' incomplete descriptions led the agent to create workflows that neither party understood. This is an anecdote, not a failure-rate estimate, but it suggests including ambiguous requests and actual users' material in a task set. A post-incident benchmark can instead ask an agent to consult logs, chat and documentation to recover a diagnosis, testing organizational context use as well as code generation. Such private tasks complement public probes; they still require evidence that the cases represent the intended workload. [Source 1](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-1) [Source 2](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-2)

Difficulty and practical value are different judgments. One speaker questioned the economic value of asking an agent to build a C compiler in Rust; another used that task family as a deliberate project-scale stress test. Neither purpose invalidates the other: a frontier capability probe needs headroom, whereas a purchasing decision needs evidence about work the buyer values. A broad coding suite can also be a small slice of possible work even if it contains thousands of tests; optimizing its score alone need not produce general capability. The warning is qualitative, not a universal minimum task count. [Source 3](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-3) [Source 4](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-4) [Source 5](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-5)

A research benchmark can make its own **capability thesis** explicit. For example, terminal-oriented tasks express a speaker's bet that command-line interaction is a useful general agent interface. That thesis guides the task choice; it does not establish that the benchmark caused adoption or broader research progress. At a more specific level, a training speedrun fixes data and target validation loss while minimizing time; an optimizer-only track narrows which changes are allowed. The two tracks test different scopes of improvement, and achieving the same loss is not proof of equal general model capability. [Source 6](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-6) [Source 7](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-7)

Artifact utility is a third, separate question. The designer of ParallelKernelBench describes selecting real inference operations lacking good kernels, so specialized solutions could become useful artifacts. That is an intended utility criterion, not a reported deployment gain, evidence of generalization, or proof that the evaluator cannot be gamed. Check both whether the artifact works for the operational need and whether the score means what it claims. [Source 8](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-8) [Source 9](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-9)

## Choose the environment, horizon and output

Specify three independent design axes: **environment realism**, **autonomy horizon**, and **output complexity**. A realistic environment need not demand sustained autonomous work; a long task need not produce a complex artifact. This is a proposed framework, not a validated universal taxonomy. [Source 10](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-10)

For example, compare a short, structured financial question with a multi-experiment scientific decision that must interpret results against prior literature, experimental design and the original goal. The latter can resemble an industry go/no-go decision more closely, but is harder to construct and verify. The described examples simulate scientific decisions, not successful autonomous drug discovery. Likewise, concatenating independent subtasks creates a longer episode without necessarily testing the state dependence that makes a long investigation difficult: a bad early log query can constrain the downstream diagnosis. Describe both the resources consumed and the dependencies, rather than equating duration with competence. [Source 11](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-11) [Source 12](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-12)

Security benchmarks need an especially explicit access model. One access-control task family gives an agent basic execution tools against live, chained applications, without source code or internet access. The agent must infer behavior and track state changes across interactions. This is different from discovering vulnerable code in a repository, and a score applies to that environment and access surface—not cybersecurity as a whole. [Source 13](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-13) [Source 14](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-14)

## Keep challenge while admitting valid tasks

A benchmark needs room to distinguish systems, but a low score alone is not proof of meaningful challenge. A speaker reports that frontier models often score below half on a multi-domain data-science suite; that suggests headroom on that suite, not coverage of every real data-science workflow. Conversely, an apparent plateau can be caused partly by unsolvable or defective remaining items, which may also bias rankings. Inspect the failures before announcing saturation. [Source 15](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-15) [Source 16](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-16)

When valid tasks genuinely stop distinguishing systems, add or update meaningful challenges; revisit the evaluation when the agent's harness changes too. Keep stable regression cases alongside new tasks so earlier requirements remain testable. Balance difficulty against completion time: an exam too easy loses signal, while one too difficult or long may not be finished. One speaker describes moving from vending machines to a cafe as models improved, but this progression is anecdotal, not a validated upgrade threshold; adaptive evaluation for changing harnesses is a proposal. [Source 17](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-17) [Source 18](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-18) [Source 19](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-19)

Admit a task only after checking that it is achievable, nontrivial, functionally correct and supported by a reliable environment. Examine pass rate alongside tool calls, output length and failure categories: a lengthy trace or low pass rate might reflect hard reasoning, an ambiguous instruction or a broken setup. Separate incomplete reasoning from environment failures. One reported accepted-task comparison used these indicators together, but did not publish enough task counts or distributions to make any one threshold a general rule. For the details of packaging and auditing an individual task, see [Specify and audit meaningful benchmark tasks](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks.html). [Source 20](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-20) [Source 21](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-21) [Source 22](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-22)

## Distinguish novelty and verifiability from score

Research-record improvement is not necessarily novel discovery. In preliminary speedrun experiments, agents could access human records; one restarted agent incorporated new human work and improved on it. The speaker assessed observed solutions as recombinations or incremental improvements rather than genuinely new optimizer mechanisms. A useful record can therefore coexist with an unmet novelty objective. If independent discovery matters, define that criterion separately; proposed no-access, papers-only and full-access conditions would distinguish what agents can use, but were not yet a completed controlled benchmark. Novelty judgments still need scrutiny. [Source 23](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-23) [Source 24](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-24)

One research arena offers a different objective: agents select problems, discuss approaches, submit solutions for automatic scoring and inspect or download one another's submissions. Where solutions can be verified and shared, this design permits cumulative work alongside competition, but it does not demonstrate a collaborative benefit. Document access to shared submissions when interpreting results: building on others' work is not evidence of independent discovery. [Source 25](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-25) [Source 23](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-23)

Deterministic checks can give clear feedback for open-ended search when the target has a well-defined verifier, but selecting only such tasks excludes important work. In changing web environments a fixed check may be brittle or reject a valid alternative; an ungrounded model judge can also misjudge. Verifiable tasks and messy iterative work should be connected by measured transfer, not assumed equivalent. Audit the verifier and its resistance to shortcutting separately; see [Verifying agent outcomes and diagnosing behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior.html) and [Protect benchmark integrity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-benchmark-integrity.html). [Source 26](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-26) [Source 27](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-27) [Source 28](#choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks-source-28)

## Choosing agent success measures and resource budgets

Defines distinct estimands and accounting; not experimental validity or task construction.

An agent evaluation can answer several different questions: whether a task is solvable at all, whether it works repeatedly, how much of a long task it completes, and what resources it consumes. None of those answers is a substitute for the others. Start with the decision the measurement must support, then state the task population, attempt policy, success criterion and denominator alongside the result.

## Repeated attempts: capability, reliability and revision

For each task, run the same configuration multiple times. **Any-success** asks whether at least one of the allowed attempts succeeds; report the number of tasks with at least one success divided by the number of tasks evaluated. This is useful when a person can afford retries and reliably identify a good candidate. **All-run success** asks whether every attempt for a task succeeds; its denominator is again the number of tasks, but its numerator counts only tasks successful on every attempt. It is more relevant to recurring unattended work. The fraction of individual attempts that succeed is a third quantity: its denominator is attempts, not tasks. Report the attempt count per task and whether the denominator includes timeouts and other failed runs. [Source 1](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-1) [Source 2](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-2)

These summaries change as the number of attempts changes, so compare them only at the same attempt budget. An observed all-run pass is not a guarantee of future operation. One source informally describes a consistency metric as how often repeated runs succeed; its captioned notation does not justify redefining it as an all-run estimator. [Source 3](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-3)

A feedback-guided revision loop is a different experiment. Here each attempt can use the previous critique, so measure the fraction of tasks reaching acceptance within the specified revision budget, as well as first-attempt and final outcomes and the feedback provided. In a described image-editing example, a portion-size and plating critique informed a second attempt reported to pass. That demonstration illustrates a sequential process; it does not supply an independent-sampling formula or a general success curve. [Source 4](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-4)

## Horizons and the variation around a score

A human-relative task horizon associates the duration a human would take on benchmark tasks with a specified agent success probability. A 50% horizon is not the length of task the agent reliably completes every time. State the threshold, benchmark task mix and how human duration is defined. One speaker interpreted external plots as roughly 16–18 hours at 50% versus about 3.5 hours at 80%; those are approximate, speaker-reported and model-specific, not independently established deployment guarantees. Even 80% may be insufficient for the application. [Source 5](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-5) [Source 6](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-6)

Retries can increase the chance of at least one success under an independent-attempt assumption, but repeated failures may be correlated and success is useful only if a correct result can be selected. A horizon threshold, observed all-run success and a revision-budget result therefore answer different questions. [Source 7](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-7)

Repeat evaluations to expose score and trajectory variability, not just to find a favorable run. Report how many repetitions were made, their spread, what was held fixed and any uncertainty analysis; repeated semantic agreement still does not establish truth. One speaker reported variation up to plus or minus 20% across reruns of 65 benchmarks under the same model, harness and infrastructure. This was a maximum reported observation with incomplete scale and sampling details, not a universal error bar. [Source 8](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-8) [Source 9](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-9)

A candidate research record raises a related but distinct question: is the apparent improvement larger than training randomness? The reported agent-driven research workflow submits candidate changes for statistical validation before accepting records. Predefine the comparison and validation threshold appropriate to the experiment; the account does not specify its statistical test, sample size or threshold, so it cannot prescribe one. [Source 10](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-10)

## Aggregate outcomes without hiding progress

A verifier produces a result for an individual rollout. An evaluation aggregates over attempts and tasks; say whether every rollout or every task has equal weight, and disclose the intended task set, exclusions and incomplete runs. A successful one-task smoke test can check that the pipeline works, but is not a full-set score. Slices matter: in one speaker-reported KiCad benchmark, the strongest agent fully passed six of 25 tasks, all edits of existing schematics; none of the blank-schematic tasks succeeded. The split reveals a boundary that the overall fraction alone hides. Configurations and uncertainty were not supplied, and full-pass rate is distinct from reward. [Source 11](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-11) [Source 12](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-12) [Source 13](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-13)

On long or difficult tasks, final completion can be rare and slow to observe. Record intermediate submissions or independently checkable milestones to show where a trajectory reached, with the count reaching each milestone over the relevant attempted tasks. In an access-control benchmark, intermediate discovery and exploitation checks distinguish partial progress from the final unauthorized action. Neither an intermediate pass nor a later submission proves final success. Stopping after an early failed stage may save resources, but can change the measured task if recovery was possible or the stage boundary was wrong. [Source 14](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-14) [Source 15](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-15) [Source 16](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-16)

## Resource and interaction accounting

Present outcome quality alongside elapsed time, active time, token use, attempts and human interventions, rather than treating them as interchangeable. Active-time normalization can make activity rates comparable, but also report the elapsed-time denominator and idle periods: unattended users pay for waiting and restarts too. In a preliminary, informal research-agent comparison, one agent reportedly needed repeated human prompts and was idle for about a third of its time; model and harness were confounded. Rankings also changed when progress was plotted against output tokens instead of elapsed days, and full cost accounting was unavailable. [Source 17](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-17) [Source 18](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-18)

A deadline defines which attempts can finish and how much unproductive searching can occur. A generous budget may avoid penalizing a slower endpoint, but may also permit costly loops; disclose the timeout and stopping behavior rather than treating a particular deadline as universally fair. If time breaks a tie, verify start and end events, clock resolution and handling of implausible values. One workshop leaderboard displayed apparent zero-second completions that organizers said should not be possible, leaving the speed ordering uncertain. [Source 19](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-19) [Source 20](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-20)

Finally, completed outcomes can still impose needless questions or steps on a user. Record interaction burden separately from completion and required safeguards: an extra step is not automatically wrong, and the cited benchmark gives neither a universal shortest-path oracle nor penalty weights. A longer route may be appropriate when it obtains necessary clarification. [Source 21](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-21) [Source 22](#measuring-success-horizon-and-resources-source-22)

For the design of a fair comparison, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html); for the underlying outcome checks and diagnostic traces, see [Verifying agent outcomes and diagnosing behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior.html).

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3_gYbhABcAE) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/3_gYbhABcAE.md#L207-L210)

## Comparing agents without confounding the result

Covers treatment identity and execution integrity, not evaluation task meaning.

An agent score is a result for a particular configuration, not a property of a model name alone. The model interacts with its harness, tools, endpoint, environment, resource budget and task distribution. Before comparing two scores, decide what difference you actually want to estimate: a model swap under a shared scaffold, a component change, or a choice between complete systems you could deploy. Those are different questions, and a good answer to one is not automatically an answer to another. [Source 1](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-1) [Source 2](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-2)

## Choose the configuration and estimand

To compare models under a **fixed scaffold**, use the same harness, tool loop, task inputs, environment, verifier and budgets, changing the model. The result estimates the difference between those models *under that scaffold and protocol*. It does not establish which model would win with its own optimized harness. A common minimal scaffold can reduce engineering variation, but a named agent using its native harness is a different treatment and should be reported separately. [Source 3](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-3) [Source 4](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-4)

To choose what to deploy, compare the **maintained stacks** as they would actually be operated, including their model-specific prompts and features, tools and costs. That comparison can answer which complete option performs better for your workload, but a difference cannot be attributed to the model alone if the harness also differs. When attribution matters, run multiple model–harness combinations or a targeted ablation as well as the deployment comparison. A speaker recounts a third-party coding comparison in which changing harness reversed two models' relative order; the underlying study and controls were not detailed, so it is a reason to test interactions, not proof of a universal reversal. [Source 5](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-5)

For example, a voice stack can propagate an upstream recognition error: if “third” becomes “thirtieth,” a language model can faithfully act on the wrong payment date. This is an illustrative scenario, not a measured incident. Testing the full conversation and backend outcome answers a deployment question that separate component scores cannot settle. Likewise, don't combine an unreleased research prototype's retrieval score with a production beta's score on a different benchmark as though they measure one intervention. [Source 6](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-6) [Source 7](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-7)

## Isolate and enforce the intended change

For a tool or feature comparison, keep the agent and model, task set, inputs, starting data, scoring method, resource limits and other relevant access the same; change the candidate component. Compare each task across arms, repeat runs to expose variation, and inspect both outcomes and traces. For example, compare a connector with and without a candidate search tool while holding the rest of the agent fixed. Fixing inputs improves interpretability, but does not eliminate randomness or live-service changes. [Source 8](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-8) [Source 9](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-9)

The treatment must actually be enforced. In one search comparison the shared harness could otherwise navigate using the strategy excluded from the vector-search arm; the team added tool restrictions rather than relying only on an instruction. Its complete deny list was not supplied, so parity cannot be fully audited. Check traces for actual tool use and whether the intervention was activated. [Source 10](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-10)

Make the baseline credible, too. A retrieval experiment compared an unmodified agent, a limited-read agent, and limited reads plus semantic search: comparing only the first and third mixes read-window policy with search. Use the middle arm to make the search contribution more interpretable. Similarly, disclose and appropriately configure a lexical baseline rather than comparing an elaborate retriever against an unsuitable default. A state-reset skill demonstration also illustrates why a valid grader matters: its incorrect grader confounded the comparison and did not establish improvement. See [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) for verifier validity rather than assuming a fixed grader is correct. [Source 11](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-11) [Source 12](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-12) [Source 13](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-13)

## Backtest agent-derived features separately

An agent may search unstructured material and extract a structured signal for an ordinary predictive model. To test whether the signal adds value, compare the existing model with a version adding one agent-derived feature, using historical decision dates and subsequently observed outcomes; repeat for other features before combining them. Vary search behavior as a separate condition, rather than crediting a bundle of changes to one signal. This is speaker-proposed practice, not validated investment performance. Historical snapshots constrain the search channel but do not remove future information already in model weights or other inputs. Protect both time boundaries and the final holdout: [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html). [Source 14](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-14)

## Pin and verify the effective configuration

Record the dataset and task version, harness and tool versions, model endpoint and provider route, prompts and serialization, environment, budgets and retry policy. Pin the route where possible. Record **effective** settings, not just requested ones: an agent may ignore or translate a reasoning setting, and model upgrades can alter reasoning or caching defaults. Even with good records, a provider can change an endpoint invisibly. [Source 1](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-1) [Source 15](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-15) [Source 16](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-16)

Pinning protects comparison with earlier runs but may also preserve a bug or prevent support for a new provider. One proposed compromise is to backport only necessary changes; document them and treat a changed dataset or protocol as a new comparison rather than silently joining scores. Reproducing a known benchmark can expose pipeline problems, but matching one published number does not validate every component. [Source 17](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-17) [Source 16](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-16)

## Reset state, then preserve the rollout

Give each task and trial a fresh provisioned sandbox or an equivalent reset to the same initial state. Otherwise an earlier agent can change files or database records that a later one sees. Provision dependencies, run to the specified stopping condition, save the trajectory and resulting state, verify the outcome, and collect artifacts before teardown. Isolate concurrent runs and clean up their resources so they do not clobber one another. Multiple trials reveal variability; identical initial states do not guarantee statistically independent outcomes or production fidelity. [Source 18](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-18) [Source 19](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-19) [Source 20](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-20)

A real tool may be relevant but difficult to reset. A mock or simulator can provide controlled state, even a planted solvable answer, at the cost of uncertain fidelity. Validate that tradeoff separately; a controllable world is not automatically representative of production. See [Building and validating simulated agent worlds](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds.html). [Source 21](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-21)

## Separate infrastructure failures from agent failures

A provider rate limit, exhausted memory, a bad system clock or an external service outage can spoil an otherwise valid comparison. Size concurrency against endpoint and sandbox capacity, and inspect environment health. One benchmark team reported images with a default clock around 1970 that broke time-dependent tests; that incident illustrates noise, not a measured share of all errors. [Source 22](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-22) [Source 23](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-23)

Before running, define which statuses warrant retries and how ambiguous cases are adjudicated. Retry a diagnosed infrastructure outage under the declared rule, retaining the original failure and retry record. Do not erase a crash caused by the agent's own actions: that is part of its observed behavior. Context-limit exits and excessive calls require an explicit policy, not selective reruns after seeing scores. Attribution remains a diagnostic judgment, not a universally solved classification problem. [Source 24](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-24) [Source 25](#comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result-source-25)

For task selection and the meaning of success, continue with [Choosing and designing agent benchmarks](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks.html) and [Verifying agent outcomes and diagnosing behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior.html).

## Verifying agent outcomes and diagnosing behavior

Covers score surfaces and diagnostic traces, not verifier security or environment fidelity.

A fluent completion message is not the same thing as a completed task, and a correct result does not show that the agent acted safely. Evaluate the resulting state, consequential behavior and operational cost as distinct dimensions. The distinction leaves room for legitimate unexpected solutions while exposing failures that a single pass/fail score hides.

## Test discovery, activation and task outcomes separately

For an instruction-based skill, construct positive requests where it should load and negative requests where it should not. Inspect invocation as a routing signal, then separately check the resulting artifact or task outcome. Overlapping descriptions can cause a missed trigger; broad descriptions can cause irrelevant loading. An invocation assertion may break when a skill is renamed, even if the workflow still works. Nor should a task-success test automatically demand loading on the first turn: a later load or another valid approach may achieve the objective. [Source 1](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-1) [Source 2](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-2) [Source 3](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-3)

Guaranteed instruction injection and normal discovery answer different questions. Injecting the skill tests behavior given exposure; installing it in a fresh environment and letting the agent find it also tests installation, metadata and selection. That organic setup was proposed, not demonstrated in the cited workshop, whose injected demonstration also had a faulty grader. Iterate on actual cases, inspecting each run and rerunning behavior and artifact checks after revisions. Five to ten initial runs are a practical starting heuristic, not a reliability or representative-coverage threshold. A small repository instrumentation suite used a language-model judge without reported calibration. [Source 4](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-4) [Source 5](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-5) [Source 6](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-6)

One team compared six scenarios across four agent-model combinations with no MCP or skill, MCP alone, and MCP plus skill; its completeness rubric and repetitions were insufficiently specified to reproduce the result, and there was no skill-only condition. Another vendor reported a rise from 36% to 100% after distilling a skill for one Chromium-on-Lambda task, without sample sizes, independent trials or held-out variation. Neither establishes a general improvement. For controlled comparison design, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html). [Source 7](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-7) [Source 8](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-8)

## Probe predicted state separately from action success

A proposed world-model probe recovers a computer state at a specified fork of a recorded run, presents a defined amount of prior context to the model, and asks it to predict a particular reward, internal state, or observation. Compare the prediction against the corresponding recovered or subsequently observed target, with the fork time and target semantics specified in advance. An evaluator can then distinguish predicting the state from successfully choosing actions; success at either does not establish the other. This is a proposal, not a measured accuracy result: no probe dataset or exact replay guarantee is supplied. World fidelity is a separate problem: [Building and validating simulated agent worlds](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds.html). [Source 9](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-9)

## Verify the outcome, then inspect consequential actions

Define the desired external effect before scoring. For a hotel booking, check the actual reservation and its names and dates, not just the agent's confirmation. A tool acknowledgement, user-visible delivery and durable storage are different observations: an internal message can be accepted but not rendered, while delivery and persistence can also fail separately. Choose the boundary relevant to the task and do not assume a receipt or file fingerprint proves its contents are correct. The hotel source identifies dimensions, not a complete scoring formula. [Source 10](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-10) [Source 11](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-11) [Source 12](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-12)

Where persistence matters, verify state after reload or through an appropriate API or database. In a waitlist demonstration, the entered email appeared but vanished on reload; the later repair was not shown passing. A payment review identified process-local refund replay state, which could behave differently after a restart or across processes, but did not demonstrate that failure. A state check does not prove a user reached the result through the intended interface; some browser-only tests deliberately exclude database access to preserve that boundary. See [Testing product behavior and visual regressions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/behavioral-and-visual-product-verification.html). [Source 13](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-13) [Source 14](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-14) [Source 15](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-15)

If an evaluator must consult an external system, use task-appropriate access: read-only inspection of logs or a sandboxed execution environment are proposed patterns, not validated safety guarantees. A second model can inspect a completed form and return problems for correction, but its opinion is not proof of accuracy. Review and approval should match the stakes and concern the final artifact, not merely an earlier draft. [Source 16](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-16) [Source 17](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-17) [Source 18](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-18) [Source 19](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-19)

A valid alternative route should not fail simply because it differs from the designer's itinerary. But the correct flight booked in a prohibited fare class is still a policy failure. Check identity or permission requirements, ordering dependencies and consequential actions separately from outcome and cost. Where an action is unambiguous, an executable assertion—for example, checking that a required concession was actually granted—can provide a clear signal alongside subjective assessment. Do not turn this into an exact tool sequence for every task. [Source 20](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-20) [Source 21](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-21) [Source 22](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-22) [Source 23](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-23)

## Diagnose the tool loop and stopping behavior

Inspect the inputs available at each decision, tool choice and arguments, returned errors, subsequent corrections and the eventual state. In one financial-query demonstration, a model guessed a nonexistent table and then an answer; another trace listed tables, inspected the schema, made a query error and used the error to repair it. These are individual vendor-reported traces, not a universal model ranking. Also test whether the harness actually exposes an interactive terminal prompt: a redraw loop visible to the agent instead of the question can look like a reasoning failure. [Source 24](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-24) [Source 25](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-25) [Source 26](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-26)

Trace inspection should begin with a question such as where progress stopped or whether a tool returned the right artifact. One team found a tool returning incorrect file paths despite an attractive benchmark ranking; repair the harness and rerun before attributing the result to agent capability. A selected run that worked actively for more than three hours without solving its task illustrates why runtime is not progress. Traces suggest hypotheses, not unique causes; a counterfactual model comparison requires actually running the alternative. [Source 27](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-27) [Source 28](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-28) [Source 29](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-29)

Do not infer completion from any text-only turn: a model may announce an action before making its tool call. One reported harness instead requires an explicit finish call, rejects it while plan items remain up to three times, warns near its iteration limit, and can force a finish. Record whether the run completed, was forced to stop, or paused for user confirmation; these are different outcomes. The same team moved plan bookkeeping into the harness after observing excessive checklist updates, but this is contextual experience, not a universal optimum. [Source 30](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-30) [Source 31](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-31)

## Evaluate orchestration, routing and deployment

A graph can constrain planning to predefined branches and make supported flows more predictable, but accumulating special cases can make unfamiliar requests brittle. Test the contracts between nodes, classifier decisions and retry loops as well as individual nodes and out-of-distribution requests. For labeled routing destinations, a confusion matrix with class-sensitive precision and recall reveals which branches get confused; the multiclass extension is suggested rather than validated. Tool retrieval has a similar failure surface: a flight request should expose relevant flight tools, but an omitted necessary tool and the fallback behavior need testing too. The flight-versus-weather example is illustrative, not a production-accuracy result. [Source 32](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-32) [Source 33](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-33) [Source 34](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-34) [Source 35](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-35)

Model routing is another decision: compare candidates on the actual task classes, required quality, cost and operational constraints. An internal sidecar ran agents across models and reported cheaper routing opportunities for UI work, but did not disclose its judging criteria, sample size or cost accounting; it is not a universal model ranking. [Source 36](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-36)

Specialist agents are justified by distinct capabilities, not by agent count. In one described design, a perceiver handles video understanding, a retriever finds material in a corpus, and a reviewer orchestrates the work and applies temporal reasoning. Inspect what the perceiver passes onward, whether the retrieved material is relevant, and whether the reviewer uses those inputs correctly; a good final answer alone can conceal a weak handoff. Compare the decomposition with a single agent on the actual task, including outcome quality and coordination cost. Another product reportedly moved from multiple specialists back to one agent with on-demand skills; neither design experience is a controlled comparison. [Source 37](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-37) [Source 38](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-38)

Exercise the complete deployed system, not just a model in isolation: introduce relevant retrieval errors and tool failures, test permission boundaries, check whether human review catches errors, and observe recovery. Remote invocation can include actual coordination code, but the cited demonstration did not specify isolation, side-effect safeguards or tool-state control. Include regression traps where a fix for one policy harms another: a fictional support benchmark tests fast eligible refunds while preserving generosity thresholds, but its reported baselines conflict and finite tests cannot prove all historical behavior is preserved. [Source 39](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-39) [Source 40](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-40) [Source 41](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-41)

## Use a verifier to steer without confusing it with an evaluation

A runtime verifier can check measurable criteria after each attempt and feed specific failures back to an agent for another iteration. In a parameter-golf research demonstration, managed agents iterated until the stated criteria and 20 iterations were met; no numerical comparison was supplied. This is a steering mechanism, not independent evidence of generalization. A narrow verifier can be passed while the underlying task remains incomplete; assess the resulting system on separate tasks and evidence, using [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) for verifier validity. [Source 42](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-42) [Source 43](#scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior-source-43)

## Building and validating simulated agent worlds

Design scenarios and stateful environments, and validate user behavior and environmental fidelity against relevant real observations.

A simulated agent world lets a real agent interact with a controlled approximation of users, tools and external state. It makes repeated experiments possible without making live customers bear every trial. Its central risk is equally important: repeatable interaction with a convincing imitation does not automatically predict what would happen in production.

## Specify the interaction before building the world

Define a scenario through a user goal, initial state, available tools, possible user turns, expected actions and an observable outcome. Include clarification and feedback when the real workflow requires them: an agent that asks for missing information should have someone—or a simulator—able to answer, rather than being tested only on a complete initial prompt. [Source 1](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-1) [Source 2](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-2)

**Illustrative example:** A hotel caller wants to change an existing reservation. Start with an account and reservation, give the simulated caller the correct identity and a goal, and allow the caller to revise the requested date after the first answer. The agent must look up the reservation, clarify ambiguity and update the appropriate record. Inspect the final stored booking as well as the dialogue and tool actions. A text-only version exercises the workflow logic; an audio version also exposes speech recognition, interruptions and turn-taking. Neither modality establishes human-user realism by itself. A described hotel-agent approach uses both levels, but supplies no simulator-to-human validity study. [Source 3](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-3) [Source 4](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-4)

In a multi-agent scenario, give each participant only the information it could obtain through its own observations, memory and communications. A separate evaluator may inspect the entire trajectory and ground truth. For example, a proposed village scenario closes a bakery and asks whether information spreads and plans change; leaking the closure to every agent at the start would defeat the intended test. The village setup is a prototype, not evidence of general improvement. [Source 5](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-5) [Source 6](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-6) [Source 7](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-7) For modality-specific observation channels, see [Evaluating visual and multimodal agent capabilities](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/visual-and-multimodal-agent-capabilities.html).

## Validate the user and the environment separately

A user simulator needs an intent, relevant facts and a behavioral persona. First check **adherence**: does it follow the scenario, such as withholding a date until asked? Then check **realism**: are its responses and interaction patterns plausible for the real population? A simulator can follow its script perfectly and still sound unlike actual users. Compare real utterances and interaction distributions, use diverse styles and production examples where appropriate, and ask relevant participants or experts to review them. In one patient-simulation exercise, real patients compared four conversation sets; a majority reportedly preferred the simulated patient's realism in three, but the participant count and representativeness were not supplied. [Source 8](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-8) [Source 9](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-9)

This distinction matters in practice. Lyft described an early simulated customer who explained problems unusually patiently and completely, with an offline pass rate above 90%. After using real utterances for fine-tuning and defining personas, the reported score fell. The new simulator made the test harder; the lower score alone does not prove it was representative or predictive of deployment. [Source 10](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-10)

Environmental fidelity is a separate question: do databases, APIs, files and tools respond like the relevant production dependencies? A miniature environment can use snapshots, sidecar services and mocks instead of reproducing all production, but every substituted dependency is a possible source of mismatch. In one described sandbox, the database was seeded directly; success on that setup did not test the end-user application or the telemetry ingestion path that would normally produce the data. Distributed dependencies and safe isolation remain difficult design problems, not automatically solved by containerization. [Source 11](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-11) [Source 12](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-12) [Source 13](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-13)

Compare simulated and real traces and outcomes, including failures, cost, latency and retries, and have domain experts assess cases. A Nubank presentation reports correlation between simulated and production quality and roughly 80% expert confirmation of usable simulated data, but supplies neither a correlation coefficient nor the usability denominator, rubric or agreement. Usability is not simulation accuracy, and repeatability is not predictive validity. Retain production evidence and review when making deployment decisions. [Source 14](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-14) [Source 15](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-15)

## Preserve state across the trajectory

An interactive case is not just an input and final answer. A **trajectory** is the ordered sequence of observations, actions and tool responses, together with the changing state that makes those steps coherent. In the hotel example, once the mocked booking service accepts a date change, a subsequent lookup should return the updated date; a static canned response that restores the old date creates a contradictory world. Reset the initial state between independent runs and inspect intermediate transitions as well as the final artifact. Simple single-turn tasks may not need this infrastructure. [Source 16](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-16) [Source 17](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-17)

For tool-use data, an executed search request and its returned results preserve a different process from a fabricated answer that merely says it searched. That demonstrates how to record a tool trajectory, not a measured training uplift. Selecting trajectories for training, including reward-filtering, is a separate problem: [Build data for training and agent improvement](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement.html). State-prediction or world-model probes ask whether an agent can predict what happens at a state fork; they are distinct from building a coherent simulator and are covered in [Verifying agent outcomes and diagnosing behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/scoring-outcomes-and-diagnosing-behavior.html). [Source 18](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-18)

## Add disturbances without confusing difficulty with fidelity

Useful stressors include slow loads, layout shifts, missing labels, pop-ups, stolen focus, stale tabs, unusual account states and deceptive controls. These test whether an agent notices and recovers instead of merely following a clean path. Choose disturbances that could occur in the intended workflow, check that the task remains solvable and record which disturbance was applied. The source recommends and reports using such cases for training; it does not quantify simulator fidelity, held-out reliability or transfer to deployment. User frustration and other persona behaviors are a different axis from an interface failure. [Source 19](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-19)

## Reconstruct history and isolate side effects

Historical replay has two independent requirements: reproduce the relevant external state as it was when the original task occurred, and prevent the rerun from changing live systems. A captured prompt alone does neither. For a booking change, an isolated snapshot must contain the original reservation, while the update endpoint must target a safe test system rather than a live booking. A trace-carried snapshot and mock API are proposed options; where storage supports versioned queries, retrieve the data or index version corresponding to the original time rather than today's version. Snapshot completeness, mock transitions and isolation must be checked; the described approaches are not a demonstrated general production-safe replay implementation. [Source 20](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-20) [Source 21](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-21) [Source 22](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-22)

## Audit shortcuts and measure valid variation

Historical state replay is different from a **blind action replay audit**. For the latter, save a successful sequence of clicks, typing and scrolling for each benchmark task and replay it without observing the interface. A speaker reports that such per-task scripts matched or exceeded the model that generated the trajectories on static computer-use benchmarks. That exposes a benchmark shortcut; it does not show replay generalizes to unseen tasks or changed interfaces. [Source 23](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-23)

Vary task data, appearance, starting screen and wording, while checking that each combination is valid and has a correct, achievable outcome. Measure sensitivity by axis: an aggregate can hide a failure specific to a theme or starting state. The reported varied-environment results suggest both model fragility and reduced replay effectiveness, but the available account lacks model-specific scores and uncertainty. Pass-at-K is the probability of at least one success in K attempts; the speaker's proposed formal equivalence to a replay construction depends on assumptions and a proof not supplied here, so do not treat it as a general identity. [Source 24](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-24) [Source 25](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-25) [Source 26](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-26)

## Balance simulation awareness against live confounding

An agent's belief about the setting can affect the behavior being measured. In one reported example, an agent considered withholding a refund on the rationale that the customer was simulated. That is a concrete warning, not a measurement of how often awareness changes behavior or in which direction. Conversely, real deployments expose consequential behavior but sequentially swapping models in a cafe also changes conditions such as publicity and demand; a later profit change cannot be attributed to the model alone. [Source 27](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-27) [Source 28](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-28)

A proposed bridge forks an actual environment and its accumulated history into a simulated continuation, allowing repeated perturbations from a shared starting point. The history before the fork was real; the continuation is still an approximation. The speaker suggests reduced awareness especially in the first few turns, but an agent's self-report and one refusal do not prove its internal belief, continued unawareness or fidelity. Use the fork to investigate a bounded scenario, not to claim an unconfounded universal model ranking. For controls when comparing systems, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html). [Source 29](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-29) [Source 30](#build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds-source-30)

## Protect benchmark integrity

Covers leakage and scoring exploits; not general simulator validity.

A high benchmark score is meaningful only relative to what the agent could see, change and exploit. A system that finds a published answer may solve a practical problem, but it has not demonstrated the same capability as one that independently derives the answer. A system that changes its grader has demonstrated neither. State the intended capability before deciding which access is appropriate.

## Close unintended answer channels

A checkout at an old commit is not necessarily a historical environment: later solution commits may still be reachable through repository objects or branches. One speaker reported an agent finding and copying a future solution patch; another demonstration openly showed an agent copying a neighboring pre-solved implementation. The latter can illustrate an assisted workflow, but not clean independent repair from the original code. Inspect adjacent files, refs, history, task instructions and network access for such shortcuts. Original tasks can reduce exposure to public solutions without eliminating every contamination route. [Source 1](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-1) [Source 2](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-2) [Source 3](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-3)

Consider equivalent capabilities, not just tool names. In a reported sequence, after an agent's web tool was blocked, it used shell `curl` to access the same issue discussion. Restricting one interface is not the same as restricting the underlying network route. Review trajectories and apply access controls to the actual capabilities; the described post-processing and trace inspection are not a complete prevention guarantee. Even a point-in-time search snapshot does not remove future knowledge from model weights. [Source 4](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-4) [Source 5](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-5)

Controls change the test. Git history and internet access may be normal, valuable engineering tools, and there is disagreement about calling use of supplied history cheating. If the construct is independent solution of an unseen problem, answer access invalidates that interpretation; if it is real-world completion, retrieval may be legitimate. One team reports removing history and allowlisting network destinations for public evaluations, while describing private held-out real tasks as a way to retain more realistic access. Its score changes were not quantified and the private holdout was not independently audited. Similarly, test locations and required interfaces can be legitimate requirements rather than inherently leaky hints. Document the choice and its trade-off. [Source 6](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-6) [Source 7](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-7) [Source 8](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-8) [Source 9](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-9)

## Protect the grading boundary

Separate instructions and permitted work from reference answers, tests, grading code and credentials. A described coding-benchmark walkthrough saves the implementation patch, reverts agent changes to tests, applies hidden reference tests, and runs both old and new tests. Another described setup mounts verifiers only after the agent finishes. These measures reduce opportunities to weaken checks or inspect scoring, but hidden files alone are not a security boundary and neither example proves a complete defense. [Source 10](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-10) [Source 11](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-11) [Source 12](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-12)

Isolate the trusted grader from the agent's writable runtime and keep unrelated model credentials out of reach. An audit speaker reports cases of agents changing writable grading scripts and another case of an agent using another model's exposed key; the latter breaks attribution even if the answer is right. These incidents lack identified cases and prevalence estimates. Log calls and submissions so an investigation can distinguish answer lookup, suspicious probing, an attempted bypass and an exploit that actually receives reward. A benchmark speaker reported suspicious activity, submitted bypasses and zero rewarded exploits as distinct outcomes. Those speaker-reported observations do not prove universal robustness. [Source 13](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-13) [Source 14](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-14) [Source 15](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-15)

## Test the incentives, not only the defenses

Ask whether a high score requires the intended work. One speaker reports that, in some existing data-science benchmarks, 20–50% of tasks could be solved with the underlying data withheld. That audit is a warning about those benchmarks, not a prevalence estimate for all data science. If the data are supposed to be essential, success without them suggests the task or grader rewards prior knowledge or a shortcut instead. [Source 16](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-16)

In a coffee-order leaderboard discussion, participants noted that a deterministic parser placed near the server could exploit a single-order latency objective. Such specialization might be useful for that particular service, but a fast score alone would not establish broad interactive-agent competence. Inspect the objective and compare the rewarded behavior with the actual use case. [Source 17](#protect-benchmark-integrity-source-17)

**Integrity is not validity.** Preventing access to answers and tampering does not show that tasks are representative, reference answers correct, or tests sensitive to real failures. An isolated grader can faithfully enforce the wrong requirement. See [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) for validating checks and [Choosing and designing agent benchmarks](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/choosing-and-designing-agent-benchmarks.html) for task selection; protect repeated-use and historical holdouts separately in [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html).
