## Evaluating retrieval, memory and learning in agent workflows

Covers informational capabilities; general experimental controls are taught separately.

An agent can fail because it never finds a fact, because it finds but misuses it, or because an old belief survives after the world changes. These are different capabilities. Measure them separately before deciding whether to change search, memory, or reasoning. For the basic distinction between active context, retrieval and persistent memory, see [Understanding context, memory and retrieval](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-memory-and-retrieval-foundations.html).

## Separate evidence access from evidence use

Compare the ordinary workflow with a condition in which relevant evidence is supplied directly. If answers improve, investigate access: query formulation, search results and harness behavior can all contribute. This contrast does not uniquely attribute the gap to the retriever, nor is supplied evidence a mathematical upper bound or necessarily a deployable method. A reported comparison lacked a complete decomposition of those factors. [Source 1](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-1)

Inspect the trace in both conditions: Was the right information found? Did the agent recognize it as relevant? Did it use it in the decisive inference? In a selected security-task demonstration, agents discovered much of the needed information without making the final logical connection; more retrieval alone would not necessarily fix that transition. A memory oracle can likewise provide the correct memory without forcing correct use. The demonstrations do not quantify how often each downstream failure occurs. [Source 2](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-2) [Source 3](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-3)

## Probe context position, delayed turns and external memory

To test **in-window** use, hold the question fixed and move a task-critical passage among positions in the supplied material. Where appropriate, include conflicting documents and check reporting-period alignment. A capacity test accepting a very long input does not establish that a small but decisive financial footnote will be used. [Source 4](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-4)

For conversational retention, preload a realistic prefix and score a subsequent response that depends on an earlier detail. One team used ten turns followed by an eleventh test; this was a setup, not a session-length limit. Another demonstration planted a learning preference, inserted filler and asked a later relevant question. Such a probe does not require a user simulator and tests a narrow fact-recovery capability, not overall tutoring quality. [Source 5](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-5) [Source 6](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-6)

For **external-memory** retrieval, deliberately place the decisive fact outside the active window and verify that the harness does not leave a copy in the prompt. Compare memory disabled, candidate recall policies and directly supplied evidence. One reported example placed the fact around step 124 and the question around step 500; the exact window and full construction were not specified. A large advertised window is not itself evidence of effective recall; one cited long-context curve was disputed, so do not turn it into a universal compaction threshold. [Source 7](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-7) [Source 8](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-8)

## Measure the search trajectory and its context

An agent may inspect results, revise a query and search again. Score the final information task and record queries, results, evidence opened and the cost of the complete loop. A one-shot ranking score is still useful for diagnosis, but does not by itself estimate success after adaptation. Conversely, a fixed-query, open-loop comparison and an agent-loop comparison answer different questions: the latter includes the agent's response to results, and a difference between them is not an isolated retriever effect. Literal matches can make refinement inspectable for identifiers, but do not establish lexical superiority on every corpus. [Source 9](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-9) [Source 10](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-10) [Source 11](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-11)

Along the trajectory, compare files, lines or symbols read with labeled relevant context. **Precision** is the fraction of retrieved context labeled relevant; **recall** is the fraction of labeled relevant context retrieved. In a vendor-reported set of 50 tasks, semantic search with windowed reads achieved approximately 87% file precision versus 65% for the baseline, while broader default exploration had higher file recall. The labels may penalize alternative valid context, and the benchmark did not directly measure completed task success. Use both measures alongside outcomes rather than choosing the higher precision alone. [Source 12](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-12) [Source 13](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-13)

## Test what memory preserves and how it changes

Specify what is written, selected, ranked, recalled and retained between sessions. Test whether important facts survive intervening tasks and whether irrelevant or obsolete material crowds them out. A proposed game-agent design caches events above a salience threshold; that is a policy to test, not evidence that its threshold or long-term consistency is optimal. [Source 14](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-14) [Source 15](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-15)

Also inject an incorrect memory as a controlled test and measure whether it is corrected, whether the error recurs and what the update costs. In one selected Pokémon example, five raw-memory runs repeated a trapdoor failure after a wrong location was stored; the speaker reported a correction with offline consolidation. The anecdote does not establish a general net benefit or a complete comparative rate. Evaluate correction quality, downstream task reward and additional compute in the intended setting. [Source 16](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-16) [Source 17](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-17)

Retaining the topic is not enough. Ask the agent to recall who supplied a claim, whether it was firsthand or a rumor, and whether later plans respect its uncertainty. A rumor repeated as a verified fact, or a known fact ignored in a plan, is a distinct failure from forgetting the words. Separating episodes from current beliefs and retaining provenance are proposed remedies, not proven guarantees. [Source 18](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-18) [Source 19](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-19)

## Design sequences that require learning

A sequence is not a learning benchmark merely because tasks occur in order. Provide new information the agent cannot already solve through offline familiarity, recurring structure that can transfer to later instances, and realistic feedback such as errors or textual corrections. For example, related database questions can reveal reusable schema information before a later question tests its application. [Source 20](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-20) [Source 21](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-21) [Source 22](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-22)

Compare reward on later instances with state retained against a reset-between-instances baseline. The difference estimates the benefit of the allowed state mechanism within that design; report absolute reward and cost too. A large gain from a low baseline is not the same as high task quality, and the contrast is not an unrestricted causal claim about all learning mechanisms. For controls and interpretation, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html). [Source 23](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-23)

Then change part of the environment—for example, rename a database column while leaving other relationships valid. Check whether the agent preserves useful experience while discarding stale assumptions. Stability can fail even without drift: in one narrated sales forecast, feedback that a prediction was too high, then too low, led the agent back to the already-rejected high prediction. This single trace illustrates oscillation, not its prevalence. The complementary plasticity test asks whether new, relevant evidence changes behavior rather than merely being stored. [Source 24](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-24) [Source 25](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-25) [Source 26](#evaluate-retrieval-memory-and-learning-in-agent-loops-source-26)

## Design evaluation distributions for decisions

Coverage and estimands rather than individual-label accuracy.

An evaluation set is not representative merely because it contains many examples. First state the decision: estimating ordinary user experience, finding severe failures, choosing a model for a particular task, and checking a proposed change each require a different population or case mix. The score is meaningful only for the distribution and conditions it actually covers.

## Ground scenarios in the work users need

Work with users and domain experts to describe expected behavior, then collect realistic workflows, ambiguous requests, ordinary successes and consequential failures. Do not restrict the test to what current connectors happen to support: one sales team wrote questions from the sales process before testing its assistant, including questions for which data was missing. Its reported accuracy lacked a disclosed rubric, but the design made unsupported demand visible. [Source 1](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-1) [Source 2](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-2)

For a financial research assistant, task variation might include unfamiliar companies, comparative and multipart requests, invalid identifiers and informal wording. A workshop's generated examples illustrate breadth, not live-user representativeness or release readiness. Likewise, experts authoring plausible repository tasks improve relevance without proving that the resulting collection mirrors all engineering work. Include common workflows and dependency failures, and disclose important absences. See [From business problem to meaningful success criteria](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/from-business-problem-to-meaningful-success-criteria.html) for defining success and [Specify and audit meaningful benchmark tasks](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks.html) for task-level validity. [Source 3](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-3) [Source 4](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-4) [Source 5](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-5)

## Choose the distribution for the estimand

Build a taxonomy of user intents, task families, populations, environments and risk conditions. Then allocate cases deliberately:

- **Production-frequency evaluation** targets performance for the traffic population represented by the sample. Estimate or document how cases were selected, the relevant period and any missing groups.
- **Risk-enriched evaluation** deliberately oversamples rare but consequential events, such as tool failure or sensitive escalation. Its unweighted failure fraction describes that enriched test mix, not the prevalence of failures in ordinary traffic.
- **Slice results** describe performance within a defined group or condition. Report its denominator and uncertainty rather than assuming the overall average protects it.

If population rates are needed from an enriched sample, use justified population weights and sampling assumptions; absent those, keep the results separate. More cases cannot repair an unidentified population or an omitted risk category. [Source 6](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-6)

An informal product-discovery pilot illustrates why prompt intent matters: the product was reportedly mentioned around 65% of the time in explicitly comparative prompts but not in a pain-focused scenario. Sample sizes and prompt distribution were not fully specified, so these are not deployment rates. A long-horizon coding benchmark likewise acknowledged underrepresenting bug localization and refactoring, while one worktree evaluation had not simulated the very long sessions of concern. State such gaps rather than generalizing beyond the observed setting. [Source 7](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-7) [Source 8](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-8) [Source 9](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-9)

Cross relevant dimensions where interactions matter: a document system may need multiple languages, historical periods, layouts and genres; a visual task can behave differently when the question language changes. One proposed Indic benchmark described such breadth, but its release, per-language counts and scoring were not established. A few multilingual visual examples are similarly not a systematic coverage study. [Source 10](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-10) [Source 11](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-11)

## Select models on the local slice

Public benchmarks are useful screening evidence and may be directly relevant when their tasks and conditions match deployment. They are not automatic certification for a different workflow. Compare actual candidate variants on the organization's task families, prompts, harness, latency and cost constraints. An image-editing aggregate can conceal different performance on object removal versus text editing; the cited vendor presentation did not provide full plotted data to verify every ranking. A modified checkpoint also needs evidence for that variant, not just the base model. [Source 12](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-12) [Source 13](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-13) [Source 14](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-14)

Record achieved task quality and realized cost per task, not only token tariffs: a cheaper token price can still yield more expensive work when an agent uses more tokens. Prompt and harness interactions can change the observed result; a small counting demonstration improved after a decomposition instruction, but cannot establish a stable model ranking. For controlled comparisons, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html). [Source 15](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-15) [Source 16](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-16)

## Replay cohorts, not anecdotes

For a proposed model or tool change, select a meaningful cohort of existing executions, replay the change and compare outcomes across cases. An expensive-case cohort answers what happens to expensive cases, not what happens to all traffic. Segment by cost, latency or risk where useful, and repeat stochastic attempts to expose within-case variability. One replay can be a valuable example but is not a reliability estimate; replay at scale costs resources, and the cited demonstration does not specify sampling, grading or fidelity. [Source 17](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-17) [Source 18](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-18)

## Quantify uncertainty for a release decision

A defect estimate below a release threshold is not enough when its uncertainty still crosses that threshold. A workshop describes an observed 3% defect rate against a 5% limit and contrasts different sample sizes; its intervals and sample-size suggestions are approximate, with no interval method or sampling design supplied. They are not universal release rules. Choose sample size and uncertainty analysis for the target population, sampling design, dependence between cases, risk tolerance and decision cost; seek more evidence or narrow deployment when the interval does not support the decision. This population-rate question is different from asking whether a deliberately enriched edge-case suite found a serious failure. [Source 19](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-19)

## Account for combinations and provenance

Count authored base scenarios separately from configurations formed by varying profile, theme or starting state. A speaker described DigiWorld as 15 apps, 387 verified scenarios and 3.2 million configurations; these are speaker-reported counts without per-axis distribution details. Millions of combinations should not be presented as millions of independent authored tasks. [Source 20](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-20)

Record where each dataset came from, what was excluded, and how labels were obtained. One tutoring study cleaned real staff-answered questions into 60 single-turn pairs, while using generated facts and filler for a different multi-turn memory probe. The former tests current question answering; the latter probes retention of planted facts. Similarly, PR descriptions and branch prefixes can suggest agent authorship, but they are proxy labels, not direct observation of autonomous work; their accuracy was not audited. Real-work capture can preserve context but may be biased or unsafe, while manufactured cases can deliberately cover missing conditions. Neither origin guarantees truth or representativeness. [Source 21](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-21) [Source 22](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-22) [Source 23](#design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions-source-23)

## Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets

Collection, refresh and incident regression rather than synthetic generation.

A production trace is evidence of what happened, not yet a test of what should happen. A useful offline case needs a reconstructable situation, an expected outcome or observation, and a way to assess a new run. Keeping that distinction lets a team learn from real work without mistaking a collection of memorable incidents for a representative sample of all users.

## Promote reviewed failures and reliable capabilities

Start with an investigated interaction, correction or complaint. A user’s correction is a lead, not necessarily an accurate label of the underlying error; review the context and decide what behavior is actually expected. Record the input, relevant state and tool responses, expected outcome or observation, and a category and owner. A clinical workflow, for example, describes turning expert trace annotations into typed cases with conversation input, expected observation and category metadata. That is a reported workflow, not a clinical-outcome study. [Source 1](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-1) [Source 2](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-2)

Make the case runnable, reproduce the baseline behavior where possible, and run the candidate on the same case. Compare its output with the original and rerun earlier cases: fixing a single failure can break something that previously worked. A workshop proposes replaying failures through a development endpoint with the production rubric, but its verification path was described rather than fully executed. Scorer quality still matters; reuse of a rubric alone does not validate it. [Source 3](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-3) [Source 4](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-4) For investigation and scorer design, see [Tracing, failure analysis and evaluator methods](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tracing-failure-analysis-and-evaluator-methods.html) and [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html).

A capability case may initially be an ambitious target; once it passes reliably enough for its intended use, keep it as a regression check. Decide whether the behavior merits a hard per-case requirement or a noisy aggregate target. In one teaching example, every financial report must name its ticker, while actionability is assessed as an average. A finite perfect run does not prove a true 100% success probability, and passing the suite says nothing conclusive about untested behaviors. [Source 5](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-5)

A growing suite preserves history but consumes time and money. Categorize cases so a relevant subset can run during iteration and a broader suite at integration; the suggested tradeoff gains faster feedback at the cost of potentially later detection. It is a proposed workflow, not a measured missed-regression rate. Owners should review redundant cases rather than blindly retaining every trace, while retaining consequential distinct failure modes. Release thresholds and promotion decisions belong to [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html). [Source 6](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-6) [Source 7](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-7)

## Refresh from real use, not just failures

Collect eligible inputs, outputs, intermediate steps, outcomes and feedback from production—or user acceptance testing when production evidence is unavailable. Select both successful and unsuccessful interactions, have knowledgeable reviewers label expected behavior, and retain provenance and selection rationale. Successes protect useful behavior that a failure-only library would miss. Usage changes can make an old suite less relevant even when the model has not changed. [Source 8](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-8) [Source 9](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-9) [Source 10](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-10)

Permission, privacy, retention and missing outcomes must be resolved before keeping an interaction. One reported benchmark effort used opt-in coding records and compensated contributors, then manually cleaned tasks; it did not publish a complete consent protocol or demonstrate representativeness. Production origin alone does not establish either. Sampled and incident-selected cases answer different questions: use [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html) when estimating performance on a population, and reserve appropriately protected tests for evaluation rather than repeated tuning. [Source 11](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-11) [Source 12](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-12)

Recheck automated judgments against newly reviewed human examples as the suite evolves; a disagreement might expose a bad application response, a bad evaluator, or an ambiguous standard. The suggested ongoing alignment check is not a demonstrated alignment trend or a prescribed refresh cadence. Online monitoring and offline experimentation are complementary; neither term inherently means batch or non-batch. [Source 13](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-13) See [Monitoring production quality and improvement](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-evaluation-and-monitoring.html) for ongoing traffic monitoring.

## Freeze comparisons while maintaining living fixtures

Maintain two explicit views: a versioned frozen set for comparing candidates on the same historical circumstances, and a living set for new usage and failure modes. Pin a code commit, injected change and expected result, or record downstream tool responses and replay them while the agent generates a fresh answer. Otherwise a changed environment and a changed agent are entangled. Recorded responses stabilize inputs, not stochastic reasoning; a frozen snapshot also becomes less current over time. [Source 14](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-14) [Source 15](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-15)

Realistic fixtures may be large because removing details can remove the trigger. Do not assume a shortened case is equivalent: rerun it against the known behavior before replacing the original. Incident.io reports an alternative to loading an entire large YAML suite: structured operations to list, add, edit or replace individual cases, with instructions for agents using the interface. This is a company workflow report, not a controlled comparison. [Source 16](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-16) [Source 17](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-17)

## Reconstruct historical work

Completed work offers another source of local tasks. In one case study, roughly twenty merged fix pull requests from one repository supplied parent commits with bugs still present; a model generated task descriptions from the fixing diffs. A candidate agent then worked against the buggy repository. That selection rule is narrow, and the account does not establish checks against solution leakage or representativeness. [Source 18](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-18)

When adapting the pattern, preserve the pre-work state, provide only information legitimately available to the agent, and decide what constitutes an acceptable result rather than assuming the historical patch is the only correct answer. Check privacy and selection bias. Archived incidents or support tickets can also generate probes for whether a knowledge base contains the information needed to do actual work; the cited scanner was a preset demonstration, not proof of enterprise-scale accuracy. [Source 19](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-19) [Source 20](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-20)

## Use shared baselines, and budget for local maintenance

A reviewed external set is a useful common starting point, not a substitute for local expert review and observed cases. One clinical team announced 200 input and 100 output guardrail scenarios, but the material was not independently inspected and does not establish clinical outcomes or coverage. Adapt and extend such a baseline for the product’s users, policies and actual failures. [Source 21](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-21)

Budget for expert task design, labeling, review, replay infrastructure and eventual replacement as well as execution. A speaker’s example of expensive benchmark construction uses hypothetical labor and cost assumptions, not a measured accounting; its lesson is to account for the quality-control and refresh work that cheap case generation can leave out. [Source 22](#build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets-source-22) For broader coverage decisions, continue with [Building and maintaining evaluation coverage](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/building-and-maintaining-evaluation-coverage.html).

## Protect holdouts and historical evidence

Separates adaptive test reuse, training exposure, entity leakage and future information.

A test can look independent while giving the system information it would not have in the intended use. The leak may come from related training examples, previously exposed benchmark answers, or evidence published after a historical decision. These are different problems: hiding benchmark answers does not make a historical web search time-correct, and an archive does not erase answers learned during training.

## Constrain historical discovery as well as page versions

For a retrospective forecast, fix a decision date before the outcome and reconstruct what the system could have known then. If an acquisition is announced later, a current search can return the announcement and turn a forecast into an answer lookup. Restrict the web tool to evidence available by the decision date, and record the cutoff, retrieved versions and their provenance. A displayed publication date alone is insufficient: a page can have been edited since that date. [Source 1](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-1) [Source 2](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-2)

There are two distinct retrieval problems. An archive lookup for a **known URL** returns an available version at or before the cutoff. Historical **search** attempts to discover relevant pages from a time-bounded index. If the evaluator picks the URL because of what happened later, the page content may be old but the selection still imports hindsight. Vendor-described historical search addresses this discovery channel, but the supplied evidence does not establish archive completeness, timestamp guarantees or exact reproduction of historical ranking. Missing pages can bias the test too. [Source 3](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-3)

Inventory every other channel: model weights, internal databases, feeds, tools and any human-selected context may contain later information. A historical web interface controls only its own channel, not future knowledge already embedded elsewhere. Disclose what could and could not be bounded; do not call the entire replay leakage-free merely because the web tool is dated. A live, unresolved case avoids a known outcome at decision time but cannot immediately establish forecast accuracy. Historical replay supplies outcomes sooner, at the cost of a harder information-boundary problem. [Source 4](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-4) [Source 5](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-5)

## Split by the generalization claim

Choose the split unit to match what the deployment claim says must be new. If the goal is performance on unseen companies, keeping questions about a company in both training and evaluation can reward familiarity with that company's facts or templates. Put companies, not just individual rows, into disjoint partitions. In the reported FinQA example, the company-disjoint split had roughly 4,000 training examples, 500 validation examples and 290 held-out benchmark examples. That boundary is useful, but the source does not establish that other leakage paths were audited. [Source 6](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-6)

Grouping is not enough if important categories disappear from the exposed or evaluation partitions. In an audience-reported prompt-optimization run, a high-scoring prompt excluded aunt and uncle relationships despite their presence in the reference. The speaker suspected those categories were absent from the optimizer's subset; that diagnosis was not established. Inspect category coverage and report results for consequential rare distinctions instead of letting common cases conceal them. [Source 7](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-7)

## Reduce benchmark answer exposure

A model can encounter public benchmark questions or solutions in pretraining, while a team can also tune repeatedly against visible test feedback. Reserve a private set for a final check, restrict who and what can see its answers, and disclose exposure risks. Fresh tasks and novel problems reduce reliance on published solutions; one coding benchmark collects recent issues on a rolling basis, while another proposal combines novel tasks with private holdouts. Neither novelty nor secrecy proves decontamination, and a fresh task may still have an answer reachable at runtime. Compare the controls to the specific exposure route rather than assuming one technique handles all of them. [Source 8](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-8) [Source 9](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-9)

Where feasible, investigate overlap or verbatim memorization and report the method and uncertainty; a speaker-reported investigation in the evidence provides neither methods nor statistical results, so it cannot supply a contamination rate. Public tasks help others inspect and reproduce work, whereas private tasks reduce answer exposure: use each for its purpose and disclose the tradeoff. Repeated visible feedback can itself encourage adaptation; preserve an independent final check rather than treating a frequently consulted regression set as untouched evidence. For runtime answer access and benchmark attack surfaces, see [Protect benchmark integrity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-benchmark-integrity.html). [Source 10](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-10)

## Separate site adaptation from unseen-site transfer

Real deployment data can reveal conditions missing from laboratory examples and help adapt a system to a particular site. But if that site supplied training data, success there estimates performance after local adaptation, not zero-shot performance at a new location. Report which sites contributed data, and evaluate the unseen-site claim on sites not used for that adaptation. These are complementary questions, not competing definitions of success.

A robotics vendor describes collecting customer-site data and later demonstrates operation at a conference without additional site data. The account is not an isolated test of data collection, and the conference demonstration gives no quantified cross-site success rate. It motivates recording the distinction, not a claim that transfer has been established. [Source 11](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-11) [Source 12](#protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence-source-12)

For controlled comparisons beyond these information boundaries, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html).

## Specify and audit meaningful benchmark tasks

Task-level construct and verifier validity rather than population coverage.

A benchmark task is a claim about what an agent should be able to do under particular conditions. A prompt alone is not enough: the agent needs a usable starting situation, a goal and a way to observe completion. Even a perfectly packaged task can be misleading if its answer is ambiguous, its checks reward the wrong thing or its inputs do not require the claimed capability.

## Construct executable tasks and matching checks

Package each task with its instruction, prepared initial state and execution environment, required data and tools, a verifier, and a stopping condition. Separate the task from the harness that runs the agent and the runtime that executes it; document which layer supplies tools, prompts and skills because that division depends on the application. A common format can help others run and extend tasks, but portability, usability and compatibility are not evidence of validity or secure isolation. A harness must actually support the task's required capabilities. [Source 1](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-1) [Source 2](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-2) [Source 3](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-3) [Source 4](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-4)

For a repository issue, preserve the issue, runnable dependencies and checks: fail-to-pass tests should fail before a fix and pass after it, while regression tests should keep passing. A test derived from the eventual fix is useful supervision, but may be flawed or demand a solution-specific detail. Another construction starts from a completed pull request, removes selected code and asks the agent to recover a reachable endpoint. Reachability does not make the historical implementation uniquely correct. [Source 5](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-5) [Source 6](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-6)

Parameterized tasks need matching state and checks, not just varied wording. In a proposed transfer task, the recipient and amount are instantiated together with mock data, initial interface state and a corresponding verifier; broken combinations must be rejected. The source describes the architecture, not the rejection criteria or verifier error rate. Likewise, a project benchmark may include external APIs, whose availability, state and cost are not automatically frozen by packaging; a shared GUI authoring interface does not prove identical semantics across platforms. [Source 7](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-7) [Source 8](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-8) [Source 9](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-9)

A compatible configurable model endpoint can sometimes let an existing harness send requests through a translating interception layer, preserving ordinary harness code while collecting sampling information. This is conditional on endpoint and protocol support, not a solution for arbitrary closed harnesses. For comparison design see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html); for validation of the checks themselves see [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html). [Source 10](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-10)

## Specify the objective without prescribing every path

Describe the user goal, starting conditions, desired behavior and genuine hard constraints. An expected result might be a correct final state, appropriate deferral, or a required tool call and arguments when that behavior itself matters. Avoid treating a particular sequence as mandatory merely because it was the author's solution: a harness upgrade or a scientifically sound alternative may achieve the objective differently. High-level tasks leave room for exploration, but can need hints and richer grading to remain solvable and fair. [Source 11](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-11) [Source 12](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-12) [Source 13](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-13) [Source 14](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-14) [Source 15](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-15)

For example, scientific analysis can admit multiple valid methods. Specify conditions that should hold across those methods rather than silently assuming one canonical path. A deterministic check can still encode an unjustified scientific choice. If correctness, useful insight and efficiency are separate goals, specify them separately: one demonstration used two model judges and a six-call rule, but did not validate the interestingness judge or establish six calls as a general limit. [Source 16](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-16) [Source 17](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-17)

## Audit the task before interpreting failures

Read the instructions, supplied artifacts, expected answer and actual checks together. Ask independent experts to attempt the task and cross-review the resulting solutions; use an adjudicator and revision when they disagree. Run agents too, because attempted execution can reveal broken environments or hidden task defects. One coding-task curation account selected extra candidates to replace defective ones and manually checked final tasks; its reported extra sample was ten percent, not a universal reserve. [Source 18](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-18) [Source 19](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-19)

In one scientific example, human attempts exposed unresolved choices about gene groups, normalization, neighborhood radius and aggregation. A disagreement with the expected number may reflect the task's ambiguity rather than poor reasoning. Decide whether a choice is essential and specify it, or accept justified alternatives; revisit arbitrary inherited thresholds before turning them into hard failures. Scientist cross-grading was the team's available proxy where no canonical answer existed, not proof of truth: no inter-rater statistic or detailed protocol was reported. [Source 20](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-20) [Source 21](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-21) [Source 22](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-22)

Also look for contradictory instructions and checks that omit a requested outcome. A significantly negative item-discrimination estimate—stronger models on the fitted scale tending to fail an item—is a reason to inspect its wording and gold answer, not automatic proof the item is wrong. One demonstration flagged an answer that counted crew when the question asked for passengers; another model's agreement with the criticism is not independent verification. [Source 23](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-23) [Source 24](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-24)

## Make the environment and evidence matter

The files, tool behavior and expected rubric must agree with one another and plausibly resemble the conditions the task claims to test. An agent should not be penalized for following its supplied evidence when the gold answer contradicts that evidence. Obvious placeholders can also alter how the agent behaves. Synthetic material is not inherently invalid, but synthesis and quality control require care. This is a task-fidelity question, distinct from whether a collection has representative sampling proportions. [Source 25](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-25) [Source 26](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-26) See [Design evaluation distributions for decisions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/design-evaluation-distributions-for-decisions.html) for the latter.

Test whether the claimed evidence is actually needed. A model might answer a public-data question from memory without using the supplied source, or answer a purported visual question from text and general knowledge without inspecting image detail. Try removing or changing the evidence and inspect whether the answer should change; for a data-analysis task, ask whether its conclusion genuinely depends on the specific supplied data. The visual-source warning is a speaker's argument, not a reported image-removal experiment or estimate of how many items have shortcuts. [Source 27](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-27) [Source 28](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-28) [Source 29](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-29)

Match fixture size and contents to the behavior under test. A small subset may suffice for a narrow correctness question; pagination or full-database behavior needs enough records to exercise it. The full-database suggestion in the cited case was prospective, not a completed load study. For design-to-code work, the needed fixture is a *paired* design and implementation: one team created toy repositories because open code paired with design files was scarce in its setting. [Source 30](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-30) [Source 31](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-31)

## Renew or shorten tests without changing the question unnoticed

When results cluster near the ceiling, inspect both task difficulty and grading strictness. Consider extending the test if it no longer distinguishes the candidates, but keep essential easy and safety checks where they serve a different purpose. High scores alone do not prove a bad evaluator, and a suggested ninety-percent signal is not a universal retirement threshold. In one word-inclusion experiment, tested models reached the original 500-word ceiling, so the author extended the lists into the thousands. The extension measures a lexical proxy, not general instruction-following capability. [Source 32](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-32) [Source 33](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-33) [Source 34](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-34)

The extended random word lists sometimes accidentally triggered safety refusals. Those are not the same failure as forgetting an instruction. The author filtered the list for one model; disclose such preprocessing and the altered input distribution when interpreting or comparing results. [Source 35](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-35)

Shortening has a different objective from finding defective items. Rank items by estimated discrimination, then check whether a selected subset preserves the original ranking for the models and benchmark in question. In one speaker-reported demonstration, about 97 of 484 items met a 99% ranking-correlation target; the speaker identified GPQA as a counterexample to generalizing the approach. Preserving that ranking does not establish preservation of absolute scores, safety coverage or other decisions. [Source 36](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-36)

## Inspect incentives in the tasks and the score

A vendor may have incentives to select impressive hard cases or sell material optimized to its own benchmark. One speaker makes that market critique while having commercial interests of his own; it is not an audited industry-wide finding. Define realism using independent knowledge of the actual work, not solely the seller's assertion. [Source 37](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-37) [Source 38](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-38)

Finally, enumerate what the score rewards and ignores. In a small acquisition-prediction exercise, correct positive predictions earned a point, false positives lost a point, and misses and passes had no effect. That objective encourages a different decision tradeoff from one that penalizes missed acquisitions; a high score does not establish investment performance. Before adopting any score, decide whether its outcome weights reflect the decision you intend to make. [Source 39](#specify-and-audit-meaningful-benchmark-tasks-source-39)

### Source 39: Backtest Your Agent Against Yesterday's Web — Ryan Ahern, Exa

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L4dUFimVDKU) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/L4dUFimVDKU.md#L55-L55)

## Generate synthetic cases without mistaking them for reality

Recipes, checks and sampling limitations; interactive simulators are treated separately.

Synthetic cases let a team exercise a behavior before real examples are available, or target rare failures that ordinary samples may miss. They answer a coverage question: “Does the system handle these constructed conditions?” They do not by themselves answer how often those conditions occur, or how well the system will perform on real users.

## Start from failures and a specification

List the behavior being tested, plausible failure modes, and the evidence needed for the expected answer. Author or generate cases across those conditions, then have a reviewer check that each case actually supports its intended label. A small diverse financial-query workshop set illustrates a useful starting point, not a representative sample of financial users. When allowed, supplement imagined cases with real-world evidence and revise the suite as usage reveals surprises. [Source 1](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-1) [Source 2](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-2)

Retention constraints can make synthetic cases particularly useful, but they are not a blanket privacy or legal guarantee. One healthcare team described contractual restrictions on retaining real records and derivatives while clinicians contributed production-inspired ideas; the permitted boundary was not resolved in the account. Establish the applicable permissions rather than assuming synthetic output makes any source use permissible. [Source 3](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-3) [Source 4](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-4)

## Build a staged recipe instead of one giant prompt

Record seeds, generation settings, dependencies and checks so a case can be traced and regenerated. Preview a small batch before scaling; inspect variety and whether later fields actually follow earlier choices. For long records, fix invariants first, generate a chronological history, plan encounters, then produce individual documents with relevant prior context. Parallel document generation can introduce contradictions, so check dates, identity and clinical facts across documents rather than assuming that shared prompts guarantee consistency. This is a reported generation design, not a measured guarantee of realistic clinical records. [Source 5](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-5) [Source 6](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-6) [Source 7](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-7) [Source 8](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-8)

Another recipe walks a knowledge graph to make multi-hop search riddles: select a seed, follow a bounded sequence of relations, and formulate a question whose answer depends on the path. Longer walks can drift away from a useful subject; the source gives inconsistent hop ranges, not an established optimum. Validate the relations and answerability rather than treating path length as difficulty proof. [Source 9](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-9)

## Construct cases backward from a check

**Illustrative example:** suppose an invented return policy accepts an unused item within 30 days and rejects it after that period. Select the intended path first: an unused item returned on day 29 should be accepted; an otherwise similar day-31 case should be rejected. Generate the surrounding customer messages and order records, then independently check that their dates, item condition and intended outcome agree. Vary templates so the answer cannot be inferred from a repeated phrase. This tests only the invented rule, not every real return-policy exception.

The same principle supports richer policy paths: a healthcare team described sampling approval and rejection reasoning paths before generating supporting records. Uniformly sampling paths can deliberately emphasize rare branches, but the resulting pass rate is not a deployment-average accuracy estimate. A contract-review practitioner described planting known problems and combining template values into code-gradable tests; their stated shorter feedback cycle was a practitioner account, not evidence of production readiness, and the source's wording about initial clause compliance is inconsistent. [Source 10](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-10) [Source 11](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-11) [Source 12](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-12) [Source 13](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-13)

Mechanically verifiable tasks are useful where requirements can be stated precisely. A proposed poem task, for example, checks word count and the presence of a chosen word; passing says nothing by itself about poetic quality. Varying constraints creates more cases, not proof that shortcuts or contamination are impossible. [Source 14](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-14)

## Expand failures without changing their meaning

From a known failure, generate neighbors that vary delivery while retaining the intent and expected decision: for a voice booking request, change speaking speed or background noise, but verify the request remains intelligible and means the same thing. Domain substitutions must also preserve meaning: gross profit and gross sales are not interchangeable just because both are financial terms. Ask experts to review questionable variants and feed identified mistakes back into the generator. Proposed voice and adversarial variations were not accompanied by a simulation-validity study or measured adversarial success rate. [Source 15](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-15) [Source 16](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-16) [Source 17](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-17) [Source 18](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-18)

## Validate examples and labels in layers

Check structure and invariants first, then test whether the content supports the label. Round-trip the generated record through an independent rule implementation where possible, review disagreements, and use domain experts to inspect a sample and hard cases. A separate model can help find issues, but may share the generator's errors; a cheap local model's label is a hypothesis, not ground truth. One financial data pipeline combined programmatic checks, an independent agent and human review; the account does not provide reviewer agreement, rejection rates or an independent audit of final labels. [Source 19](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-19) [Source 20](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-20) [Source 8](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-8) [Source 21](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-21)

For retrieval training, another proposed backward construction generates questions and answers from documents, checks answerability using other grounded models, then removes the initial retrieval support so the learner must find the evidence. Checking the easy, grounded version helps construct supervision; it does not independently prove the resulting harder task or every label is valid. [Source 22](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-22)

For training data, budget for a funnel: generate more candidates than needed, filter invalid or unhelpful examples, record generated and retained counts, and evaluate the trained model on separate relevant evidence. A speaker reported 50,000 seeds yielding roughly 7,000 retained records and a search-benchmark change from zero to 30% after training. The model setup, baseline protocol and ablations were not supplied, so the report neither isolates the cause nor proves transfer to production. [Source 23](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-23)

## Ground personas without claiming new human evidence

If personas are meant to resemble a population, use aggregate data and conditional relationships rather than sampling every attribute independently. For example, an age–income joint distribution can keep combinations in plausible proportions where the source data supports them. This does not establish individual realism, predictive validity or a formal privacy guarantee; the proposed method did not report distribution-fit or disclosure-risk measurements. [Source 24](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-24)

Repeatedly asking an unchanged synthetic persona the same question can estimate that model's response distribution more precisely, but it creates no new independent human observations. A tighter Monte Carlo estimate is not evidence that the model predicts the population more accurately. This caution concerns reruns without new real-world input, not every kind of data augmentation. [Source 25](#generate-synthetic-cases-without-mistaking-them-for-reality-source-25)

For ongoing use, connect synthetic stress tests with [permitted production-grounded evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html); keep the two purposes and their limitations visible when reporting results.

## Collect and interpret human judgments

Human labeling and evidence quality rather than test-distribution design.

Human feedback becomes useful evaluation evidence when its origin, context and uncertainty remain visible. A click, a reasoned expert judgment and a later edit answer different questions; treating them as interchangeable can turn convenience into false confidence.

## Preserve an independent first judgment

Show a reviewer the task and relevant evidence before showing the model's verdict. Save that first assessment, then reveal the model's reasoning and record any revision and why it changed. In a browser-verifier experiment, experts assessed full trajectories first; the verifier sometimes surfaced details they had missed. Independence protects the reference from immediate anchoring, not from human error. [Source 1](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-1)

Test whether reviewers actually deliberate. One copy-typing study inserted false alerts into legitimate historical sessions without affecting customers; reviewers sometimes accepted the signal despite strong calibration scores. Its sample size was not disclosed. If uncritical approvals are later reused as labels, they could reinforce the original errors; that feedback loop is a proposed mechanism, not a measured effect in the study. [Source 2](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-2) [Source 3](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-3)

Acceptance-weighted adaptation is a separate concern. A code-review system can use accepted and rejected suggestions to adjust what it offers, but a team can reject an important security warning. Keep mandatory rules and independent expert review separate from popularity; the described weighting safeguards are unspecified. Past review history can supply context without becoming the standard of correctness, and noisy utility feedback can misassign credit. [Source 4](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-4) [Source 5](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-5) [Source 6](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-6) For measuring held-out judge alignment with these references, see [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html).

## Capture the reasoning and the evidence

Ask domain practitioners, including nontechnical experts, to inspect real outputs and explain the judgment, correction and significance of each error. Walk through completed cases: what did the expert look for, why did it matter, and what would have prompted a stop or question? Retain the sequence and constraints as well as the final artifact; otherwise a finished product can hide the decisions that made it acceptable. A small first set is useful for elicitation, not a guarantee of domain coverage, and expertise does not ensure experts agree. [Source 7](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-7) [Source 8](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-8) [Source 9](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-9) [Source 10](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-10)

Attach each label to its supporting evidence and record the depth of verification: for example, whether a reviewer inspected only an extracted field or checked the original source. This makes a conclusion distinguishable from the work supporting it; it does not prove the conclusion correct. One campaign-finance case reports evidence-bearing labels, but their completeness was not independently audited. [Source 11](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-11)

Make that work practical. Present traces in the form the domain expert recognizes, with a short set of decisions and room for comments. For visual review, associate a comment with a marked region or relevant component rather than leaving the recipient to infer its target. A demonstration exported located feedback as structured data, but did not disclose its full schema; neither a tailored view nor deterministic capture establishes that the annotation or proposed fix is correct. [Source 12](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-12) [Source 13](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-13) [Source 14](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-14)

## Interpret disagreement rather than erase it

Specify the dimension before resolving disagreement. Two reviewers may disagree whether a visual element meets a stated alignment requirement, suggesting a definition or inspection problem. They may also genuinely prefer different styles; averaging those tastes into one label can erase useful information. Record the reviewer’s relevant perspective, preference and conditions, and select experts across meaningful styles or media rather than relying on a large undifferentiated pool. The boundary between an objective requirement and taste itself needs definition; proposed preference vectors and diversity benefits have not been validated here as training results. [Source 15](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-15) [Source 16](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-16) [Source 17](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-17)

Separate perceptual observation from policy. In the hearing-aid example, detecting an apparent ear device may be correct while the device is permitted. A single “violation: no” label would incorrectly suggest the detector failed. Record whether the observation is supported and, separately, whether the applicable policy makes it a violation. This is a design remedy, not a measured accuracy improvement. [Source 18](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-18)

Repeated verdicts or a committee can prioritize disagreements for human inspection. A disputed borderline case may expose missing context or an unclear decision rule; independent refinements of a vague specification may also reveal ambiguity. But inconsistency has other causes, unanimous models can share an error, and a disagreement-only queue misses consistent mistakes. Include other cases in review. [Source 19](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-19) [Source 20](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-20) [Source 21](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-21)

For source-sensitive extraction, an alternative is independent duplicate work: give workers the same source and instructions without showing each other's outputs, require provenance, and reconcile differences against the source rather than by majority vote. The reported case uses agents; independence of presentation does not eliminate correlated model errors or substitute for professional sign-off. [Source 22](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-22)

## Treat behavioral feedback as a clue

A complaint starts an investigation: ask what was wrong and inspect the relevant output. A staged demonstration produced a complaint that its author could not substantiate; it shows the value of clarification, not a measured false-report rejection rate. Likewise, capture what happened after acceptance: an edit may reveal a defect, a preference, a changed requirement or unrelated work. [Source 23](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-23) [Source 24](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-24)

A later editor snapshot can inform an earlier prediction, but the user's intent or the code may have changed in between. One experimental approach takes a snapshot after ten seconds without edits in a region, not after a commit. It compares samples from the original context with that later state, using closeness as a heuristic for predictability; it considers very distant examples noisy and intermediate cases potentially useful. Neither the pause nor text similarity proves satisfaction or semantic correctness, and thresholds, selection bias and training gains were not established. [Source 25](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-25) [Source 26](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-26) [Source 27](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-27) [Source 28](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-28)

Historical diffs have similar limits. Before inferring expected review flags, check that original and revised documents and relevant decisions exist. One contract project retained only final versions, and negotiation complicated interpretation, so its proposed diff-based route was unavailable. [Source 29](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-29)

## Audit the collection, not just its volume

Preference data can teach the wrong signal. A video judge reportedly learned overall polish and artifacts instead of the intended storytelling, physics or camera axes. Real-versus-generated pairs can also make origin or encoding a shortcut for quality. Normalize obvious nuisance differences across pairs and test challenging counterexamples for each axis; shared encoding and annotation do not prove all provenance confounding is gone. The diagnosis and improvement are internal, qualitative reports without an isolating ablation. [Source 30](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-30) [Source 31](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-31)

Inspect locally controllable properties—expert selection, evidence links, specificity and quality checks—even when downstream model-training feedback is unavailable. These properties make data more inspectable; they do not establish a causal training improvement or a universal quality-over-volume law. [Source 32](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-32)

Finally, a public invitation alone does not ensure broad participation. Provide dataset hosting, access to relevant models and interpretable write-ups so contributors are not excluded merely by infrastructure or API costs. Access broadens the opportunity to contribute; it is not a statistical-validity guarantee. [Source 33](#collect-and-interpret-human-judgments-source-33)

## Evaluate and represent retrieval corpora

Retrieval and corpus preparation rather than final-answer grading.

A retrieval system decides which pieces of a corpus are available for a later task. A fluent answer can hide a retrieval failure, and finding the right document does not establish that an answer is supported by it. Evaluate evidence access on its own, then use [grounded-answer evaluation](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers.html) to examine support and abstention.

## Define what retrieval must find

For each realistic query, identify the relevant unit: a page, passage, file, document, or exact entity. The right choice depends on the task. A question about a policy may need a particular passage; an equipment inventory may need every matching asset, including names differing by one character. Treat the latter as an identity problem rather than assuming semantic similarity will distinguish near-collisions. Lexical search can help with identifiers and import chains, while semantic search can find related code described in different words. In one exploratory code-search comparison each approach helped on different tasks; neither was universally superior. [Source 1](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-1) [Source 2](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-2)

Build judgments from real questions and have knowledgeable people label relevant results and plausible but misleading near-matches. One team reports assembling about 200 such examples in under a week, though it did not report a full labeling protocol or representativeness study. Pooling candidates from multiple systems before judgment can expose results that a single system would never return. In a separate pooled-ranking case, a grounded model judge reportedly agreed with human *system rankings* at 0.87; the agreement statistic was unspecified and does not mean 87% of individual labels were correct. [Source 3](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-3) [Source 4](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-4)

A complementary shortcut begins with a known page: generate a question about it, run retrieval, and check whether the originating page appears. This provides a code-checkable target without repeatedly asking experts to find an answer. It does not guarantee the question resembles a real user's request or that the originating page is the only valid evidence. Retain real-user cases alongside synthetic queries. [Source 5](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-5)

### Choose denominators that match the decision

* **Precision at K** is the number of relevant results among the first K divided by K. It reflects the irrelevant material in a fixed-size reading window. State what happens if fewer than K results are returned.
* **Recall at K** is the number of relevant items found in the first K divided by the total number of relevant items in the judged corpus for that query. It asks what was missed; incomplete relevance judgments make this denominator uncertain.
* A **hit rate** can ask whether at least one target was found. It is useful when one suitable source suffices, but does not show whether all relevant sources were found or how much irrelevant material accompanied them.

**Illustrative calculation:** suppose a judged corpus has four relevant documents and the top five results contain three of them. Precision at five is 3/5, or 60%; recall at five is 3/4, or 75%. If the query needs all four documents, the missing item matters even though the result list contains useful evidence. If a user can read only five, the two irrelevant entries also matter. A code-search example returned 295 files when six were needed, illustrating the burden of excess material; its full relevance labels and a numerical F1 were not supplied. [Source 6](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-6)

Rank-sensitive measures can distinguish a relevant result at the top from one near the cutoff. Define the exact measure and relevance grades before comparison; one source's captioned metric names are too imprecise to reconstruct its formula. A tutor team compared retrieval configurations by whether the correct lesson page was found, rather than assuming its hybrid settings were optimal. The underlying tuning experiments and sample sizes were not shown. [Source 7](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-7) [Source 8](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-8)

Keep reported results tied to their definitions. A rulebook project reported that hybrid search raised retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions, with no previously found question lost; the hit definition and per-question results were not supplied. Another team initially defined precision at ten and reported about 60%, then described a later 90–95% result using an ambiguous “recall at 10 or precision at 10” label. Do not silently call that later number precision. Neither small, speaker-reported comparison proves that a search design generalizes. [Source 9](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-9) [Source 10](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-10)

The precision–recall distinction is not limited to retrieval, but the population changes. For an incident detector, precision concerns flagged incidents and recall concerns all actual positive incidents—not retrieved documents. One synthetic detector account provisionally reports perfect precision and 0.8 recall; that would still miss positives. Its English interpretation is uncertain because the automatic captions render English speech in Devanagari and contain errors. It is not evidence of production incident coverage. [Source 11](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-11)

## Represent the material before indexing it

A chunk is the unit search can return. Pick boundaries based on what makes sense to retrieve and what context the reader needs: functions, classes or methods for code; paragraphs and sections for prose; intact tables where a split would sever labels from values. Overlap can protect context at boundaries but duplicates content. A rulebook system instead used nonoverlapping chunks with document name, page, section path and chunk index, enabling a tool to fetch and reconstruct the surrounding section. Its heading rules were tailored to those rulebooks, not validated across all formats. [Source 12](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-12) [Source 13](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-13) [Source 14](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-14) [Source 15](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-15)

Metadata should support actual downstream operations: locating a source, filtering by applicable role, or expanding a hit to its section. Code comments and generated document summaries may help convey meaning beyond the raw chunk, but comments can be stale and summaries inaccurate; the cited accounts did not isolate their benefits. Richer query-like code representations were suggested, not tested in the raw-code embedding experiment. [Source 16](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-16) [Source 17](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-17) [Source 15](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-15)

### Recover PDF and table structure

Many PDFs describe positioned glyphs and graphic lines rather than explicit paragraphs and tables. Extraction must infer reading order and structure; recognizing the characters alone can put the right value under the wrong heading. PDFs vary, so inspect representative outputs rather than assuming every document has the same internal form. [Source 18](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-18)

For example, a table may visually show a transaction category spanning several fee rows. If extraction leaves the category only on the first row, a later retrieved fee loses its meaning. Expand the spanning label into each applicable structured row, retaining column headings and a route back to the source. A rulebook team used CSV for this; its fee example was a dummy illustration and the reported improvement was qualitative, not an isolated numeric test. [Source 19](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-19)

The best representation for search need not be the best one for reasoning. One practitioner describes indexing natural-language descriptions of tables to match questions, while passing structural HTML for reasoning about merged cells; simpler tables may fit Markdown. This is a reported practice without retrieval metrics, so test it against your own table types. [Source 20](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-20)

## Ground search plans and test transfer

Before a search agent plans a series of queries, show it an initial semantic search and the metadata facets actually available. The preview can reveal corpus vocabulary and usable filters, rather than letting the agent invent them. The cited account does not isolate how much this preview improves results. [Source 21](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-21)

Test the actual input regimes in which the system will operate. A code-search author reported that recall fell almost to zero on a 396-file mixed-responsibility repository after better results on more modular files; the account does not isolate repository size, organization or model capacity as the cause. A credit practitioner likewise distinguished standardized public information from challenging private-loan files, spreadsheets and PDFs, without a comparative extraction benchmark. A successful result on one corpus is a reason to test the next, not proof of transfer. [Source 22](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-22) [Source 23](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-23)

## Build traceable references and keep them current

A structured reference can make a corpus easier to navigate. One company organized product capability cards by what a product does and why it matters to defined personas, retaining citations back to connected sources. Another described research documents enriched with concepts, markets and time periods; an API context graph linked services and endpoints to code and production traces. These structures support inspection, but links alone do not prove the compiled claims, complete governance, or point-in-time correctness. [Source 24](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-24) [Source 25](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-25) [Source 26](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-26) [Source 27](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-27)

Inventory each source's location, format, update pattern and task consequence, then choose a refresh cadence appropriate to that source. In a hypothetical claims workflow, a policy document and newly arriving claim decisions change on different schedules; example annual, quarterly and hourly intervals are assumptions, not prescribed rules. A perfectly retrieved stale document can still mislead. Preserve dates and source trails so a user can tell what information was available and when. [Source 28](#evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora-source-28)
