## Build data for training and agent improvement

Training-data selection rather than independent evaluation outcomes.

Training data is not just a collection of inputs. It embodies decisions about which situations are generated, which outcomes count as desirable, which targets are trusted, and what the student should learn. Those decisions can improve the training signal while also introducing biases that a separate evaluation must detect.

## Generate and filter synthetic interaction trajectories

A proposed approach runs an agent in a simulated environment, generates candidate interaction trajectories, scores them with a reward, and rejection-samples the apparently desirable trajectories for training. Real customer conversations may inform the simulated user. The reward determines which behavior is selected; the simulator determines which situations the agent can encounter. Consequently, both shape the resulting data, including their blind spots. [Source 1](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-1)

**Illustrative example:** If a support simulator rewards ending conversations without human handoff, it may select a trajectory that keeps a distressed caller talking when escalation would have been appropriate. A high reward would then certify the proxy, not the user's welfare. Review the reward and selected examples against the intended outcome, including cases that deserve escalation. This is a vendor proposal, not independently validated evidence of improved real-user outcomes. For designing and checking the simulated world itself, see [Building and validating simulated agent worlds](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-validate-simulated-agent-worlds.html).

## Curate teacher targets and behavioral hints

A teacher can label realistic task contexts, but a stronger model is not an infallible labeler. One editor team described collecting opt-in production snapshots containing the context available at an edit request and asking a frontier teacher for a prediction. Snapshot inputs connect training to actual tasks, but opt-in alone does not establish representativeness or describe all privacy handling. [Source 2](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-2)

The team checks predictions for concrete violations, such as undoing what the user just typed or changing text outside the editable region. A failing prediction goes to another model with the failure explanation for repair before use as a training target. This controls identifiable failure modes, but the account gives neither repair accuracy nor remaining error rates; checks can miss bad labels and repairs can be wrong. Inspect targets and measure downstream student behavior rather than treating the repair step as a guarantee. [Source 3](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-3)

When trustworthy traces are scarce, one speaker recommends keeping a smaller, human-inspected golden subset and testing a higher training weight for it. The same speaker suggests that some failed reasoning traces might sometimes help smaller students. Those are conditional hypotheses to test through mixtures and student measurements, not a general instruction to discard every failure or train on all errors. No supporting experiment for the alleged benefit of failed traces is supplied. [Source 4](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-4)

A complete ideal answer is not always available. Another proposed distillation approach gives the teacher privileged information about a specific behavior to improve, such as an undesirable formatting pattern or a tendency to continue rather than wrap up. The hint narrows supervision without supplying a perfect response for every task. It still needs validation: hints may be unreliable, downstream quality can regress, and the approach is not guaranteed to work for every enterprise task. [Source 5](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-5)

## Select the skill, difficulty and verifier

Start with the intended skill, then select tasks that exercise it and can be executed safely. For reinforcement learning, tasks that are always trivial or impossible provide little useful learning signal; seek a productive difficulty range for the current agent and revise it as capability changes. The source gives qualitative guidance, not a universal success-rate target or selection algorithm. Match the verifier to the outcome: an equality check, compiler, unit test, database lookup, or rubric-guided judge may fit different tasks, but each creates its own training signal and can reward the wrong thing. See [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) for verifier validity. [Source 6](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-6)

A visual reasoning company described purpose-built multimodal data and a loop involving evaluations, agents, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. The transferable decision is to target the missing visual skill rather than presume a generic image-text corpus covers it. The company did not disclose the dataset composition, recipe, filtering, or measured gains, so this is not proof that its flywheel works. [Source 7](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-7)

## Feed observed gaps back into the data

An OCR team described using evaluation results to update training inputs, combining synthetic examples and real documents when labels are scarce. The operational loop is: inspect a failure, identify the missing training pattern, add or improve relevant examples, then measure the changed model. Annotation quality and contamination safeguards were not described in the account, so the loop is not itself evidence of generalization. Keep independent assessment separate from data used to tune the system; see [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html). [Source 8](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-8)

Internal records may also contain knowledge absent from public data: failed experiments, trade theses and explanations of why a decision did or did not work. Preserve the context and outcome rather than training only on apparently successful decisions. A speaker proposed such proprietary negative data as a differentiator; neither the business advantage nor the claimed ease of quickly structuring it was demonstrated. [Source 9](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-9)

## Keep execution receipts and bootstrap flow specifications

Retain the journey as well as the final status: actions, errors, timings and final state can help reviewers diagnose a run and curate future examples. A reported e-commerce journey, for instance, includes login, catalog loading, cart actions and abandonment. A receipt records what happened; it does not by itself define a correct outcome or become an executable test. Proposed overnight aggregation and autonomous fixes were not demonstrated results. [Source 10](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-10)

A related proposal would enrich nontechnical UI feedback with recordings, console logs and network requests. Its live integration did not run and only initial mocked tests were reported. Treat the added context as potentially useful evidence, not a verified automated improvement pipeline. [Source 11](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-11)

Where written flows are missing, one described tool performs a one-level surface crawl of the current website and generates Gherkin user flows. This is a starting point for human review: a shallow crawl observes existing behavior and visible links, not the intended requirements, hidden paths, or complete acceptance criteria. A current defect can be reproduced as if it were a requirement unless someone checks it. [Source 12](#build-data-for-training-and-agent-improvement-source-12)

## Preserve meaning and interpret measurements

Measurement semantics and reproducibility rather than evaluator sampling.

A successful query, a reconciled total, or a large dataset can still answer the wrong question. Interpret a measurement by tracing what was observed, how it was transformed, and which decision the result is meant to support.

## Protect business and label semantics

Before changing a transformation, state what one row represents and which business predicates define the metric. Then trace downstream consumers: changing a customer-month table to customer-week can repeat a monthly revenue value across weeks, so a downstream sum may inflate revenue even though the SQL runs. Removing a paid-customer filter may similarly turn paid churn into a metric that includes trials. These are illustrative failure modes, not measured incident rates; map lineage and check consumer assumptions before the change, rather than waiting for a successful build. [Source 1](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-1) [Source 2](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-2) [Source 3](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-3)

The same rule applies to test and training transformations. Gross profit and gross sales are not interchangeable paraphrases, and a horizontal flip of a directional traffic sign or a color change to a traffic light may change the label. Whether a transformation preserves meaning depends on the task and domain, not on its mechanical validity. Consult domain owners about the permissible variations; executable checks alone do not establish the intended semantics. See [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) for executable verification. [Source 4](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-4) [Source 5](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-5)

## Model the decision, not just the field

A useful conceptual framing distinguishes four things: what the source can observe, what storage preserves, what the decision needs, and what the model assumes. Billing may mean the payer by “customer,” while support means the caller; one universal entity definition can erase a distinction relevant to either decision. This four-part schema is a proposal for reasoning, not a validated taxonomy. Explicitly record the decision and entity definition before mapping fields. [Source 6](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-6) [Source 7](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-7)

A financial numeral also needs a type: value, unit, magnitude scale, reporting period and document location. A prior-year revenue figure in a later filing is not automatically revenue for the filing year, and a table-wide billions annotation can sit far from the number. Preserve those associations before comparing or calculating. [Source 8](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-8)

Reconciliation is necessary but not sufficient. In one speaker-reported debugging case, row counts and dollar totals matched while date parsing left nearly all dates empty. Other cases involved missed categories or changed signs. Check missingness by field, category coverage, sign conventions and representative source-to-output records as well as aggregates. Those cases illustrate a mechanism, not an estimated error rate. [Source 9](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-9)

A zero result has a boundary too. A demonstrated query found no hotels listed in its Antarctica database; that supports “none listed in this database,” not “none exist anywhere.” State the dataset, query scope and any known completeness limits when reporting absence. [Source 10](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-10)

## Ask what the measurement channel can see

In cell modeling, DNA, RNA expression, proteins and morphology or spatial measurements describe different aspects of biology. RNA sequencing is relatively scalable; protein measurements can be closer to functional activity but are described as lower throughput. Abundance makes a modality convenient, not sufficient for every biological question. Improving measurement fidelity alongside scale is a research direction, not a demonstrated out-of-distribution guarantee or a quantified cross-modality ranking. [Source 11](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-11) [Source 12](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-12)

A single-cell profile is also a snapshot of a changing system: cell cycle and bursts of expression can create genuine differences. Labs and instruments add technical variation. Record time, preparation, laboratory and instrument context where available, and consider both explanations before treating all variation as error or all of it as biology. The cited account does not supply a method for partitioning or correcting those effects. [Source 13](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-13) [Source 14](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-14)

## Specify the workload, not only its name

A serving benchmark needs its request-generation protocol. Record sampling and truncation, input and output length distributions, termination behavior, cache reuse and multi-turn structure. Specify whether requests arrive at a constant rate, via a stated stochastic process, or under a constant concurrency target, and verify the actual schedule. Two harnesses in a reported experiment produced different input-token workloads from the same named dataset because of sampling and truncation. A shared catalog can make scenarios reproducible, but does not by itself prove they represent a deployment. [Source 15](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-15) [Source 16](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-16) [Source 17](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-17) [Source 18](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-18)

Channels matter outside serving too. One speaker reported word error rates of 11.4% for a headset-oriented speech benchmark and 26% for the same model on a central room microphone, with different distance and speaker conditions. Full replication details were not supplied. Compare channel and recording conditions before attributing a score difference to the model. [Source 19](#preserve-meaning-and-interpret-measurements-source-19)

## Validate judges against human labels

Alignment and classifier errors, not truth or probability calibration.

A judge can score thousands of answers consistently and still apply the wrong standard. Validate it as a classifier against human judgments for the intended task, then inspect the kinds of errors it makes. Agreement with those labels is useful evidence of alignment—not proof of truth, task success or reliable predicted probabilities.

## Error costs, precision and recall for the stated positive class

First define what counts as positive. Suppose positive means a **failure that should be flagged**. A true positive is a real failure flagged by the judge; a false positive is a flag on an acceptable answer; a false negative is a failure the judge misses. Then:

- **Precision** = true positives / (true positives + false positives): of the flags, how many are real failures?
- **Recall** = true positives / (true positives + false negatives): of the real failures, how many did the judge flag?

**Illustrative example:** On a labeled set, a judge flags 12 answers, 9 of which are actual failures. Three more failures go unflagged. Precision is 9/12 = 75%; recall is 9/12 = 75%. The denominators happen to match here but measure different populations. If a denominator is zero, report the metric as undefined rather than inventing a percentage. Show counts, prevalence and uncertainty alongside rates: an aggregate agreement score can conceal a failure class that the judge rarely catches. [Source 1](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-1) [Source 2](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-2)

Choose an operating point according to the downstream action. When a flag sends a case for review and a miss reaches users, greater recall may be worth extra false alarms. When a flag itself triggers a costly accusation, precision may matter more. These are conditional choices, not rules for an entire field. One workshop first uses cancer screening to motivate recall and later describes medical use as favoring the opposite; its captions do not resolve that tension. Specify the positive label, the consequence of each error and who bears it instead of silently choosing one remark. [Source 3](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-3)

## Establish the human reference

Select raters who represent the relevant users or have the required domain expertise. Give them a common rubric and concrete borderline cases, and examine where people disagree before treating a single adjudicated label as a reference. Ask whether the disagreement is due to missing context, ambiguous instructions or a genuine difference in values. Revise the criteria or record the disagreement and its resolution; do not assume that additional labels alone settle an incoherent standard. Human–human agreement and judge–human agreement are different measurements, and neither makes a subjective judgment automatically true. There is no universal human-agreement threshold established by these sources. [Source 4](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-4) [Source 5](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-5)

Have humans label cases independently of the judge's verdict before comparing them, so the model's answer does not become the reference by default. Use multiple raters where practical; a single knowledgeable rater can be a starting point but leaves variation less visible. For collection and adjudication details, see [Collect and interpret human judgments](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/collect-and-interpret-human-judgments.html). [Source 6](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-6)

## Validate against held-out labels

Collect representative positive and negative cases, including relevant difficult slices. Retain the application outputs and context so judge revisions can be tested on the same material without rerunning the application. Separate examples used for prompt development and iteration from independently labeled held-out cases used for the final estimate. Run the frozen judge on each held-out case with the permissible task context and intended reference facts, but withhold the held-out human verdict and adjudication. Have the judge generate its verdict independently before comparing it with the human label; otherwise it could copy the answer instead of judging the case. [Source 7](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-7) Report the confusion counts, precision, recall and overall agreement, the sample and label process, and uncertainty or limitations. Revisit representativeness as the application and traffic change. [Source 8](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-8) [Source 6](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-6)

Inspect disagreements in both directions. Read the case and judge rationale: a false alarm can expose an overstrict judge, while a missed failure may reveal a rubric gap, missing context or insufficient model capability. The human label can also be wrong. Resolve the actual issue, update the development set or instructions as appropriate, and evaluate the revised judge on fresh held-out data rather than repeatedly tuning to the reported test. A team whose critic excused real bugs found it useful to read full traces and adjust the critic where its judgments diverged from humans; that account is qualitative rather than a quantified reliability study. [Source 9](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-9) [Source 10](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-10)

For contrast, a browser-verifier experiment described roughly 50 trajectories for development and about 100 held out, with two paid annotations per held-out trajectory. The speakers reported false positives falling from almost half to zero on their gold evaluation and a kappa of 0.58. Confusion-matrix counts, uncertainty and full adjudication details were not supplied, so this is not evidence of zero false positives in general. [Source 11](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-11) [Source 12](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-12)

A different actionability workshop used approximately random purported human labels. Its displayed disagreement and precision/recall numbers illustrate mechanics only; they do not validate the judge. Another workshop's 46% agreement likewise used deliberately random labels. Do not promote either demonstration result into a quality estimate. [Source 13](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-13) [Source 9](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-9)

## Probe bias, not just the average

To test presentation sensitivity, swap the order of paired answers while keeping their content fixed and compare verdicts; blind model identity where possible; and inspect slices for preference for length, confidence, style or model family. A reversal under an order swap is a diagnostic, not a complete bias benchmark. Blinding names cannot remove all stylistic cues, and using a different judge family or provider does not guarantee independent errors. A small same-family demonstration also confounded origin with wording, so it does not establish the magnitude of a family effect. [Source 14](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-14) [Source 15](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-15) [Source 1](#validate-judges-against-human-labels-source-1)

Finally, separate three questions: **human–judge agreement** asks whether verdicts match a chosen reference; **precision and recall** characterize classifier errors for a specified positive class; **probability calibration** asks whether stated probabilities correspond to observed frequencies. A high value on one is not proof of the others. For what agreement can and cannot establish, see [Agreement, truth and the limits of evaluator proxies](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies.html); for confidence calibration, see [Compare systems, confidence and behavior without mixing estimands](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands.html).

## Agreement, truth and the limits of evaluator proxies

Epistemic and construct-validity limits, not the operational labeling procedure.

A score can be consistent, reproducible and still answer the wrong question. Before using an evaluator to choose or improve a system, distinguish three things: agreement with a reference, the validity of that reference or proxy, and the real outcome the decision depends on. They are related evidence, not interchangeable measurements.

## Agreement is useful but not independent truth

Agreement tells you that judgments coincide. It can help prioritize disagreements for inspection and measure alignment with a reference, but the parties may share assumptions or training influences. Different model providers, model families or reviewer roles do not by themselves establish statistical independence. In one finance case, four model families reportedly produced the same total while sharing a sign convention different from the answer key. That is one shared-error example, not an estimate of how often consensus fails. [Source 1](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-1)

In an exploratory credit exercise, two reported bankruptcy probabilities started at 62% and 25% and converged near 25% after structured reasoning, with both models favoring restructuring. The future was unresolved in the account. Convergence shows changed agreement under that process, not calibrated probabilities or predictive advantage; the prompts and repetitions were not specified. [Source 2](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-2)

Unexpectedly perfect agreement can prompt checks for leakage, repeated familiar cases or overfitting. One speaker proposed rejecting 100% agreement outright, but provided no held-out evidence that perfection necessarily means overfitting. Do not turn that concern into an automatic upper-bound rejection rule. When possible, examine fresh cases and independent evidence of correctness; use [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html) for the distinct problem of measuring agreement with human labels. [Source 3](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-3)

Adding another model reviewer does not make the chain infallible. Generated tests and reviews can themselves omit the relevant failure, and repeated evaluation of transcripts may reach the limit of what a platform knows about the customer’s intended outcome. The customer may have additional task-specific ground truth that the platform lacks. [Source 4](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-4) [Source 5](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-5)

## Ask what the reference and proxy actually establish

Start with the outcome, then state the narrower claim a measurement supports. A booking record can establish that a flight was booked; it cannot alone establish that it was the best option for a particular traveler. A self-evaluating teacher’s pass signal may simply reproduce its own interpretation of “best.” [Source 6](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-6)

Some outcomes cannot be observed on the development timescale. A speaker’s hypothetical smoking-cessation agent illustrates the gap: a long-term health outcome might take decades, whereas a forbidden-word check is immediately executable. The forbidden-word check may be a useful safety signal, but it does not measure the eventual health outcome, which is impractical to observe during development. Similarly, noting differences between a clinical encounter and a generated note is not the same as deciding which omission threatens safety; that requires domain judgment. [Source 7](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-7) [Source 8](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-8)

Intermediate criteria are also hypotheses about success. In exploratory scientific work, a team tested domain-informed checkpoints at common nodes in analysis paths. Their scores were reported to correlate only loosely with verifiable outcomes, and the speaker withheld confidence in using them for reinforcement learning or benchmarking. No coefficient or controlled optimization result was given. A plausible checkpoint should therefore be compared with outcomes before its score becomes an optimization target. [Source 9](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-9)

Where a task has stable, checkable evidence, source-anchored deterministic scoring can be preferable to asking a second model for an opinion. But a deterministic scorer can implement the wrong rule, and even a gold fact may be wrong or stale. Check the reference against its source and test scoring behavior separately from whether the criterion captures the outcome. A workshop described citation scoring and scorer unit tests; another system used separate conceptual and programmatic critics, yet later failures show that critic agreement was a safeguard attempt, not proof of correctness. [Source 10](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-10) [Source 11](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-11)

The evaluator itself needs scrutiny for reliability, scenario coverage and applicability to the deployed configuration. One vendor described tracing and an internal judge-based suite for its monitoring agent, without reporting judge validation or results. Instrumenting an evaluator is valuable visibility, not independent validation of its conclusions. [Source 12](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-12) [Source 13](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-13)

## Separate preference from realism and usefulness

A preference score is meaningful when liking is the intended outcome. It is weaker evidence for realism, historical fidelity or usefulness. In an internal comparison described by a vendor panel, participants reportedly preferred generated videos over real counterparts, potentially because generated images looked more polished. No sample size or reproducible protocol was supplied; the example illustrates the distinction rather than a general preference rate. [Source 14](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-14)

A designer also qualitatively reported a visual judge favoring crowded first viewports. More content can satisfy an easy proxy while worsening the intended design; a functional check that required content is visible answers a different question from taste. This account does not establish that automated taste assessment is impossible. [Source 15](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-15)

Likewise, a coverage rubric can reward several hedged alternatives when a workflow needs one usable recommendation. Evaluate whether the answer commits when the task warrants it, while preserving appropriate uncertainty and alternatives when the evidence really is uncertain. [Source 16](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-16) A separate proposed historical-persona mechanism warns that raters may prefer familiar cultural portrayals over documentary accuracy; record-aware expertise can test a different objective, but no preference-training ablation was reported. [Source 17](#agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies-source-17)

When building criteria for the actual task, see [Turn task quality into actionable evaluation rubrics](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics.html); for supplying judges the necessary evidence, see [Give judges the evidence and context they need](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need.html).

## Give judges the evidence and context they need

Evidence access and verification, not judge error-rate estimation.

A judge can only assess a property for which it receives relevant evidence. A plausible verdict on the wrong trace span, an empty tool result or a stale reference is still a verdict about the wrong input. Treat the judge's data contract as a separate design decision from the rubric and from the question of whether the judge agrees with trusted labels.

## From criterion to resolved evaluator inputs

Start with the specific question, then identify the observations needed to answer it. For a final itinerary, the judge needs the user's request and the itinerary; a root span containing both can be appropriate. To assess what a tool returned, select the relevant tool-call span instead. For tool-use judgments, include the applicable tool definitions, available actions and execution evidence as well as the response. [Source 1](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-1) [Source 2](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-2) A root conversation observation may not expose the system prompt that a separate generation observation contains. [Source 3](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-3) [Source 4](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-4)

Keep the evaluator's variable names independent of source-specific field names. An **illustrative mapping** might bind `request` and `answer` to dataset columns for an offline batch, but to the request and response fields of a production root span for live traces. A tool-return check would instead map its tool result from the relevant tool span. Before executing, inspect the actual resolved values for representative records: are they present, from the intended run and observation, and complete enough for the question? Missing or wrong values should make a result ungradable, not silently become evidence of failure or success. Mapping makes the evaluation runnable; it does not validate the rubric or the judge. [Source 5](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-5) [Source 6](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-6)

Evidence modality matters as much as field selection. Text can convey words but cannot itself establish tone, audio timing or interruptions. In one demonstration, a reviewer could operate a music-making app but could not hear its output; functional controls did not establish that the music was good. That limitation concerns the demonstrated setup, not all audio-capable models. Audio-based judging is a possible response, but the advice does not establish its reliability. [Source 7](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-7) [Source 8](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-8)

For long trajectories, selecting evidence by criterion can make review tractable. A demonstrated verifier ranks screenshots for each rubric item and checks selected images for satisfaction and contradiction. Selection can nevertheless miss the decisive image or a contradiction: inspect what was selected and treat gaps as uncertainty, not proof of absence. Visual overlays can expose apparent fit, but do not by themselves verify every numerical property of a box. [Source 9](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-9) [Source 10](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-10)

For collecting traces, see [Tracing and diagnosing production behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-observability-and-diagnosis.html); for designing criteria and testing whether a judge's judgments are reliable, see [Turn task quality into actionable evaluation rubrics](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics.html) and [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html). Supplying inputs is not a substitute for either.

## Evaluate faithfulness to supplied evidence

A source-faithfulness question asks whether the answer's claims and decisions follow the evidence supplied, not whether that evidence is true. Give the judge the original retrieved material as well as intermediate research notes when needed; compare numerical claims and their context, not just fluent wording. Inspect whether tool results were empty or unusable and whether the answer discloses such failures. A tool call that completed is not proof that its output supports the answer. [Source 11](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-11) [Source 12](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-12)

In one financial workshop, a correctness judge relying on its own knowledge marked all thirteen reports incorrect when it treated current events as unknowable future facts. A faithfulness judge given research-turn context classified seven as unfaithful and six as faithful. These were judge outputs in a particular demonstration, not validated financial facts or proof that correctness judges generally fail. A faithful report can faithfully repeat a false or stale source. [Source 13](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-13)

Also preserve the sequence of a conversation. A clinical-note example discussed more than one plan but recorded the option the participants had rejected rather than the final decision. The rejected words really appeared in the source, yet matching them was not faithful to the choice. This is a case example, not a measured prevalence of such errors. [Source 14](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-14)

## Verify sources and critic objections

Before relying on a citation, inspect the retrievable source for existence, relevance, support and sufficient currency for the claim. Distinguish measured observations from source-checked statements, inferences and assumptions; verify or explicitly qualify the latter. [Source 15](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-15) Check a critic's objection against the underlying evidence before changing the artifact: an adversarial reviewer can also be wrong. [Source 16](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-16)

A speaker recounted a search example in which an answer and its verifier agreed with a stale seed, while later search contradicted it. The ownership details were tentative; the lesson is shared-source failure, not a verified corporate-history claim. Asking the same model to confirm its own citation likewise does not create independent evidence. Even a fresh source can be incomplete or wrong, so source checking increases the basis for confidence rather than guaranteeing truth. [Source 17](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-17) [Source 18](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-18)

## Supply policy, case context and qualified behavior signals

Give the judge the applicable policy and the environment's available tools and contracts. A helpful-sounding refund response is not compliant if it violates a non-negotiable return rule. Make the task specification explicit: if a noninteractive agent must return a report inline rather than write a file, tell it so and judge against that actual environment. A proposal to give judge and producer comparable retrieval access can reduce an information mismatch, but shared access is not independent verification and can reproduce the same retrieval error. [Source 19](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-19) [Source 20](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-20) [Source 2](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-2)

The significance of an omission can depend on the case. A speaker contrasts two travel-history omissions in otherwise similar clinical scenarios, one described as irrelevant and the other as potentially decisive. The claim is contextual, not a universal medical rule. One proposed design retrieves relevant expert corrections, prior judgments and guidance for each case while keeping general instructions stable. It may make evolving standards inspectable, but retrieval relevance, conflicts and propagation of mistaken corrections remain unresolved; it is not proof that fixed rubrics or learned weights always fail. [Source 21](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-21) [Source 22](#give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need-source-22)

For personalized tasks, profiles and session behavior can help interpret an ambiguous request, but listening history or reformulation is a proxy, not the user's explicit intent or satisfaction. Shared-device use and other context can distort it. Judge with the available context while preserving those uncertainties; check the reference and proxy separately where the decision warrants it. ## Turn task quality into actionable evaluation rubrics

Criteria and score labels, not comparative estimands or evaluator architecture.

A rubric turns “this answer should be good” into a standard someone can apply, explain and revise. It identifies the task, the artifact being judged, the conditions that matter and what a failure means. A clear rubric defines the intended target; it does not by itself prove that a human or model applies the target reliably, or that the target captures the real-world outcome.

## Write a criterion someone can act on

Begin with the user’s task and ask a domain owner what successful work must do, what unacceptable work looks like and which exceptions matter. Replace a generic helpfulness score with observable conditions. For a travel planner, a workshop describes checking the requested number of days, budget and use of trip details in follow-up answers. A different team illustrates a possible offline check that would penalize reports with more than three suggested fixes to control verbosity; that limit is a local presentation choice, not a general rule or a measure of diagnostic correctness. [Source 1](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-1) [Source 2](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-2)

**Illustrative rubric excerpt: travel follow-up.** The task is to answer a user's question about an existing itinerary. Judge whether the answer uses the trip details relevant to that question.

- **Pass:** addresses the follow-up using the relevant itinerary constraint, or explicitly says the needed detail is unavailable.
- **Fail:** gives generic advice while ignoring an available, relevant trip constraint, or invents the missing detail.
- **Not applicable:** the follow-up does not depend on the itinerary.
- **Failure reason:** identify the ignored or invented constraint and the relevant passage, so the team knows what to investigate.

This excerpt is a proposed local standard, not a validated travel evaluator. The owner must decide, for instance, whether acknowledging missing information is acceptable for the actual task. Lyft’s described support rubric distinguishes excessive repeated education from escalating too early: both can be wrong, but fixing one by always doing the other would miss the goal. In a clinical case, clinicians defined expected behaviors and hazards, and a judge returned pass/fail, triggered hazard and reason; structured reasons help inspection but do not independently prove clinical correctness. [Source 3](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-3) [Source 4](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-4)

Maintain rubric text as evaluation logic: version criteria and examples, review changes with the domain owner, and test their effects. Separating instructions, candidate material and examples makes their roles legible, but delimiters such as XML are not established prompt-injection protection. Detailed failures can also inform what behavior-specific training data to collect even when a separate scalar reward is used for training. Mapping the right evidence into a judge is a separate prerequisite: [Give judges the evidence and context they need](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need.html). [Source 5](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-5) [Source 6](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-6)

## Separate dimensions without making every clue mandatory

A single overall rating can conceal distinct problems. A response may be fluent but use the wrong year, as in a prepared travel-agent example; relevance to a question is also different from covering every part of it. A visually attractive video may contain inconsistent events. These are separate properties because a pass on one does not entail a pass on another. [Source 7](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-7) [Source 8](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-8) [Source 9](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-9)

Separate hard constraints from informative measures: a safety requirement may block release, while a style preference informs improvement. Separate genuinely independent outcomes so a failure is diagnosable, but do not turn every helpful signal into a required criterion. For an investment report, a valuation ratio might support a useful recommendation without being mandatory for every good recommendation. Ask the stakeholder whether the signal defines success or is only one possible route to it. [Source 10](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-10)

More granular criteria can point to specific repairs and training needs. They also make consistent application harder as the list grows, especially for difficult tasks; proposed checks for coverage, no-op behavior, variability and expert agreement are not themselves evidence of reliability. Choose enough detail to identify a meaningful failure, not a fixed number of bullets. [Source 11](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-11) [Source 12](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-12)

## Choose labels for the decision

Use a binary issue label when the question is a concrete occurrence, such as whether a required constraint was violated, and define which label is the problem. Binary wording alone does not make the criterion sound. If partial success changes the decision, define anchored labels such as correct, partially correct and incorrect; use **not applicable** when the condition genuinely does not arise rather than silently counting it as pass or fail. State what improvement means and request a reason tied to the artifact. [Source 13](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-13) [Source 14](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-14) [Source 15](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-15)

For qualitative tone, one practitioner reports using a category first and then a finer rating with examples and textual justification. That may preserve distinctions a binary label would lose, but the report does not establish that the staged format is universally more reliable. Score format is a design choice, not a substitute for defining quality. [Source 16](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-16)

## Use examples to clarify boundaries, not dictate a template

Positive, negative and borderline examples can show how a criterion applies. Vary their surface form so an evaluator does not learn that one writing style or layout is the only acceptable answer; label the examples clearly apart from the candidate. Compare a rubric with and without examples on separate held-out cases, then inspect disagreements rather than assuming either version wins. Examples embedded in a prompt are not independent validation cases. [Source 17](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-17)

In a small 16-report workshop, removing examples slightly increased agreement with the presenter, but inspection revealed that the presenter had accepted a report without risks while the examples demanded them. The discrepancy was partly about the standard itself, not simply the judge: the team had to decide whether risks were required and reconcile the labels and rubric. This small experiment cannot establish that examples are generally helpful or harmful. [Source 18](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-18)

For independent assessment of whether a judge applies the intended standard, see [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html); for how reference judgments are collected and interpreted, see [Collect and interpret human judgments](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/collect-and-interpret-human-judgments.html). A well-worded criterion and a reliable evaluator are different accomplishments.

## Make ownership of subjective standards explicit

Taste can be specified without pretending it is universal. Ask the owner for strong and weak examples, the differences that matter, and reasons behind tradeoffs; translate those into named dimensions and any deliberately chosen weights. One team’s design critic used design, originality, craft and functionality, weighted weaknesses more heavily and used reference sites to express its own taste. Those choices are local to that team, not objective proof of universal aesthetic quality or safety. [Source 19](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-19)

An agent may draft the rubric or evaluator, but the responsible person should decide whether its distinctions actually express the intended standard. A recruiting example proposes judging whether sourcing overemphasizes well-known employers rather than less-visible candidates; generating such a judge does not demonstrate that it is correct or that the preference produces better recruiting outcomes. Likewise, simulated newsletter audience reactions can suggest edits but are exploratory, not observations of the real audience. Retain human editorial judgment and test downstream outcomes separately. [Source 20](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-20) [Source 21](#turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics-source-21)

## Compare systems, confidence and behavior without mixing estimands

Statistical comparison and confidence, not judge implementation or truth claims.

A system can agree with itself, disagree with an incumbent, be preferred in a pair, and be wrong—all at once. Before choosing a metric, name the estimand: the particular population-level quantity the comparison is intended to estimate. A reliability measure, a calibrated probability and a signed quality difference answer different questions.

## Use confidence only for the decision it supports

An agent's self-reported confidence or an “inferred answer” flag can help prioritize human review; neither proves the answer correct. A narrated incident demo reported increasing confidence after experts supplied context, but did not independently validate incident resolution or calibrate those scores. [Source 1](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-1) [Source 2](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-2)

For action gating, define the outcome and obtain representative labeled examples. If a score means probability of a correct action, compare predicted probabilities with observed correctness in score bands, including important subgroups and the proposed action region. Assess uncertainty and monitor shifts; good aggregate calibration need not guarantee every subgroup is calibrated. A voice-system example assumes a reasonably calibrated single score, even though a real cascade may have several signals. That assumption must be tested, not inferred from the model's confidence wording. [Source 3](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-3)

Choose between acting, asking for confirmation and human review using the costs of mistakes, delay, review capacity and the observed performance of each option. A low-score queue can help allocate review, but inspect high-confidence errors too, and measure both coverage and error among automatically handled cases. There is no universal threshold. Probability calibration is not the same as [agreement with human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html) or precision and recall. [Source 4](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-4)

## Absolute acceptance and relative preference

Pointwise evaluation asks whether one response satisfies a criterion; pairwise evaluation asks which of two responses is better on a defined axis. Use the first for an absolute policy gate and the second, for example, to compare storytelling quality. The preferred answer can still fail policy, and a tie or an unsure judgment can be meaningful. Reverse or randomize presentation order to check position sensitivity rather than assuming the comparison is neutral. [Source 5](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-5) [Source 6](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-6)

For image edits, a comparison can assess faithfulness, completeness and realism as well as visual appeal; stakeholders must define what improvement means. The proposed pairwise advantage in storytelling agreement was not measured in the cited account, and the image criteria are not fully disclosed. Relative preference does not automatically establish absolute validity. [Source 7](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-7)

## Repeatability is not truth

Run the same version repeatedly on identical inputs, holding and recording the judge model, prompt, inference engine and settings fixed. Also test sensitivity to a mild challenge separately: a verdict changing under pressure is a different observation from changing on an exact rerun. Consistency does not establish correctness; inspecting the source and rubric matters too. In one project five of twelve apparent evaluation flips failed to reproduce, and a supposedly hallucinated date was present in the source. The project did not report a formal variance estimate. [Source 8](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-8) [Source 9](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-9) [Source 10](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-10)

In a separate speaker-reported case, an incumbent disagreed with itself about 7% of the time across repeated runs, while a candidate differed from historical production answers about 18% of the time. The former is a repeatability baseline, not a mathematical ceiling on candidate accuracy; neither number alone says how often the candidate is worse. Sampling, configuration and uncertainty were not supplied. [Source 11](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-11)

## Behavioral drift versus paired quality gain

Measure cross-version disagreement on the same inputs alongside within-version disagreement. One proposed diagnostic subtracts the average within-version disagreement from cross-version disagreement to highlight changes beyond baseline variability. Its statistical assumptions and derivation were not supplied: do not treat it as a universal correction, an accuracy estimate, or a signed gain. Behavior can change for better, worse, or into another acceptable response. [Source 12](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-12) [Source 13](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-13)

To estimate *quality gain*, review paired incumbent and candidate outputs for each request against the relevant outcome criteria, classifying improvements, regressions and acceptable alternatives. Define the target population and sampling procedure. A signed net gain can be the population share of improvements minus the share of regressions, with acceptable alternatives contributing zero under that definition. If only disagreements are reviewed, their sampling probabilities and the unreviewed population must be accounted for before making a population-wide claim. Pair each comparison by request and keep repeated runs from one conversation grouped when estimating uncertainty; correlated repeats are not independent conversations. The source recommends this design but does not specify a confidence-interval estimator or reviewer sampling protocol. Inspect high-risk slices as well as the overall difference, and make a release decision against a prespecified tolerance rather than a positive point estimate alone. [Source 13](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-13) [Source 14](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-14)

These comparisons are not automatically causal evidence about a single change: if models, prompts, tools or traffic differ together, the observed difference is a system-level comparison under that protocol. See [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html) for controlled comparisons, and [Agreement, truth and the limits of evaluator proxies](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies.html) for why agreement alone is not truth.

## Fidelity to a reference distribution

For quantization, compare output distributions of the compressed model and its original reference on specified calibration inputs; KL divergence is one proposed measure. This asks how closely one model follows a particular reference, not whether either is correct on the application. Report the input distribution, divergence direction and aggregation, and choose an acceptance threshold for the purpose. The source does not specify those choices, so no universal cutoff follows. Pair fidelity checks with independent task evaluation rather than substituting them for it. [Source 15](#compare-systems-confidence-and-behavior-without-mixing-estimands-source-15)

## Choose and combine judge methods

Evaluator architectures and process grading, not their continuing operations.

A judge architecture should follow the property being checked, not the other way around. A parser, a model critic, an expert and a tool-equipped investigator can all contribute, but they answer different questions and introduce different errors. Keep their results separate long enough to understand what each actually establishes.

## Separate production, review and review signals

An agent’s statement that it completed a task is not a completion check. Give a reviewer a distinct fault-finding job and fresh context: the artifact and relevant original evidence, without the producer’s drafting history or conclusions when the aim is to avoid anchoring. A reported demand-letter review used opposing legal perspectives to find a renewal clause while a separate auditor checked arithmetic. These were agent personas, not demonstrated professional legal review. [Source 1](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-1)

A reviewer can be another model, but a different model or context does **not** make errors statistically independent: reviewers can share data, assumptions and blind spots. Nor does an objection automatically justify a change; [check criticisms against their sources](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/give-judges-the-evidence-and-context-they-need.html), and keep approval authority separate from review. A booking demonstration separates execution, validation and approval, but its selected cases do not establish that this eliminates correlated errors. [Source 2](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-2)

You can also keep review signals blind until synthesis. For example, one branch examines design quality while another collects mechanical defects; the synthesizer then considers both. Otherwise a large defect count can anchor the qualitative review, while an empty page can look excellent merely because it has no detectable polish violations. This architecture was described by its author; the intended subagent execution was not clearly shown live. [Source 3](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-3)

## Match the grader to the property

Use a repeatable code check when the requirement and reliable evidence can be expressed directly: JSON parsing, a required field, an unambiguous tool argument or an authorization limit. Use expert or model judgment for meaning that cannot be captured reliably that way. A tool-equipped judge can investigate an open-ended case, but extra model calls add cost and require their own validation. [Source 4](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-4)

Deterministic does not mean comprehensive. In a workbook example, the same inputs are supplied to a reference and generated workbook and their outputs compared, testing behavior without demanding identical formulas. The example does not specify input coverage, tolerance or engine fidelity, so a pass cannot establish correctness for every spreadsheet. [Source 5](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-5) A contract team reported that its model judge introduced substantial noise, but did not quantify it; that experience supports using reliable code checks where available, not assuming all legal meaning is mechanical. [Source 6](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-6)

Conversely, a keyword may measure the wrong property. In a constructed returns example, requiring “cannot” also passes an acceptance that says the customer cannot pay shipping. In a separate waitlist demonstration, persisted state does not make a message promising a confirmed seat true. Check persistence directly and assess whether the message matches the business outcome; neither demonstration establishes semantic-judge accuracy. [Source 7](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-7) [Source 8](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-8) Likewise, OCR can help check required rendered text while aesthetic quality may still need human judgment; OCR can miss errors too. [Source 9](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-9)

Keep dimensions visible: a summary can have valid JSON, structurally valid references, faithful content, appropriate length and acceptable latency, each with a different failure mode. Combining methods does not validate their references or cover every possible error. For designing the criteria and testing judge alignment, see [Turn task quality into actionable evaluation rubrics](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/turn-task-quality-into-actionable-evaluation-rubrics.html) and [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html). [Source 10](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-10)

## Separate outcome from trajectory

A final result and the path to it are different evaluands. A correct-looking artifact obtained by escaping a sandbox to inspect hidden tests is not a valid success. Conversely, an agent that searches correctly but cannot buy an out-of-stock item may deserve process credit even though the purchase outcome remains unsuccessful. Checking the trajectory is a detection aid, not a replacement for isolation or authorization controls. [Source 11](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-11) [Source 12](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-12)

Avoid making one arbitrary action sequence the definition of success when alternative paths are legitimate. Score essential constraints and relevant intermediate work separately. For instance, a task can penalize choosing the wrong person while still crediting a correct report about the person actually chosen; partial credit does not turn the overall answer into a success. Nor should an invented requirement be added merely because it sounds useful. [Source 13](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-13) [Source 14](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-14) [Source 15](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-15)

This distinction also matters for training feedback: in a simplified outcome-reward illustration, giving every step the final outcome’s positive reward can reinforce a wrong intermediate step. Step-level supervision can distinguish it, but human labeling is costly and model-generated labels introduce verifier errors. This illustration is not a complete account of reinforcement learning. [Source 16](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-16)

## Judge open-ended reasoning and adaptive paths

When competent people can reach different conclusions, assess whether the necessary evidence and reasoning support the conclusion rather than forcing a single golden recommendation. An investment benchmark describes this approach for different defensible calls, but its results are preliminary and its rubric reliability was not measured. [Source 17](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-17) A separate attribution workflow has analysts produce evidence-backed opinions and a synthesis judge weigh their reasoning; if agreement is insufficient, it may expand the jury. The source supplies no threshold, stopping rule or validation. Consensus is an input to a decision, not proof of a uniquely true causal allocation. [Source 18](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-18) [Source 19](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-19)

Appropriate uncertainty can itself be a target: one team reports penalizing shaky assumptions and encouraging a clarifying question for ambiguous document fields. Asking also imposes user work; the source does not measure the costs of asking too often or too rarely. [Source 20](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-20)

For a highly variable execution, a tool-equipped judge can inspect the observed trajectory and choose further checks—for example, following a suspicious handoff to inspect its tool arguments. This is a per-case investigation, not cross-trace discovery, and its findings are hypotheses to verify. Proposed adaptive judges supplement rather than replace fixed checks and ordinary model judges; superior discovery of unknown failures has not been established in a controlled comparison. [Source 21](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-21) [Source 22](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-22)

## Choose an ensemble rule for the decision

Specify what a positive verdict means before combining votes. Requiring multiple reviewers to agree before **raising a finding** can suppress noisy alerts, but may also suppress real defects when any reviewer misses them. A speaker described such multipass review and cited separate research reporting improvement, without establishing the false-negative cost. [Source 23](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-23)

For **accepting training examples**, requiring every judge to approve is restrictive in a different direction: it can reject useful data. In a vision-labeling demonstration, one small judge rejected heavily, so the presenter accepted an example if either judge approved, preserving more data at a possible quality cost. Validation was incomplete and the source’s recall remarks are ambiguous. [Source 24](#choose-and-combine-judge-methods-source-24) Neither rule is universally best: compare missed harms, false alerts and lost coverage for the actual decision, and remember shared errors can defeat a voting scheme. [Agreement is not truth](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies.html).

## Operate and improve evaluation systems

Maintenance, triage and feedback loops, not initial architecture design.

An evaluation system is not finished when its judge produces a score. The score must help someone decide what to inspect or change, and the judge itself can become inaccurate as tasks, user behavior, and standards change. Operate it as a monitored component, not as a source of unquestionable ground truth.

## Turn verdicts into bounded action

Keep the dimension, verdict, and reason together. An advertisement can be acceptable for brand safety yet factually inaccurate; a single fail would conceal which property needs repair. A rater's explanation can point a developer toward the offending claim or missing context. A model-generated explanation is useful evidence to inspect, not proof that the verdict or the explanation is correct. [Source 1](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-1) [Source 2](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-2)

Use that feedback to direct a specific revision, then assess the revised artifact again. A refund agent, for example, can be checked against the store's eligibility rubric, rather than a vague helpfulness criterion. Set a maximum number of attempts and an escalation or stop condition; a retry loop consumes resources and can repeatedly optimize against the same faulty grader. The refund example does not establish grader accuracy or convergence. A separate demonstration uses an overall session rubric and bounded retries, but its prior financial scorecard was not independently verified, and its session-level outcome was not an individual grade for each delegated subtask. [Source 3](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-3) [Source 4](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-4) [Source 5](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-5)

## Spend human attention on disagreement—and on passes

Use disagreements between the agent, verifiers, or distinct judges to prioritize cases where a domain expert can resolve ambiguity or find a defective criterion. Production signals such as a possible frustrated follow-up can also find candidates, but a flag is not a confirmed failure. One support-workshop example interprets a follow-up using conversation history; it was staged and did not validate the disagreement label. [Source 6](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-6) [Source 7](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-7)

Do not spend the whole review budget on flagged cases. In one vendor case study, all reported errors among 200 held-out families fell within six disagreements, but a separate example had four model families share the same wrong sign convention. In a generated clinical-note exercise, the presenter reported serious errors in one in five apparent clean passes, often omissions; its denominator, labeling method, configuration and uncertainty were not supplied. Neither result is a general error rate. Together they explain why agreement and passing verdicts also deserve sampled review, including targeted checks for known shared blind spots. A selectively reviewed queue cannot by itself estimate overall prevalence. [Source 8](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-8) [Source 9](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-9) [Source 10](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-10)

Human reviewers should also use the product and inspect complete traces, not just the judge's final label. An apparently poor answer may arise from failed retrieval, a bad tool call, or reasoning after a correct tool result; the repair differs. For the distinction between agreement and truth, see [Agreement, truth and the limits of evaluator proxies](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies.html). [Source 11](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-11) [Source 12](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-12)

## Maintain a changing judge without losing comparability

Regularly compare sampled human and judge decisions and inspect reasons, including examples from new user populations and failure types. Record the task, input distribution, judge/model and rubric versions with results. When experts reveal a missing criterion, update the rubric and relevant examples, then revalidate against independently held-out judgments reflecting the new standard. These are practical safeguards, not a prescribed numerical threshold: the cited teams did not disclose a universal sampling rate, agreement target, or complete calibration protocol. [Source 13](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-13) [Source 14](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-14)

A stable rubric is useful for comparing implementations; an evolving rubric is necessary when the old one misses what matters. Preserve the old version or run both versions on a common set when feasible, and label the break: a score increase after changing the definition does not on its own show the agent improved. A clinical-note presenter reported qualitatively better performance from a judge updated with expert feedback on the same generated-note dataset, but did not provide split hygiene, exact scores or prospective outcomes. Treat the loop as a hypothesis to validate, not proof that iterative feedback generalizes. [Source 15](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-15) [Source 16](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-16)

## Select and improve the judge on its actual task

Start with a clear property and a simple baseline judge on relevant traces. Inspect its errors with domain reviewers; test whether a capable model can do the task before trying cheaper models and adapting their instructions. Compare candidates on independent human-labeled cases, including important error types and cost, not on a generic leaderboard alone. A reported legal trace-judging collaboration used this capability-first approach, but disclosed neither detailed cost accounting nor judge-agreement data. Prompt inspection makes a proposed change reviewable; it does not validate it. [Source 17](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-17) [Source 18](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-18) [Source 19](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-19)

Feedback volume depends on the task and what is being trained. One vendor describes small batches of roughly 10–20 human examples to improve a judge and larger production feedback sets for reward models; that is not a universal sample-size rule. Keep examples used to optimize the judge or agent separate from the independent evaluation used to decide promotion. Otherwise a system may learn to satisfy its own reviewer while both repeat the same mistake. See [Choose and combine judge methods](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/choose-and-combine-judge-methods.html) for method selection and [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html) for holdout protection. [Source 20](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-20) [Source 21](#operate-and-improve-evaluation-systems-source-21)
