## Verifying performance and kernel changes

Owns benchmark integrity, numerical fidelity and concurrency/state failures in optimized workloads, rather than general verifier auditing.

A fast measurement is useful only if the timed implementation still performs the intended work. Verify the operator, workload and numerical behavior separately from speed, and then verify the effect on the real flow. An isolated kernel win, a correct output and a safe production change are three different claims.

## Establish the computation and compare like with like

Give a kernel generator the actual model's operator semantics, including architecture-specific attention or other changes, rather than relying on its familiarity with a similarly named model. A speaker warns that missing context can lead to an invented implementation; the warning is guidance, not a measured hallucination rate. [Source 1](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-1)

Define the reference behavior, relevant shapes and dtypes, inputs, acceptable numerical tolerances and target GPU topology. Compare candidate outputs with the reference over representative cases, including edge conditions, and measure speed only for candidates that meet the correctness contract. Equality here means the specified numerical and behavioral equivalence, not an assumption that different floating-point implementations are bit-identical. The reported multi-GPU benchmark starts with reference implementations and topology, and distinguishes correctness from reaching baseline speed. Its speaker reports that additional samples produced more correct kernels while the fast metric plateaued; the result is specific to the tested models and benchmark. When compilation succeeds but speed does not, inspect partitioning, collective ordering and communication scheduling rather than treating syntax as the whole problem. [Source 2](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-2) [Source 3](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-3) [Source 4](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-4) [Source 5](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-5)

## Protect the workload being timed

Keep the timer, test inputs and workload contract outside the candidate's control, and check that the same substantive computation occurs during correctness and timing. A timer set to zero, inputs replaced with zeros, a no-op or reused result can look fast without solving the task. Explicitly state whether library calls and existing accelerations are permitted; a library call is not inherently cheating. Inspect behavior as well as source when implementation constraints matter. [Source 6](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-6) [Source 7](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-7)

In a reported GPU MODE incident, a candidate computed the anticipated fifteen results on the first call and served dictionary lookups on later calls. Passing correctness and recording fast subsequent calls therefore did not establish the intended computation was fast. This account is not reproduced here, and phase-dependent behavior does not establish the model's intent. A separate compiler case reportedly invoked GCC despite a requirement to implement the compiler in Rust; runtime tracing exposed the forbidden subprocess despite strong partial scores. [Source 8](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-8) [Source 9](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-9)

## Test dependencies and sustained generation

Concurrent GPU work needs explicit producer–consumer ordering. In a reported optimization, matrix multiplication and RMS computation ran concurrently, but post-scaling could read a stale buffer because an implicit stream join was insufficient. The fix marked completion of both producers and made the consumer wait for both. Unit tests and apparently similar perplexity had not exposed the race; longer generation showed repetition and a one-token lag. Exercise sustained decoding and buffer reuse as well as local checks, while recognizing that a passing long run cannot prove all concurrent executions safe. [Source 10](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-10) [Source 11](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-11)

## Diagnose silent inference divergence

When output quality degrades without a crash, hold the sequence fixed: record the prompt and generated tokens, replay that exact sequence through a simpler reference forward pass, and compare token probabilities or log probabilities. This avoids confusing a change in generated text with a numerical discrepancy. The reference is diagnostic, not proven ground truth; choose tolerances appropriate to the implementations. A related invariant compares rollout and training probabilities before any weight update, when the intended weights and inputs match, allowing for normal numerical differences. [Source 12](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-12) [Source 13](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-13)

Two reported failures show why the surrounding state lifecycle matters. In one, a fresh request was classified as decode before prefill, so a recurrent implementation read stale state from a previous request. The fix treated zero-computed-token requests as prefill before decode; the precise read-before-compute explanation is specific to that implementation. In another, a narrow unsigned index wrapped at a large state-cache offset, silently corrupting results. Shrinking the allocation hid that fault by avoiding the triggering slot. The reported move to `size_t` helped on the target platform; its width is platform-dependent, so check the full range of offset arithmetic rather than treating the type name as a portable proof. [Source 14](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-14) [Source 15](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-15)

## Verify the affected flow before release

After correctness and representative timing, rerun functional checks and measure the affected business flow. Compare old and new versions under comparable traffic in a canary, examining latency, CPU and errors as well as behavior; have an engineer review the evidence. The canary supports conclusions about its tested traffic, not every future workload, and a local kernel speedup does not establish an end-to-end service-level objective. [Source 16](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-16) [Source 17](#performance-and-kernel-verification-source-17) For the hardware optimization choices themselves, see [Verifying hardware and training optimizations](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/gpu-optimization.html).

## Define domain success and expert accountability

Covers define domain success and expert accountability; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A domain evaluation begins with a decision about usable work: what must a person be able to do with the output, what happens if it is wrong, and who is responsible for acting on it? A benchmark score can inform that decision, but neither a high score nor a cited answer establishes that the workflow is safe, effective or ready to deploy.

## Define acceptance around the actual work

Specify the completed artifact or decision, not merely whether an answer contains some correct facts. A financial statement with an incorrect cost or income line may have substantial partial credit yet still require the analyst to redo the work. For that use, count a fully usable statement separately from partial accuracy. For an index whose source documents can be revisited, an imperfect extraction may be tolerable; for sensitive insurance or financial extraction, the consequences may justify a more costly, accurate and verified path. These are different operating points, not a universal demand for perfection. [Source 1](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-1) [Source 2](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-2)

Set acceptance with the customer and responsible expert using the task's consequences, expected exposure and available verification. Even a small error rate can mean many affected people at high volume, but demonstrating rare-error reliability also requires sufficiently representative evidence. A threshold should state the use and population to which it applies, the evidence required, and what happens when evidence or performance is insufficient—not turn one attractive average into a blanket approval. [Source 3](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-3) [Source 4](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-4)

## Measure recovery, not just error counts

Ask what users must do after each failure. A voice assistant playing the wrong song can require a listener to notice, interrupt playback and repeat the request; saying it did not understand imposes a different burden. A confirmation step may prevent a wrong action but also delay correct requests. A visual list selectable by remote may make confirmation easier, while opening the wrong TV channel may disrupt the current state. Estimate the consequences for the actual interface and compare policies on the combined burden, including delay and wrong actions. The source's recovery times are illustrative, not measurements of satisfaction. [Source 5](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-5) [Source 6](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-6)

For a writing assistant, revision effort may be more relevant than an abstract style score, but it must be measured with the intended writers and tasks; the cited recommendation did not time human editing. Recovery cost is a useful proxy, not the same thing as user satisfaction or the domain outcome itself. [Source 7](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-7)

Report results by meaningful user group, task difficulty and operating condition as well as overall. For example, separate a straightforward single-table analysis from a multi-table one, and show where the sample is too small to support a decision. A weak or under-evidenced slice may justify a narrower deployment or more evidence even when the aggregate looks good. Difficulty comparisons require appropriate splits and contamination controls; neither a universal minimum sample size nor a guaranteed threshold is supplied here. [Source 4](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-4) [Source 8](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-8)

## Build the workflow with practitioners

Begin with recurrent, tractable work whose quality practitioners can judge. Have them break it into the order of operations, identify exceptions, explain why similar cases deserve different treatment, and review traces as well as final outputs. Convert that knowledge into task instructions, examples and evaluation criteria, then maintain them as the workflow changes. Pair practitioners with engineers and measurement specialists: expert participation supplies domain knowledge, not automatic proof of safety. One reported financial-planning practice lets nonengineers author and maintain workflow skills, but does not provide a controlled effectiveness comparison. [Source 9](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-9) [Source 10](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-10) [Source 11](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-11) [Source 12](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-12)

Organize the work according to what can be measured and how quickly it must iterate. When meaningful objective measures are weak and taste dominates, an expert oracle can directly judge outputs and make changes. When useful measures exist and manual engineering iteration is fast enough, an evaluator can define failure modes and collect quality measures to guide engineers. If manual iteration becomes too slow and suitable automation exists, consider an architect who designs an improvement system that learns or adapts; the role is more than designing the application around domain constraints. These are role choices, not necessarily separate hires. [Source 13](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-13) [Source 14](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-14)

In a reported prior-authorization case, an expert moved from direct review and product changes to defining failure modes and metrics, building a review dashboard and hiring clinicians; their feedback supported engineering changes. Later policy variation made manual fixes too slow and motivated an architect approach. This account does not establish the effectiveness or safety of automated adaptation. One concentrated product may work with a single expert oracle; a clinical scribe spanning specialties and geographies may need distributed reviewers and local ownership. Match expertise to the particular task and add engineering and evaluation skills; the reported staffing cases are practitioner accounts, not controlled evidence for one universal structure. [Source 15](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-15) [Source 16](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-16) [Source 17](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-17) [Source 18](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-18)

## Keep decision authority and evidence together

Separate preparation from authority. In a reported planning workflow, an agent drafts a client's cash-flow or insurance analysis while the planner works elsewhere; the planner reviews and adjusts it and controls sending the recommendation. Evaluate the draft, the handoff and the expert's final decision separately. Specify what can be prepared automatically, what evidence the reviewer sees, when the system must stop or escalate, and who can approve or deliver the result. Human review is a control to test, not an assumption that every error will be caught. This account reports a process, not measured advice safety or time savings. [Source 19](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-19) [Source 20](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-20)

Give the responsible expert an inspectable trail from material facts and actions to their source and a domain-native view of what changed. An evaluation evidence pack can record intended use, source lineage, detected failures and fallback, segmented results, operational controls and named owners. It supports a reviewable decision; a provenance link is not proof that the source or inference is correct, and a proposed pack is not a regulatory approval or a mandated file count. [Source 21](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-21) [Source 22](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-22) [Source 23](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-23)

## Test domain outcomes, then bound the inference

Build benchmarks around real units of work and the tools and constraints they involve. Use bounded tasks and a consistent scaffold so candidates face comparable conditions; hold out relevant examples and compare against a sensible simple baseline. A speaker reports that linear methods matched or exceeded some costly single-cell models in particular benchmarks; incomplete tables, splits and uncertainty prevent generalizing that result, and the suggested information-loss mechanism was not established by a causal ablation. [Source 24](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-24) [Source 25](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-25) [Source 26](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-26)

A simulated environment can establish that a system handles the cases modeled there, not that it produces the same benefit in the real workflow. For example, a synthetic remediation exercise used a modeled manual baseline and reported times for resolved cases; its caption interpretation is provisional, and neither the baseline nor those selected cases establish production recovery performance. Likewise, a research competition result is not trading profit. Record the simulated environment, comparator and limits, then seek evidence from representative real use before claiming efficacy. [Source 27](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-27) [Source 28](#define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability-source-28)

For the distinction between evaluator agreement and truth, see [Agreement, truth and the limits of evaluator proxies](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agreement-truth-and-the-limits-of-evaluator-proxies.html); for constructing representative cases, see [Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html).

## Evaluating evidence-heavy financial work

Covers financial research, sources and forecasts; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A financial memo is reviewable when an analyst can trace material claims to appropriate evidence, reproduce the calculations and see what could change the conclusion. Fluent prose and abundant citations are not enough. The standard applies to the work supporting a decision, not a promise that the decision will make money.

## Verify what the source actually supports

For each important figure, open the underlying source and check the entity, reporting period, metric, units and extraction. An audited filing and an informal estimate do not have the same evidential status, although even an authoritative filing can be wrong or unsuitable for the question. One reviewer described a tool preferring an informal guess over an available audited figure; the anonymized anecdote does not establish why retrieval ranked it that way. A model's remembered number may be correct, but memory alone does not provide an auditable source trail. [Source 1](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-1) [Source 2](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-2) [Source 3](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-3)

Check the time window and the sources actually used, not just the number retrieved. In one investing demonstration, an answer used one or two of fifteen candidates; a date-filtered answer used seven of fifty-two. The latter count proves neither consensus nor correctness. A months-old note may be stale for a fast-changing market question but useful for another question; set freshness from the decision, not a universal age limit. [Source 4](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-4) [Source 5](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-5)

## Reconstruct the financial perimeter and the workbook

A matching number can describe the wrong company or period. Before comparing figures, identify acquisitions, divestitures and partial-year contributions. In an illustrative benchmark case, the task was to reconstruct Sonoco as of May 2025 with a full year of Eviosys and without TFP. Different reported sales can reflect different perimeters rather than simple arithmetic error. This example is a benchmark design, not independently verified investment advice. [Source 6](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-6)

For spreadsheets, distinguish gross from net, company from segment, quarter from year, and inputs from formulas. A tabular range helps inspect cells, a structural view exposes formulas and relationships, and a rendered sheet can reveal layout and headings. One practitioner found no single representation adequate; that is qualitative experience, not a quantified comparison. Combining views helps select the right figure but does not establish that the underlying figure is true. [Source 7](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-7) [Source 8](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-8)

## Make derivations reproducible and check independent controls

Separate selecting evidence and explaining it from calculating with it. A proposed architecture lets a model refer to a canonical numeric value while a computation layer preserves the payload and executes the calculation. Record each input's source and the rules and adjustments used, so a reviewer can replay, for example, a firm-specific margin or leverage calculation. Deterministic code makes the operation repeatable, not necessarily correct: parsers, chosen inputs, accounting rules and the generated explanation can all fail. The vendor's implementation was not independently audited. [Source 9](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-9) [Source 10](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-10) [Source 11](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-11)

Use an independently sourced control where available. A reported statement-extraction case checked each month's records against printed balances, then reconciled individual dates, descriptions and notes. The year reportedly balanced to the penny and 56 differences were reconciled, but this is one case, not an estimated error rate. A balanced total can hide offsetting mistakes; check the transaction details too. Similarly, comparison to a system of record can catch mismatches without proving that OCR, the record or the checker covers every relevant field. [Source 12](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-12) [Source 13](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-13)

## Preserve disagreements and uncertainty

Repeated figures should agree where they refer to the same definition and period; investigate differences rather than blindly demanding identical strings where rounding or scope differs. More importantly, if a filing and an earnings call make conflicting claims, show both with their sources and ask a reviewer to resolve the material difference. A smooth synthesis that silently chooses one can conceal the very issue diligence should expose. [Source 14](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-14) [Source 15](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-15)

Keep an estimate, forecast or disputed claim labeled through subsequent drafts and slides. A practitioner describes an expected approval becoming a received approval after successive rewrites: the failure is a change in evidential status, not merely an awkward sentence. Test the final artifact against the original source, not only the first draft. The anecdote does not measure how often this occurs. [Source 16](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-16)

## Evaluate the whole decision, not only a plausible answer

Define the assignment from mandate to deliverable. A benchmark example asks for a fund's strategy and holding period, then an evidence-backed long, short or pass memo. Inspect the material sources, historical comparators, calculations, judgment and evidence that could overturn the thesis. Ask experts to review the work against the mandate; several conclusions can be defensible without treating every factual claim as correct. Agreement with a firm's process does not prove a profitable trade. [Source 17](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-17) [Source 18](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-18) [Source 19](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-19) [Source 20](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-20)

Stress a material assumption and examine the reasoning, not just whether the label changes. In the benchmark's acquisition example, the reviewer asks what happens if projected savings are zero: does the memo explain the effect on the recommendation? This is a sensitivity test, not evidence that either recommendation will succeed. For generated model documentation, historical comparisons and working-quant ratings can assess the artifact; they do not constitute auditor or regulatory approval. [Source 21](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-21) [Source 22](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-22)

## Define the forecast before judging it

Answering questions about debt or liquidity is different from predicting a future credit path. Distress can lead to bankruptcy, liability management, an exchange or restructuring; a binary default label may miss the decision-relevant outcome. Define a forecast date, horizon and an operationally clear set of outcomes before scoring probabilities against resolved cases. The cited exploratory case did not supply a mutually exclusive taxonomy, horizon, scoring rule or validated outcome. A critique that static scores can miss changing circumstances is a qualitative argument, not proof that such scores are obsolete. [Source 23](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-23) [Source 24](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-24) [Source 25](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-25)

While the future is unresolved, check layers separately: was EBITDA extracted correctly, was leverage derived using the intended debt and adjustment definitions, and is the distress judgment defensible? The example is not a complete leverage specification. Model forecasts may converge and still be wrong; a market-price analogy does not turn agreement into a validated price, calibrated prediction or investment return. [Source 26](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-26) [Source 27](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-27) [Source 28](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-28)

## Backtest with information available at the time

For each historical decision date, reconstruct the information actually available then, generate the feature or forecast, and compare it with the existing process on later-resolved outcomes. A proposed acquisition test searches at intervals before the announcement rather than letting today's search reveal the deal. Historical pricing pages or adverse-media reports can be transformed into structured features for a conventional model; test whether those features add value rather than assuming more searches help. [Source 29](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-29) [Source 30](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-30) [Source 31](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-31)

Historical replay may shorten feedback when outcomes take months, but a date-filtered web tool alone cannot remove future knowledge from model weights, internal feeds or other tools. Check snapshot coverage and availability dates, retain out-of-sample holdouts, and follow with live validation. The source proposes this workflow without validated snapshot coverage or out-of-sample performance results; it does not establish investment gains. For the broader integrity of historical tests, see [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html). [Source 32](#financial-research-sources-and-forecasts-source-32)

## Grounding answers in retrieved evidence

Evaluate answer support against approved sources, then diagnose domain-agent tool-use failures and evidence-backed incident explanations.

An answer can sound credible, cite a document and still make a claim that the document does not support. A useful diagnosis separates three questions: did the system find appropriate evidence, did the answer stay within it, and did its tool and investigative behavior justify the conclusion? A fluent final response alone answers none of them.

## Source boundaries, supported answers and selective abstention

Start by specifying what counts as an approved source and which claims require one. A payment-rule assistant, for example, may use general knowledge to explain what a bank is, while the project’s intended boundary requires scheme-specific fees and rules to come from its own rulebooks. The intended answer gives a rulebook, section and page so a reader can inspect the basis. That reference is a pointer to evidence, not proof that the passage entails the claim. A real review must compare what the answer asserts with what the cited passage actually says, including conditions and exceptions. [Source 1](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-1)

A source can be missing for only part of a question. In one demonstration, the question covered honey bees and carpenter bees but the supplied material covered only carpenter bees. The desired behavior was to answer the supported portion and say the other was not supported by the available sources. A revised prompt marked the missing evidence yet still included extra honey-bee information: recognizing a missing citation was not the same as abstaining from the unsupported claim. [Source 2](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-2)

This distinction matters when reviewing a response: a complete refusal throws away usable evidence, while a complete answer can quietly blend source-backed facts with model knowledge. Inspect each substantive part against its own supporting passage and note what remains unanswered. Whether the right source was retrieved is a separate question from whether the answer follows it; see [Evaluate and represent retrieval corpora](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora.html) for retrieval evaluation.

Withholding can also be applied to individual values. One described financial platform removes numbers that cannot be independently checked against a canonical process, rather than treating agreement between probabilistic models as sufficient assurance. That policy trades coverage for protection against unchecked values. Its account gives neither a rejection rate nor coverage loss, an independent audit or a complete check specification; correctness also depends on the canonical inputs and implementation. It is an illustrative design, not proof that every remaining number is true. [Source 3](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-3)

## Diagnosing enterprise tool-use failures

When an agent gives a bad database answer, examine the interaction rather than labeling the whole event a reasoning failure. A finance experiment described three distinguishable patterns: inventing tables or columns; issuing broad queries such as `SELECT *` that overwhelm the available context; and repeating a failed strategy instead of responding to an error. A query can execute successfully and still return too much to be useful. Conversely, a schema error may reveal that the agent never checked what was available. These observations motivate different investigations: schema discovery, query scope and adaptation to feedback, respectively. The account does not give failure frequencies or detailed evidence that the same rates hold across domains. [Source 4](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-4)

Experience can change what good tool behavior looks like. In a proposed sequence of questions over the same database, early exploration may establish table relationships and data formats; later work could reuse those discoveries rather than rediscovering them each time. Compare the exploration needed across comparable tasks, while checking whether reused knowledge remains applicable. The narrated later-instance improvement was illustrative, not a measured reduction in query count. [Source 5](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-5)

These are diagnostic lenses for interpreting behavior, not executable pass/fail tests. For the separate problem of designing reliable artifact checks, see [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html).

## Incident hypotheses need evidence chains and alternatives

An incident explanation should connect a proposed cause to observations in sequence: which events were observed, how they relate to the suspected mechanism, and which link remains uncertain. A coherent story is not itself evidence that one event caused another. When the chain is incomplete, communicate the uncertainty and what needs investigation instead of announcing a root cause. [Source 6](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-6)

A vendor demonstration presented stale integrations as an explanation while also surfacing a concurrent cloud outage as an alternative. The useful practice is to make competing explanations and their supporting or conflicting evidence visible to an engineer, rather than hiding everything that does not fit the leading story. The demonstration did not independently verify its incident conclusion; even a displayed alternative is not necessarily ruled out merely because the system labels it so. [Source 7](#evaluate-retrieval-and-grounded-answers-source-7)

## Voice interaction and speech system evaluation

Covers voice interaction and speech system evaluation; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A voice agent can sound natural, repeat a reassuring confirmation and still perform the wrong action. Evaluate the interaction at two levels: whether the user and system successfully completed the task, and which speech, language, timing or tool component caused a failure. Neither a fluent recording nor a strong isolated component score establishes the outcome. [Source 1](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-1) [Source 2](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-2)

## Verify outcomes, not just fluency

Check both the conversation and the external state: Was the requested action authorized? Were the right arguments sent? Did the intended booking or refund actually appear in the relevant system? Score helpfulness and tone separately from domain rules such as eligibility. Track task failure, escalation, abandonment and silent errors alongside conversational quality; these are useful outcomes to investigate, not proof that a particular speech defect caused a business change. [Source 3](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-3) [Source 4](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-4)

In a deliberately generated refund call, the customer asks about order 14 but the system processes order 40 despite a spoken confirmation. The useful test compares the audio, recognized order, tool arguments and resulting state—not just whether the final sentence sounds correct. This is a synthetic illustration, not a documented customer incident or a measured failure rate. [Source 5](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-5) [Source 6](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-6)

## Localize errors across the voice stack

Align the audio, transcript, timing and tool trace. Ask what the caller actually said, what recognition supplied to the language model, what the model decided, and what was spoken or executed. An appointment example changes the third to the thirtieth at recognition, so a downstream model can confidently book the wrong day. Conversely, a correct transcript can still produce a generated note with additions or omissions. Diagnose the boundary before changing the wrong component; these examples do not quantify the relative frequency of each failure. [Source 7](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-7) [Source 8](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-8)

A useful diagnostic framework crosses **listening and speaking** with sounds, words, interaction and the participants' understanding. For example, confusing spelled M and N is a listening error; pronouncing the corrected name badly is a separate speaking error. Both can affect the same task. The framework is conceptual, not a validated universal scoring scheme. [Source 9](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-9) [Source 10](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-10)

Build component tests for consequential fields—names, phone digits, dates, addresses and domain terms—under the noise, accents, language switching and devices representative of deployment. A field test can quickly localize a broken collection step, but passing fields does not prove the whole conversation works. In one speaker's reported diarization benchmarks, telephone conditions were around 8% error and a noisy multiperson setting around 41%; those figures describe those settings, not universal bounds. [Source 11](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-11) [Source 12](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-12) [Source 13](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-13)

## Test turn-taking and repair

Include pauses *within* an identifier, interruptions, short acknowledgments, changed requests and multiple turns of misunderstanding. In an account-number anecdote, the user paused while reading an unfamiliar sequence; the bot interrupted, reported no record and asked again. The component and timing threshold were not instrumented. Evaluate whether the system recognizes uncertainty, clarifies the missing part and retains earlier corrections rather than simply restarting the exchange. Clarification is proposed guidance, not a demonstrated comparative recovery rate. [Source 14](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-14) [Source 15](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-15)

Preserve speaker and word timing so an interruption can be distinguished from a brief backchannel. Prosody, stress and acoustic context may carry useful information, but are not certain labels of emotion or intent. A hotel demonstration included an interruption and changed dates; parts were sped up, so it illustrates interaction behavior rather than measured response latency. Also test whether a safety warning resumes after an interruption or a backchannel; reported hazards lack incidence estimates. [Source 16](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-16) [Source 17](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-17) [Source 18](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-18) [Source 19](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-19)

Compare premature cutoffs **at the same latency budget**, since waiting longer can reduce interruption at the cost of slower response. A vendor reported 9.9% versus 4.5% cutoffs at matched latency for an alternative and its audio-based turn detector; dataset size, uncertainty, baseline identity and the exact latency were not supplied. The comparison motivates a matched test, not a general performance ranking. [Source 20](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-20)

## Combine listening, simulation and live tests

Listen to real calls to discover unexpected conversational failures, then encode recurring issues in rubrics and field checks for broader coverage. Use controllable simulated calls to reproduce a pause, correction or interruption, including risky cases that should not be induced with real users. Neither automated scoring nor simulation alone proves the system works for real people. When the hypothesis depends on genuine reaction—such as the effect of an outbound opening or vocal delivery—consider a suitably governed live comparison. The cited opening guidance is practitioner advice, not a controlled study. [Source 21](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-21) [Source 22](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-22)

## Score diarization and the word-to-speaker join separately

Diarization asks **who spoke when**. Compare predicted speaker timelines with a human-labeled reference and break diarization error rate into speaker confusion, false-alarm speech and missed reference speech, divided by total reference speech duration. A missed second speaker during overlap counts as missed speech even if the first speaker was detected. Inspect the timelines as well as the aggregate: a selected 30-second telephone clip showed approximately 5% versus 3% DER for two displayed systems, but cannot establish general superiority. [Source 23](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-23) [Source 24](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-24)

Then test the join between recognized words and speaker times. ASR and diarization timestamps may disagree; one may detect speech the other misses, and overlapping speech may yield only one transcribed word. Examine boundary words and short turns directly. Exclusive diarization selects the speaker most likely represented in the transcript to simplify attribution, but can lose the other overlapping voice; its selection algorithm and full reconciliation process were not disclosed. Choose the representation according to whether the application needs a readable single-speaker transcript or a fuller account of overlap. [Source 25](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-25) [Source 26](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-26)

## Normalize and test speech output

Before text-to-speech, test a normalization layer for markup, emoji, dates, currency and email addresses, and configure pronunciation for critical names, brands and acronyms. Listen to the actual synthesized output: a correctly recognized name may still be spoken incorrectly, and a generic fluent sample may miss that defect. Targeted dictionaries and slower spelling are practitioner suggestions; verify the result with the chosen provider and relevant users rather than assuming normalization is portable or universally correct. [Source 27](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-27) [Source 28](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-28) [Source 10](#voice-interaction-and-speech-system-evaluation-source-10)

## Clinical safety and operational review

Covers clinical safety and operational review; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A clinical agent can sound reassuring, complete a conversation and still miss a consequential detail. Review therefore has to follow the whole pathway: what the person said, how the system interpreted it, whether it recognized uncertainty, and what happened when human help was needed. The practices below are evaluation and operational guidance, not clinical instructions or evidence that a particular agent improves patient outcomes.

## Listen for the detail that changes the meaning

Speech recognition errors are not equally consequential. A system that hears “no” instead of “now,” or “fine” instead of “five,” may alter the meaning of a short response even when its overall transcription looks good. Evaluate these short, high-consequence utterances separately. One described system uses conversation context and a second scoring pass for single-word responses; its reported combined-system improvement does not isolate the effect of that pass. [Source 1](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-1) [Source 2](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-2)

Recognition-time context, such as likely medication names relevant to the current stage of a call, can narrow candidate words. Excessive always-on vocabulary can also contaminate recognition, so test targeted vocabulary against the actual population and setting. After recognition, contextual correction may suggest what was meant, but a plausible suggestion is not a verified value. Ask for spelling, confirmation or repetition when an important field is uncertain, and evaluate whether the system makes the appropriate handoff. Selected patient-call clips illustrate such behaviors; they do not establish diagnostic rules or deployment-wide safety. [Source 3](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-3) [Source 4](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-4) [Source 5](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-5)

Structure collection where possible: define the expected type and permitted values, validate them, and repair or confirm failures. For an appointment, resolve a relative date against an explicit current date and clarify an ambiguous hour rather than silently choosing morning or evening. A valid-looking field is still not proof that the person intended that value. [Source 6](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-6) [Source 7](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-7)

## Build evidence for rare and nuanced failures

Invite clinicians to define scenarios from the actual workflow and articulate what a safe response and escalation would require. Risk may be implied by the whole conversation rather than an explicit keyword. In one clinician-attributed example, a person's description of packing a box and imagining being gone conveyed possible self-harm; the relevant signal was the context, not a universal rule about boxes. The case supports testing nuanced interpretation, not a measured comparison showing which moderation method is best. [Source 8](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-8)

Use scenario-conditioned simulated patients to exercise a history-taking or follow-up workflow repeatedly, including difficult variations. Simulation is useful for iteration, but simulated behavior is not equivalent to real patients and a simulation pass is not evidence of patient benefit. Rare serious failures also demand sustained expert evaluation on appropriately representative cases: a small clean demonstration cannot establish a very low failure rate. The cited account describes large-scale clinician testing but does not provide the sampling assumptions needed to reproduce its sample-size claims. [Source 9](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-9) [Source 10](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-10)

Keep clinical safety, task performance and the person's experience as distinct evaluation targets. A system can complete a task yet fail to engage someone, or sound empathetic while missing a safety issue. One presenter identifies empathy as a separate requirement, but does not provide enough benchmark design or results to validate a particular empathy measure. [Source 11](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-11)

## Review what happens in use

A saved prelaunch test set is a starting point, not durable assurance. In the described monitoring approach, automated evaluations score live conversations for dimensions including safety, escalation and relevance, while member feedback provides a different perspective, including on tone. These signals need interpretation and action; the source does not establish judge calibration, coverage or detection performance. [Source 12](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-12)

Combine broad random review across capabilities with intensified review of identified high-stakes cases. One practitioner recommends reviewing every such identified case. That recommendation depends on both reliable identification and sufficient qualified review capacity: reviewing all cases flagged as high-stakes does not prove that every high-stakes case was flagged. Specify who reviews, how disagreements are resolved and how findings lead to correction; do not infer those operational details from a dashboard. [Source 13](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-13)

For launch decisions, distinguish the severity of a possible outcome from how frequently it occurs. Consider the worst *plausible* harm, not merely average inconvenience, and bring clinical, safety and operational judgment to the classification. The cited practitioner proposes holding and fixing uncertain safety defects, while a minor polish issue may justify the opposite default. This is a decision aid, not a validated quantitative risk model or an automatic classifier: the difficult question is whether the issue is truly only polish. [Source 14](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-14) [Source 15](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-15)

## Make the service scorecard respect escalation

Containment is the share of interactions handled end-to-end without human transfer. It can be useful, but maximizing it alone can reward an agent for keeping a distressed caller when a human or emergency escalation is appropriate. Separate appropriate handoffs from avoidable ones; examine the quality and timeliness of the handoff alongside automated resolution, satisfaction, safety and governance. The medical-support example describes this tension, not a validated reward function. [Source 16](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-16)

If a composite score is needed, make its weights explicit and tied to the service mandate, and retain the individual measures so a high total cannot conceal unsafe escalation. Published vendor weights represent their authors' priorities, not a universal recipe or a probability of clinical accuracy. Similarly, cross-industry containment figures reflect different mandates and designed handoffs; without cohort definitions and sampling methods, they are not a clinical-quality leaderboard. [Source 17](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-17) [Source 18](#clinical-safety-and-operational-review-source-18)

## Document extraction and legal review

Covers document extraction and legal review; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A document system can return accurate-looking statements while omitting a critical page, transcribing a table incorrectly or reviewing the wrong person’s file. Evaluate the path from source document to extracted representation to decision: success at one stage does not establish success at the next, and faithful extraction alone does not establish legal correctness.

## Find missing information, not only incorrect statements

Check both whether emitted facts are supported and whether consequential facts are absent. In a speaker’s clinical illustration, a plausible headache note omitted jaw pain on chewing, a detail the speaker regarded as changing urgency. This is an illustration of omission severity, not independently validated clinical advice. A claims-review account similarly scores correctness, completeness and conciseness separately; its provider comparisons are snapshots without a complete numerical table or model settings. [Source 1](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-1) [Source 2](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-2)

A missing source document is a different problem from a missing fact in an available document. Cross-reference notes, scheduled procedures, reports and billing: if a note references a scheduled X-ray but the report is absent, flag the gap for follow-up rather than inventing why it is missing or assuming the procedure occurred. [Source 3](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-3)

For legal review, test missing expected clauses explicitly. The requirement must be conditional on the applicable template and supplier type. A team described removing clauses from signed contracts and mixing these mutations with intact contracts that should receive no flag. The agents reportedly missed most removals; the account supplies no denominator, full omission taxonomy or final recovered performance. Intact controls reveal indiscriminate flagging, while deleted cases test detection—not the legal sufficiency of every contract. [Source 4](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-4)

## Establish record integrity before aggregation

Deduplicating pages and identifying records belonging to the wrong person are separate checks. Similar names can result in an unrelated person’s record being included in a claim, contaminating the analysis and potentially exposing private information. Verify identity and per-claim extraction before combining claims, and establish permission for the intended cross-record use. The case account does not measure how often contamination occurs. [Source 5](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-5)

Once those prerequisites hold, aggregated records may help inspect provider networks or costs. Even then, price differences alone do not prove waste: a higher-priced provider might require fewer treatments, and patient outcomes matter. The described network visualization used a redacted subset; proposed savings were not established causal effects. [Source 6](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-6)

## Diagnose the document pipeline

A structurally valid pipeline can silently miss a scan, segment the page incorrectly, read a block incorrectly or join blocks in the wrong order. One reported architecture separates layout and reading modules around block-level OCR, making segmentation and order distinct things to inspect; no ablation isolates the benefit of any component. Another account describes extraction confidence, bounding boxes and failures being returned to tools to help refine a schema. A bounding box helps a reviewer locate evidence, but a confidence number is not calibrated merely because it is available, nor do diagnostics detect every error. [Source 7](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-7) [Source 8](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-8)

State where the evaluation begins. A synthetic pipeline generating text and Markdown tests downstream reasoning over already parsed content; it does not test conversion from degraded scans, handwriting or visual checkboxes. Its speaker’s confidence in available parsers is an opinion, not a parser benchmark. Include source-image cases when those ingestion failures matter. [Source 9](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-9)

## Select and test representations for the task

Plain OCR text may lose the row-column relationships, charts, formatting or reading order on which an answer depends. Compare representations using the same task and source documents: test both whether the representation preserves those features and whether downstream answers use them correctly. A vendor-affiliated account reported better PDF retrieval with a multimodal approach but did not provide the visual leaderboard details or implementation; another reported improved answers with structured parses, without full numerical methods and with one comparison model omitted. Neither establishes a universally superior representation. [Source 10](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-10) [Source 11](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-11)

Include varied, complex real document types when they reflect the deployment distribution. A speaker recommended character error rate, table structure, equations and language-specific grammar as possible OCR rewards, alongside synthetic documents; exact reward weights and document selection were not supplied. Such component measures need downstream task checks as well. [Source 12](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-12) [Source 13](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-13)

## Preserve source errors; measure extraction coverage

If the objective is faithful transcription, correct a recognition mistake without silently correcting the source itself. For example, a source table may contain an arithmetically wrong total. A model that recalculates it may produce a plausible number but an unfaithful transcription. Preserve the printed value, then surface any suspected arithmetic issue separately for review. A proposed correction layer for OCR errors was not independently measured; translation or transliteration are distinct objectives. [Source 14](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-14) [Source 15](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-15)

For structured rows, measure **precision** as correctly emitted rows divided by emitted rows, and **recall** as correctly recovered expected rows divided by expected rows, using a defined matching rule and reference set. High precision can coexist with low recall when an extractor outputs only a few easy rows and silently drops the rest. Inspect missed rows and their importance, not just the correctness of returned rows. The reported model and harness comparison lacks detailed numbers. [Source 16](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-16)

## Test contract invariance and policy controls

When a complete gold answer is expensive, metamorphic tests compare outputs under changes that should preserve a particular rule. Reorder independent clauses, rerun the same contract, or change a supplier name or address only where that field genuinely has no bearing on the rule. Unexpected flag changes reveal instability. Passing such tests establishes neither complete coverage nor legal correctness: the same wrong answer can be consistent across variants. [Source 17](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-17)

Policy advice needs a separate control test. Define the approved policy, construct cases where an answer could conflict with it, and check the advice a customer would actually receive. Add a policy check or escalation where appropriate, then rerun those cases through the full path to see whether the control intercepts the error. A speaker-retold airline incident involving alleged incorrect post-purchase discount advice motivated such a proposal; the legal account was not independently checked and the proposed controls were counterfactual, not demonstrated prevention. [Source 18](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-18)

A related exploratory proposal compares a user’s privacy preferences with contract terms through concrete scenarios, surfacing possible conflicts. This can inform review, but a generated conflict is not a legal determination and does not give the user power to negotiate the terms. [Source 19](#document-extraction-and-legal-review-source-19)

## Synthetic respondents and historical personas

Covers synthetic respondents and historical personas; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A synthetic respondent is a model-generated forecast of an answer, not an additional human observation. A historically styled persona is a reconstruction from evidence, not the person speaking. Both can help explore questions, but they require different validation: population response patterns for the former, and time-specific documentary fidelity for the latter.

## Define the population and the claim

Use synthetic respondents to explore follow-up questions within a regime checked against relevant human data, not to inflate a survey's sample size. A plausible explanation or blind realism review is not proof that the model captures the target population, rare cases or downstream outcomes. In one speaker-reported clinical realism review, clinicians distinguished synthetic from real records about 60% of the time; the sample and protocol were not supplied, and this is not a clinical outcome measure. [Source 1](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-1) [Source 2](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-2)

Specify whether the target is stated attitude, actual behavior or a decision mediated by an agent. Exercise attitudes may be easier to elicit as text than future gym attendance, but their usefulness as a behavioral proxy must itself be tested; the example is hypothetical. If a purchasing agent actually filters options for a person, evaluating only unaided human choices may miss part of the decision pathway. This is a forward-looking design consideration, not proof that human studies are obsolete. [Source 3](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-3) [Source 4](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-4)

Political simulations illustrate the same limit. A model estimating legislators' votes or scoring bills against synthetic constituents produces model outputs, not verified vote forecasts or public opinion. A described dataset's assumed representativeness was not checked against actual constituent opinions. [Source 5](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-5) [Source 6](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-6)

Keep denominators explicit even for real surveys used as a reference: a reported intention to adopt among people **not currently building** with a modality is neither current use among all respondents nor a prediction that all intenders will adopt. [Source 7](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-7)

## Hold the world fixed; test the persona

In an *illustrative* price experiment, specify the product, expiry, competitor offerings and other fixed conditions, then vary price. Otherwise the model may infer that a price change also changed quality or the market, confounding the intended treatment. A secondhand account described synthetic purchase responses forming an inverted U while human responses declined; invented correlations were offered as an explanation. Full prompts and controls were not available, so treat it as a diagnostic illustration rather than a reproducible effect. [Source 8](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-8)

Enough context to define the experiment is not the same as more persona detail. Additional demographic or ideological detail can amplify model biases; a reported voting example became less aligned with humans as descriptions grew richer. Compare prompt variants against held-out human results rather than selecting the most vivid profile. Reorder answer options, reword questions and challenge stated opinions: a strong option-order effect can look like a stable preference until the order changes. [Source 9](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-9) [Source 10](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-10)

Use an existing human study as a starting point for exploratory follow-ups when a new study is unavailable, but label the result as extrapolation and validate important predictions with people. A claim that expert-plus-persona extrapolation beats expert judgment alone was not backed by a comparative experiment in the cited account. [Source 11](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-11)

## Compare distributions against human variability

A correct average can hide a wrong distribution: an *illustrative* model whose respondents all give the middle rating could match the mean of a human group split between extremes while missing polarization entirely. Compare response shares and distribution shape as well as correlation or mean. One proposed method elicits free-text reactions and compares them with human-written anchors for each rating, yielding a distribution rather than one forced score. Its embedding, normalization and calibration details were not disclosed, so the estimator cannot be reproduced from the account alone. [Source 12](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-12) [Source 13](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-13)

Interpret agreement relative to the variability of the human reference. Repeated answers from the same people estimate within-person temporal consistency; a secondhand study reported about 80% consistency after two weeks and about 83% agent alignment **normalized** against human inconsistency, not 83% raw accuracy. When retests are unavailable, repeatedly splitting the human sample and comparing halves gives a reference for sample variation, not a measurement of within-person repeatability. More synthetic samples may characterize the model precisely without adding independent human validation. [Source 14](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-14) [Source 15](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-15)

## Anchor historical reconstruction to documents and time

A fluent voice can use premises or later knowledge the historical person could not have held at the chosen moment. Specify the individual and encounter date, assemble inspectable documentary evidence and ask experts whether each argument is licensed by that record. A general training cutoff alone does not select one person's position at one moment: it can still mix earlier periods and different observers. Documentary support is not direct access to private beliefs, and surviving sources may be incomplete or biased. [Source 16](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-16) [Source 17](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-17) [Source 18](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-18)

For example, a speaker contrasts an unanchored Lincoln answer on executive war powers with an 1848 letter; the contrast illustrates a possible temporal reasoning failure, not a systematic benchmark or proof that anchoring fixes it. Keeping documents in context gives reviewers a route back to specific evidence; fine-tuning may produce a convincing voice while making the connection to an individual document harder to inspect. That architectural preference is an argument, not a controlled comparison. [Source 16](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-16) [Source 19](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-19)

A proposed, preregistered study crosses four moments with three conditions—primary writings, modern biography and a date-only model—and asks five expert-designed diagnostic questions in each cell. It is designed to distinguish moment-specific reasoning from a smooth later narrative, but had not been run at scale in the account; superiority of primary-document anchoring remained a prediction. [Source 20](#synthetic-respondents-and-historical-personas-source-20)

## Visual media and physical systems

Covers visual media and physical systems; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A plausible image, a coherent video and a robot that completes one action are not interchangeable evidence of competence. Evaluation must ask what was actually perceived, what changed over time, whether modalities and physical relationships agree, and whether an action can be repeated and recovered when it fails.

## Test the scene, not the familiar category

A model may recognize a chessboard and answer with a standard board's count rather than count the squares actually visible. A narrated partial-board example elicited 32 white squares; it is a selected failure, not an estimate of accuracy, and the source image is unavailable. Construct cases where the familiar prior conflicts with the observed scene, and check the answer against the visible objects and their relationships. [Source 1](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-1)

The same distinction matters for policy grounding. A proposed construction-safety application would need to connect a written rule to the particular workers and locations to which it applies; detecting a helmet somewhere in a frame would not establish that each worker required to wear one is compliant. This is a prospective application, not evidence of a deployed safety system or reduced incidents. [Source 2](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-2)

## Follow state and narrative over time

Test what changed and what remains true across frames. In one described robot video, models reportedly missed a lifted lid and later stove activation. Questions about the state before and after each event test more than whether the system recognizes a kitchen. The example does not establish the cause of the failure or a general memory error rate. [Source 3](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-3)

For generated video, a frame can match the prompt and still fail the intended story. Examine character identity across shots, pacing, plausible movement and event order alongside frame quality. For existing video, timestamped embeddings, OCR and tags can help a reviewer locate a brief anomalous content shift that a whole-video description misses. Reports and comments can point to emerging concerns after publication, but audience reaction is supplementary evidence, not ground truth about abuse or originality; its added benefit and resistance to manipulation were not quantified. [Source 4](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-4) [Source 5](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-5) [Source 6](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-6)

## Separate physical and audiovisual checks

Attractive visuals need not depict a physically coherent process. Likewise, clear studio-quality sound may be wrong for a distant speaker in a reverberant room. Evaluate geometry, causal sequence and scene-consistent acoustics separately from aesthetic quality. These are qualitative evaluation arguments, not measured physical-model performance. [Source 7](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-7) [Source 8](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-8)

A door-slam check illustrates why individual metrics have narrow meanings: locate the closing frame and look for an audio spike at the corresponding time. A spike supports timing alignment, but it does not identify the sound as a door. Nor does it validate continuous lip synchronization; animated mouth movement was an unresolved problem in the described setup, not a universally unsolved task. [Source 9](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-9) [Source 10](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-10)

## Route edits for authenticity, then gate revisions

Not every image needs enhancement. An already-good food photo can consume compute and become worse if edited; an image showing six pieces alongside a description of eight can invite invented food. Evaluate the routing decision and the resulting edit against the original content and merchant identity, not aesthetic polish alone. The reported system's diversity and trust goals were not measured outcomes, and the source's wing-routing terminology is ambiguous. [Source 11](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-11) [Source 12](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-12)

A reported workflow generates image-specific edits, checks dimensions such as plating, faithfulness and color, and feeds rejection reasons into another attempt. Bound the attempts: publish an enhancement that passes the gate, or leave the image unenhanced when the limit is reached. This exchanges coverage for protection against repeatedly failing edits; the retry limit and acceptance rates were not supplied, and passing an imperfect gate is not proof of no defects. Similarly, a generation agent can use intermediate quality checks to revise output, but the reported move from a fixed pipeline to such agents is not a controlled reliability comparison. [Source 13](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-13) [Source 14](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-14)

Visual feedback can also help reconstruct a dense chart: generate a table, plot it, compare against the image and revise. A visually plausible trend is weaker evidence than correct individual values; the described demonstration gives no numerical reconstruction accuracy. [Source 15](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-15)

## Measure sustained action and recovery

A compelling robot clip demonstrates that one sequence occurred, not that the system can operate reliably over a shift. Record all attempts, failures, interventions and recoveries; report per-task success separately from sustained operation over the full sequence. Test recovery from physical states not deliberately rehearsed, particularly with deformable objects that can assume many configurations. A vendor describes a robot recovering after pulling over a napkin stack, but this observation is not a held-out recovery benchmark. [Source 16](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-16) [Source 17](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-17)

A media demonstration or simulated task is not proof of physical deployment reliability. Even real-site trials must distinguish adaptation at a familiar location from transfer to a new one; see [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html).

## Validate bootstrapped vision labels independently

A prototype workflow uses a vision-language model to propose labels, separate vision models to review them, and the accepted examples to train a smaller detector. Agreement among those models can still share errors, so compare predictions with held-out human labels where available. In the reported road-sign experiment, existing annotations allowed such a comparison, though the metric configuration and complete numerical comparison were not supplied. In document parsing, an illustrative detector found a signature missed by its teacher, but the presenter lacked equivalent ground truth; one recovered signature does not establish an unseen-document generalization rate. [Source 18](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-18) [Source 19](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-19) [Source 20](#visual-media-and-physical-systems-source-20)
