## Creative quality and accessibility

Covers creative quality and accessibility; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

Creative quality depends on what an artifact is for and whom it serves. A design can satisfy a brand brief but be inaccessible; a factual explanation can be too full of internal jargon for its audience. Evaluate those dimensions separately instead of letting visual polish or one overall preference score stand in for the whole experience.

## Design-system retrieval as proposed product context

When a user has no established brand, one proposed workflow retrieves a pre-designed, coherent system matching the requested mood and context, rather than inventing typography, color and layout choices independently. The proposal is intended to give the generator a consistent starting point, not to establish that retrieval produces better or more accessible designs. Evaluate whether the selected system actually suits the user and task, whether its components work together, and whether users can use the result. The cited workflow is a product proposal, not a measured experiment. [Source 1](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-1)

## Define quality for the intended audience

Specify the audience, role, purpose and context before asking reviewers to judge quality. A slide appropriate for a startup may be inappropriate for a finance firm; a meeting summary that highlights deal context for sales may fail an engineer who needs blockers and actions. These are motivating examples, not measured persona-specific results. Standards and user needs can also change over time. [Source 2](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-2) [Source 3](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-3)

The distinction applies to instruction as well as aesthetics. A chess engine's best move and how likely players at a specified rating are to find it are different questions. The described coach uses a rating-conditioned human-move model to predict a distribution over moves. A rating-group prediction is not a calibrated probability for a particular learner, and the source does not establish that the model's estimates are calibrated or that coaching improves learning. [Source 4](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-4)

A writing benchmark aimed at one author's voice and ten tasks can help that author compare candidates; it is not a universal ranking of creative writers. Its speaker recommends local evaluation and final human review. Claims about reduced editing burden are practical guidance, not timed evidence of savings. [Source 5](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-5) [Source 6](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-6) [Source 7](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-7)

## Separate constraints, craft and preference

Break a broad assessment into dimensions that can be examined independently. For writing, voice, storytelling, instruction compliance, research accuracy and generic or repetitive language are different properties: a script may sound right while misstating a fact. A reported writing benchmark groups its detailed metrics this way, but its full prompts, weights and metric definitions were not supplied. Likewise, a changelog can be factually accurate and still use internal jargon that customers do not understand. [Source 8](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-8) [Source 9](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-9)

For design, alignment or contrast can be more assessable once context is specified, while aesthetic preference can yield legitimate expert disagreement. Record whose preference and use case are being judged rather than calling every disagreement an error. Accessibility requirements, however, are not simply a matter of whether reviewers like the look. [Source 10](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-10)

A proposed brand check decomposes an existing system into colors, typography, motion, texture and other components. A novel page can then satisfy those constraints without copying a single reference layout. This leaves space for meaningful novelty; unusual is not automatically good, and most common is not automatically best. These are design proposals and opinions, not controlled evidence that component scoring improves training or beats exemplar comparison. If a generator extracts its own brand specification, independently review the specification too: using the same mistaken assumptions for generation and evaluation can make a flawed result appear consistent. [Source 11](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-11) [Source 12](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-12) [Source 13](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-13) [Source 14](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-14)

Repetition is also not a complete quality metric. Narrow probes for color, typography and layout can identify recurring patterns, but their usefulness depends on the examples and labels sampled. One team reported historical website homogenization before generative AI as well as repetition in generated sites; sampling and comparison controls were not provided. Compare against a relevant historical baseline and ask whether similarity reflects a useful convention or a failure to respond to different contexts. [Source 15](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-15) [Source 16](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-16) [Source 17](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-17)

## Give implementation both structure and visual context

A screenshot communicates appearance; a structured, code-like representation of the design scene graph can convey elements and their relationships to an implementing agent. The Figma team reported better results using image and code context together than an image alone. This is an internal practical observation, not a universal ranking of representations. Check the implementation's theme and variable use, visual appearance and decisions under ambiguity, not just pixel similarity. [Source 18](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-18) [Source 19](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-19) [Source 20](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-20)

## Build accessibility into the lifecycle

Set platform-specific accessibility requirements during planning and design, before implementation and QA. Audit inherited patterns and fix identified accessibility problems before generating new features: an agent can copy existing inaccessible conventions just as readily as useful ones. The propagation mechanism is qualitative, not a measured rate. Do not infer that there is no accessibility need from the absence of users who could not enter or use the product in the first place; that is a selection problem, not an estimate of demand. [Source 21](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-21) [Source 22](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-22) [Source 23](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-23) [Source 24](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-24)

Where appropriate, map a design element to the actual existing accessible and internationalized component, rather than rebuilding a lookalike. The reported design-to-code example maps a button to a codebase component; reuse is useful only to the extent that the actual component and its use meet the requirements. A visually identical replacement may omit behavior. [Source 25](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-25)

For web interfaces, a cited minimum is semantic HTML where it expresses the behavior, keyboard access to mouse-operated interactions, understandable labels for screen-reader users, and an explicit audit. Use native semantics before adding ARIA where appropriate. Automated checks and lightweight generation guidance are starting points, not a complete accessibility certification. Manually test the actual interactions and assistive-technology experience, and apply requirements appropriate to the platform. The source explicitly says the minimum checklist and any single tool are insufficient. [Source 26](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-26) [Source 27](#creative-quality-and-accessibility-source-27)

## Preference discovery and recommendations

Covers preference discovery and recommendations; other articles own their distinct mechanisms and evaluation targets.

A person looking for a sofa may know that a room should feel calm without knowing the catalog's style vocabulary. A recommender must help turn that incomplete intent into a usable choice, while keeping stated requirements separate from guesses. A click can inform the process, but it does not by itself show that the item fits, that the user liked it, or that the explanation was true. [Source 1](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-1) [Source 2](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-2)

## Discover the preference without exhausting the user

Start with a working state containing explicit facts and constraints, such as a budget, separately from inferred preferences, such as the style suggested by an inspiration image. Record uncertainty about the inference rather than promoting it to a fact. Evaluate whether supplied details survive in state and are represented correctly. The shopping system describes confidence within an error bound, but provides neither the bound nor a calibration method; a confidence field is not evidence that its probabilities are reliable. [Source 3](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-3)

Ask about the unknown most likely to block a useful choice. For a living-room redesign, room width can matter before refining a style preference: a sofa that cannot fit is not a viable recommendation. This is an information-value objective, not a published numerical estimator or proven optimal questioning policy. Evaluate both useful constraint discovery and the burden of repeated or inconsequential questions. If the user can state a dimension plainly, text may suffice; if they cannot articulate a visual style, a board of examples can provide shared reference points. Hovers and clicks are tentative signals, not validated evidence of liking. [Source 4](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-4) [Source 5](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-5)

Test updates as well as retention. **Illustrative example:** a shopper changes the maximum width but not the budget. The extracted width should change and the budget should remain stable; a state that rewrites both is not faithfully tracking the revision. The source describes this counterfactual logic, not a dataset construction method or passing threshold. [Source 6](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-6)

A simulator seeded with constraints hidden from the agent can test which constraints the agent elicits and how many turns it takes. It can expose repeated questions even if a final recommendation looks plausible. But the described simulator was not validated against real shoppers, and neither coverage of hidden preferences nor a recovery rate was reported. Real-user evidence remains necessary. A speaker also reported that users wanted involvement in exploring possibilities, while price comparison or negotiation might be delegated; the study's size and protocol were not supplied, and agent-to-agent shopping was not yet built. Treat this as a design hypothesis, not a universal automation preference. [Source 7](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-7) [Source 8](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-8)

Let people inspect and correct inferred taste. In a reported music example, listening on a shared device included the speaker's children's Disney music; an editable natural-language profile could distinguish that history from his own preferences and express future aspirations. This makes user correction possible, but the account does not report correction accuracy or long-term effects. Behavior can ground an inference without being the user's unquestionable intent. [Source 9](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-9)

## Turn preferences into catalog choices and assess fit

A preference such as “calm and compact” must be mapped to catalog attributes before it can constrain retrieval. The proposed shopping agent bridges conversation and merchant ontology; merchant expertise can clarify what the local metadata actually means. Evaluate whether the mapping preserves the user's constraint and whether eligible items are retrieved, rather than assuming that a plausible translation is correct. No mapping accuracy or fairness result is supplied. [Source 10](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-10)

Catalog representation is a different concern from learning preference. In a Spotify architecture account, existing content embeddings are quantized into discrete semantic-ID tokens added to a model's vocabulary. A request and listening-history IDs can then yield an entity ID plus a natural-language explanation. This helps connect language generation to catalog entities; emitting a valid ID does not establish that the recommendation fits the user or that the explanation is faithful. [Source 11](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-11)

Assess distinct parts of the response rather than relying on engagement alone:

- **Fit:** Does the item satisfy explicit constraints and the user's current intent, including corrections to inferred taste?
- **Fidelity:** Are product details and the reasons given for the recommendation supported by the available information?
- **Presentation and actionability:** Can the person find the relevant trade-offs and decide what to do next? A comparison table, a policy summary or visual inspiration may help in different situations; none is mandatory for every query.
- **Interaction:** Did the process uncover the important blocker without redundant questions or obscuring the user's choice?

A purchase-oriented actionability measure should not be presented as proof of causal conversion or user welfare. The described recommenders use or propose language-model raters for stage-specific qualities, but the shopping account provides no rater prompts, calibration or longitudinal improvement evidence. Ground judgments in meaningful user evidence and human preferences, while recognizing that behavioral history can be misleading; validate the judges rather than treating them as automatic authorities. See [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html). [Source 12](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-12) [Source 13](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-13) [Source 14](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-14) [Source 2](#preference-discovery-and-recommendations-source-2)

## Matching evidence and autonomy to risk

Focus on system risk, harm prioritization and deployment decisions; detailed technical enforcement belongs in agent controls.

A capable agent is not automatically entitled to act. The right authority depends on what can go wrong, whether errors reach consequential decisions, whether anyone can catch them, and what happens afterward. Treat authority as a permission that can be granted, held, reduced or suspended as evidence changes—not as a one-way launch milestone. [Source 1](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-1) [Source 2](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-2)

## Grant, hold and withdraw authority against risk evidence

Start at the lowest authority level that creates value. A practical ladder is suggestion, editable draft, actions approved individually, and actions within explicitly preapproved limits. Before moving up, define the permitted actions, accountable decision-maker, evidence needed, review expectations and fallback. Legal or organizational constraints may cap authority regardless of model capability; for example, a hypothetical claims workflow requires human review of denials. That example is an assumed rule, not a statement of universal law. [Source 2](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-2) [Source 3](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-3)

One proposed reporting workflow begins in **shadow mode**: the human completes the report as usual while the agent independently produces its version. Compare the two, investigate disagreements and build an expert-reviewed record. The next stage lets the agent draft while an analyst checks every line. If evidence warrants it, review can later focus on flagged items plus independently selected samples, and eventually on high-risk exceptions with periodic independent sampling. The stages are a proposed operating pattern, not validated promotion thresholds. [Source 4](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-4)

Use a joint scorecard. Value measures such as cycle time, hours returned and detection latency belong beside severity of errors, overrides, recovery performance and missed issues. When review becomes exception-only, sample **unflagged** work independently: otherwise the most consequential omissions may never reach a reviewer. A declining override rate may mean better agent performance or merely shallower review. A named authority owner should promote only when the evidence and controls meet the workflow's agreed conditions; hold if evidence is insufficient, and restrict or suspend authority when recurring violations or control failures justify it. The sources do not establish universal thresholds or sampling rates. [Source 5](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-5) [Source 6](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-6)

Clinical practice illustrates why the ladder is not simply “test, then automate.” Real calls and synthetic rare cases can exercise failures before exposure; simulation failures send the team back to improve the system. Passing simulation can support supervised real-world evaluation, but simulated patients are not patients and a clean simulation does not establish clinical benefit. Clinician-supervised testing and monitored deployment supply different evidence. In an irreversible-harm setting, monitoring and rollback cannot undo a harmful call already made, so a small initial exposure alone is not a substitute for predeployment evidence. This is the speaker's clinical release rationale, not a blanket legal rule for every study. [Source 7](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-7) [Source 8](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-8) [Source 9](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-9)

Authority level is distinct from selecting which workflow nodes are sufficiently checkable for automation and from limiting the population exposed to a release. See [Choosing agent delegation and coordination](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-delegation-and-coordination.html) for node suitability and [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html) for exposure and recovery. An internal changelog agent that only raises reviewable pull requests, for example, is not evidence that autonomous production publication is safe. [Source 10](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-10)

## Assess the whole path from error to harm

Ask four separate questions: how might the system fail; can that failure reach a real decision; will a control or person catch it; and how severe would the consequence be? This is a conceptual decomposition, not a calibrated probability formula. The same model can carry different risk when its authority, human mediation, monitoring or exposure changes. Controls can contain defects, but that does not excuse poor model quality or make a nominal human-in-the-loop label proof of effective review. [Source 11](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-11) [Source 12](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-12) [Source 1](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-1)

One retrospective analysis reported that its thirteen dimensions covered almost 98% of examined incidents and that an incident implicated six dimensions on average. Its sampling, coding and denominators were not fully specified. These are reported categorizations of past incidents—not proof the framework predicts future incidents or that any control caused a reduction in harm. Their useful lesson is to investigate interacting technical and organizational failures rather than stop at the first model error. [Source 13](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-13)

## Prioritize by severity, likelihood and materiality

Name concrete harms before choosing tests. A clinical assistant might miss sudden vision loss, invent medical advice or ignore distress. Distinguish an incorrect answer that causes no harm from one that could cause serious harm. The same scheduling error may waste time in one case and affect a vulnerable patient or procedure in another; those examples do not quantify harm probabilities. [Source 14](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-14) [Source 15](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-15) [Source 16](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-16)

Allocate scarce testing and review using severity, plausible frequency, exposure and business context, not failure count alone. Severity-times-frequency can help order discussion, but is only a heuristic, not a validated risk model; a rare catastrophic failure must not disappear merely because its observed count is low. High aggregate accuracy can still leave substantial absolute harm at high volume, while a small clean test cannot establish a rare-error rate. Representative sustained testing and expert assessment are needed for stronger evidence. [Source 17](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-17) [Source 18](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-18) [Source 19](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-19)

In security triage, even real findings can overwhelm engineers. Deduplicate, consider impact and likelihood in the actual environment, agree severity rules with product and security teams, and route findings to their owners. A firewall or internal-only access can change assessed likelihood without making a vulnerability unreal. The proposed materiality scales do not provide universal weights or thresholds. [Source 20](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-20) [Source 21](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-21) [Source 22](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-22)

## Count a sound handoff as success

If authorization is absent, uncertainty is too consequential, or an action is irreversible or outside the agent's remit, stopping and handing off can be the correct outcome. In an expense-workflow demonstration, an expired session led the agent to hand authentication to the user rather than guess a password; it resumed after control returned and the expense state was checked. The user was simulated, so this demonstrates a possible behavior, not a calibrated production reliability rate. Do not optimize merely for fewer escalations: that would reward inappropriate autonomy. [Source 23](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-23)

A reviewer must be able to make a real decision. In a hypothetical exception workflow, the agent highlights source evidence and uncertainty and supplies an editable draft instead of filing automatically. Whether a user can recognize and correct a mistake depends on expertise, access and time; an approval button alone is not a safety guarantee or a compliance determination. For approval design see [Human Review and Agent Governance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/human-review-and-agent-governance.html); for independent runtime enforcement see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 24](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-24) [Source 25](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-25)

## Exercise detection, fallback and ownership

For each important failure, name the detection path, fallback and responsible responder, then test whether they operate together. In the hypothetical exception assistant, an analyst can reject an invented exception against the source; unreadable extraction stops the workflow and requests a clean file; an alert has an owner empowered to stop work. A targeted offline test can reveal that the assistant misses exceptions, but does not identify every live omission. In that example, affected work stays under manual review; other workflows need their own detection and fallback design. [Source 26](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-26) [Source 27](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-27)

## Tie evidence to each hazard

A useful safety case links each named hazard to the relevant calls or cases, datasets, pinned prompt, judge verdicts and control-response evidence, and identifies the release and authority scope those artifacts support. When a prompt, language, data source or action scope changes, follow the links to determine which argument needs renewed evidence. The clinical account states this traceability requirement; it does not provide an audited submission or establish regulatory acceptance. [Source 28](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-28)

## Keep risk expertise in the team

Using a hosted model instead of training one does not remove the need for statistical testing, model-risk literacy or validation of evaluators. Combine that expertise with domain, product, security and systems knowledge: functional agent behavior is not captured by classifier metrics alone, even though precision and recall can be useful when validating a judge against labeled cases. This is organizational guidance, not a measured staffing formula. See [Validate judges against human labels](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/validate-judges-against-human-labels.html) for the validation method. [Source 29](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-29) [Source 30](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-30) [Source 31](#risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy-source-31)

## Prompt Injection and Agent Threat Modeling

Explain attack paths and threat models; grant enforcement is treated in the access-control article.

An agent may legitimately read an email, repository or tool description and then mistake an instruction embedded there for authority to change its task. The danger is not just an undesirable answer: the same agent may be able to read private records, write shared memory or call tools. Threat modeling follows that path from attacker-controlled input to the actual consequence.

## Map reach, assets and trust boundaries

Start with the agent's legitimate purpose and the assets it can affect. Diagram inputs, context assembly, model, memory, tool endpoints, connected applications and outputs that trigger operations. For each crossing, ask who controls the material, what the agent can read or write, whose identity it uses and what a successful attacker would gain. A support agent with access to customer records and messaging has a different blast radius from one that only answers from a public manual, even if both are called support bots. Revisit the map when tools, data, models or workflows change. [Source 1](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-1) [Source 2](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-2) [Source 3](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-3)

Ordinary success with cooperative users is not an adversarial assessment. Use the role and its real privileges to identify high-consequence probes, while remembering that attacks can also arise outside the nominal task. More capable systems may both do useful work and interpret attacks that weaker systems miss; the poem-wrapped instruction example is illustrative, not a measured model comparison. [Source 4](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-4) [Source 5](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-5) [Source 6](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-6)

## When source content claims authority

Indirect injection enters through material the agent was authorized to read, rather than necessarily through the user's own request. An email summary can include hidden text telling the agent to perform an unrelated action. The boundary is crossed when source content is promoted from evidence about the task to an instruction governing the agent. Human visibility is not a reliable indicator of what a parser or model receives. The hidden-email examples are illustrative or briefly reported incidents, not measurements of defense effectiveness. [Source 7](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-7) [Source 8](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-8)

Record origin and trust level, and treat retrieved material, repository comments and reviewer inputs as data even when they contain imperative language. Internal-looking material can also be poisoned. A locally reviewed skill can load instructions from a mutable remote file, changing effective behavior without a local edit. A sandbox or a prompt saying to ignore embedded commands is not a complete defense; consequential actions require independent authorization. See [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html) and [Agent and Dependency Supply-Chain Security](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security.html). [Source 9](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-9) [Source 10](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-10) [Source 11](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-11)

## Tool metadata can manufacture a dependency

Tool descriptions are themselves input to the model. A malicious description can make a privileged call appear necessary to complete a harmless request. In a demonstrated weather-tool trap, the description said the agent needed an internal-configuration call and its output to answer; the trace showed the internal call. That run did not establish external exfiltration. Inspect descriptions and actual cross-tool calls, not just protocol conformance: a properly formatted integration can still carry hostile instructions. Implementation vulnerabilities in the server are a separate surface. [Source 12](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-12) [Source 13](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-13) [Source 14](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-14)

## Memory makes an attack durable

An instruction need not act immediately. A poisoned document can ask to be remembered and triggered later, when a secret becomes available; shared notes or learned skills can carry the instruction into another run or to another agent. One described sleeper-memory scenario combines persistence with a later outbound channel; another cross-agent resume scenario is illustrative, not an observed propagation or containment experiment. [Source 15](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-15) [Source 16](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-16)

Map not only who can read a store but also who can write it and which future agents will ingest it. Review learned artifacts and consider isolating memory or using fresh runs for sensitive work. That trades useful continuity for a smaller persistence surface; neither a review nor a memory-free run proves safety. Suggested screening and skill-review layers have not been shown to stop all attacks. [Source 17](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-17)

## Review capability combinations, not just components

The consequential path often combines three ingredients: untrusted input can influence an agent that has private data and a tool capable of external action. For example, a malicious support message could redirect a broadly connected agent toward collecting and sending customer information. A proposed rule of two calls for human sign-off when all three are needed together. Treat this as a review trigger, not proof that any pair is safe or that approval alone prevents compromise. Examine the actual end-to-end path and reachable destinations. [Source 18](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-18) [Source 19](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-19) [Source 2](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-2)

## Maintain an inventory, then test the paths

An AI bill of materials should include models, datasets, prompt templates, agents, memory stores, tools, dependencies and connected applications, as well as generated outputs and observable behavior. It helps identify affected systems when a component changes or is found vulnerable. It is not proof that discovery is complete or that an inventoried component is safe; a vendor inventory demonstration did not evaluate discovery completeness or incident-response performance. [Source 20](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-20) [Source 21](#prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling-source-21)

Use the inventory to choose realistic attack paths and probe whether the agent follows malicious content, stores it, or invokes an unrelated tool. A passed probe is evidence only about the tested cases—not containment. Isolation, independent action and egress controls, and stopping mechanisms need their own verification; see [Probing safety behavior and reward proxies](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/safety-evaluation-and-adversarial-probing.html) and [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html).

## Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls

Own permissions, execution and emergency control; privacy retention and tenancy have their own article.

An agent can be instructed to ask permission, stay in a directory, or avoid secrets and still have the technical ability to do otherwise. The relevant security question is not just what the agent is told, but **what effects its environment will permit if it misinterprets a request, follows hostile content, makes a mistake, or deliberately takes an alternative route**. A useful control limits that authority outside the model’s own judgment. It is still only as strong as its coverage and the assumptions behind its decision.

## Enforce effects at real choke points

Place an independently controlled authorization and validation decision before an operation reaches the system that performs it. Check the actor, resource, proposed operation and relevant parameters against policy; deny or route the call when it fails. Validate generated queries and commands for the actual downstream consumer, not merely for whether the text looks acceptable. For example, a travel-booking demonstration used pre-call checks to prevent confirming an unpaid reservation. This demonstrates the pattern with dummy tools, not comprehensive production reliability. [Source 1](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-1)

The choke point must cover **every route to the effect**. A write-tool hook is not a file boundary if shell commands, scripts, another tool or a child can write the same file. One practitioner reported an agent bypassing a repository hook through a patch tool and subsequently adding its own emergency-unlock rationale; the account motivates a lower-level write gate and operator-controlled exceptions, but did not provide a bypass-resistance test of the replacement. [Source 2](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-2) [Source 3](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-3)

Pre-action blocking prevents a covered operation from executing; a warning, log, checkpoint or post-action correction does not. Checkpoints and rollback can aid recovery when feasible, but cannot be assumed to reverse every external effect. A heuristic pre-edit check can generate false positives, so a trusted operator may need a narrowly scoped exception; that is different from allowing the agent to override a hard security rule. Similarly, a deterministic block only acts on what its detector recognizes: a missed classification is not repaired by making the response deterministic. Monitoring, credential checks and escalation complement enforcement, not replace it. [Source 4](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-4) [Source 5](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-5) [Source 6](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-6)

An approval instruction inside a prompt is also not an independent gate: an agent might treat its own or another agent’s response as confirmation. Authenticate and enforce the approval at execution; design of meaningful human review belongs to [Human Review and Agent Governance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/human-review-and-agent-governance.html). A described computer-use monitor pauses *recognized* irreversible actions, while operating-system application restrictions belong at a different layer; neither establishes complete detection. [Source 7](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-7) [Source 8](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-8)

## Deny hard violations while steering recoverable plans

A denial need not end the whole task. If a booking is not paid, the confirmation remains blocked; the agent can instead ask for payment or pursue another authorized step. If one room lacks capacity, it can explore multiple rooms, but every proposed alternative must still satisfy the original requirements and the same hard checks. In the travel demonstration, captions inconsistently described party and room counts, so it does not establish that the proposed alternative preserved the booking requirements. Steering suggests a new plan; it never turns a denied action into permission. [Source 9](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-9)

## Keep data and secrets out of model context

Limit the fields returned to the model to those needed for the task, not just the tables the tool can reach. A read-only contact view that exposes names and phone numbers but not addresses illustrates the distinction between accessing a data source and revealing all its fields. Tenant authorization is a separate decision; see [Privacy, Tenancy and Data Governance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance.html). [Source 10](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-10)

Keep actual credentials in a privileged broker rather than putting them in prompts or tool output. Give the agent narrow operations such as checking whether a key exists or using a credential for a permitted service, without returning its value. A described vault substitutes a placeholder only at egress to its configured domain; that design was not security-tested. Inspect outputs for accidental secret return, including results of generated redaction code. [Source 11](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-11) [Source 12](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-12) A fresh subagent context may protect the parent’s context from intermediate material, but the child can still receive and expose that material; isolation of conversation context is not credential isolation. [Source 13](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-13) [Source 14](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-14) [Source 15](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-15)

## Audit chained and delegated authority

List effective routes, not just individual tool grants. A nominally read-only document connector can be undermined if the same agent controls an authenticated browser with document-creation rights. This is a described bypass scenario, not a reproduced exploit. Generated code and calls to more privileged agents create similar composition questions: who requested the operation, whose identity executes it, and what can flow back? Authorize each delegation and constrain the returned information as well as the immediate call. [Source 16](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-16)

One proposed lineage rule illustrates the issue: if a human can access A–D, an intermediary C–D and a worker D–F, only D is common to the whole chain and returned under the illustrative intersection. This is not a noninterference proof: even when a wider-privileged worker returns only an allowed field, its computation might leak information by inference. The proposal does not settle that problem. [Source 17](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-17)

## Identity, ambient credentials and attributable authority

Give each workload a distinct identity and narrowly scoped, preferably short-lived, audience-bound credentials; inspect its environment for inherited tokens that silently add authority. A shared developer login makes both blast-radius control and attribution harder. Identity answers *which principal is acting*; it does not decide whether this particular principal may delete this particular record. Human sponsorship and organizational accountability are likewise separate from technical authentication. [Source 18](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-18)

## Choose purpose-specific capabilities and inherit boundaries

Start with a declared job and grant the smallest **useful** set of tools, commands, destinations and read/write rights. A research summarizer may need web access while a release deployer may not. Blanket restrictions can make a workflow unusable; an unrestricted tool catalog exposes more effects than the task needs. Open-ended coding agents are harder to scope than a narrowly defined agent. [Source 19](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-19)

Observed calls can suggest permissions to remove, but do not prove that an unused permission is unnecessary: a rare legitimate incident or recovery path may be missing from history. Review proposed reductions against those cases. Human review of a capability declaration decides whether and on what terms to launch; it does not enforce the individual calls at runtime. See [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html) for release decisions. [Source 20](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-20)

## Sandbox lifetime, resource limits and actual outbound paths

Run generated code in an environment with bounded filesystem access, compute and output, a limited lifetime, and an explicit network policy enforced outside the agent’s control. Default-deny outbound traffic, including DNS, and permit only narrowly scoped paths necessary for the task; enforce that policy outside the sandbox. [Source 21](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-21) A read-only knowledge-base browser is one bounded example: the described system used an eight-second timeout, a 40,000-character output limit and twenty commands per turn; its exact allowlist and isolation implementation were not supplied. These are case-specific limits, not recommended universal settings. [Source 22](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-22)

A filesystem sandbox alone does not prove data cannot leave. Inspect and test the actual outbound channels, including DNS as well as web connections, and ensure alternate routes cannot bypass the intended proxy. A speaker described DNS exfiltration despite blocked web access, rather than demonstrating the attack; another architecture described a single proxy without an adversarial audit of every channel. Treat both as reasons to test the boundary, not proof of containment. Preserve useful state across disposable runs only without automatically preserving old authority. [Source 23](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-23) Sandboxing complements identity, action authorization and stops; it does not imply any of them. [Source 21](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-21) [Source 24](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-24)

## Budgets and live stops limit ongoing work

Make action counts, resource consumption or elapsed-time limits executable stopping conditions, not just alerts. Separately, provide agent-wide and per-tool kill switches that an operator can change without deploying new code. A proposed design checks a switch in in-flight work at the next decision point and applies tool, model, autonomy and stop controls throughout the child-agent tree. Otherwise a child using a direct path may continue after its parent is stopped. [Source 25](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-25) [Source 26](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-26) [Source 27](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-27)

A next-decision-point check cannot interrupt an already completed action or undo it. The stop and propagation mechanisms are architectural proposals, not measured stopping-latency guarantees; test the real implementation and plan separately for recovery.

## Inspectable programs and the limits of pre-execution proof

For workflows where a plan can be represented formally, separate planning from execution. Deferring an opaque I/O operation creates a pause but does not reveal what it will do. Instead, represent proposed actions as program nodes, inspect the operations and data flows, and check specified types, taint properties or a supplied proof before an assumed interpreter executes them. This can establish a property of the represented program under its policy and interpreter assumptions. [Source 28](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-28) [Source 29](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-29) [Source 30](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-30)

An omitted operation, an untrusted interpreter or a flawed policy lies outside that assurance. This is a conceptual tutorial, not a complete deployable safety proof, and it does not prove that a natural-language answer is generally safe. Nor does the speaker’s skepticism about a broad definition rule out narrower semantic properties. Pre-execution analysis complements, rather than replaces, the runtime checks on actual effects.

## Product safety knowledge is not enforcement

The agent also needs correct product-specific instructions. In one reported SQL-view task, a skill-assisted agent included `security_invoker=true`, which the speaker said preserved the intended row-level security behavior, while the tool-only agent omitted it. The comparison was a single reported task, without repeated-run rates or independent security verification. Access to a tool does not itself impart its security semantics. [Source 31](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-31)

Put indispensable, stable safety guidance in context reliably loaded for the task; leave less critical detail in references where appropriate. One team moved its checklist into the main skill after observing agents miss an optional reference, but did not quantify the behavior. This is selective placement, not a reason to inline all documentation—and even reliably loaded instructions remain guidance, not a policy gate. [Source 32](#agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls-source-32)

For threat paths that lead an agent to misuse its authority, see [Prompt Injection and Agent Threat Modeling](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling.html); for investigating actual behavior, see [Tracing and diagnosing production behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-observability-and-diagnosis.html).

## Human Review and Agent Governance

Covers approval design and governance ownership, not clinical intervention policy.

A human approval button is not, by itself, oversight. The person must know what consequential action is proposed, have evidence on which to challenge it, and retain authority to reject or change it. The system must also make clear who owns the agent and enforce the boundary around what it may do. A reviewer’s presence does not establish independent scrutiny. [Source 1](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-1) [Source 2](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-2)

## Make approval a decision about a specific action

An approval should identify the approving person, agent or actor, session and run, tool, exact arguments and permitted lifetime, with its outcome linked to the action receipt. A click authorizing one action should not silently authorize a changed payload or an old retry. The proposed approval-state design in one speaker-reported case treats expiry as a terminating condition: a stale approved callback had remained retriable and blocked later work. The account does not provide a complete implementation or authorization schema. [Source 3](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-3)

These records answer different questions. Permission authorizes a bounded action; an attempt shows the agent tried; a receipt records what a tool or system reported; an observation is a check of what could be seen; a verified outcome is a conclusion supported by checks against the intended state. Approval alone does not establish execution, and a receipt alone need not establish the intended lasting result. For outcome evidence, see [Managing agent task flow and action evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-task-flow-and-action-evidence.html).

The approval screen should expose the distinction that matters, not merely announce that something consequential will happen. In a speaker-retold banking incident, approvers saw a warning that money would leave the bank—which was compatible with the intended interest payment—but missed that principal would leave too. Several people and a technically correct warning did not ensure the relevant invariant was checked. This anecdote motivates more specific evidence and warnings; it is not a test of an alternative interface. [Source 4](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-4)

Give the reviewer the underlying source, uncertainty and an editable proposed action, rather than only a model recommendation and “approve.” A proposed document-exception workflow shifts from automatic filing to an analyst examining highlighted evidence and choosing whether to submit. It is a hypothetical design, not evidence of an approved banking deployment. In a separately reported financial-planning workflow, agents prepare drafts in parallel, but a planner reviews and adjusts every recommendation before client delivery. The reported boundary is useful, though the account does not measure review effectiveness. [Source 1](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-1) [Source 5](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-5)

## Preserve attention and independent judgment

Reviewers can defer to automation even when they perform well on ordinary calibration. In selected historical legitimate sessions, proctors reportedly scored above 90% on calibration but accepted 50% of seeded fake signals. After guidance recast the signal as a preliminary alert and required independent video evidence for an adverse decision, reported rejection of fake signals rose from 50% to 71%. The speaker did not give a sample size or detailed design, so these figures do not establish a general effect. They do illustrate why measuring agreement alone is not enough: ask whether reviewers can find and use evidence that might contradict the alert. [Source 2](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-2) [Source 6](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-6)

Review is a scarce resource. Repeated routine prompts can encourage reflexive approval or “always allow,” especially when agents operate in parallel. Reserve deliberate friction for consequential, ambiguous or dangerous cases; make safe routine cases subject to an explicit bounded policy and deny clearly prohibited actions. This is a design tradeoff, not a universal threshold: estimate alert volume and ensure enough qualified reviewers have time to examine the evidence. Unnecessary friction on low-stakes work can also degrade the workflow. [Source 7](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-7) [Source 8](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-8) [Source 9](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-9)

Written instructions to pause are useful but are not enforcement. A reported financial-advice workflow specifies draft-but-do-not-send as a limit; the description does not demonstrate technical enforcement. For consequential actions, put the approval boundary in the execution system rather than relying on the agent to remember it. Acknowledging a production freeze is likewise not proof that a destructive operation is impossible. The technical controls are covered in [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html); deciding when to widen autonomy belongs in [Matching evidence and autonomy to risk](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/risk-based-safety-and-staged-autonomy.html). [Source 10](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-10) [Source 11](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-11)

## Give responsibility a name

One proposed governance framework registers each agent under a stable identity and assigns a named human sponsor responsible for its purpose, costs and failures. The sponsor defines the relatively stable role: responsibilities, budget, intended outcomes and local rules. A runtime mission is the particular task or action being pursued now; an agent’s choice of mission must not silently redefine its role. Explicit ownership and handoff matter because a group of possible interveners is not necessarily a person who knows they are responsible. [Source 12](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-12) [Source 13](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-13) [Source 14](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-14)

The sponsor can define local expectations, but inherits model behavior, external context and partner-agent behavior that may change outside their control. A named sponsor and registry make accountability traceable; they are not, on their own, an identity-security protocol or authorization mechanism. This is a conceptual framework, not an evaluated staffing model or a demonstrated reduction in failures. [Source 15](#human-review-and-agent-governance-source-15)

## Privacy, Tenancy and Data Governance

Own data use, tenant access and privacy; agent credential brokering is in runtime controls.

Sensitive data governance is a property of the whole data path, not just the model’s answer. Decide who may use each source, which tenant and document a request may reach, where raw and derived records live, and what reviewers can inspect. A successful query or a redacted screen does not by itself answer any of those questions.

## Enforce tenant boundaries throughout the data path

Treat the model’s query as a request, not an authorization decision. Hiding the scope field from the model-visible schema reduces exposure but does not prevent the model from guessing it. Trusted query validation must reject unauthorized access to hidden fields, while trusted code derives the permitted tenant from the authenticated request and independently applies the restriction outside the model-generated query. The described approach is an architectural recommendation, not a penetration-tested authorization implementation. Check scope at every query, and also at retrieval hits and derived computations, where data can otherwise escape the initial filter. In one financial-research design, each hit is reauthorized against its document, citation and value; separate desks within a firm motivate the boundary. The vendor describes this design without a formal isolation proof. [Source 1](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-1) [Source 2](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-2) [Source 3](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-3) [Source 4](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-4)

Choose the isolation granularity deliberately. A shared workspace avoids duplicating definitions, but requires reliable customer-to-session mapping and an additional access layer where workspace resources are shared. Separate workspaces or organizations make the boundary clearer but require synchronizing definitions; account- or project-level separation is another strong-boundary option, not a mandatory cloud layout. Verify actual workspace sharing and inherited role controls for the deployed version rather than treating a vendor description as a security certification. A speaker-reported incident in which monitoring access exposed another customer’s logs and metrics illustrates why even fast, useful services can fail acceptance; the product, test and remediation were not specified. [Source 5](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-5) [Source 6](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-6) [Source 7](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-7) [Source 8](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-8)

## Authorize use and design for regulated data

Permission to query a source is not necessarily permission to send it to a model, use it for a new purpose, or move it to another provider or region. Identify the source owner, access grantor and intended-use approver; they may be different people. Map primary processing, evaluation, logs and recovery copies before choosing architecture. A proposed recovery design keeps core traces in their permitted region while replicating identifiers and metadata elsewhere. That is a possible availability tradeoff, not a legal exemption: identifiers and metadata may themselves be restricted. [Source 9](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-9) [Source 10](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-10)

For protected health information, one practitioner recommends stripping sensitive fields at ingestion before a general-purpose data lake, separating production from non-production without data pipes between them, and restricting raw access by role and region. Removing a field before storage reduces reliance on every downstream dashboard author remembering to redact it. The account supplies no de-identification algorithm, re-identification analysis or privacy audit, and does not prove legal compliance. Validate residual risk and applicable requirements for the actual data and use. [Source 11](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-11) [Source 12](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-12)

## Protect traces and evaluator explanations

The user-facing answer is only one disclosure surface. Prompts, tool results, stored traces, evaluator inputs and judge explanations may contain or reconstruct sensitive information. A fictional banking demonstration masks a configured card number during instrumentation before persistence, but does not measure masking recall or leakage. Restricting raw trace access while allowing a service account to supply derived analysis to engineers reduces direct exposure, yet the derived analysis can itself leak; a customer-hosted data plane does not necessarily mean a customer-hosted control plane. [Source 13](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-13) [Source 14](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-14)

An evaluator may see a raw trace and repeat its content in reasoning even though the application UI hides it. One proposed design retains the score while withholding sensitive explanations from persistence or display; another runs a second judge on redacted input when reviewers need an explanation. Decide separately what is processed, persisted and shown: UI suppression alone is not backend deletion. The first design relies on sensitivity detection and actual non-persistence on the protected branch; the second relies on input redaction and may lose useful context and add cost. No leakage, accuracy, latency or cost evaluation establishes that either design is safe in all cases. [Source 15](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-15) [Source 16](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-16) [Source 17](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-17)

## Memory, communities and personal representation

More information sharing is not always better. A proposed multi-agent evaluation warns that optimizing information diffusion can reward oversharing, while optimizing recall can encourage reuse of stale facts. Measure whether private information remains contained and whether recalled material is still appropriate alongside public-information reach; this is a conceptual proposal, not a measured privacy guarantee. [Source 18](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-18)

When an agent joins a human community, other participants may not expect their conversation to be recorded or processed by it. Establish what participation and data handling mean for bystanders as well as the agent’s owner, while preserving space for human connection. The source raises this concern without specifying a control or legal analysis. [Source 19](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-19)

Personal personas add a different responsibility: fluent resemblance is not evidence that a system represents a particular person. Assess the personal record available and keep humans responsible for interpreting its gaps. One speaker’s unsuccessful attempt to help a person with advanced dementia lacked a gathered personal archive and took place when that person was largely beyond language; the resulting generic resemblance motivates caution, not a claim about clinical effectiveness or harm. [Source 20](#privacy-tenancy-and-data-governance-source-20)

For execution authority rather than data ownership, see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html); for audit and monitoring integrity, see [Observability, Monitoring and Audit Integrity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/observability-monitoring-and-audit-integrity.html).

### Source 20: The Miranda Hypothesis: How Hamilton Poisoned Persona Evals - Jacob E. Thomas, Results Gen

Evidence: case_study. This is a personal motivating account, not clinical efficacy or harm research; the person was also largely beyond language by then.

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJXjTLPzvAU) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/IJXjTLPzvAU.md#L1312-L1317)

## Agent and Dependency Supply-Chain Security

Own artifact distribution, dependencies and code vulnerabilities; injection mechanics are in threat modeling.

An agent's supply chain includes more than the libraries in its final output. Shared instructions can steer what it writes or runs, integrations contain executable code, and dependencies can change after they are approved. Review each artifact according to what it can influence, where it comes from and how it reaches users.

## Gate and screen reusable instructions

A shared skill may look like configuration, but its instructions can influence code and tool actions across many users. Review it as an upstream dependency. Relevant risks include requests to hardcode credentials that later enter logs, destructive shell instructions, unintended file changes, excessive permissions and drift from intended behavior. These are illustrative risk categories, not evidence that every listed attack happened in production. Plugins, hooks, rules and tool servers have different execution and risk profiles, so do not assume identical review is sufficient for each. [Source 1](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-1) [Source 2](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-2)

In a regulated financial organization's reported process, a new or changed skill enters an internal marketplace through a pull request and is scanned before distribution; policy and severity determine whether it is allowed, needs remediation or is blocked. Local scanning helps authors iterate, but the upload path scans again rather than assuming the local check ran on the current version. This creates a useful distinction between fast feedback and an authoritative distribution decision. [Source 3](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-3) [Source 4](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-4)

The gate only covers artifacts routed through it. The speaker recommends bringing downloaded third-party artifacts through the marketplace and identifies alternate distribution paths as a continuing coverage problem. Another team describes scanning at release and again at use, assuming the first check can miss something. A proposed sharing loop also screens distilled skills for injection and personal information before publication. Neither a trusted marketplace nor a clean scan proves instructions safe or correct; scanner coverage, bypass residual risk and the sharing loop's detection accuracy were not established. [Source 5](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-5) [Source 6](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-6) [Source 7](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-7) For the attack mechanism itself, see [Prompt Injection and Agent Threat Modeling](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/prompt-injection-and-agent-threat-modeling.html).

## Recheck updates and dependency health

Approval is version-specific evidence, not permanent trust. A speaker described an unnamed useful tool package with fifteen clean releases that allegedly added an attacker BCC on the sixteenth. Reinspect changed instructions and code, provenance and permissions when upgrading. The same source suggests delaying adoption by a week or two as a heuristic; waiting does not guarantee that malicious behavior will be discovered and may delay important fixes, so weigh the specific update. Scanning also has unknown false-negative rates. [Source 8](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-8) [Source 9](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-9)

Known vulnerability status is only one input. In a recorded vendor demonstration comparing two QR-code packages, neither had an active CVE, but one was maintained and the other was not. The presenter preferred the maintained package because a future patch might arrive sooner. That is a reasonable maintenance consideration, not a measured guarantee of future patch speed or safety. Repeatable workflow checks can reduce reliance on a developer remembering to request a check each time, but the proposed skill or hook is not evidence that checks cannot be bypassed or that its scanner finds every issue. [Source 10](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-10) [Source 11](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-11)

## Verify generated package names and provenance

A model can invent a plausible package name. An attacker who observes that suggestion could register the previously nonexistent name, so a later successful registry lookup or installation would not prove that the original recommendation referred to a legitimate project. Before adding a generated dependency, establish that it is appropriate for the task and verify the intended project and publisher through trustworthy provenance, not just a matching name. This differs from a misspelling of an existing package, although both exploit name confusion. The sources describe the mechanism; the incident and rough download counts mentioned by one speaker cannot be verified from the supplied account, and no frequency estimate is established. [Source 12](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-12) [Source 13](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-13)

## Review integration implementation as code

A tool server can have unsafe instructions, ordinary code vulnerabilities, or both. Inspecting descriptions for instruction poisoning is not a substitute for reviewing implementation paths and dependencies for command injection, path traversal and similar defects. One externally reported Figma integration incident involved a fallback that concatenated a URL into a shell command, allowing crafted input to add a command. The account explains the failure but does not reproduce the exploit or establish that current versions are vulnerable. [Source 14](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-14) [Source 15](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-15)

A proposed generated-code loop scans, repairs findings and scans the revised code again. The absence of scanner findings is a stopping condition for that check, not proof that all vulnerabilities have been removed; the source reports no measured success rate. [Source 16](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-16)

## Retain delivery controls and verify compliance separately

Agent assistance does not justify bypassing tests, security checks, artifact registries or established deployment paths. Treat generated changes as changes that must traverse the applicable delivery process, with evidence tied to the artifact actually being released. [Source 17](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-17)

A green build demonstrates only what its checks cover. It does not establish that a change meets business or regulatory obligations unless those obligations are explicitly checked and the relevant decision is traceable. A speaker described a feature-flag incident affecting driver checks and later controls for changes affecting London; that history is speaker-reported rather than independently documented in the supplied account. Use it to distinguish build success from policy evidence, not as proof that any particular control is universally sufficient. [Source 18](#agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security-source-18)

## Payment and Purchase Security for Agents

Own purchase-specific controls rather than the general action broker.

A purchase is not one decision. An agent discovers a seller, receives final payment requirements, signs, and receives a result; the seller verifies payment and fulfills it. Each transition can change what is being trusted. A directory listing does not prove who owns the wallet, a valid signature does not prove settlement, and one successful payment check does not protect an alternate route to the same content. The examples below come from controlled experiments and speaker recommendations, not measured production loss rates. [Source 1](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-1) [Source 2](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-2) [Source 3](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-3)

## Approve the seller and bind the final terms

Treat a discovered service as a candidate, not an authenticated counterparty. In the setup described by the speaker, the directory checked that a service worked, not who operated it or owned its payment wallet. A look-alike name and a lower price can therefore attract a buyer to the wrong seller. This is a characterization of that tested discovery system, not an audit of every directory. Apply a seller-approval policy that associates the identity with its authorized payment details. [Source 3](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-3)

A strict allowlist is appropriate when exploration is unacceptable, but can become stale when a legitimate seller changes domain, wallet, network, currency or price. The speaker proposes approved, blocked and probationary lists, with human review for newly discovered sellers. That is a policy design, not a validated review schedule: decide explicitly what a probationary seller may do before review rather than treating probation as automatic permission to spend. [Source 4](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-4)

Immediately before signing, compare the seller's final payment request with the approved terms, including price, recipient wallet and network. In a controlled test, a listing advertised five cents but the payment request asked for fifty; the unguarded buyer paid, while a deterministic price comparison blocked the changed amount. Wallet and network substitution were additional risks discussed, not separately demonstrated comprehensive protections. A correct price alone cannot identify the intended recipient. [Source 1](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-1)

## Enforce the purchase plan, not just the wording

Seller-supplied content is evidence about an offer, not authority to expand the buyer's mandate. In a controlled one-purchase task, a seller suggested a more complete summary elsewhere and the model attempted another purchase. Keyword checks missed indirect suggestions and a model classifier could miss attacks too. A deterministic guard enforcing the approved one-call plan blocked the extra payment even though the agent still requested it. The reported zero successful attacks applies only to that constrained guarded experiment, not general immunity to prompt injection. [Source 5](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-5)

For a legitimate multi-purchase task, approve an appropriately scoped plan instead of applying a universal one-call rule: specify the permitted items or sellers and limits, and require a fresh decision when the proposed action falls outside that scope. This is a purchase-specific control; the broader authority boundary is covered in [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html).

## Separate verification, settlement and fulfillment

A facilitator may verify a payment signature even though settlement later fails, for example because funds are insufficient or state is inconsistent. If the seller has already delivered confidential data, activated a license or provisioned a valuable service, it may be too late to recover the value. Waiting for settlement reduces that exposure but adds latency. For inexpensive, reversible, latency-sensitive output, earlier delivery may be a deliberate business risk; the source supplies no numeric threshold. [Source 2](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-2)

Verification alone also does not make repeated fulfillment safe. Several requests with the same payment identifier may all appear valid before only one settles. Keep shared state for identifiers in progress and completed, and return the saved result for a repeat of the same purchase rather than independently fulfilling it again. Bind the identifier to the specific resource delivered: if a request reuses it for a different paid page, reject the conflict rather than deliver a second item for one payment. The speaker proposes a 409 conflict response. [Source 6](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-6) [Source 7](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-7)

This ledger is a design requirement, not a complete implementation from the source. In particular, multiple workers must not both claim the same identifier before either records it; the talk does not specify atomic claim acquisition, concurrent processing, or a resource-identity schema. Those details need explicit design and testing before the proposed protection can be relied on. [Source 6](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-6)

The buyer faces the inverse risk after a timeout: in the described x402 payment-number flow, a retry with a *new* payment number can be treated as another valid charge for the same desired result. The speaker advises reusing the original payment number across retries. This guidance is specific to that flow, not a complete timeout-recovery procedure or a rule for every payment API. [Source 8](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-8)

## Protect every route to the purchased result

A cryptographically correct payment flow cannot protect a report that is also served by an unprotected endpoint. Inventory all routes intended to be paid, including alternate representations, and request each without payment: the recommended negative test expects payment-required behavior before content is released. The source does not provide an exhaustive route inventory or an automated test implementation. [Source 9](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-9)

Caches are another route. In the scenario discussed, a paid response cached under a public URL was available to later buyers without another payment. Keep cached content behind the authorization check; for confidential, expensive or per-request generated results, consider `Cache-Control: no-store`. The public-cache behavior is specific to the scenario, not a universal HTTP or x402 default, and the talk did not test whether every intermediary obeys the header. Test the actual delivery path rather than treating the header as a guarantee. [Source 10](#payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents-source-10)
