## Tracing and diagnosing production behavior

Evidence capture and root-cause investigation, not a proof of user-visible success. Owns trace collection, privacy, triage, attribution and cost; it does not itself decide release readiness. Owns live discovery and incident handling; release gates and memory maintenance are separate.

A user reports that an agent gave an unhelpful answer. The final response alone cannot tell you whether the agent never called a needed tool, called it with the wrong arguments, received empty results, or ignored useful evidence. A trace connects the interaction to the steps that actually ran, making those competing explanations inspectable. It is evidence for diagnosis, not proof that the user’s task succeeded or that every relevant event was captured. [Source 1](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-1) [Source 2](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-2)

## Capture the execution you need to explain

Treat a task or conversation as a parent trace and the model calls, tool calls, retrievals, and other meaningful operations as nested spans. At each important boundary, capture the input and output or a safe reference to them, the operation’s identity, timing, status, and relevant state changes. Record prompt and model versions, settings, tokens, retries, and costs per attempt. Network logs alone miss local retrieval, in-process tools, and memory operations; instrumenting semantic nodes makes those steps visible too. [Source 3](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-3) [Source 4](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-4) [Source 5](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-5)

Keep enough context to connect an operation to the user's goal, the available tools, prior steps, and any stated reason for the action. These annotations help formulate hypotheses, but an agent’s explanation or reported belief is not verified access to the model’s internal causal reasoning. For a browser workflow, also capture what happened in the browser: a plausible decision log cannot establish that navigation, a download, or a click actually worked. Make the resulting sequence legible to product and support staff as well as engineers. [Source 6](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-6) [Source 7](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-7) [Source 8](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-8)

Correlate components using trace context and relevant domain identifiers: an interaction ID can link a user request to its specialists and dependencies; a payment ID can connect intent, the seller called, and its response. Check context propagation at process boundaries. In one case, passing the parent span ID into a coding-agent subprocess exposed turns and commands that had been orphaned; that solution is an example, not a universal propagation contract. Trace repair agents as well as the application when they investigate or change it. A missing child span remains a visibility gap, not evidence that no action occurred. [Source 9](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-9) [Source 10](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-10) [Source 11](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-11)

### Make evidence queryable and replayable

Attach evaluation results, classifications, and version or task metadata to the trace that produced them. A decline in a quality score can then lead to the individual spans behind it: for example, did a model stop calling the intended tool, or did the tool run and return bad results? Count adoption alongside answer quality and cost; using a tool is not the same as benefiting from it. Query labels to select candidate cases, then inspect inputs, outputs, and contrasting successes. A workshop demonstrated this query-and-drill-down workflow on prepared support traces; filters cannot find unlabelled failures reliably and do not make the retrieved cases representative. [Source 12](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-12) [Source 13](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-13) [Source 14](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-14)

For a hard-to-repeat failure, preserve the recorded decisions and state transitions rather than demanding that a new model call reproduce the same text. Reconstruct the old run, or substitute recorded outputs at selected boundaries while inspecting the remaining behavior. This is useful precisely because a fresh generation can take a different path. Selective replay still depends on what was recorded: live tools, unrecorded external state, or unstubbed model calls can change the result, so it is not automatically deterministic. [Source 15](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-15) [Source 3](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-3)

### Findings must tell someone what to do

When a check blocks a workflow, retain the failed gate, the contract it tested, the reason, and the evidence needed to investigate. Deliver a proposed remediation in the place the responsible person works—for example, alongside a change under review—and preserve a machine-readable finding for issue or security workflows. A readable report helps action; neither its structure nor the gate’s decision proves the underlying finding is correct. [Source 16](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-16) [Source 17](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-17)

Apply the same discipline to CI. Distinguish a suspected flaky test from an infrastructure failure or a likely code defect before responding. A retry may unblock a change but does not repair the flaky test, and an automated classification can be wrong. Aggregate failure categories across changes to decide whether test reliability or infrastructure deserves investment; counts of feature, fix, and refactor PRs describe workflow allocation, not business value. [Source 18](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-18) [Source 19](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-19)

## Move from individual traces to operational patterns

One successful trace is not a picture of production. Compare branch frequencies and their latency, retries, and quality signals; then open examples from both common and rare routes. A rare branch can hide a serious defect, while a frequent but mildly inefficient route can dominate cost. Observed frequencies are only estimates for the traffic and period captured, not permanent properties of the system. [Source 20](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-20)

Track economics at the same task and span level. A cheap model call may produce a costly task if it requires many more calls or tool steps. Record input and output tokens, cached tokens, per-step timing, model selection, and whether interventions such as summarization actually occurred. Tag costs by feature, tenant or organization where appropriate, provider, and environment so teams can compare workloads rather than guess from the total bill. Combine those measures with task-specific quality evidence before deciding on routing, limits, or procurement; cost attribution alone does not establish quality or reconcile a bill. Cost and replay overhead can remain unpredictable even with managed infrastructure. [Source 21](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-21) [Source 22](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-22) [Source 23](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-23) [Source 24](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-24)

Compare a change in failures or latency with an appropriate historical baseline, including workload and load, then overlay model, application, dependency, and configuration changes. This gives an investigator a narrower set of hypotheses—not a proven cause. A change coinciding with a spike might be unrelated; check the affected path and contrasting cases before assigning blame. The proposed baseline-and-change approach in the source does not establish detection thresholds or early-warning accuracy. [Source 25](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-25) [Source 26](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-26)

### Store useful evidence without creating a new exposure

Detailed traces may contain conversation text, nested tool results, or media and must support both fresh incident lookups and large historical searches or annotation. Test those different workloads against actual data and latency needs; a vendor’s scale claims do not establish the right database for every team. Operating a trace platform also means maintaining access controls, masking, and retention—not just displaying a dashboard. [Source 27](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-27) [Source 28](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-28) [Source 29](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-29)

Collect only what a diagnostic purpose warrants. A user can paste sensitive information into free text even when a separate secure collection flow exists. Where possible, remove or mask sensitive input before it reaches retained telemetry; restrict access and test the full capture path, including downstream copies. A proposed scrubber is not a universal guarantee that nothing sensitive will be stored. [Source 30](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-30)

## Find issues, then identify the responsible layer

Start with a change in a known failure category, a deterministic indicator such as a keyword spike, or a broad signal such as user frustration. Use it to retrieve and read examples, including cases the signal may have missed. Inspect cases independently and cluster recurring patterns; domain experts can reject false positives, intended behavior, or irrelevant clusters before work is assigned. Deep inspection can yield cheaper indicators—specific content patterns or tool sequences—for ongoing surveillance. Those indicators inherit the blind spots of their definitions. [Source 31](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-31) [Source 32](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-32) [Source 33](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-33) [Source 34](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-34) [Source 35](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-35)

Make an issue a persistent, reviewable record of a suspected repairable mechanism, with supporting and counterexample traces, onset, affected-user share, severity, and owner. Deduplicating occurrences reduces noise, but do not equate a semantic cluster with an issue: wrong price quotes and wrong refund calculations can look alike while requiring different fixes. Clusters can also drift over time, so revisit their boundaries and distinguish a new mechanism from a recurrence. Prioritize prevalence and impact, while retaining rare high-severity cases. [Source 36](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-36) [Source 37](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-37) [Source 38](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-38)

**Worked source example — planted defect.** In a shopping-agent demonstration, searches used human-readable category names while the stored values were lowercase hyphenated slugs. The trace showed empty results and fallback searches; inspecting the tool arguments alongside the repository’s data contract pointed to normalization, rather than necessarily a weak model. A candidate repair can be checked against the recorded case and other relevant cases. This was an intentionally planted workshop defect, not a measured production failure rate. [Source 39](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-39)

Use that sequence as a diagnostic habit, not a fixed answer: compare the request and tool arguments, the actual result, the implementation or service behavior, and the final outcome. A bad result might come from an incorrect prompt example, a tool interface, sandbox execution, an upstream provider, an inference failure, or a product expectation the system never supported. Route a supported model gap to model evaluation, an interface or infrastructure defect to engineering, and a missing capability or expectation mismatch to product. Do not infer that every bad answer is an engine bug, or that an accessible sandbox automatically explains a failure. [Source 40](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-40) [Source 41](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-41) [Source 42](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-42) [Source 43](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-43)

## Run diagnosis as an operational loop

An incident playbook connects detection to an accountable responder, trace-based diagnosis, containment, repair, and regression checks. If appropriate for the service, containment might mean rolling back a change or routing affected work to a person while the cause is investigated. Join the report and trace to the relevant code or dependency; write down the hypothesis, supporting evidence, missing context, and assumptions. Persist intermediate artifacts so another investigator can resume or challenge the analysis. A coding agent can prepare evidence or a proposed fix, but a plausible report is not a verified diagnosis, and larger fixes may need human leadership and review. [Source 44](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-44) [Source 45](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-45) [Source 46](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-46) [Source 47](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-47)

Choose the trigger to match the question. An engineer can investigate on demand; a periodic sweep can find patterns that no single alert captures; a quality, latency, or cost alert can initiate a faster targeted investigation. A short-window monitor for stuck sessions and a slower cross-session analysis answer different questions, so use both when warranted. Set thresholds and cadence for the application rather than copying a demo threshold. The described modes have not been shown equally reliable or inexpensive. [Source 48](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-48) [Source 49](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-49) [Source 50](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-50)

After repair, feed the diagnosed case and its relevant variants into offline development and regression evaluation, then continue reviewing live usage for new patterns. Post-merge observation can reveal surprises tests missed, but cannot undo an irreversible action or replace preventive controls. Code throughput and deployment counts are activity or downstream signals, not proof of stability or user benefit. For how to maintain production-grounded cases, see [Learning from production evidence and regression tests](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/learning-from-production.html); release decisions have their own owner in [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html). [Source 51](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-51) [Source 52](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-52) [Source 53](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-53) [Source 54](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-54)

### Read success and feedback carefully

A tool returning HTTP success may still return empty or irrelevant content. A completed task can have a wrong price or fail the user’s actual intent; a successful final answer can also conceal repeated failures and lucky recovery. Examine the content and intermediate struggles as well as availability and error status. A toy shopping demonstration exposed empty results despite successful spans; its small uncontrolled results do not establish a production failure rate. [Source 55](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-55) [Source 56](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-56) [Source 57](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-57)

Collect reviewer overrides, their reasons, and feedback on cited evidence in the normal review workflow. Changes in override frequency or review time can direct investigation, but an override is not automatically a correct label, and a long review may have several explanations. Likewise, clicks, copies, and user ratings are behavior or feedback signals, not correctness measurements. [Source 58](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-58) [Source 59](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-59) [Source 60](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-60)

Repeated requests, complaints, and abandonment can suggest a user is stuck; absence of further messages does not establish resolution. Investigate whether the task is supported but needs better guidance, or whether the product has a bug or missing feature. For sessions genuinely resolved, examine what information would have helped earlier, generalize across similar examples, and have reviewers check the proposed guidance before introducing it. That is a reported workflow, not proof that guidance caused the observed outcomes; ongoing knowledge maintenance belongs to [Maintaining agent context, memory and knowledge](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/reliable-agent-context-and-memory.html). [Source 61](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-61) [Source 62](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-62) [Source 63](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-63)

Agents can also report environmental friction: a selective feedback tool may surface missing tools, conflicting instructions, or platform failures, while an end-of-run retrospective asks every run and may find issues a thresholded report omits. Neither method has a demonstrated universal signal-quality advantage. In one reported case, continued complaints after a filename fix exposed non-breaking spaces that ordinary-space handling had missed; developers reviewed proposed fixes. Spikes in complaints can be incident leads, but fallible, incomplete self-reports do not replace independent monitoring. [Source 64](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-64) [Source 65](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-65) [Source 66](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-66) [Source 67](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-67) [Source 68](#agent-observability-and-diagnosis-source-68)

## Learning from production evidence and regression tests

Improvement processes and feedback, not raw execution controls. Behavioral suites and predeployment evidence rather than continuous production monitoring. Owns task verification, comparisons and replay; incident management is separate.

A production trace is evidence about what happened, not an automatic specification of what should happen next. A useful improvement loop moves from observed behavior to a reviewed hypothesis, a repeatable test, a candidate change and comparative evidence. It preserves uncertainty at each step: a cluster may be misleading, a regression suite is finite, and passing it is not the same as authorization to release.

## Construct repeatable behavioral evidence

Ask domain experts to create diagnostic cases, expected outcomes, a rubric and held-out references. Run candidates against the same instrument after a prompt, model or skill change, retaining individual outcomes as well as aggregates. Automated scoring can provide an initial pass; experts remain needed for disputed cases and interpretation. One team described a roughly 200-task nightly suite, but its reported aggregate comparison lacks uncertainty and per-task regression details. The expert-instrument proposal likewise does not establish judge calibration or deployment outcomes. [Source 1](#learning-from-production-source-1) [Source 2](#learning-from-production-source-2)

Make results available to the decision process rather than treating a favorable average as approval. The thresholds, exceptions and promotion authority belong to [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html); continued observation after deployment is a different activity. No finite offline suite proves safety outside its coverage. [Source 3](#learning-from-production-source-3)

## Train recovery from observed disruptions

A training environment that silently resets after a tool or infrastructure error may never exercise the recovery behavior a user needs. Preserve the disruption in the task and evaluate whether the agent refreshes, backtracks, compares state, waits, abandons or escalates as appropriate. Gather failures under protective operation, then reconstruct representative tasks and decide what successful recovery and its reward should mean. For instance, an **illustrative** expired-session case could require the agent to stop and request reauthentication rather than repeatedly submitting the same action. [Source 4](#learning-from-production-source-4) [Source 5](#learning-from-production-source-5)

Turning user feedback into faithful environments and reward signals is still an open engineering and research problem; the cited approach does not isolate a reliability gain. A proposed thinner future harness is not evidence that safeguards can be removed. Live recovery limits and independent enforcement are covered by [Running and resuming agent sessions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-sessions-and-long-running-work.html) and [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 6](#learning-from-production-source-6)

## Discover patterns, then review what they mean

Known scores detect known failure categories; examining many interactions together can expose recurring frustrations or goals that the existing rubric never anticipated. A useful discovery pipeline selects trace material, applies a facet such as task or issue, summarizes it, embeds the summaries and groups similar representations. Each choice affects what can appear: if relevant tool metadata is omitted during preprocessing, an issue may disappear before clustering begins. Review representative underlying interactions before turning a cluster into a requirement or a new regression case. Clusters are leads, not proof of novelty or error. [Source 7](#learning-from-production-source-7) [Source 8](#learning-from-production-source-8) [Source 9](#learning-from-production-source-9)

In a synthetic support workshop, a generic issues facet yielded no topic, while a custom support-workflow facet surfaced record-lookup failures. The product required at least 100 matching facet outputs at the time: too few matches and an ill-fitting representation were different possible explanations for an empty result. That cutoff was product-specific, not a general statistical rule; the workshop did not measure discovery recall. [Source 10](#learning-from-production-source-10)

Once reviewed, a failure can become a case with an explicit expected outcome and a suitable evaluation method. The complementary work of selecting and maintaining production-derived examples is detailed in [Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html).

### Maintain skills through reviewed changes

Separate the agent doing a task from a maintenance process that examines its outcomes and human corrections. In an issue-triage case, the maintenance agent gathered reactions and comments and proposed a versioned skill change for human review. A shared procedure should have a named owner and a reviewer other than its author, because rules and workflows change and one mistake can repeat across future work. Human review is a safeguard, not a measured guarantee; reactions can be noisy or contradictory. A proposal to consolidate experiences into skills also illustrates why stale SQL-column guidance needs revision, but its suggested consolidation counts were inconsistent and should not be treated as a threshold. [Source 11](#learning-from-production-source-11) [Source 12](#learning-from-production-source-12) [Source 13](#learning-from-production-source-13) [Source 14](#learning-from-production-source-14) [Source 15](#learning-from-production-source-15)

### Share experiments without losing history

Domain experts need appropriate access to inspect traces and try controlled changes, not an engineering export for every question. A demonstrated remote evaluation exposed selected prompt, tool-description and model parameters while execution stayed on the server and results returned to a playground. Keep source assets, versions, authorship and synchronization under change control even when a managed interface makes experiments accessible. The demonstration does not specify a complete authentication or promotion policy. [Source 16](#learning-from-production-source-16) [Source 17](#learning-from-production-source-17) [Source 18](#learning-from-production-source-18)

### Revisit the objective, not just the implementation

A candidate can improve a fixed score while missing what users value. Compare qualitative feedback, behavior and product outcomes with the rubric and ask whether the proxy needs a new dimension. Keep the existing evaluation stable for an apples-to-apples comparison of candidates, then version a revised objective separately so the reason for a changed score is visible. Automatically turning feedback into a faithful objective is proposed research, not a validated procedure. [Source 19](#learning-from-production-source-19)

## Broaden and place tests deliberately

Keep behavioral specifications and unit, integration and penetration tests versioned independently of a particular agent framework. On migration, run the same obligations against the new implementation instead of redefining success to match it. This is a design recommendation; the source does not demonstrate a finished portable specification format. [Source 20](#learning-from-production-source-20)

Generate domain-grounded synthetic edge cases before customer records are available, for example a difficult but plausible support-policy boundary reviewed by an expert. They accelerate iteration when real examples are sensitive or scarce, but cover only modeled scenarios; passing generated cases alone cannot establish real-world coverage or authorize shipping. [Source 21](#learning-from-production-source-21) [Source 22](#learning-from-production-source-22)

Security testing adds a different evidence stream. A proposed process brings context-sensitive offensive checks closer to code changes, validates candidate exploits and gives developers actionable remediation guidance. More frequent scans or findings do not demonstrate coverage, and the source shows neither a completed automatic patch nor successful retest. Retest the fix rather than equating a report with remediation. [Source 23](#learning-from-production-source-23) [Source 24](#learning-from-production-source-24)

Execution and scoring can live in different places: a candidate might run locally and send outputs to a separate evaluation service. Record candidate execution failure separately from evaluator failure. In a demonstration a code evaluator failed and an LLM judge was used instead; that fallback was not shown to have equivalent validity. [Source 25](#learning-from-production-source-25)

## Evaluate the whole task, not just the final sentence

Use different checks for different questions. Deterministic checks can validate syntax, counts and required fields; semantic evaluation addresses meaning and grounding; behavioral checks inspect tool selection, loops and repeated actions. Post-processing can enforce a length or reference-count rule, but neither a valid structure nor a good-looking answer establishes factual correctness. One small thread-summary experiment reported structural success after post-processing; its size and partly model-derived labels limit generalization. [Source 26](#learning-from-production-source-26) [Source 27](#learning-from-production-source-27)

Also check completion against every requested deliverable. A polished response may stop halfway. If a research assignment requires both a user-facing scorecard and a durable memory update, inspect both artifacts and their substantive content rather than crediting a fluent opening. The cited financial demonstration did not independently verify the scorecard values or supply a complete rubric. [Source 28](#learning-from-production-source-28) [Source 29](#learning-from-production-source-29)

## Compare changes under realistic conditions

Running the same agent code in simulation and production reduces implementation drift; one team reported synchronizing the two environments. It does not make simulated users, data, external tools or failures realistic. Document those differences when interpreting offline results, and use customer-perspective checks as a complement: a browser-using agent can exercise the visible interface and reveal issues absent from code or logs, though computer use adds latency and token cost and the cited account does not establish broad coverage. [Source 30](#learning-from-production-source-30) [Source 31](#learning-from-production-source-31)

A telemetry trace usually records emitted events, while an execution checkpoint aims to retain enough state—such as variables, files, code and environment—to resume. Tracing systems differ, so verify what your own record captures. A checkpoint can support a controlled branch: restore the same point, change one factor such as a model or policy lookup, then compare decisions and artifacts as well as cost. Confirm replay fidelity and avoid treating the branch as proof of what production would have done. [Source 32](#learning-from-production-source-32) [Source 33](#learning-from-production-source-33) [Source 34](#learning-from-production-source-34)

In a vendor demonstration, a cheaper-model replay looked equivalent on one case, but a subsequent cohort verdict was not to ship. The cohort size, grading and raw results were not given; the lesson is to challenge the attractive example with broader evidence, not to infer a population effect from the demo. [Source 35](#learning-from-production-source-35)

Finally, test whether injected knowledge helps rather than assuming more context is better. One team described withholding an otherwise relevant entry from a small comparison group and comparing downstream project success with the injected group. Use such evidence to reconsider or retire stale entries after model or product changes, but the account lacks effect sizes and a full assignment and analysis design, so it does not establish a causal effect. [Source 36](#learning-from-production-source-36) [Source 37](#learning-from-production-source-37)

## Maintaining agent context, memory and knowledge

Knowledge and retrieval state, not transactional execution guarantees. Owns retention, retrieval and maintenance of working knowledge; external-source provenance is separate. Procedural knowledge and recurring jobs, not generic trace storage. Owns reusable knowledge lifecycle; working-session context belongs to execution.

An agent does not remember a fact merely because it mentioned it. Reliable reuse requires a place where the fact is owned, a way to find it again, and a reason to trust it for the next task. That place might be a project record, a source document, a worklog, or a curated memory store. The material in the current prompt is only the working view of that larger body of knowledge.

The design challenge is to carry forward enough context to avoid repeated discovery without turning yesterday’s guesses into today’s unquestioned instructions. Knowledge continuity is also distinct from resuming an execution or retaining authority: see [Running and resuming agent sessions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-sessions-and-long-running-work.html) and [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html).

## Make project knowledge recoverable

For each fact a later task may need, name its system of record and the path by which a person or agent can recover it. A friendly acknowledgement is not proof that the fact was stored. Record a finding in the issue system, a code decision in the project’s maintained documentation, or a task-specific lesson in a memory store linked to the investigation. A recurring diagnostic agent can then revisit earlier weak signals as evidence accumulates instead of treating every run as a clean slate. This supports continuity, not an automatic guarantee that the old conclusion remains correct. [Source 1](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-1) [Source 2](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-2)

A shared code index and project memory can give different coding tools a common retrieval layer; one reported implementation indexes locally, but that does not establish that downstream model requests stay local. Starting a fresh session can encourage useful decisions to be written somewhere discoverable, but it is a practitioner’s preference, not a rule: continuing a session may be more convenient, especially with larger contexts and better retrieval. [Source 3](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-3) [Source 4](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-4)

Preserve reasons as well as outcomes. A decision record should say what was chosen, why, and how the rule is meant to be enforced, with references to relevant evidence or checks. A worklog adds the changing situation: the plan, attempts, evaluations, fixes, results, and surprises. The plan alone cannot tell a successor what actually happened. One practitioner reports that a fresh session resumed a presentation from a worklog; another describes timestamped breadcrumbs for later agents. These are handoff practices, not measured guarantees of continuity. Documentation does not itself enforce a rule; link it to actual checks where appropriate. [Source 5](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-5) [Source 6](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-6) [Source 7](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-7)

Important decisions that remain discoverable can also help after compaction. One speaker reports tolerating repeated compactions because decisions could be looked up again, but that personal experience does not establish lossless retrieval or a safe universal compaction policy. Indefinitely appending everything is not a maintenance strategy either: longer-lived memory may need revision and compression, an area for which the proposed lifetime-scale architectures remain unsettled. [Source 8](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-8) [Source 9](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-9)

## Retrieve the right shape of evidence

Different questions call for different retrieval operations. An overview search can show the landscape; detailed semantic retrieval exposes the content of a few promising matches; metadata filters restrict a search to an appropriate time, project, or category; exact matching finds a known identifier or phrase. One harness reports overview summaries of up to 50 chunks and full semantic content for its top 10, plus filtering and grep. Those numbers describe that harness, not optimal defaults. The decision is about the information shape needed for the task, not a universal preference for semantic search. [Source 10](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-10)

Task relevance also matters within memory. A refund workflow may need the procedural lesson to check settlement before refunding, not an unrelated interface preference. That example illustrates a policy rationale rather than a measured financial deployment. [Source 11](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-11)

### Build grounded, inspectable context

Where structure can be computed, derive it before asking a model to interpret it. For data transformations, parse the implementation to identify lineage and grain, then profile actual data to check properties such as key uniqueness. SQL parsing alone cannot prove that real join keys are unique. Only after those steps ask narrow semantic questions—for example, classify one column using its type, comments, and local context—and retain the output for inspection and correction. A grounded summary can still be wrong. [Source 12](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-12) [Source 13](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-13)

A context graph is one way to persist typed assets and relationships with their supporting evidence, so an agent can fetch a relevant dependency subgraph rather than reconstructing an entire system. It can connect catalog facts and warehouse profiles to transformation models; it does not replace the catalog. Update relationships as their sources change. The workshop’s educational graph is not the production implementation, and its broader cross-system workflow was an incomplete vision. A graph is an option, not a prerequisite for all useful project memory. [Source 14](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-14) [Source 15](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-15)

For each curated memory, retain its source run, version and scope, permit correction or deletion, and record which memories a later run used. A decision record can connect evidence and policy to the plan, tool calls, results and cost; sharing relevant records with other agents or human teammates can make prior work reusable. These records describe observable execution, not faithful access to the model’s internal reasoning. Shared context does not by itself establish safe access controls or improved multi-agent outcomes. In one memory demonstration, the source-run link was partly blocked, and a claimed speedup was not controlled. [Source 16](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-16) [Source 17](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-17) [Source 18](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-18) [Source 19](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-19)

### Let outcomes inform retrieval, cautiously

A trace and a score become useful memory only if a later run can use the lesson. One proposed loop converts evaluated outcomes into guidance for selecting context or broadening a future search. Initially, before enough reviews exist, the described system falls back to semantic search; the source does not establish how many reviews or how much diversity are enough, and noisy feedback can mislead. [Source 20](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-20) [Source 21](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-21)

In a demonstration, a gaming-mouse search first returned nothing; after feedback pointed to a wireless mouse, a later run searched more broadly and returned related inventory. The informative observation is the changed tool trajectory, not merely a different answer. The example has no held-out test and does not prove the returned product met all gaming requirements. [Source 22](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-22)

## Keep long work usable without keeping everything in the prompt

### Recover omitted session material

Compression must preserve a way back to information that a later turn may need. In one reported system, keeping only the first 100 characters made follow-ups lose their referents: after an answer about common inputs, a question about input B looked like a new conversation. An unconstrained model summary also inconsistently omitted important details. These are failures of particular implementations, not proof that all summaries fail. [Source 23](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-23) [Source 24](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-24)

The team’s compromise kept the first and last 100 characters of long material, stored the omitted middle, preserved the system prompt and latest results, and exposed IDs, positions and previews for fetching earlier messages or tool calls. This makes omission different from deletion, although the agent must still recognize when to retrieve. The team reported months of usefulness while revisiting the heuristic; neither fragment length nor retrieval accuracy was established as generally optimal. Test follow-ups that refer to earlier results, not just whether the first response fits the window. [Source 25](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-25) [Source 26](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-26)

A store of omitted messages within one session is not automatically cross-chat memory. At the time of that account, a new conversation could not recall previously discussed issues; ID storage also did not establish prompt-cache reuse. For execution lifecycle rather than knowledge retention, see [Running and resuming agent sessions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-sessions-and-long-running-work.html). [Source 27](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-27) [Source 26](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-26)

### Isolate heavy analysis

A trace-analysis agent can generate more spans while investigating its own failures. Retrying against that growing input can make the original overload worse. One team moved searches over hundreds of spans and intermediate results into a separate subagent context; the main conversation received a compact result and could retrieve more material as needed. This is a context boundary, not evidence that adding agents inherently improves reasoning. The reported improvement was qualitative, and provider-limit failures remained. For coordination choices beyond this boundary, see [Choosing agent delegation and coordination](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-delegation-and-coordination.html). [Source 28](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-28) [Source 29](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-29)

## Turn experience into maintained knowledge

A memory lifecycle can ingest an experience, extract candidate facts, consolidate them, and retrieve the resulting information later. Different records serve different purposes: a critique and a user’s accepted exception can help a later polishing session, while a prior failed query can inform a shared organizational librarian. Human overrides, low-confidence moments and clarifying questions can identify candidate guidance updates. None of these observations proves that an entry is correct, current, or safe to generalize; the reported systems do not establish a universal consolidation policy or quantified improvement. Updating surrounding guidance is not necessarily updating model weights. [Source 30](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-30) [Source 31](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-31) [Source 32](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-32) [Source 33](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-33)

### Combine examples, rules and review

Episodic memory offers a particular previously labeled case as a reference. Semantic memory states a reusable rule, such as a customer-specific distinction clarified by reviewers. They complement each other: retrieve a genuinely comparable precedent, apply the current rule, and send an unresolved or poorly matched case to a person. The proposed allocation depends on retrieval and escalation identifying those cases correctly; the source gives no verified similarity threshold. Customer-specific security judgments should not be generalized into universal policy. [Source 34](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-34) [Source 35](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-35) [Source 36](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-36)

Persisted errors can repeatedly mislead. Offline consolidation can compare memories with prior traces, correct false or overly local conclusions, and retain abstractions useful beyond one task. A selected Pokémon example reports five of five raw-memory runs falling through a trapdoor after a wrong location was stored; an offline correction enabled progress in the illustrated case. This is not a general success rate. A comparison of different model generations also suggests that the ability to write useful memories matters, but does not isolate model capability as the cause. Evaluate the quality and compute cost of consolidation in the actual application rather than assuming a net gain. [Source 37](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-37) [Source 38](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-38) [Source 39](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-39) [Source 40](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-40)

### Close gaps without exhausting experts

Use a concrete task to expose a missing definition or procedure, ask the responsible expert targeted questions, and curate the answer so the next task can retrieve it. One demonstration used prepared answers and flat files standing in for enterprise systems; it is not evidence of enterprise-wide completeness. An audience concern was that agents can keep asking follow-ups and overload staff, while tickets themselves may be incomplete. The speaker therefore favored starting with one small team and an available expert, bounding the questions, and repairing context offline before operational retrieval. The reported couple of weeks concerned discovering gaps, not necessarily filling them. [Source 41](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-41) [Source 42](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-42) [Source 43](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-43)

Observed user demand can expose a different gap: one sales-assistant account describes using frequent questions and product material to create enablement content and return it to retrieval. The account does not demonstrate content approval, factual checking, or a measured accuracy gain. In a separate reported banking incident, a changed interest-rate policy had not reached the vector index; traces led the team to repair freshness instead of replacing the model. For source ingestion and external provenance, see [Managing production retrieval, data and provenance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/retrieval-evidence-and-provenance.html). [Source 44](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-44) [Source 45](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-45)

## Design and distribute reusable procedures

A skill or playbook packages instructions for an applicable kind of work. Keep a maintained map to current authoritative documentation for volatile details, rather than duplicating an entire changing API reference. Conversely, keep stable safety-critical guidance visible where it is needed: agents may skip a reference. An example product workflow changes a database schema in development or staging, runs security and performance advisors, fixes their findings, and only then creates a migration. It is not permission to make unrestricted production changes. [Source 46](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-46) [Source 47](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-47)

Route instructions by task and audience. For example, a rule favoring distinctive typography on a brand landing page may conflict with a native-feeling product interface; separate instructions avoid turning either into a universal ban. The reported benefit is not a quantified comparison with a monolithic prompt. Relevant accessibility guidance should be reliably loaded for UI generation, but the cited recommendation did not demonstrate a complete mandatory-loading mechanism, and instruction exposure is neither enforcement nor a substitute for manual accessibility testing. [Source 48](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-48) [Source 49](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-49)

Task-specific catalogs can preserve confirmed patterns and antipatterns across projects and model changes. A shared human-readable repository may be sufficient to start; a vector database is not mandatory. Bringing confirmed knowledge into authoring or review earlier is a proposal that may also increase latency and context cost. One practitioner’s build-versus-buy heuristic favors buying generic infrastructure and building local practices, while acknowledging ambiguous cases rather than proving a cost advantage. [Source 50](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-50) [Source 51](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-51) [Source 52](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-52)

Content portability is not distribution compatibility. Repository packages, plugins and central services are different ways to make skills discoverable, and some formats are environment-specific. A described central service selects organizational skills by query and role; verify actual client support and policy behavior instead of assuming universal compatibility or always-current delivery. Version packages and their dependencies so a procedure matched to one product version is not silently applied to another. [Source 53](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-53) [Source 54](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-54) [Source 55](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-55)

### Distill a skill from evidence, not just a topic

Choose a coherent source scope first: a conversation, an entity-centered subgraph, or another bounded collection may fit better than an entire workspace. Structural processing can organize that source while limited language generation synthesizes descriptions. In one described pipeline, most steps were asserted to be deterministic, but the full pipeline and its reliability were not independently established. [Source 56](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-56) [Source 57](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-57)

Check support for each instruction and step, not just whether the overall topic has sources. A patient-intake demonstration linked a previously generated skill’s steps to tool calls and entities; it did not show successful execution or clinical validation. If the selected graph spans unrelated communities, splitting the skill may improve coherence, but community detection is only a heuristic and step-level provenance alone cannot prove completeness. [Source 58](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-58) [Source 59](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-59)

## Operate knowledge as a maintained system

### Ownership, versioning and freshness

Assign knowledgeable owners to shared instructions, review changes, and update or retire skills when products or workflows change. An accessibility specialist maintaining a reusable skill is one reported example; another account notes that writing a review skill is much easier than running it consistently and economically at scale. A large experimental collection can be useful locally while a production environment carries only the maintained set it needs. A repository and pull-request review are one collaborative option, not proof that repositories outperform other stores. [Source 60](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-60) [Source 61](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-61) [Source 62](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-62) [Source 63](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-63)

Version not only the skill text but also the relevant instructions, source material, model and configuration used in a run. For each change, record the failure that prompted it and the intended correction; a diff without rationale may be hard to interpret later. Versioning enables comparison and rollback, not deterministic replay across changing models or proof that a new rule is correct. [Source 64](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-64) [Source 65](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-65)

Age and duplicate flags identify candidates for review, not truth: an old document may still be correct and a newly updated one may be wrong. Track dependencies from skills to their underlying evidence, and flag changed, removed or contradictory sources; the proposed mechanism does not prove automatic repair. Keep graph edges and evaluation expectations current too: in one impact-assessment case, new consumers appeared between an evaluation’s authoring and execution. A newer model can also confidently repeat an obsolete product reference. Check current documentation and retire stale or irrelevant context rather than assuming a model upgrade fixes it. [Source 66](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-66) [Source 67](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-67) [Source 68](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-68) [Source 69](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-69) [Source 70](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-70) [Source 71](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-71)

### Repair procedures from feedback

Review recurring failures, corrections and trace patterns for a specific reusable lesson; propose a change to the applicable playbook, have an owner review it, and make the reviewed version available to later runs. One team reported putting reviewer steering in a version-controlled feedback file loaded into subsequent runs. The account does not quantify recurrence reduction or explain conflict resolution. A skill update described for new sessions does not establish that already-running sessions receive it automatically. [Source 72](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-72) [Source 73](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-73)

Track whether rules are used and whether users find them useful, not just how often they fire; frequency alone is not validated utility. Failure-triggered repair avoids routine probing cost but discovers drift after a user-visible failure. Scheduled sample runs or audits can find problems earlier at ongoing cost; the cited healing and audit workflows are proposals or working theories, not established guarantees. Production-derived regression sets have a separate lifecycle: [Build and maintain production-grounded evaluation sets](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/build-and-maintain-production-grounded-evaluation-sets.html). [Source 74](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-74) [Source 75](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-75) [Source 76](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-76)

Reserve capacity for this work. Agent and harness failures compete with feature delivery, and their timing and repair effort are hard to predict. Explicit prioritization can help avoid maintenance being silently dropped or displacing a deadline; the evidence does not prescribe a staffing percentage. [Source 77](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-77)

### Choose stores and protect what they contain

Choose the simplest inspectable substrate that supports the required scope and operations. One team reported a separate Markdown file per user, capped at 8,000 characters and updated after sessions; that is a local design, not a validated universal limit. Files and databases can both offer programmable memory, and one speaker found overly prescriptive schemas restrictive in their setting; this does not mean structured schemas always fail. User and organizational stores can be combined, but export through an API does not prove a drop-in migration, and the cited account does not specify authorization or tenant isolation. [Source 78](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-78) [Source 79](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-79) [Source 80](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-80)

Workflow definitions themselves may disclose valuable institutional procedures, not just the data processed by them. Private deployment with approved models is an option when appropriate, but keeping textual workflows on premises does not by itself establish privacy, security or regulatory compliance. Apply the relevant access and isolation controls separately: [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 81](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-81)

### Give experts and recurring work a durable home

Domain owners should be able to maintain the logic they understand. In one reported pipeline, a clinician could add a customer-specific intake-form skill without an engineering code change. That illustrates an editing interface, not a complete clinical governance process, skill schema or regression suite. Expert ownership still needs reviewed changes and appropriate verification. [Source 82](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-82)

For recurring work whose desired output is understood, bind a reusable procedure or contract to an event or schedule. Start with one bounded job—such as a proposed weekly flaky-test hunt—rather than forcing an exploratory, one-off question into a fixed obligation. A CI iteration that produces a reviewable change is a possible hosting pattern, but the cited example does not provide complete security or authorization controls; triggering a job is not approval to deploy its output. [Source 83](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-83) [Source 84](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-84) [Source 85](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-85) [Source 86](#reliable-agent-context-and-memory-source-86)

### Source 86: Loop Engineering from First Principles — Kyle Mistele, HumanLayer

Evidence: speaker_guidance. The transcript does not provide workflow code or security controls; it describes a deployment pattern rather than a turnkey safe CI configuration.

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xIt_mTQp6mY) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/xIt_mTQp6mY.md#L145-L147)

## Operating secure, governed agent environments

Security-specific threats and controls, distinct from general release decisions. Workload execution, access and infrastructure testing rather than semantic product quality.

A secure agent environment is an operating system of people, tools, data, policies and evidence—not just a sandbox or a prompt. Controls should make actual activity visible, constrain consequential actions, and test whether the environment supports the intended workload. None of these measures alone proves containment or complete security.

## Discover what is running and govern what changes

Build an inventory of actual agent activity, not just approved applications or employee-initiated chats. A gateway collecting session and tool-call records can reveal scheduled, triggered and SaaS-connected agents; map the observed systems to tasks, owners and risks. The inventory covers what its collection points can see, not necessarily personal devices or other uninstrumented paths. One organization reported more than 300 daily agents in a company of roughly 50–60 people, using a broad, unaudited definition; it is an illustration of the possible discovery gap, not a prevalence estimate. [Source 1](#security-and-agent-operations-source-1)

Separately, maintain an AI bill of materials covering models, datasets, dependencies and tools. Compare each build with an approved baseline: an unexpected addition should stop the build for review before an authorized baseline update. This governs changes to the deployed inventory, whereas activity discovery asks what is actually being used. The cited presenter showed an inventory interface but did not demonstrate the separate baseline CI action running. [Source 2](#security-and-agent-operations-source-2) For deeper dependency risks see [Agent and Dependency Supply-Chain Security](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-and-dependency-supply-chain-security.html).

Restrictions without a workable alternative can push activity into personal accounts or devices. Offer approved tools and a justified exception path, and explain concrete risks such as unauthorized data transfer while retaining enforceable boundaries. The cited workaround stories are anecdotes; the effectiveness of education or any claimed reduction is not established by a controlled study. [Source 3](#security-and-agent-operations-source-3) [Source 4](#security-and-agent-operations-source-4) [Source 5](#security-and-agent-operations-source-5)

## Make runtime activity observable without preserving authority

A run may produce issues, traces or learned artifacts worth retaining after its sandbox is torn down and its credentials and repository access removed. The distinction is continuity of knowledge versus continuity of authority: a later run can use reviewed findings without inheriting old access automatically. The described architecture does not establish a credential-isolation or retention policy, and retained artifacts themselves need review. [Source 6](#security-and-agent-operations-source-6)

Users may not see every background action. Action logs and a separate monitor can flag unexpected behavior such as an attempt to access secret storage, providing a basis for investigation even when nobody watches continuously. The proposal has no measured alert quality or detection latency and is not a preventive guarantee. [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html) covers enforcement boundaries. [Source 7](#security-and-agent-operations-source-7)

Visibility also creates privacy exposure. When raw prompts and responses cannot be exported, send categorical evaluation results instead: aggregate signals remain available, but diagnosing an individual failure becomes harder. Private hosting is another option where richer inspection is allowed. Categories and metadata can themselves reveal sensitive information; minimizing raw content is not a privacy guarantee. [Source 8](#security-and-agent-operations-source-8)

## Review artifacts and act on findings

Let developers scan agent skills locally for quick feedback, then repeat current checks at the authoritative distribution boundary. A local pass may be missing or stale by upload time. Backfill the historical catalog too: a new gate cannot retroactively examine artifacts already published. Distinguish numbers of findings from numbers of affected skills, because one skill can contain several findings. The cited first-party program did not establish scanner precision or complete coverage, including across alternative distribution channels. [Source 9](#security-and-agent-operations-source-9) [Source 10](#security-and-agent-operations-source-10)

Triage involves two different questions: is the finding valid, and should it block release? In one demonstrated product, an accepted finding is valid but nonblocking, a confirmed finding affects quality gates, and a false positive is marked separately. Those labels are product-specific, not a universal taxonomy. Record the risk decision and remediation owner rather than treating nonblocking as equivalent to invalid; broader release acceptance belongs to [Production governance, readiness and release](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/production-governance-and-release.html). [Source 11](#security-and-agent-operations-source-11)

## Protect transactions and changing counterparties

In the described x402 payment-number flow, a buyer retrying after an ambiguous timeout should reuse the same payment number: issuing a new number may create a second independently valid charge. On the seller side, repeated requests with the same verified payment number can otherwise receive multiple valuable responses even though only one payment settles. Shared state should distinguish pending and completed IDs and return the saved result rather than perform independent fulfillment again. These are complementary protections against duplicate charging and duplicate delivery, not interchangeable controls. The seller example does not specify atomic locking; concurrent requests require a concurrency-safe implementation. This retry advice is specific to the described flow, not every payment API. [Source 12](#security-and-agent-operations-source-12) [Source 13](#security-and-agent-operations-source-13)

A strict seller allowlist can limit exposure but makes discovery difficult and can become stale as legitimate domains, wallets or prices change. A proposed alternative maintains approved, blocked and probationary categories, with human review of new identities and interactions. The proposal does not define what probation permits or establish a safe review interval; an operator must decide those constraints rather than assuming discovery itself implies trust. See [Payment and Purchase Security for Agents](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/payment-and-purchase-security-for-agents.html) for the wider purchase boundary. [Source 14](#security-and-agent-operations-source-14)

## Prepare data, documentation and execution

Before assigning autonomous work, check that the underlying records, people, infrastructure and governance can support the intended outcome. A fluent interface cannot recover missing comparable outcomes from records that never captured them. For large mixed-media records, one described approach preprocesses PDFs and images, extracts information, and human-verifies a summary before higher-level analysis. A benchmark starting with clean data does not validate OCR, extraction or cleanup upstream. [Source 15](#security-and-agent-operations-source-15) [Source 16](#security-and-agent-operations-source-16)

Make the working environment usable as well as controlled: clear documentation, understandable data relationships, modular code, reliable tests and an environment that can execute changes. Identify the specific CLI, API and log access needed and resolve production-data governance before granting access. Placing a debugging sandbox inside a private network is one deployment option for sensitive connections, not proof of isolation or compliance. These are readiness considerations, not a validated readiness score. [Source 17](#security-and-agent-operations-source-17) [Source 18](#security-and-agent-operations-source-18) [Source 19](#security-and-agent-operations-source-19)

Check documentation through the agent’s actual retrieval path. A page that looks complete in a browser may omit important content for a fetcher if that content appears only after JavaScript runs. Inspect what the agent receives rather than assuming either that all crawlers fail or that a particular page format is universally required. [Source 20](#security-and-agent-operations-source-20)

## Test the workload through the deployed interface

Test complete workflows through the same interface agents will use, both locally and in the remote deployment environment. A code interpreter and a cloud browser stress different primitives: package execution and PDF creation are not the same workload as opening tabs, filling forms or downloading screenshots. Use generated exploratory workflows to find surprises, but retain deterministic checks and useful oracles. A team’s thousand generated tests were an arbitrary wide net, not evidence of representative coverage or a validated detection rate. Queryable result storage can make large runs manageable; the example’s SQLite usage did not disclose its schema or concurrency safeguards. [Source 21](#security-and-agent-operations-source-21) [Source 22](#security-and-agent-operations-source-22) [Source 23](#security-and-agent-operations-source-23) [Source 24](#security-and-agent-operations-source-24) [Source 25](#security-and-agent-operations-source-25)

Check artifact integrity, not merely successful API calls. In one test an uploaded image differed after download; the team traced the mismatch to an encoding layer in the tool wrapper. The source does not specify the exact comparison or repair. Browser workloads also ran out of sandbox memory when opening tabs, with no allocation or failure denominator reported. Both failures show why a model-level diagnosis alone can miss environmental causes. [Source 26](#security-and-agent-operations-source-26) [Source 27](#security-and-agent-operations-source-27)

Exercise filesystem read, write and execute permissions, mounts and persistence; check process creation, installed package discovery and memory under realistic workloads. If a workflow requires a particular tool or skill, preflight it and stop if missing rather than silently changing the task. An instruction-level preflight is not an independently proven security boundary. Failing a workload under a restriction is a reason to diagnose and design an appropriate solution, not to remove the restriction indiscriminately. [Source 28](#security-and-agent-operations-source-28) [Source 29](#security-and-agent-operations-source-29) [Source 30](#security-and-agent-operations-source-30)

## Separate business guards from policy distribution

Some requirements depend on both arguments and prior state. In a booking demonstration, a pre-execution rule checks dates and capacity and requires recorded payment before confirmation. Test legitimate paid bookings as well as invalid dates and unpaid confirmations: a guard that blocks everything is not correct business behavior. The selected scenarios do not establish that all invariants were covered. [Source 31](#security-and-agent-operations-source-31)

Changeable rules can be stored outside the agent and delivered by a runtime control service: agent events go to the service and steering decisions return without redeploying the agent. This changes distribution, not the correctness of the policy or the strength of enforcement. The local service was demonstrated; the managed production mapping was a proposal, not a tested complete security design. For independent per-action enforcement see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 32](#security-and-agent-operations-source-32) [Source 33](#security-and-agent-operations-source-33)

When using an external operator assessment, check its scope. A rating of managed GPU clusters concerns that service and its division of operational responsibility relative to peers; it cannot automatically certify the provider’s bare-metal service, where the customer may operate more of the stack. The publisher’s scope description is not itself a disclosed scoring rubric or evidence for a particular rating. [Source 34](#security-and-agent-operations-source-34)
