[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SQMCtZX3trg) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/SQMCtZX3trg.md#L606-L606)

## Designing agent-facing product interactions

Own interaction surfaces and application-facing workflows; not the tool catalog or authorization contract.

An agent can act through a desktop, share a view with a person, manipulate application state or answer through a structured interface. These are product interaction choices: they determine what the person can see and do while the agent works. They are distinct from the executable interface contract and the permissions that govern actions.

## Choose an execution desktop without blocking the user

A computer-use agent that takes over the mouse and keyboard can leave the person unable to work on the same desktop. If concurrent work matters, consider a separate execution desktop that the user can inspect or return to. One team moved toward separately hosted desktops after users complained about foreground contention. This is a usability response to those complaints, not a measured productivity gain or a requirement to use cloud hosting. A separate device is also not, by itself, proof of security isolation. [Source 1](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-1) For security controls, see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html).

## Elicit intent and ground it in shared visible context

The application can ask for missing intent at the moment of interaction, when the user's immediate purpose is available. Carry the clarification into generation and checking rather than expecting general model training to supply this particular context. This is an architectural argument, not a controlled comparison. [Source 2](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-2)

Shared visible context can make that conversation more precise. In an early design-oriented demonstration, a user could identify a heading spatially and associate feedback about its styling with the target, rather than reconstructing the page entirely in prose. The proposed benefit is less explanation and lost intent, but explanation savings were not measured and the visual demonstration is only partly accessible. [Source 3](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-3)

Distinguish this annotated, turn-based interaction from the aspiration of an agent that reacts while a person continues working. The latter has a different timing objective from submitting a batch request and waiting; the source did not demonstrate a complete real-time collaborator or establish its latency. [Source 4](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-4)

## Let agents interact with application state

Not every interaction has to be a visual click. A product can expose structured access to the state the user is already viewing, allowing an agent to read current data or change a setting in the application. In one reported implementation, a frontend-bound programming surface in a web worker used two-way browser-state binding; the agent could change a time range and read application data. The product consequence is that both participants can work with the same state rather than requiring every operation to be reconstructed visually. The account did not provide a reproducible task or measured reliability. [Source 5](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-5)

This product-facing state-sharing choice is not itself an execution protocol or permission grant. See [Tool interfaces](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tool-interfaces.html) for executable interfaces and [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html) for enforcement.

## Show useful progress while structured components arrive

Time to first readable output and total answer latency are different. A single-client case initially waited for a complete validated structured answer before rendering anything; the reported median answer time was roughly 38 seconds in that pipeline. The team changed the experience to stream readable Markdown and append a structured source card after the answer. A person could start reading sooner while the later card preserved a clickable structured component. [Source 6](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-6)

This reduces blank waiting in the reported design; it does not establish faster retrieval or a shorter total answer. Nor does the initial complete-object constraint prove that partial structured streaming is impossible in other designs. The latency figure is a speaker-reported case metric, not a general estimate.

## Separate domain expertise from presentation control

In a shopping agent, a merchant may know how user constraints map to its own catalog metadata. That knowledge need not give each merchant control over how options from different merchants are presented. One team retained response-format decisions with the agent to support a consistent cross-merchant experience while using merchant knowledge for mapping. This is a product-specific authority choice, not proof of fair comparisons or a universal commerce standard. [Source 7](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-7) Broader preference evaluation is covered in [Preference discovery and recommendations](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/preference-discovery-and-recommendations.html).

## Evaluate discovery, onboarding and use separately

An agent may recommend a product to a person, discover it as a potential tool, onboard to it and then use it directly. Test these as distinct stages: being recommended does not establish that setup will succeed; being usable does not establish that an agent will find or recommend it. The proposed framing is an advocacy framework, not evidence that agents always make purchasing decisions. A speaker also argues that multiple sales interactions can obstruct onboarding; no controlled onboarding experiment was presented. [Source 8](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-8) [Source 9](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-9)

Use observed questions and traces to locate friction. A documentation search endpoint can return relevant chunks while recording agent queries; those queries are leads about missing documentation, not proof of the user's intent. In another case an agent recovered from a parameter mismatch using the error message but spent a turn doing so. Route patterns to product and engineering, while treating specific interface repair as the responsibility of [Tool interfaces](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tool-interfaces.html). A proposed content campaign would test whether clearer use-case messaging changes search-based recommendations; no causal lift was reported. [Source 10](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-10) [Source 11](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-11) [Source 12](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-12) [Source 13](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-13)

Simplification can itself trade off against discovery. One team replaced a visible worktree selector with a slash command, reducing maintenance and allowing mid-chat switches but making the feature harder to find; feedback was mixed. The team accepted that tradeoff for a power-user feature, not as a general rule to hide advanced functionality. [Source 14](#agent-product-interaction-surfaces-source-14)

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WE_Gnowy3uw) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/WE_Gnowy3uw.md#L400-L404)

## Comparing task quality, cost and value

Covers outcome economics and controlled comparisons, not inference-server tuning. Accounting and value proxies, not inference-server configuration.

A cheap model call is not necessarily a cheap completed job. It may produce an answer that needs more retrieval, retries or human correction, and a faster response may still take longer to turn into usable work. Compare systems at the boundary where a defined task is accepted, while keeping quality, money and time visible as separate outcomes. [Source 1](#decision-economics-source-1) [Source 2](#decision-economics-source-2)

## Observe the workflow to usable work

Trace a task from request through retrieval, model and tool calls, retries, review and correction. Record which configured system ran, token use, expenditure, elapsed time and the human effort needed to reach a usable result. Keep request latency, total elapsed time and reviewer time distinct: each answers a different question. Context can grow and a model can change even when request volume is stable, so record those changes with the traces. [Source 3](#decision-economics-source-3) [Source 4](#decision-economics-source-4) [Source 5](#decision-economics-source-5)

For example, a speaker reported that a code-mode change used 43% fewer tokens and cost 31% less, while latency stayed roughly constant because of sandbox overhead. The comparison lacks the full task set, trial counts and raw data; it illustrates why the axes can move differently, not a general expected saving. Another retrospective coding account estimated a roughly fivefold speedup only after including planning, coordination and review; it was not a controlled productivity study. [Source 6](#decision-economics-source-6) [Source 7](#decision-economics-source-7)

## Attribute avoided input to an explicit alternative

A counterfactual saving compares what was actually sent with what a specified alternative policy would have sent. Name that alternative, the workload and the assumed prices, including whether caching applies. If you assign the difference to retrieval or compression, explain the accounting order and assumptions. Priced avoided input is an estimate against that policy, not an observed reduction on an invoice or proof of a better end-to-end workflow.

In one speaker-run test, 20 questions on a 53-file FastAPI project were compared with repeatedly sending all files: approximately 83,000 input tokens versus 4,900 retrieved and 523 compressed. That baseline makes the comparison interpretable but is weaker than a capable modern coding agent; code-finding accuracy is not correctness of a generated patch. A separate 247-query savings attribution lacks enough billing, cache and pricing detail to establish realized savings. [Source 8](#decision-economics-source-8) [Source 9](#decision-economics-source-9)

## Control attribution when comparing interventions

Choose the question before running the comparison. Holding total resources fixed asks which strategy uses a given budget better; sweeping budgets asks how quality changes as spending changes. Use comparable tasks and acceptance rules, repeat runs, and record model, harness, reasoning effort, generation settings, precision and runtime environment. Report meaningful changes rather than attributing every observed difference to the intervention. For detailed experimental design, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html).

In a reported financial-task comparison, an initial strategy used roughly 39,000 tokens while another used roughly 600,000. When strategies received the larger budget, reported scores were 76 and 89 for two approaches. The example motivates budget control, but the available account does not supply sufficient uncertainty or replication to establish a general ranking. In a separate serving comparison, a temperature-zero default rather than the intended roughly 0.7 workload explained an apparent throughput advantage; matching configuration matters even when the metric is speed rather than quality. [Source 10](#decision-economics-source-10) [Source 11](#decision-economics-source-11)

## Full lifecycle cost per accepted task versus first-attempt reliability

For a defined workload, period and acceptance rule, calculate:

**Cost per accepted task = total lifecycle expenditure in the period / verified acceptable tasks completed in that period.**

The numerator includes failed runs, retries, escalation and human supervision or repair, plus allocated infrastructure, integration, maintenance and optimization labor. The denominator is not requests, generated answers or tokens: it is accepted work. Apply comparable task mix and quality standards across alternatives. If no tasks are accepted, report the cost and zero accepted outcomes rather than a finite ratio. GPU rent and token tariffs are inputs, not the full price of delivered work; additional serving output can spread fixed costs but the people and software required to achieve it also cost money. [Source 12](#decision-economics-source-12) [Source 13](#decision-economics-source-13) [Source 14](#decision-economics-source-14)

**Illustrative accounting example:** over the same period, system A costs $1,200 across all work and produces 80 accepted tasks; system B costs $1,000 and produces 50. Their computed costs per accepted task are $15 and $20, respectively. This does not show either system has positive business value, and it is comparable only if the workloads and acceptance standards match. It also does not establish how much of the cost was caused by the AI change.

Report first-attempt success separately: accepted first attempts divided by eligible first attempts. It matters when a user cannot wait for retries or a mistake has consequences; the cheapest eventual accepted result need not be the most reliable first result. Retry expense depends on the actual retry policy, dependence between attempts and whether success can be recognized—not an assumed fixed number of attempts. For autonomous benefits, also track which work is eligible, whether people adopt the system, straight-through completion and accepted quality; do not multiply rates as independent or infer financial value without a defensible model. [Source 15](#decision-economics-source-15) [Source 16](#decision-economics-source-16) [Source 17](#decision-economics-source-17)

## Task-specific cost–quality frontiers and quality gates

Treat each model, harness and reasoning configuration as a separate candidate. Measure task-appropriate quality, actual task cost and latency, along with relevant constraints such as licensing. A candidate is dominated if another is at least as good on the dimensions being compared and strictly better on one. Among candidates that satisfy the application's requirements, a nondominated choice may be preferable to either the largest model or the lowest token tariff. Local inference avoids provider fees but still consumes hardware and energy. [Source 18](#decision-economics-source-18) [Source 19](#decision-economics-source-19) [Source 20](#decision-economics-source-20)

Repeat the comparison for important slices: a reported spreadsheet benchmark found that the leveraged-buyout subset changed which model was on the frontier, although the underlying plotted data and uncertainty were not supplied. Preference scores and accuracy also measure different things; do not substitute one for the other without justification. For systems that learn across tasks, report absolute reward, gain relative to a reset baseline, and cost separately: a strong starting model can score well without learning much. [Source 21](#decision-economics-source-21) [Source 22](#decision-economics-source-22) [Source 23](#decision-economics-source-23)

Before replacing an incumbent, inspect critical categories and uncertainty rather than treating a point estimate or lower bill as equivalence. One proposed release workflow uses repeated comparison, disagreement review and a positive lower confidence bound for net gain, with critical categories holding up; that is guidance, not proof of production savings. Check the replacement after deployment as well. The details of choosing and allocating capabilities belong in [Allocating models and deployment resources](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/routing-and-deployment.html); hard optimizer constraints belong in [Search and objective integrity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/search-and-objective-integrity.html). [Source 24](#decision-economics-source-24) [Source 25](#decision-economics-source-25)

## Interpret workload spending and adoption

Attribute shared spend by team and use case so an unusual bill can be investigated against task mix and results. Long-context, multi-turn agents can have a very different consumption profile from isolated short automation. Review anomalies and use budgets or quotas appropriate to the stage of adoption, but do not turn either high or low token consumption into a productivity leaderboard. A higher bill may purchase trusted work; very low usage may expose an adoption problem. Early exploration still needs safeguards. [Source 26](#decision-economics-source-26) [Source 27](#decision-economics-source-27) [Source 28](#decision-economics-source-28) [Source 29](#decision-economics-source-29)

An adequate cheaper option may be more attractive if it is fast enough for the workflow, but the reported adoption pattern is observational. Compare people or teams cautiously: differences in tasks and experience confound raw usage, and the sources do not provide a validated normalization formula. [Source 30](#decision-economics-source-30) [Source 31](#decision-economics-source-31)

## Intermediate value proxies and trusted throughput

Some outcomes, such as financial performance, arrive too late or are too entangled with other factors to guide every iteration. Define an intermediate proxy that can be checked now: for example, what counts as a useful insight, useful insights per analyst-day, and the cost per useful insight. Specify the observation window and assess whether reviewers agree. These measures can guide learning, but a faster research process or more counted insights does not establish realized ROI. [Source 32](#decision-economics-source-32)

Similarly, a merged change is not automatically valuable. Complexity-weighted merged work may capture effort that line counts miss, but the proposed scoring is not validated as a measure of customer value. Keep objective checks, human maintainability review and production outcomes as distinct evidence of trusted throughput, rather than silently treating them as a validated composite score. Use [Measuring useful outcomes and business value](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/measuring-business-value.html) for whole-workflow baselines and eventual outcome attribution, and [Budgeting evaluation and monitoring](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluation-infrastructure.html) for the separate cost of evaluation itself. [Source 33](#decision-economics-source-33) [Source 34](#decision-economics-source-34)

## Allocating models and deployment resources

Covers task routing, provider selection and specialization rather than low-level serving internals. Application model quality and choices, rather than hardware-level serving metrics.

A model allocation decision has two parts: which capability should perform each piece of work, and where should that capability run? A low token price or a high leaderboard score answers neither question on its own. Compare alternatives on the application’s tasks, quality requirements, latency and full operating costs; public benchmarks are useful partial evidence, not a substitute for that comparison. [Source 1](#routing-and-deployment-source-1) [Source 2](#routing-and-deployment-source-2)

## Route capability by task, risk and role

A task router chooses a model for a request or a workflow stage. It can use explicit task classes, expected difficulty, risk, latency and organizational preferences. The goal is the least costly option expected to meet the requirement, not the cheapest option regardless of outcome. That predicted threshold must itself be tested: a vendor’s proposed difficulty classifier and savings claim do not disclose enough calibration detail to establish that its routes are correct. [Source 3](#routing-and-deployment-source-3) [Source 4](#routing-and-deployment-source-4)

For example, a session-analysis demonstration used inexpensive parallel extraction and stronger synthesis. That split saves nothing useful if the extractors omit the evidence needed by the synthesis step; the demonstration did not establish comparative quality or optimal cost. Similarly, a code-review system may spend more capability on complex, risky changes, but it needs evidence that its risk classification and subsequent review actually catch defects. [Source 5](#routing-and-deployment-source-5) [Source 6](#routing-and-deployment-source-6)

Routing at the outset is different from **escalation after a detectable failure**. An invoice example retries tax extraction with more reasoning if the simple extractor fails. Test both the trigger and the retry: a plausible but incorrect extraction may not trigger escalation at all. Compare the entire policy with a stable route and a single-model baseline, including router errors, retry frequency, final task quality, latency and total spend. For code review, replay known incident-causing changes to check whether a cheaper model or context filter quietly misses serious defects; fewer comments or lower cost do not demonstrate preserved recall. [Source 7](#routing-and-deployment-source-7) [Source 8](#routing-and-deployment-source-8) [Source 9](#routing-and-deployment-source-9)

Switching models also has a price: rebuilding context, routing overhead and reduced prefix-cache reuse can erase savings. A stable task-level choice may beat a flexible per-turn choice; the suggested limit of two or three models is a vendor heuristic, not an established optimum. A live demonstration reported a 14-cent routed session versus 44 cents for a comparison, but it did not establish equivalent correctness with repeated, executed quality tests. Measure your own policy instead. Task routing chooses *which model* handles work; distributing requests among replicas of a model is a serving decision, not the same routing problem. See [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html) for cache economics and [Measuring inference serving performance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/inference-serving.html) for serving measurements. [Source 10](#routing-and-deployment-source-10) [Source 11](#routing-and-deployment-source-11) [Source 12](#routing-and-deployment-source-12)

## Compare compression and specialization by task economics

A smaller task-specific system can be built in different ways. Distillation trains a student to reproduce useful teacher behavior; quantization represents an existing model more compactly; a native-small model starts with a smaller architecture; and an adapter adds task-specific parameters to a shared base. Compare these candidates on the actual task, including quality on difficult cases, latency, throughput, memory, training, serving and maintenance. A compact reranker, for instance, need not preserve every open-ended generation capability of its teacher. [Source 13](#routing-and-deployment-source-13) [Source 14](#routing-and-deployment-source-14)

At similar storage sizes, a compressed larger model may retain better quality while a native-small model may run faster. The cited comparison is speaker-reported, not a universal ranking. Shared-base adapters can let several specialized versions use one inference pool, potentially avoiding per-tenant reserved GPUs; deeper full tuning offers different control and allocation tradeoffs. In the cited account, hosted full fine-tuning was forthcoming rather than demonstrated as generally available. [Source 15](#routing-and-deployment-source-15) [Source 16](#routing-and-deployment-source-16)

A nominal bit width does not describe the entire precision format or prove quality on a particular device. For precision allocation, calibration and hardware validation, use [Model selection and runtime efficiency](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency.html) rather than treating a compression label as a result.

## Keep a portfolio without multiplying operational chaos

Different tasks may warrant different models, including a mixture of open-weight and hosted proprietary options. Standardizing the shared interface, evaluation and operating practices is compatible with keeping that portfolio: standardization need not mean selecting one model for everything. A builder-heavy survey reported both multi-model use and movement toward fewer AI tools; its open- and closed-model categories overlap, so they are not mutually exclusive market shares or evidence of model quality. [Source 17](#routing-and-deployment-source-17) [Source 18](#routing-and-deployment-source-18)

Give routes understandable task labels and make the mapping inspectable, with explicit rules for preferences and a way to revise a poor route. Changing the model behind a label still requires testing; a common interface does not make the replacement behaviorally equivalent. Revisit choices as models, tools and workloads change. For controlled local comparisons, see [Comparing agents without confounding the result](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/comparing-agents-without-confounding-the-result.html); for how multiple agents coordinate, see [Choosing agent delegation and coordination](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-delegation-and-coordination.html). [Source 19](#routing-and-deployment-source-19) [Source 20](#routing-and-deployment-source-20) [Source 21](#routing-and-deployment-source-21)

## Choose where inference runs

Hosted APIs, dedicated capacity and local execution expose different tradeoffs. Dedicated GPUs can be attractive when demand keeps them busy or data-placement requirements justify control; sporadic demand pays for idle capacity, and running infrastructure requires expertise. Even the same weights can exhibit different reliability, speed and price across providers. Compare providers with the application’s actual prompt and output lengths, traffic, repeated prefixes, quality and reliability requirements. [Source 22](#routing-and-deployment-source-22) [Source 23](#routing-and-deployment-source-23) [Source 24](#routing-and-deployment-source-24)

One internal repository comparison reported a hosted option at about $2.50 per task versus $11 for a self-hosted option, in half the time. That is a useful warning against assuming self-hosting is cheaper, not a general crossover point: utilization and complete accounting were not disclosed. Conversely, local execution can provide control over data and traces; in one particular M3 Ultra setup, lack of batching for the chosen configuration made an evaluation run serially for days with thermal concerns. That constraint is specific to the setup, not local inference in general. [Source 25](#routing-and-deployment-source-25) [Source 26](#routing-and-deployment-source-26)

## Decide whether specialization will pay back

Frequent, latency-sensitive work can justify a specialist even when a general model is capable. Edit prediction on every keystroke is one motivating case, though the account supplies no measured general-model comparison. Estimate whether repeated per-task savings over the useful life of the specialist outweigh data preparation, expert review, training, evaluation, deployment and maintenance, including retuning when models or tasks change. Narrow, high-volume extraction may justify work that a low-volume broad task does not. [Source 27](#routing-and-deployment-source-27) [Source 28](#routing-and-deployment-source-28)

A reported reinforcement-learning run cost roughly $420 in compute and $40 in judge fees on eight H100s; that is not the cost of the whole specialist project, because data, experts, engineering and deployment are excluded. Likewise, replacing expensive teacher sampling with a student for data filtering is a proposed economy only once the student is sufficiently capable; the cited account provides no quantitative quality or financial validation. [Source 29](#routing-and-deployment-source-29) [Source 30](#routing-and-deployment-source-30)

## Decoding and long sequences: preserve what matters

Model choice is not the only quality-cost lever. In a recommendation task, constrained decoding can restrict generated identifiers to a permitted catalog or subset, while beam search explores candidate sequences at added latency. Spotify reported 98% valid identifiers without constraints and found top-p sampling less accurate than beam search in its experiment. The validity figure is not recommendation relevance, and the account omits sample size, accuracy metric, settings and latency measurements. Test allowed-output validity, relevance and response time separately before choosing a decoding strategy. [Source 31](#routing-and-deployment-source-31) [Source 32](#routing-and-deployment-source-32)

Long documents introduce a different tradeoff: processing blocks or using a different sequence architecture may reduce computation while losing information needed for recall. The cited architecture comparison is qualitative and provides no cost–recall curve. For video, one described system groups similar frames around temporal changes into timestamped segments rather than analyzing at a fixed frame rate. Test whether brief or rare anomalies survive that representation; the account supplies no missed-anomaly rate or compression ratio. This within-video representation is distinct from skipping an entire upload. [Source 33](#routing-and-deployment-source-33) [Source 34](#routing-and-deployment-source-34)

## Designing efficient agent workflows

Covers delivery loops and replay, not retrieval context or production serving. Trajectory and development workflow design, not evaluator scheduling.

An agent can produce a correct answer and still make the workflow slower or more expensive: it may repeat a tool call, wait on a shared test suite, or produce changes faster than people can review them. Design for **accepted work per unit of time and cost**, not just generation speed. The useful question is where flexibility is necessary, where work can be reused, and what actually limits delivery.

## Extract and maintain reusable production procedures

Begin with the desired outcome and allow flexible exploration where the path is uncertain. When similar requests recur, inspect successful traces for stable mechanics that can become parameterized code. In an insurance-portal architecture, a reusable authentication component prepares a browser, an agent handles variable navigation, and one tool bundles downloading a document and transferring it to the runtime. An SOP can guide the flexible stage without pretending the SOP itself is executable. The proposal reduces model decisions, but does not measure savings or reliability; its authentication and session-security details are not specified. [Source 1](#workflow-design-source-1) [Source 2](#workflow-design-source-2) [Source 3](#workflow-design-source-3) [Source 4](#workflow-design-source-4)

Run the extracted procedure on later requests only after checking that parameters, preconditions and outcomes preserve the user's constraints. Detect failures or drift and fall back to adaptive execution or repair. A schedule-lookup demonstration saved actions as code and changed the day parameter; replay hit a hiccup and fell back to a vision-language agent. This hybrid is experimental, not a guarantee of reliable replay. Browser shortcuts such as encoded URLs can bypass fragile UI interactions, but selected demos do not prove that every site constraint is preserved. [Source 5](#workflow-design-source-5) [Source 6](#workflow-design-source-6)

Compare the initial discovery bill and ongoing maintenance against expected reuse, rather than assuming the cheaper path pays off on its first use. Reactive repair avoids routine probe costs but lets a user encounter stale behavior; scheduled sample runs spend resources to find drift earlier. The proposed repair approach was still a working theory, not a demonstrated universal maintenance policy. Security boundaries for the components remain a separate concern: see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 7](#workflow-design-source-7) [Source 8](#workflow-design-source-8)

## Use captured model outputs in deterministic regression tests

Production procedure reuse runs extracted actions on a new request. A different kind of replay tests application code against **already observed model decisions**: capture the model outputs and context, substitute them into the test, and run the deterministic nodes to see whether a code change handles that known case correctly. To avoid fresh inference, stub every relevant model node. A demonstrated test stubbed the planner but left a later language model active; it was not itself a zero-model-call run. Even fully stubbed tests still use infrastructure and may miss hidden external dependencies. They cannot tell you how a changed model behaves on new inputs, so retain live behavioral tests. [Source 9](#workflow-design-source-9)

## Find the delivery bottleneck

Map elapsed time from specification through generation, validation, review and release. Faster coding helps little if review or the release queue is saturated. One speaker's hypothetical monthly release growing from 20 to 200 pull requests illustrates the queue problem, not a measured result. Another reports roughly tenfold faster builds after a tool change; that is a build-time observation, not a tenfold improvement in total delivery. Failed centralized checks can also impose long waits and interrupt human flow. [Source 10](#workflow-design-source-10) [Source 11](#workflow-design-source-11) [Source 12](#workflow-design-source-12)

Use fast feedback suited to the current task: for example, browser iteration for UI changes or a coverage- and change-selected test subset during editing. Keep broader final CI checks rather than treating a locally green subset as acceptance. Deep security scans may warrant a different cadence: one vendor demo described a roughly hour-long scan, but one project does not establish an optimal schedule or scaling rule. [Source 13](#workflow-design-source-13) [Source 14](#workflow-design-source-14)

## Budget verification and repair

Separate uncertainty about *how to do* a task from uncertainty about *what counts as right*. A task with a variable path and a repeatable, inexpensive check is a promising agent candidate; if checking effectively requires redoing the work, automation may not save effort. This is a proposed task-selection framework, not a validated complexity classification. Include model and tool costs, checker runs, human review, infrastructure and maintenance. False positives matter too: an unnecessary automated fix costs effort and can introduce another defect. [Source 15](#workflow-design-source-15) [Source 16](#workflow-design-source-16) [Source 17](#workflow-design-source-17) [Source 18](#workflow-design-source-18) [Source 19](#workflow-design-source-19)

Checks may make a failed first attempt repairable, but neither correctness nor lower accepted-work cost follows automatically. The idea that stronger harnesses enable cheaper models is a hypothesis to test on the actual workload. A selected game-making demonstration reported about $200 and six hours for a successful harness run, without a controlled cost comparison. An under-tested recruiting integration reportedly produced repeated formatting errors and costly workarounds; the account supplies no retry counts or measured savings. Inspect such loops and stop unproductive repair, rather than judging only the final artifact. [Source 20](#workflow-design-source-20) [Source 21](#workflow-design-source-21) [Source 22](#workflow-design-source-22)

## Measure complete trajectories

Record completion against the original requirements, calls and retries, tokens, elapsed time and timeouts alongside answer quality. A correct account-balance answer can hide three database calls; some repeated calls may be justified, so investigate rather than treating minimum call count as the objective. A minimal file-creation probe reportedly exposed a 70-fold token difference between unnamed models in one harness; absent full run conditions, this is a reason to probe your own setup, not a model ranking. [Source 23](#workflow-design-source-23) [Source 24](#workflow-design-source-24)

Per-step accuracy is also not the same as end-to-end completion. A thought experiment with 100 required steps at 99% independent success gives roughly 37% success without recovery; correlated failures or recovery change the result. It is not a measured browser-agent reliability figure. [Source 25](#workflow-design-source-25)

## Allocate work by structure and dependency

Use a script for a fixed procedure; use a model where interpretation or selection is genuinely uncertain. A financial example has the model select what to calculate while code extracts inputs and computes the result. Deterministic arithmetic does not validate the chosen sources, definitions or plan. Similarly, selecting among approved responses may be a classification problem rather than open-ended generation, but the classifier itself still needs evaluation. Generated code can batch structured exploration; constrain its effects because flexible code can bypass intended mutation paths or lineage. [Source 26](#workflow-design-source-26) [Source 27](#workflow-design-source-27) [Source 28](#workflow-design-source-28) [Source 29](#workflow-design-source-29) [Source 30](#workflow-design-source-30)

Parallelize independent work, not dependent decisions. In a travel example, flight and hotel searches can run together, but a budget check needs both prices and an activity search needs the remaining budget. The application must dispatch calls concurrently for the suggested parallelism to matter. Isolate standardized evaluation environments before running them in parallel, and account for capacity and orchestration. Serialize conflicting writes where necessary; one team's account favored parallel read-only research but serial feature changes after simultaneous workers produced conflicts. [Source 31](#workflow-design-source-31) [Source 32](#workflow-design-source-32) [Source 33](#workflow-design-source-33)

A different, speculative proposal duplicates an implementation across several candidate repository bases, hoping one will fit a rapidly moving shared state. Unlike independent reads, this spends extra compute on alternatives and still needs reconciliation and validation. No measured benefit or scheduling policy was supplied. [Source 34](#workflow-design-source-34)

## Enforce limits, not just intentions

Set separate runtime limits for steps inside an attempt, retries across attempts, elapsed time and total spending. A prompt saying “search sparingly” or an iteration limit is not a hard session-wide monetary cap. Inspect repeated searches for genuinely new evidence; one team prompted the agent before a sixth call to reconsider, but that instruction was not an enforced cap. For automated test-and-repair, protect test integrity and stop when the budget is exhausted rather than letting a loop weaken tests to pass. Choose timeouts for the actual startup and execution environment, not a demo's numbers. [Source 35](#workflow-design-source-35) [Source 36](#workflow-design-source-36) [Source 37](#workflow-design-source-37) [Source 38](#workflow-design-source-38) [Source 39](#workflow-design-source-39)

For the distinct problem of staging evaluation and monitoring budgets, see [Budgeting evaluation and monitoring](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluation-infrastructure.html).

## Managing context, retrieval and cache costs

Covers retrieval and context policies, not tool catalog interfaces or inference cache billing. Covers prefix placement, replica locality and billing rather than general KV sizing. Context, knowledge and retrieval economics, not model-selection economics.

An agent needs enough evidence to make the right decision, not necessarily every available document. But removing context is not free: search, indexing, summaries, cache misses and repeated retrieval all add work, and a shorter prompt may omit the one fact that changes the answer. Choose a context policy by testing the complete task, not by minimizing tokens in isolation.

## Select evidence without losing the way back

Filter, aggregate and deduplicate **before** sending material to the model: a short answer cannot recover input cost already incurred. For code, an overview of signatures can orient the agent, followed by expansion to the relevant implementation and callers. Remove overlapping retrieved chunks, but retain identifiers or locations so the agent can inspect the original. These are design strategies, not demonstrated guarantees of coding quality. [Source 1](#context-and-retrieval-source-1) [Source 2](#context-and-retrieval-source-2) [Source 3](#context-and-retrieval-source-3)

A diagnostic system illustrates the tradeoff: it clusters exceptions, ranks them by relevance and timing, presents truncated top results and lets the agent request the full log for an exception. The recovery path matters because ranking or truncation can hide the decisive clue; the reported improvement in signal-to-noise was not accompanied by measured diagnostic accuracy. For numerical questions, a query such as SQL aggregation can answer directly rather than paginate every trace into context. Generated redaction or summaries require separate validation; neither is a privacy guarantee. [Source 4](#context-and-retrieval-source-4) [Source 5](#context-and-retrieval-source-5)

Keep bulky traces, intermediate results and media in a queryable store, passing references or selected results instead of repeatedly embedding whole payloads. Make retrieval completeness, permissions, retention and read load part of the design: external storage can relocate rather than eliminate cost. Separately referenced images can also avoid base64 text bloat; that example is not a general performance benchmark. [Source 6](#context-and-retrieval-source-6) [Source 7](#context-and-retrieval-source-7) [Source 8](#context-and-retrieval-source-8)

## Choose the context policy by workload

Compare full context against retrieval, clearing, summarization and fresh sessions on the same representative tasks. Track answer or action quality, latency, actual charges, retained evidence and replacement work. In a reported literature-review experiment, the relevant corpus fit in the window and memory variants added cost without improving performance; this does not establish that full context wins on larger corpora. Conversely, a local setup with a 32K window could not fit some lessons: a cache discount does not increase physical window capacity. [Source 9](#context-and-retrieval-source-9) [Source 10](#context-and-retrieval-source-10)

Clearing a useful tool result may force the agent to retrieve it again. A compact summary saves space but may lose a qualification or drift; a fresh session can also discard useful history. Test the downstream consequences and cost of reconstruction rather than adopting either continual retention or mandatory reset as a rule. Maintain indexes as the underlying corpus changes. See [Running and resuming agent sessions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-sessions-and-long-running-work.html) for session recovery and compaction in the longer-running workflow. [Source 11](#context-and-retrieval-source-11) [Source 12](#context-and-retrieval-source-12) [Source 13](#context-and-retrieval-source-13)

## Budget the retrieval pipeline

Measure query construction, embedding inference, index construction and maintenance, search, reranking and the answer task—not just vector-search latency. Start with an approach appropriate to the corpus: some practitioners favor hybrid lexical and semantic retrieval from the outset, while others start with lexical search and add semantic infrastructure only if it improves a relevant failure. A cross-encoder scores query and candidate together and can improve a shortlist, but doing that for every document increases query-time work. Stop adding stages when the improvement in relevant task outcomes no longer justifies their cost; no universal threshold follows from these examples. [Source 14](#context-and-retrieval-source-14) [Source 15](#context-and-retrieval-source-15) [Source 16](#context-and-retrieval-source-16)

Limit sequential search rounds and, when helpful, search independent aspects in parallel; breadth still consumes resources. One knowledge harness uses bounded rounds and parallel aspects as a design choice, not a proven optimum. Retrieval relevance and fast search are intermediate measures: separately verify whether the final answer uses the right evidence. [Source 17](#context-and-retrieval-source-17)

Corpus organization also determines search work. A layout arranged by year can make a cross-year question expensive to traverse. Indexing and embeddings move work upfront and require refresh, potentially paying off across repeated queries. Multiple indexes at different chunk scales can find both local details and document-wide context, but use more storage and fusion work; parallelism is an argument for latency, not a measured guarantee in the cited example. [Source 18](#context-and-retrieval-source-18) [Source 19](#context-and-retrieval-source-19) [Source 20](#context-and-retrieval-source-20)

For a recurring hierarchy, an alternative is to give the model a compact description of paths and let code resolve the selected structure to underlying instances. This avoids listing every asset in the prompt only when the hierarchy is repetitive and the index, filters and selected plan are correct. The reported scaling example does not prove a bound for arbitrary graphs; measure total validation work as well as per-query tokens. [Source 21](#context-and-retrieval-source-21) [Source 22](#context-and-retrieval-source-22)

When choosing an engine, distinguish the relevance scoring method from the implementation that finds top results. Test representative concurrency, metadata filters and authorization. Filtering after retrieval can remove eligible results from a small candidate set; filtering first can cost speed. Compare recall as well as latency under real load. A vendor's native-filtering claim is not a universal optimum. [Source 23](#context-and-retrieval-source-23) [Source 24](#context-and-retrieval-source-24) [Source 25](#context-and-retrieval-source-25)

## Reuse prefixes and price the whole run

A stable shared prefix can avoid repeated prefill computation if the serving system actually retains it. Put shared instructions before changing request content, then compare cold and warm requests. If caches are local to replicas, routing a repeated prefix to a different replica can miss even though the text matches. The cited warm-prefix demonstration lacks enough controls to predict a production speedup; verify cache hits and latency for the actual deployment. [Source 26](#context-and-retrieval-source-26) [Source 27](#context-and-retrieval-source-27) [Source 28](#context-and-retrieval-source-28)

Inference reuse and billing are related but distinct. Calculate charges for cached and uncached input, output, summary calls and any prefix changes, using the provider's actual terms. Compaction can make a shorter history more expensive if it invalidates a cheap cached prefix. In one reported 36-turn configuration, roughly 1.78 million tokens and 97% cached input made retaining history cheapest among the tested strategies. The limited trials and provider-specific pricing do not establish a general break-even. [Source 29](#context-and-retrieval-source-29) [Source 30](#context-and-retrieval-source-30)

Whole-response caching is different again: it reuses an answer, not merely computation for a prefix. Consider it for genuinely equivalent requests only when a key accounts for changing context, model or instruction versions, freshness and access permissions. A previously correct answer can be stale or unauthorized for a different user. A claim that much repeated spending is redundant lacks the dataset and method needed to generalize. [Source 31](#context-and-retrieval-source-31)

Warm development environments and checkpointed histories are also distinct from response caching. Reuse may avoid rebuilding state, but test isolation and invalidation; summaries need factual-retention checks. Availability of provider caching alone does not establish a hit rate or savings. For tool catalogs and progressive disclosure of interfaces rather than general context policy, see [Tool interfaces](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tool-interfaces.html). [Source 32](#context-and-retrieval-source-32) [Source 33](#context-and-retrieval-source-33) [Source 34](#context-and-retrieval-source-34)

## Tool interfaces

Tool affordances and invocation, schema discovery and progressive loading of instructions.

An agent can only use an interface it can find and understand. A long list of opaque API endpoints is not automatically a useful toolset: schemas consume context, names may hide the intended action, and the result of a call may not give the agent enough information to proceed. Design the individual operation, its discovery path and its invocation environment as separate choices.

## Discover capabilities progressively and tune schema selection

For a small, stable set of tools, loading every schema may be simpler than maintaining a router. When a large catalog makes context or selection costly, expose a search mechanism or concise capability descriptions first, then load complete definitions for relevant candidates. An embedding-based router can index descriptions and retrieve a shortlist for each request; test the smallest shortlist that meets your required recall, including uncommon tasks. A smaller shortlist costs less context but can omit the only suitable operation; wider retrieval or a second search costs more and may add a handshake. Suggested catalog sizes and shortlist lengths are starting heuristics, not universal thresholds. The reported catalog experiments have incomplete methods and conflicting counts, so they do not establish a portable accuracy or savings figure. [Source 1](#tool-interfaces-source-1) [Source 2](#tool-interfaces-source-2) [Source 3](#tool-interfaces-source-3)

The same staged pattern applies differently to procedural skills and documents. A skill's name and trigger description help select a playbook; the body and specialized references are loaded when needed. A document interface might expose a short index description and then retrieve the relevant schema or passage. Test whether the agent actually selects the right skill and follows its references: merely making a reference available does not ensure it is read. A large database schema can be disclosed in chunks only if the extraction interface can return chunks; a prompt asking for partial results cannot create that capability. An experimental filesystem-shaped documentation interface and suggested semantic augmentation have no measured retrieval advantage in the source. [Source 4](#tool-interfaces-source-4) [Source 5](#tool-interfaces-source-5) [Source 6](#tool-interfaces-source-6)

## Replace the per-turn active tool registry

Selection and registry maintenance are distinct. Once the current request's candidates are selected, replace the previous active shortlist rather than continually adding to it. Otherwise a conversation can eventually carry the whole catalog again. Check the framework's actual behavior and ensure the current task still has the tools it needs. The demonstrated replacement hook was described orally, not as a complete implementation. Crucially, removing old schemas does not remove chat history: history compaction and broader context economics are separate concerns in [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html). [Source 7](#tool-interfaces-source-7)

## Compose calls and intermediate results in code

A program can run independent reads in parallel, wait for a result before issuing a dependent call, branch on that result and reduce structured intermediates before sending a concise answer to the model. For example, an **illustrative** inventory lookup could fetch stock for several warehouses concurrently, then request a reorder quote only for locations below their threshold. Check failures and partial results before treating the aggregate as complete. This avoids requiring a new model turn for every intermediate operation, but is not itself evidence of speed or safety. [Source 8](#tool-interfaces-source-8)

Choose an execution language the intended model can use and test the generated program, including numerical behavior and error handling. Large images or binaries need not be serialized into model context: an appropriately access-controlled reference can identify an artifact for later use. The source's warnings about language arithmetic and smaller-model fit are qualitative, not a controlled comparison with native tool calls. Execution permissions and isolation are separate: see [Agent Authority, Isolation and Runtime Controls](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-authority-isolation-and-runtime-controls.html). [Source 9](#tool-interfaces-source-9)

## Make individual tool meaning and first-call affordances legible

A tool description should answer what its identifiers identify, what the operation changes, and how failures appear. An experienced developer may know what a delete-item endpoint deletes; an agent seeing only a schema and docstring does not inherit that product history. State, for example, whether the identifier is an item or a collection ID, whether deletion is reversible, and what a not-found response means. These are illustrative contract fields, not claims about a specific endpoint. [Source 10](#tool-interfaces-source-10)

Names, inputs and output shape also affect adoption. A practitioner observed agents falling back to familiar grep and file reads rather than using a graph tool; a search-like name, multi-keyword input and evidence-bearing grep-like results can make the first call easier to interpret. Test actual trajectories instead of assuming familiar formatting guarantees use. [Source 11](#tool-interfaces-source-11)

## Encode known workflow steps in executable tools

If product rules already say which operations form a valid workflow, do not make the model rediscover every rule from generic CRUD calls. In one document-pipeline rebuild, a classify-to-extract operation replaced repeated generic step creation, with validators, contextual next-step guidance and occasional automatic chaining. This embeds a known valid path while leaving judgment where it is needed. The reported reliability improvement was qualitative, without a controlled prompt-versus-architecture comparison. A valid pipeline can still extract the wrong information; inspect [action evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-task-flow-and-action-evidence.html) as well as structure. [Source 12](#tool-interfaces-source-12)

## Maintain a discoverable catalog and diagnose contract drift

Give each catalog entry an owner and version alongside its name, intent-oriented description and schema. When a description or schema changes, refresh its search index. Record candidates retrieved, the eventual call, failures and fallback paths; inspect rare operations and use the terms users actually use. If the required operation is absent from the shortlist, widen the search, retry or fall back to a broader group, then improve the entry if its description caused the miss. [Source 13](#tool-interfaces-source-13) [Source 14](#tool-interfaces-source-14)

A retrieval miss is not the same as a permission or configuration mismatch. Separately compare instructions with the tools actually exposed and permitted. One speaker reported hundreds of runs requesting an unavailable tool; the case does not quantify comparative reliability. Finding a tool never grants authority to execute it. [Source 15](#tool-interfaces-source-15)

## Select retrieval primitives and fit uneven clients

Teach the harness which retrieval primitive fits the information need: literal grep-like search finds exact strings; BM25 uses lexical term matching and ranking; semantic search can find conceptually related wording. They are different interfaces with different failure modes, not interchangeable labels. Supply concise index and field descriptions so the agent can formulate useful queries, and evaluate whether the returned evidence answers the task. General retrieval selection and context management are covered in [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html). [Source 16](#tool-interfaces-source-16) [Source 17](#tool-interfaces-source-17)

Connector compatibility is a separate issue. A team found uneven support for server-level instructions and repeated relevant guidance in tool calls. In another workaround, prompts asked permission to map unlinked design components and then requested candidate matches, imitating missing elicitation and sampling features. These are context-specific adaptations, not proof that prompts reproduce native protocol guarantees. [Source 18](#tool-interfaces-source-18) [Source 19](#tool-interfaces-source-19)

## Layer local access over remote connectors

A shell-friendly local client can provide familiar command discovery while a remote protocol handles connector interaction; CLI and MCP need not be mutually exclusive choices. A demonstration used browser authentication, OS-keychain storage and persistent sessions shared across agent invocations. It did not audit credential isolation, revocation or multi-user access. For long operations, submit, check progress and collect later only when both server and client support asynchronous tasks; the demonstration did not establish cancellation or failure recovery. See [Running and resuming agent sessions](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-sessions-and-long-running-work.html) for the broader session lifecycle. [Source 20](#tool-interfaces-source-20) [Source 21](#tool-interfaces-source-21) [Source 22](#tool-interfaces-source-22)

## Choose interaction flow, state access and predictable behavior

Flags are often convenient for independent, single-pass inputs. If the next choice depends on a live response or an earlier answer, an interactive flow can preserve situational guidance and escalation, though flags can encode conditional logic too. For an existing terminal UI, a multiplexer can send keys and capture the screen, but the agent must interpret redraws. A structured side channel can instead expose machine-readable state, choices and inputs while retaining the human UI. In the workshop's low-inventory illustration, include the remaining quantity and whether the agent should ask for confirmation or select a backup, not just the displayed button text. The side channel is a proposal, not a controlled comparison. [Source 23](#tool-interfaces-source-23) [Source 24](#tool-interfaces-source-24) [Source 25](#tool-interfaces-source-25) [Source 26](#tool-interfaces-source-26)

Keep each tool's semantics predictable so the model can reason about its result rather than invoke another opaque decision-maker inside every call. Predictability does not mean identical output when external state has changed: a stock query may correctly return a different quantity later. [Source 27](#tool-interfaces-source-27)

## Compose domain operations and revisit discovery with stateful scripting

Batching several operations in one script and preserving state across scripts solve different problems. A spreadsheet team exposed roughly fifteen operations as JavaScript functions in a REPL: one call could combine results, while retained variables let a later call inspect and extend an earlier investigation. TypeScript definitions described the model-facing methods while the domain engine remained in C#. The team had also found that a rigid, one-time discovery handoff blocked further investigation; planning was useful, but the agent needed to return to discovery as new facts emerged. [Source 28](#tool-interfaces-source-28) [Source 29](#tool-interfaces-source-29) [Source 30](#tool-interfaces-source-30) [Source 31](#tool-interfaces-source-31)

The stateful-versus-stateless observations were not a controlled comparison, and the source does not establish the sandbox's security properties. Test the interface with the actual workload and protect execution independently rather than treating the REPL as a security guarantee.

## Measuring inference serving performance

Covers inference phases, metrics, concurrency and KV capacity, not user-facing voice or specific decoding techniques. Service performance and resource provisioning, not business ROI or kernel algebra.

A serving configuration has no single meaningful speed. Its capacity depends on the request mix, concurrent demand, hardware, scheduling and the latency users can tolerate. Measure it under the workload and service objective you intend to operate, rather than choosing the largest isolated tokens-per-second number.

## Set interaction-dependent latency objectives

Start with the interaction. Immediate review may require a tighter deadline than a coaching response where users accept a longer wait for better reasoning. Choose a measurable event and a percentile objective as well as acceptable quality and cost; a mean completion time does not guarantee a good tail. A model's first token may itself be reasoning rather than a usable answer. For speech, time to first audible response includes more than model serving; see [Interactive latency](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/interactive-latency.html) for those boundaries. [Source 1](#inference-serving-source-1) [Source 2](#inference-serving-source-2)

Also compare delivered words for the languages users actually speak. Tokenizers may use different numbers of tokens per word across languages, so equal token throughput does not imply equal time to words. That observation comes from a speaker's account, not a controlled universal comparison. [Source 3](#inference-serving-source-3)

## Diagnose the request and its metrics

**Prefill** processes the input and builds attention key-value (KV) state; **decode** generates subsequent tokens with dependencies on earlier tokens. Record prompt and output lengths and repeated prefixes to determine which phase dominates. Long-document analysis with a short answer can be prefill-heavy; long generation puts more weight on decode. Speeding decode alone does not remove long-prompt processing. Prefix reuse is a separate design decision; see [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html). [Source 4](#inference-serving-source-4) [Source 5](#inference-serving-source-5) [Source 6](#inference-serving-source-6)

Track at least time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency or per-request generation rate, end-to-end completion latency, and aggregate request or token throughput. These answer different questions: throughput is total work delivered, not the pace experienced by a single user. In one speaker-reported low-reasoning test, raising concurrency from 32 to 64 produced about 1.9 times the throughput but sharply worsened P95 TTFT; exact tail times are not reliably available. A separate dashboard demonstration changed batch-token settings and saw inter-token latency change with little first-token change. Neither result is a universal tuning rule. [Source 7](#inference-serving-source-7) [Source 8](#inference-serving-source-8)

## Sweep load against the SLO

Construct a representative workload including prompt and output distributions, prefix repetition, arrival pattern and expected concurrency. Keep model, precision, hardware, replica count, workload and objective explicit when comparing a candidate with a baseline. Sweep offered load and relevant serving settings, recording achieved throughput and latency percentiles at every point. The **knee** is where additional load no longer produces proportional throughput while latency rises; the safe operating point can be below it if the SLO is already violated. A knee belongs to that configuration and workload, not to the model in general. [Source 9](#inference-serving-source-9) [Source 10](#inference-serving-source-10) [Source 11](#inference-serving-source-11)

**Illustrative decision:** for an interactive document assistant, compare two configurations using the same long-input/short-output trace and a chosen P90 TTFT deadline. Reject a higher-throughput configuration if its P90 violates that deadline; among conforming points, compare completed load and cost. Repeat at the intended replica scale and check answer quality when changing numerical precision or the model. This is a decision procedure, not a measured result or a claim that a single SLO captures the whole product. An eight-replica code-generation comparison illustrates the importance of the scale and baseline, but its available account lacks full hardware and repeated curves. [Source 12](#inference-serving-source-12) [Source 13](#inference-serving-source-13)

The load generator itself must be measured. Record scheduled versus actual send times and delivered requests per second, client CPU and streaming collection delays, alongside server-side timestamps. In one incompletely specified experiment, a requested 200 QPS became only 38 QPS because of client limitations; another reported substantial client-side streaming delay. Central scheduling with multiprocess execution is one design for reducing client contention, not a server optimization. Test the generator independently before treating an apparent server knee as real. [Source 14](#inference-serving-source-14) [Source 15](#inference-serving-source-15) [Source 16](#inference-serving-source-16)

## Budget memory and place the phases

Weights are only part of the accelerator memory budget. Concurrent requests also retain KV state for system prompts, user inputs, tool results and generated tokens. Estimate using actual length distributions and simultaneous demand, then load-test: an advertised maximum context window is not the same as every request's typical memory requirement. A hierarchy can hold hot KV blocks on GPU and colder blocks in CPU memory or disk, trading capacity for transfer time. [Source 17](#inference-serving-source-17) [Source 18](#inference-serving-source-18)

Prefill and decode may be placed on different hardware to suit their different demands, but the KV state must be located and moved between them. Compare any phase-specific benefit with transfer and scheduling overhead at the actual request mix; the described heterogeneous placement is an architectural proposal without a measured head-to-head or cache-transfer cost. It is not caching a final answer. [Source 19](#inference-serving-source-19) [Source 20](#inference-serving-source-20)

## Schedule workers and provision readiness

For many small, fast requests, one described design puts annotated requests in a shared queue; workers pull work and form batches using local capacity rather than depending entirely on possibly stale central worker state. Keep gateway processing lightweight and large payloads outside the queue. If a worker pulls too many items, returning them over the network costs time; local coordination among colocated GPUs is one proposed remedy. The source does not establish its fairness or measured latency. [Source 21](#inference-serving-source-21) [Source 22](#inference-serving-source-22) [Source 23](#inference-serving-source-23)

Small models introduce a separate residency decision: dedicated warm pools for each model may waste capacity, while sharing a GPU can require pinned popular models plus lazy loading and eviction under memory pressure. That is a proposal without a detailed policy or measured outcomes; test load-time delays, memory contention and scheduling behavior for the intended mix. [Source 24](#inference-serving-source-24)

For procurement, compare usage pricing with dedicated capacity against measured baseload, allowed bursts and utilization; dedicated hardware is not automatically cheaper when idle. Readiness matters too: in computer-use workloads a GPU can wait while a large sandbox starts or resets. A demand-sized warm sandbox pool can move preparation ahead of need but pays for unused environments. Evaluate resource prices, startup delays and pool utilization rather than assuming savings; the described pool provides no measured hit rate or break-even. Runtime image size can similarly trade cold-start time against steady-state performance. [Source 25](#inference-serving-source-25) [Source 26](#inference-serving-source-26) [Source 27](#inference-serving-source-27) [Source 28](#inference-serving-source-28)

## Compare hardware and rental exposure on common terms

Compare accelerators on the same model, request mix, quality, latency objective and achieved utilization—not on relative speedup alone. Include service scope, networking, energy, software and operating costs: a managed cluster and bare-metal rental can leave different work with the buyer. More output at the same interactivity can improve capacity economics, but optimization and maintenance also cost money; a GPU hour is an input, not an acceptable completed task. [Source 29](#inference-serving-source-29) [Source 30](#inference-serving-source-30) [Source 31](#inference-serving-source-31)

If using a rental-price reference, inspect its sampled providers, service and contract terms, and whether it represents offers or completed trades; neither necessarily equals your realized rent. A proposed rent hedge depends on how changes in the reference move with changes in your own price, not just on similar price levels. This is a market-design argument, not a validated hedge or protection against operational risk. [Source 32](#inference-serving-source-32) [Source 33](#inference-serving-source-33)

## Speculative decoding

Covers token-level speculation, not speculative voice pipeline execution.

Speculative decoding can make generation faster by using a cheaper process to propose future tokens and asking the target model to check a block at once. It is an optimization of token generation, not an independent check of whether the answer is factually correct. Whether it helps depends on accepted work *and* the cost of producing and checking it.

## Draft and verify token blocks

In ordinary autoregressive generation, the model advances one token at a time. With a draft-model approach, a smaller model proposes several next tokens; the target evaluates the candidates together, accepts suitable ones and corrects rejected work before generation continues. One speaker gives three to five draft tokens per cycle as a typical illustrative setting, not a universal optimum. The opportunity is to advance through several useful tokens with fewer expensive sequential target steps. [Source 1](#speculative-decoding-source-1) [Source 2](#speculative-decoding-source-2)

This is target verification of token proposals, not verification against external evidence. Nor does this high-level account specify the acceptance and rejection algorithm needed to establish identical sampling distributions under every decoding setting. A speaker’s assertion that quality is unchanged is not a substitute for a distribution-preservation argument or a comparative quality experiment. Check the implementation and its validity for the intended sampling settings separately from the speed measurement.

Token speculation is also different from overlapping stages of a workflow or a voice pipeline: the latter may begin useful work before another stage finishes, whereas this mechanism proposes token continuations for target verification. For user-facing readiness and first audible speech, see [Interactive latency](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/interactive-latency.html).

## Choose a drafter and measure net benefit

A draft must be cheap enough to pay for itself and compatible enough with the target to produce useful candidates. A tiny model that is frequently rejected wastes its own work and still incurs target checking; a more accurate but expensive drafter can also eliminate the saving. One speaker recommends a much smaller model with the same tokenizer and ideally the same model family. A suggested size ratio is guidance for starting experiments, not a proven optimum. [Source 3](#speculative-decoding-source-3) [Source 4](#speculative-decoding-source-4)

There are other ways to propose tokens. A model-based drafter adds model compute and may improve acceptance; a model-free strategy can reuse patterns from the prompt or earlier output with lower overhead, especially when the continuation resembles that context. Compare actual net cost, not acceptance alone. Acceptance is the fraction of proposed tokens the target accepts; it explains how much speculative work survived, but is not itself latency, throughput or output quality. [Source 5](#speculative-decoding-source-5) [Source 6](#speculative-decoding-source-6)

Task and generation settings matter. Code, JSON and SQL are plausible candidates for better agreement than less predictable creative continuations, but one demonstration changed temperature as well as task type. It therefore does not isolate the effect of task structure. A drafter that works on coding may fail on specialized prose; remeasure when either the workload or sampling settings change. [Source 7](#speculative-decoding-source-7) [Source 8](#speculative-decoding-source-8)

## Compare the loaded service with its baseline

Compare speculation on and off using representative prompts, output lengths, sampling settings and traffic. Record accepted draft fraction, generation speed, user-visible latency, throughput and resource cost together. Drafting, target verification and rejected proposals all consume time. The additional model and caches also require memory; under higher concurrency they can compete with capacity needed for other requests. A single-request improvement need not translate into a better loaded service. [Source 9](#speculative-decoding-source-9) [Source 10](#speculative-decoding-source-10)

The evidence illustrates both directions, not a universal expected gain. A structured example on a Blackwell setup reportedly generated about 1.6 times faster; it was a single demonstration without repeated trials or a throughput curve. In a different demonstration, generation at concurrency one fell from about 58 to 16 tokens per second. The speaker attributed the loss primarily to draft incompatibility, but did not isolate that cause experimentally. [Source 6](#speculative-decoding-source-6) [Source 4](#speculative-decoding-source-4)

A vendor describes adapting draft strategy to request and workload because per-request gains can impose validation overhead on a batch. That is a reasonable decision to investigate, not a separately ablated proof that adaptive speculation wins. Use [Measuring inference serving performance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/inference-serving.html) to interpret service throughput and latency, and measure the complete application outcome separately: faster token production does not verify a report’s sources or establish its time to usable completion. [Source 11](#speculative-decoding-source-11) [Source 9](#speculative-decoding-source-9)
