## Verifying hardware and training optimizations

Covers kernels, precision and training-memory tradeoffs, not service-level SLO sweeps. Kernel mechanics and training architectures, not general model routing.

A GPU optimization is a hypothesis about a particular workload and machine, not a transferable speedup. First identify where wall-clock time and memory go; then choose a transformation, verify it on the target stack and measure both isolated and combined effects. [Verifying performance and kernel changes](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/performance-and-kernel-verification.html) covers the separate correctness and integrity gates.

## Profile before choosing a kernel

Distinguish compute saturation from memory movement, launch overhead and dependency waits. A low-FLOP operation can still cost time if it is invoked repeatedly or launches many small kernels: the normalization example in one talk illustrates this, but its invocation count depends on the model. Inspect CPU hot paths too. In one vendor case, a tensor-merge path involving repeated immutable-map copies accounted for a reported 8.8% of sampled CPU in one service and period; that sample is not a fleet-wide savings estimate. [Source 1](#gpu-optimization-source-1) [Source 2](#gpu-optimization-source-2) [Source 3](#gpu-optimization-source-3)

Try a compiler baseline before paying the development cost of a custom kernel. One speaker reports a newer compiler outperforming handwritten normalization in displayed comparisons, but exact compiler versions, hardware and code are unavailable. Treat that as a reason to measure, not a rule that custom kernels are obsolete. Give an optimizer accurate device-generation and interconnect capabilities, and inspect the model's actual architecture: experience can transfer, while an existing kernel may not. Benchmark on deployment hardware at relevant shapes, precision and workload ranges, with a communication-aware baseline for multi-GPU paths. A local open implementation makes this test possible, not automatically successful. [Source 4](#gpu-optimization-source-4) [Source 5](#gpu-optimization-source-5) [Source 6](#gpu-optimization-source-6) [Source 7](#gpu-optimization-source-7) [Source 8](#gpu-optimization-source-8)

A specialized kernel can win for some context lengths and lose elsewhere. Measure each regime and dispatch to a validated fallback where necessary; the source's example range is not a portable threshold. Re-measure the combined stack because improvements may interact and eventually meet hardware limits. One vendor reports roughly 25% improvement from bare-metal changes and a threefold combined gain with kernels, without controlled attribution or a complete workload and stability protocol. Neither is a guaranteed kernel-only speedup. [Source 9](#gpu-optimization-source-9) [Source 10](#gpu-optimization-source-10) [Source 11](#gpu-optimization-source-11)

## Memory movement and recomputation are different levers

Fusion and cache reuse reduce intermediate transfers or repeated loads; a row-wise fused loss can avoid materializing the full logits tensor, with savings dependent on dimensions and context. Gradient checkpointing instead retains selected activations and recomputes omitted intermediates during training. It can lower memory at the cost of extra work and longer runtime. One speaker reports roughly 70% memory reduction and 10–15% slower training in an example; neither number is a general bound. Measure memory, runtime and quality for the chosen implementation. [Source 12](#gpu-optimization-source-12)

## Three distinct normalization transformations

1. **Offline gain folding:** where the algebra and architecture permit, combine a normalization gain with adjacent weights in a transformed checkpoint, avoiding repeated communication during inference. This is not the same as removing normalization altogether. [Source 13](#gpu-optimization-source-13)
2. **Deferred scaling:** rearrange compatible work so matrix multiplication and RMS computation run concurrently, then apply post-scale only after both finish. This needs lower-level scheduling and correct synchronization; algebra alone does not establish a correct or faster implementation. [Source 14](#gpu-optimization-source-14)
3. **Conditional elimination:** the speaker proposes dropping a redundant normalization only in a particular two-normalization structure when the relevant scale-invariance argument applies. It is not permission to delete arbitrary layers. The available account omits the exact algebra, full architecture proof and independent equivalence tests. [Source 15](#gpu-optimization-source-15)

Test each change and its combination with the actual compiler, quantization and serving stack; reported compatibility is not a versioned support matrix. [Source 16](#gpu-optimization-source-16)

## Schedule communication with computation

Multi-GPU performance depends on transfer and synchronization as well as arithmetic. In the NVIDIA-specific discussion, a host-initiated copy engine suits large transfers while conserving compute resources; device-initiated tensor-memory mechanisms can support finer-grained overlap, and register-based instructions can enable in-network reductions at different resource costs. Select for message size, registers, processor availability and topology rather than assuming one mechanism wins everywhere. [Source 17](#gpu-optimization-source-17)

When communication and compute data patterns align, different warps may overlap the work; when their requirements do not align, specialization across processors may be preferable. Both approaches still depend on data readiness and the interconnect. Compare against a baseline that includes communication, not a compute-only ideal. [Source 18](#gpu-optimization-source-18) [Source 8](#gpu-optimization-source-8)

## Overlap training without ignoring stale policies

Long agent rollouts finish at different times. A synchronous trainer waits for stragglers to preserve a fresher policy; an asynchronous design overlaps generation, grading and training, but some trajectories were generated by older policies. The learning recipe must handle that off-policy lag and be checked for stability—no universal safe lag or controlled throughput advantage is established by the cited workshop. [Source 19](#gpu-optimization-source-19)

One proposed architecture separates environment execution, inference replicas and the trainer behind services, with an orchestrator collecting and batching rollouts. This allows their counts to scale independently and an environment to run as an evaluation without starting a trainer. Large multimodal artifacts and mixture-of-experts router metadata can be moved out of process memory into object or file storage while preserving what is needed to reconstruct training inputs. These are architectural recommendations, not measured savings. [Source 20](#gpu-optimization-source-20) [Source 21](#gpu-optimization-source-21)

An anecdotal classifier example used a provisioned sandbox for an agent to compare and train candidates, test, clean up resources and report hosting considerations; classifier metrics were not disclosed. It illustrates bounded experimentation, not proof of model quality. [Source 22](#gpu-optimization-source-22) For request-level latency and service objectives, see [Measuring inference serving performance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/inference-serving.html).

## Interactive latency

Covers voice stage readiness and overlap, not aggregate inference throughput.

A voice user does not experience a first token or a network byte. The relevant conversational gap starts at the caller’s last syllable and ends when meaningful agent speech becomes audible. Measuring that interval per utterance, alongside the boundaries of the intervening stages, reveals delays that a fast component metric can conceal. [Source 1](#interactive-latency-source-1) [Source 2](#interactive-latency-source-2)

## Measure audible response and downstream readiness

Instrument the caller’s last syllable, the turn-completion decision, recognition and model readiness, the first text the speech stage can use, the first synthesized byte and the first meaningful sound heard by the caller. Record function calls and handoffs where they lie on the response path. The end-to-end gap answers the experience question; the intermediate markers help locate the delay. Overlapping stages need their actual timestamps: adding all component durations as if they were serial can misstate the critical path. [Source 1](#interactive-latency-source-1) [Source 3](#interactive-latency-source-3)

A TTS service can send bytes that contain initial silence. One speaker reports observing up to 750 milliseconds of silence after an early response byte, but does not name providers or give sample counts, distributions or the silence-detection method. That report motivates measuring audible onset; it does not establish a typical delay or a ranking of providers. [Source 2](#interactive-latency-source-2) [Source 4](#interactive-latency-source-4)

Likewise, the first language-model token is useful only if the next stage can consume it. In the described pipeline, speech synthesis waits for a complete sentence, so time to first sentence can matter more than time to first token. A different streaming synthesizer may accept a smaller unit: measure the actual readiness boundary for the deployed pipeline rather than imposing the sentence assumption everywhere. A model that wins on token onset can lose on time to usable speech. [Source 5](#interactive-latency-source-5) [Source 6](#interactive-latency-source-6)

The speakers suggest 500–600 milliseconds as a more human-like target and around 1.5 seconds as a tolerable upper region. These are practical heuristics, not controlled perception thresholds or universal accessibility requirements; related presentations should not be counted as independent confirmation. Choose a budget appropriate to the interaction, then preserve useful and reliable behavior inside it rather than selecting the fastest component regardless of its effect on the task. [Source 1](#interactive-latency-source-1) [Source 7](#interactive-latency-source-7)

These per-utterance timestamps answer a different question from an aggregate serving SLO, and neither is the same as a GPU kernel microbenchmark. A fast kernel does not guarantee a quick spoken response if turn detection, sentence buffering or synthesis dominates. Conversely, an average voice gap alone does not guarantee acceptable tail behavior. For serving measurement and SLOs, see [Measuring inference serving performance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/inference-serving.html); for isolated hardware performance verification, see [Verifying performance and kernel changes](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/performance-and-kernel-verification.html).

## Overlap voice processing provisionally

A turn detector can decide that speech has ended while automatic speech recognition is still finalizing its text. Instead of waiting serially, start model work on a provisional transcript and compare it with the final transcript. If the words agree, the work already done may move the response closer to the caller. The speaker reports a possible half-second saving in this matching case; it is not a measured guarantee for other workloads. Synthesis can begin once this pipeline has the speakable unit it requires. [Source 3](#interactive-latency-source-3)

The mismatch case determines whether the optimization is safe. If final recognition changes a date, amount or intent, provisional output may be wrong. A design needs a policy for discarding or revising speculative work, cancelling stale output and preventing premature tool side effects; the presentation does not specify those mechanisms. Until such handling is established, treat early work as provisional rather than as authority to execute an irreversible action. Measure both the matching-case benefit and the cost and consequences of corrections. [Source 3](#interactive-latency-source-3)

This is overlap between voice pipeline stages, not the token-level target-verified mechanism described in [Speculative decoding](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/speculative-decoding.html). Slow external operations create a separate conversational design problem; see [Voice-agent operations](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/voice-agent-operations.html).

## Budgeting evaluation and monitoring

Covers evaluation feedback and monitor budgets rather than product-task quality itself. Evaluation, verification and monitoring economics, not serving configuration.

A useful evaluation system returns decision-relevant feedback soon enough to act on it, while retaining coverage of consequential failures. Faster execution is not itself a better model, and an evaluation that runs successfully is not evidence that its output is factually acceptable. Budget the checking system as a workload in its own right: generation, scoring, human review, infrastructure and the time needed to revise tests.

## Shorten the feedback loop without changing the claim

Parallel rollouts can reduce wall-clock waiting by executing independent cases concurrently, subject to capacity and cost. They do not make the agent more competent. In one demonstration the parallel benchmark did not finish, so it establishes neither a completed score nor a measured speedup. A separate team reports simulation compressing feedback that previously took days or weeks to hours or less than a day; exact timing and simulation-to-production correlation were not established. Use simulation to screen changes, not as automatic proof of live performance. [Source 1](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-1) [Source 2](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-2)

Measure feedback delay, coverage, annotation quality and infrastructure spend separately. A self-service annotation platform may lower handling costs and shorten loops, but its reported savings did not establish label reliability or judge accuracy. Similarly, a monitor capacity ablation can reveal unnecessary expense: one speaker reported a four-times expansion sparse autoencoder matching a 32-times version in one synthetic SQL-injection backdoor setting with a 40% poison fraction, one model and four tested middle layers. No adaptive attacker was tested, so the comparison does not establish general production-monitoring coverage. Recheck detection of the failures that matter before reducing capacity. [Source 3](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-3) [Source 4](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-4)

## Select and stage checks around decisions

Start with the decision: what failures would block a release, require a fix, or change a model choice? Select the smallest set of signals that covers those failure modes, not the smallest count of metrics. A rare severe failure can justify a dedicated check even if most cases pass. [Source 5](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-5) [Source 6](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-6)

Run cheap, relevant regression subsets while iterating, then the broader suite at integration. Categorizing cases by failure mode helps select a meaningful subset; it does not guarantee early detection of regressions outside it. The suggested schedule is a cost-control proposal, not a measured miss rate or universal cadence. Where a recurring convention error can be expressed in a maintained lint rule, weigh the rule's authoring and maintenance against repeated review and correction; cheap rule generation does not eliminate maintenance. [Source 7](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-7) [Source 8](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-8)

Check artifacts as soon as a defect is observable. In a video workflow, comparing starting frames can catch identity drift before generating clips; a bad clip can be repaired before a long assembly. Still evaluate the assembled sequence for temporal or story-level defects that a frame check cannot see. This is a workflow argument, not a quantified savings result. [Source 9](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-9)

For objective structure, use code before a model judge. **Illustrative:** parse a text-to-JSON response, check required fields and reject nulls; only then spend semantic-review capacity on whether the values are supported by the source. Passing the schema is not factual acceptance. Likewise, known-pattern filters may precede a classifier, but regex cannot provide comprehensive prompt-injection protection. [Source 10](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-10) [Source 11](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-11)

## Account for the whole evaluation bill

One case can involve an application call and several judge calls; repeated stochastic trials multiply both. Include generation, judges, expert labels, audits, engineering, compute for checkpoints, and renewing stale tests. Do not reduce sample sizes merely to make the bill look smaller: the remaining comparison must still be informative for the decision. The Game Arena speakers report roughly 400,000 poker hands for a stochastic comparison and discuss pairings to reduce games; they do not provide a sample-size derivation or significance threshold. [Source 12](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-12) [Source 13](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-13) [Source 14](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-14)

Save outputs and their relevant context so a rubric edit can be tested by rescoring fixed material rather than rerunning the application; a generation prompt change generally requires new outputs. Compare judge decisions against domain-expert labels and investigate disagreements as possible evaluator errors, not just application errors. A writing benchmark's speaker reported over $2,000 for a rubric change versus over $4,000 for a generation-input change, specific to its approximately 120 models, ten tasks and five drafts—not a general price schedule. [Source 15](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-15) [Source 16](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-16)

A cheap initial answer can also have an expensive audit. One reported case put checking—including second opinions, disagreement resolution and audit—at roughly four times first-answer cost; inconsistent currency captions prevent reconstructing its exact bill. Keep this evaluation budget distinct from the deployed cost per accepted task discussed in [Comparing task quality, cost and value](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/decision-economics.html). [Source 17](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-17)

## Monitor live behavior according to risk

Offline regression fixtures protect against known failures; production sampling discovers cases the fixtures miss. A cheap regex can track aggregate frustration trends, while a specialized classifier or model judge can inspect more nuanced cases. Neither a high pass rate nor a mature system alone proves an evaluator can be retired: consider severity and what a missed case costs. One workshop suggests 5–10% judge sampling after establishing a baseline, but gives no statistical-power or rare-event justification; it is an example, not a safe default. [Source 18](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-18) [Source 19](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-19) [Source 20](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-20)

A cascade may send obvious cases through cheap checks and escalate uncertain or high-impact cases to deeper analysis. Audit a sample of bypassed cases, including known incidents and adversarial or changed inputs, and measure misses by severity. Similarity and creator-metadata bypasses have been proposed for video analysis, but their false-negative rates were not reported. A low-cost first pass can silently remove the very context an expensive reviewer needs. [Source 21](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-21) [Source 22](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-22) [Source 23](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-23)

## Decide whether a specialist judge pays for itself

A small distilled judge is a separate investment from training the model being judged. Compare its held-out agreement with expert labels and the existing committee, failure modes, feedback latency, per-item serving cost, and the cost of collecting labels, training, deployment and replicas. At low volume, the existing committee may be cheaper overall; at high volume or when feedback must sit close to generation, a specialist may justify the up-front work. A video team preferred a smaller judge over a reportedly better but slower larger one; it supplied neither a quantitative accuracy comparison nor a universal break-even threshold. [Source 24](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-24) [Source 25](#evaluation-infrastructure-source-25)

**Illustrative cost calculation:** if a committee costs $0.10 per item, a specialist costs $0.02 per item, and curation, training and deployment cost $800, the simple financial break-even is 10,000 items: $800 divided by $0.08 saved per item. This excludes ongoing maintenance, replication, labeling and the cost of additional errors; a cheaper judge that misses consequential failures may not be acceptable at any volume.

### Source 1: Everything Is a Rollout — Alex Shaw + Ryan Marten, Terminal-Bench, Harbor, Laude Institute

## Evaluation-driven improvement

Covers experiment design and regression evidence, not the optimizer’s search algorithm.

An evaluation becomes useful for improvement when it does more than announce a score: it identifies a failure, helps locate a repair, and tests whether that repair preserves what already worked. Even then, a passing set establishes behavior only on the cases and conditions examined. The aim is a disciplined cycle of focused learning and broader verification, not a claim that repeated testing makes an agent generally correct.

## Turn a new capability into a protected behavior

Start with a behavior the system cannot yet perform reliably. Keep examples that expose that failure together with examples it already handles correctly. Work on the new capability, then retain its checks as regression tests when the behavior is sufficiently reliable for the intended use. The point of the transition is to keep a subsequent improvement from silently undoing an earlier one; a workshop's suggestion of a 100% transition is a teaching model, not a validated production threshold. [Source 1](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-1)

Use the failure subset for inexpensive iterations, but periodically run the broader corpus and do so before a release decision. A financial-agent workshop reported that six selected failures passed after a prompt revision; it did not show repeated trials or freeze live search results, and this selected-case result did not establish broad improvement. A candidate can fit those six cases while damaging others. [Source 2](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-2)

## Diagnose before choosing the repair

A final wrong answer is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Read the input, retrieved evidence, intermediate decisions, tool requests and outputs around representative failures. Compare cases that changed between candidates, not just their aggregate scores. Traces provide a denser explanation of a failure than pass/fail alone, while the outcome still matters: a convincing trajectory is not a substitute for completing the task. [Source 3](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-3) [Source 4](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-4)

For example, an agent citing a stale policy and skipping escalation might have outdated memory, a weak instruction, malformed tool data, a missing workflow gate or a reasoning problem. That scenario is illustrative, not a validated root-cause classifier. Investigate the evidence and repair the responsible layer: update the source when it is stale; fix the harness for context overload; enforce a schema at the interface when structure is the defect. A prompt prohibition is not automatically the right remedy. [Source 5](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-5) [Source 6](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-6)

Causes can combine. In a selected international-stock demonstration, adding country information did not resolve failures until the outdated tool was also updated. The reported final success rate is bounded by an unspecified dataset size and judge calibration; the failed intermediate attempt is the more useful lesson than the headline gain. Prioritize recurring defects by consequence as well as frequency, while keeping enough contextual evidence to investigate them responsibly. For instrumentation details, see [Tracing and diagnosing production behavior](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/agent-observability-and-diagnosis.html). [Source 7](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-7) [Source 8](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-8)

## Compare candidates under controlled conditions

Save the baseline configuration and compare it with the candidate on the same inputs, evaluator and, where possible, environment and retrieved data. Change a bounded component when the question is causal: if the model, prompt and tools all change at once, a whole-system comparison can show which configuration performed better on the test, but not which change produced the difference. Repeating stochastic cases helps estimate typical behavior, at a compute cost; one favorable run is weak evidence of a small improvement. Fixed inputs and a fixed judge do not eliminate sampling or live-retrieval variation. [Source 9](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-9) [Source 10](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-10) [Source 11](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-11)

Version history and an attractive new prompt establish what changed, not that it improved outcomes. Check the actual outputs and disagreements as well as the metric, and use a broader or held-out set that has not guided every iteration when making a generalization claim. Even an optimized aggregate can leave the original failure intact: in one workshop a selected political-relation extraction still misclassified a sports commentator after optimization. That was a demonstration, not an independently validated production result. [Source 12](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-12) [Source 13](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-13)

## Protect more than the headline score

Define the dimensions that must not be traded away: task completion, factual grounding, critical slices, tool behavior, cost or latency, and any relevant safety requirements. An overall average can conceal a regression in a capability that a particular user needs. Likewise, adaptation for a specialist task should be checked against relevant general capabilities, rather than assuming they survive. [Source 14](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-14) [Source 15](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-15)

One small financial-report workshop illustrates why separate checks matter. Adding explicit recommendation instructions improved measured actionability across repeated outputs, yet faithfulness remained poor. An actionable form is not a sound recommendation, and the demonstration's small, nondeterministic experiments are not evidence of financial usefulness. Keep the unresolved grounding failure visible rather than averaging it away. [Source 16](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-16)

## Make iteration fast without weakening the release decision

Fast, inexpensive, low-noise checks allow more useful experiments. Run a compact, representative regression subset and the current failure set during development; use reusable cases and structured feedback to reduce setup and diagnosis time. Compression saves effort but may omit an important failure, so periodically restore broader checks and investigate whether the fast suite still represents the behaviors it is meant to protect. An agent may exploit gaps in an evaluator; inspect the outputs behind a rising number. [Source 17](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-17) [Source 1](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-1)

A release gate should combine evidence that the targeted defect improved with checks for previously passing behavior and critical dimensions. Thresholds must be chosen for the application and its risk; a workshop's replay threshold is a local decision, not a universal safety guarantee. After release, continue evaluating real interactions and add coverage for newly discovered failure classes: a detector can help find recurrence, but does not itself prevent it. [Source 18](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-18) [Source 19](#evaluation-driven-improvement-source-19)

For how candidates are constructed rather than compared, see [Prompt and harness optimization](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/prompt-and-harness-optimization.html); for the integrity of the objective being optimized, see [Search and objective integrity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/search-and-objective-integrity.html).

### Source 19: Guardrails First: Engineering Member-Facing Health AI — Rashi Agrawal, Hinge Health

[Watch original](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YXEqC05WEI0) · [Transcript lines](https://github.com/flaviusapop/ai-engineer-evals/blob/main/transcripts/YXEqC05WEI0.md#L319-L320)

## Search and objective integrity

Covers objectives, governance and acceptance decisions, not domain-specific candidate-generation methods.

An optimization loop can get better at its score without getting better at the job. Before letting it try many changes, state the user outcome, the evidence that would count as success, and the boundaries a solution must respect. A reward or business KPI is a proposed representation of that intent, not proof that the representation is faithful. Domain experts should own the underlying success criteria: see [Define domain success and expert accountability](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/define-domain-success-and-expert-accountability.html). [Source 1](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-1) [Source 2](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-2)

A creative-editing case illustrates the gap: a rejection-driven loop overcorrected toward a generic ceramic bowl. The pixels changed, but the speakers regarded the result as commercially meaningless. This is an illustrated failure, not an estimate of how often it happens. Check the usefulness of accepted changes, not just whether they avoid explicit rejection. [Source 3](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-3)

## Stable comparisons, evolving objectives and nonmonotonic search

For a comparison, hold the task, scenarios, scorecard and evaluation configuration stable while candidates change. Otherwise, a score increase may reflect a changed measuring stick rather than an improved implementation. Stability for a comparison does not mean the scorecard must never change: when production learning exposes a missing objective, review the change, version the new scorecard, and rerun the baseline and candidates under it. Report which version produced each result; scores across different versions are not automatically comparable. [Source 4](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-4) [Source 5](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-5)

List the dimensions separately before combining them: task success, latency, cost, reliability, privacy or other relevant risks. If search requires a scalar, assign explicit weights, or set non-negotiable constraints and optimize one remaining dimension. A weight allows tradeoffs; a constraint excludes candidates outside its limit. Neither approach supplies the right weights or limits automatically. A cheaper or faster candidate can fail the task: in one selected demonstration a later iteration reduced latency and turn count but failed after an earlier iteration passed. This is not a convergence test. [Source 6](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-6) [Source 7](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-7)

The optimizer's chosen weights and constraints are a **decision policy**, not the empirical cost–quality frontier. The latter describes observed candidate tradeoffs under a particular workload and measurement setup; see [Comparing task quality, cost and value](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/decision-economics.html). Do not infer equivalent quality from a lower price, or from two similar-looking scores without the evidence needed to assess their difference.

Prioritize experiments using expected impact and frequency together with deployment risk and the human effort required to review them. A frequently used payment flow can warrant attention that an infrequent operation does not, while a risky migration can cost more review than a small change. This is a decision consideration, not a supplied ROI formula. [Source 8](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-8)

Keep process validity separate from task accuracy. An inspectable, constrained process can leave useful evidence even when the answer fails or experts reasonably disagree over the ground truth. Conversely, a valid process does not make the answer correct. One team reported internal task-success gains while changing several components, but did not disclose enough to attribute the improvement to its harness alone. [Source 9](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-9)

## Search and objective integrity

### Protect the measurement surface

Freeze the cases, harness and metrics for the comparison; explicitly grant the optimizer access only to intended artifacts, such as selected prompts, memory policies or retrieval rules. Preserve a known version and a way to undo edits. A prompt telling an agent not to change the evaluator is not itself evidence of a hard access control; use an appropriate enforced boundary when the risk requires one. Even a protected scorecard can encode the wrong goal. [Source 10](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-10) [Source 11](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-11)

For example, an integration-skill optimizer rewarded fewer turns and proposed removing documentation-fetching instructions; other missing criteria allowed it to remove trace-linking guidance. The sandbox could not evaluate an approval gate for data leaving the machine. Humans accepted only three of six suggestions after review. A missing observable cannot be protected merely by assuming that a passing score covers it. [Source 12](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-12)

### Run a conditional keep-or-revert loop

1. Establish a baseline and a concrete failure surface: task examples and checks that can reject a fluent but wrong answer. Specify budget, time and access limits. [Source 13](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-13) [Source 11](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-11)
2. Propose a bounded change and record its parent version and diff. Rerun the same cases and complete scorecard, including correctness and guardrails.
3. Keep the candidate only if the decision rule is satisfied; otherwise revert to the known version. Inspect individual regressions and uncertain results rather than accepting a marginal aggregate improvement blindly. [Source 14](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-14) [Source 15](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-15)
4. Preserve candidate versions and results as branches: extend promising alternatives, revisit earlier ones, and record why each was retained or rejected. In a prepared prompt-optimization walkthrough, the presenter selected version five after reaching version ten because later changes regressed; the small evaluation does not establish held-out generalization. [Source 16](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-16) [Source 17](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-17)

A local metric can hide an end-to-end regression: a kernel may look faster after a surrounding acceleration is disabled while the full inference path becomes slower. Retain the real operating conditions in the acceptance question. The correctness-and-speed loop is guidance, not a complete specification of tolerances, timing or statistical acceptance; selected winners still need independent validation. For verifier design and its limits, see [Tests, oracles and verifier validity](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tests-oracles-and-verifier-validity.html) and [Protect holdouts and historical evidence](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/protect-holdouts-and-historical-evidence.html). [Source 18](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-18) [Source 14](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-14)

### Govern search, feedback and decisions

Automation can explore parameters, analyze recurring failure patterns and propose patches; people retain responsibility for requirements, objective-defining data and evaluator changes, and promotion. Give an improvement agent the product requirements and recurring failure themes, not only instructions to make individual tests pass. A proposed fix or automatically generated evaluator is an artifact for review, not evidence that autonomous repair worked. In one speaker's experience, human structural ideas and agent parameter tuning played different roles; that anecdote is not a comparative benchmark. [Source 19](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-19) [Source 20](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-20) [Source 21](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-21)

Separate the inner task execution from an outer improvement loop: capture trajectories, rewards and relevant artifacts; analyze failures; propose a change; then test it under the controlled scorecard. Rollouts can feed different learning or prompt-improvement methods, but reuse of infrastructure does not turn training material into independent held-out evaluation. Rewards themselves can be gamed. [Source 22](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-22) [Source 23](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-23)

Finally, choose action, confirmation, stop or human-review thresholds using the relevant outcome distribution and the costs of mistakes and interruptions. A stop can prevent a wrong action but also delay someone whose request was understood correctly. The voice-assistant example in the source uses illustrative request and recovery-cost assumptions, so its preferred threshold is not a portable default. In a clinical example, a missed red flag is treated as more costly than an unnecessary follow-up question; clinicians must determine the applicable tradeoff, not a flat accuracy score. [Source 24](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-24) [Source 25](#search-and-objective-integrity-source-25)

## Prompt and harness optimization

Covers prompt, orchestration and memory updates, not weight-training algorithms.

An agent can improve because its instructions became clearer, its execution environment changed, or it was given more opportunities to try—not necessarily because the underlying model changed. Optimize the system against the actual task, keeping a simple baseline and a separate evaluation for changes that may make it worse.

## Choose retention and compaction for the actual constraint

First identify what binds: context capacity, latency, cost, or the ability to recall a detail. Retaining history may be the simplest useful baseline. If a few tool outputs dominate the window, try truncating outliers with the omission clearly marked, clearing expendable results, or retaining a recent-turn window before adding a model-generated summary. Selective summaries can preserve decisions while losing details needed later; clearing material can also force expensive retrieval again. Compare downstream task success and total cost, including re-retrieval, rather than treating a shorter context as automatically better. [Source 1](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-1) [Source 2](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-2)

In one workshop, cached full history won the initial comparison, which involved only one or two trials. Its speakers nevertheless described an operational compaction cutoff without reconciling it with those longer-history findings. Another team used downstream behavior because it lacked a principled intrinsic measure of context quality; passing those evaluations supports only the tested heuristic. Details on cache economics belong in [Managing context, retrieval and cache costs](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/context-and-retrieval.html), and loading tool details on demand in [Tool interfaces](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/tool-interfaces.html). [Source 2](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-2) [Source 3](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-3)

## Make instructions a testable task specification

State the outcome, relevant authoritative reference, input interpretation, and conditional procedures needed for this task. Start with a minimal version and add observed local gotchas instead of copying a complete manual into every run. A rule should say when it applies: a workaround for one framework location may be harmful elsewhere. Compare the same task with and without guidance; an instruction can be well written and still distract the model. One practitioner reported 77% correctness with a skill and 97% without it, but supplied no trial count or uncertainty, so this is a reason to test, not a general estimate of skill harm. [Source 4](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-4) [Source 5](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-5) [Source 6](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-6)

Minimal does not mean never giving rich examples. In voice-sensitive writing, positive samples and concrete counterexamples can communicate a target that a short instruction misses. The guidance is experiential, without a controlled prompt-length ablation. Evaluate added context against the smaller baseline on the actual writing task. [Source 7](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-7)

## Search prompts with diagnostic feedback

Fix the task contract and scoring checks, then propose instructions, run representative cases, inspect failures, and revise. Reflection can use intermediate outputs, tool responses and errors rather than only a scalar score; that extra diagnostic information matters when rollouts are costly. A prompt found this way can encode the component's role and task-specific constraints, not just a collection of magic phrases. For example, one reported search learned to avoid a library header incompatible with its target hardware generation; the baseline improvement ratio was caption-ambiguous. [Source 8](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-8) [Source 9](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-9) [Source 10](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-10)

A search that keeps only the aggregate leader may discard a candidate that handles a rare case particularly well. Retaining candidates that win on individual examples preserves alternative strengths for further edits or combinations. This Pareto-style frontier is search diversity, not a guarantee of global optimality or unseen performance. In one classification experiment the speaker reported improvement from 68% to about 83% during iteration and 80.2% on an untouched test set; labels were author-selected and sometimes subjective. Those are different estimands, not interchangeable accuracy claims. [Source 11](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-11) [Source 12](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-12) [Source 13](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-13) [Source 14](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-14)

For mechanically checkable requirements, a program specification can generate candidates and test constraints directly: a demonstration searched for numbered lines with specified word counts and initials. It did not report held-out performance. Keep a final test independent of repeated selection and inspect failures of the checks themselves; a score is only as meaningful as the specification. [Source 15](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-15)

## Compress and adapt without changing the contract

Instruction compression is not model-weight compression or conversation-history compaction. Hold input, output schema and task requirements fixed while searching for fewer instruction tokens, then separately test correctness and cost. A fictional classifier example reported a 51% reduction in instruction tokens, not proof of production savings or preserved quality. Historical production answers can seed training labels, but they may be inconsistent or wrong: review disagreements so a genuinely better answer is not rejected merely for differing from the old system. Reoptimizing for a smaller model is distinct from copying the larger model's prompt; downsizing trials can still overfit or fail the release gate. [Source 16](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-16) [Source 17](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-17)

Whole-prompt rewriting can discover useful details but accumulate instructions. Selecting a bounded subset of prepared components would cap growth while limiting what the search can express; that approach was proposed, not experimentally established as optimal. Similarly, model-specific corrections may help one family and overcorrect another. Ablate skills, compile only applicable rules, and retest scaffolding after a model upgrade; remove workarounds only when the new combination passes the relevant tasks. A speaker's argument that stronger instruction following can make precise prompts more valuable is a hypothesis, not a scaling law. [Source 18](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-18) [Source 19](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-19) [Source 20](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-20) [Source 21](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-21)

## Search the harness and allocate the budget

When prompt changes plateau, the editable artifact may be control flow, tool availability, state handling, or which role does what. A reported experiment changed a short model-call program into a process involving rule induction, code synthesis, execution, tracing and debugging. This shows an explored search surface, not proof that any scorable program can be optimized reliably. Before adding architecture, test whether supplying domain context and explaining available tools solves the problem; that priority is practitioner guidance rather than a controlled comparison. [Source 22](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-22) [Source 23](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-23) [Source 24](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-24)

At a fixed inference budget, compare an execution-only system with alternatives that reserve some compute for an adviser, a grader, or coordination. An adviser can be consulted mid-task; a grader can request revision; a later reflection can help future runs. A strategy that spends more tokens is not evidence that its orchestration is intrinsically better. Composing these roles is an architectural proposal, and results from particular financial tasks should not be generalized to every workflow. [Source 25](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-25) [Source 26](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-26) [Source 27](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-27)

## Bound repair and make room for divergence

Feed validator errors or critic feedback back to the agent, but limit attempts and inspect the final result. In a query demonstration, a prohibited regular expression was repaired into an allowed exact-title match that found nothing; adding full-text search addressed the information need. Validity and usefulness were separate outcomes, and this was a staged demonstration, not a recovery-rate estimate. If repeated revisions remain below the target, permit a restart rather than preserving a failing approach indefinitely. For voice writing, one practitioner warns that too many critique cycles can make the draft generic; that limit is experiential rather than measured. [Source 28](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-28) [Source 29](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-29) [Source 30](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-30) [Source 31](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-31)

Creative work has a different objective from passing a syntactic check. Banning a familiar style may merely elicit the next familiar default. External inspiration, a sampled starting color, or fresh-context ranking can introduce diversity; assess whether the result fits the brief, not whether it is merely different. These examples are qualitative, not measured guarantees of originality. [Source 32](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-32) [Source 33](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-33) [Source 34](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-34)

## Carry verified lessons into future runs

A within-run critique changes the current attempt. Cross-run learning instead distills a success or failure into scoped guidance that a later run can retrieve or use as a revised procedure; neither changes model weights. For example, a retrospective might notice repeated identical tool calls and store a framework-specific lesson where it applies, rather than burdening every task with it. Replay the triggering case and regression cases before promoting the lesson, and check that future agents actually use it. The cited memory systems report no longitudinal proof that accumulated lessons improve outcomes; automatic pruning remains future work in one example. Runtime retrieval and slower consolidation into persistent guidance can coexist rather than being mutually exclusive. [Source 35](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-35) [Source 36](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-36) [Source 37](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-37) [Source 38](#prompt-and-harness-optimization-source-38)

For the broader improvement loop, see [Evaluation-driven improvement](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluation-driven-improvement.html).

## Retrieval and query optimization

Covers retrieval and tool-access mechanisms, not general context compaction or downstream model training.

Optimize retrieval for the question and decision, not for a single impressive search score. Exact identifiers, paraphrased concepts, broad documentary evidence and structured counts have different failure modes. Compare candidate strategies on representative tasks and include the quality and cost of the answer that uses them.

## Combine complementary searches

Lexical search can find an exact error code or function name but miss a synonym; semantic search can find the synonym but confuse similarly described functions. Run both when both failure modes matter. Their raw scores need not share a scale, so adding them directly can give one retriever arbitrary dominance. [Source 1](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-1) [Source 2](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-2)

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines ranked positions instead of the original score magnitudes, with a tunable rank constant. This lets the two searches contribute without assuming their raw scores are directly comparable. Alternatively, normalize scores and tune weighted combinations against query–document relevance judgments. This retains score information but depends on the normalization, weights and labels. Tune on the intended query mix; RRF is a starting point, not a universal winner, and automatically generated relevance labels are not automatically trustworthy. [Source 2](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-2) [Source 3](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-3)

## Choose query strategy, filters and reranking

Use a natural description for semantic search when the intended meaning is broad, but use a literal pattern or keyword for an exact identifier. Route recognized query types to explicit templates—for instance, a hybrid search or a hybrid search followed by reranking. A real date, location or category constraint can filter the candidate pool before ranking; an inferred but incorrect constraint may exclude the answer. The template architecture is not evidence of continuously learned autotuning. [Source 4](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-4) [Source 5](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-5) [Source 6](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-6)

After candidate generation, thresholds decide which weak matches survive. A single fixed cutoff can reject a relevant result for a short or unusual query, while a permissive cutoff sends noise onward. One search tool used a query-sensitive heuristic instead of a slower model judge; its reported timings and quality are setting-specific and its threshold method is not fully specified. Tune against both missed evidence and irrelevant context. [Source 7](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-7)

A reranker can compare candidates more carefully. Pointwise scoring examines each query–candidate pair separately; listwise comparison considers competing candidates together, potentially useful when near-duplicates differ in one decisive detail. Joint comparison costs resources and time, and the cited workshop gives no comparative benchmark proving it is always superior. [Source 8](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-8)

## Vary evidence granularity

A small passage may answer a focused fact question; a broader question may need context spread across a document. A fixed chunk size selected for average corpus performance can conceal those differences. In one research design the same corpus was indexed at several scales, each query searched all copies, and chunk hits were mapped to shared document identities before their document rankings were fused. This avoids comparing unlike chunk identities, but multiple copies and searches cost storage and work, and whole-document context has its own cost. [Source 9](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-9) [Source 10](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-10) [Source 11](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-11) [Source 12](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-12)

A hindsight oracle that picks the best scale using known answers measures potential headroom, not a deployable selection policy. The reported multi-scale recall gains are benchmark-specific; incomplete protocols and ambiguous percentage definitions prevent a clean universal effect size. Number of scales and fusion choices remain open. For production index lifecycle and provenance, see [Managing production retrieval, data and provenance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/retrieval-evidence-and-provenance.html). [Source 13](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-13) [Source 14](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-14)

## Demand task-level benefit

Compare additions to a simpler baseline on the same representative questions, including exact-detail probes and final answer quality, latency and cost. A tutoring case found that adding filesystem browsing to its hybrid retriever increased latency by roughly half without improving relevant-page recall on its student questions; that does not rule out browsing for tasks with more cross-document dependencies. A separate reported long-context probe found lexical retrieval retained buried exact facts that its dense setup missed, but omitted the details needed to generalize the comparison. [Source 15](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-15) [Source 16](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-16)

Define target documents and relevance measures with [Evaluate and represent retrieval corpora](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/evaluate-and-represent-retrieval-corpora.html); retrieval recall is not itself proof of a correct final answer. A narrow adaptation can be tested too, but a reported German legal retrieval improvement lacks the metric and protocol needed to transfer its numerical claim. [Source 17](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-17)

## Select useful memories and executable resources

Semantic similarity alone does not mean a prior memory helps. Consider ranking candidate memories by both task relevance and observed usefulness, while recognizing that credit assignment can be noisy and new memories lack outcome history. In a reported 68-question experiment, a ranked decision ledger outperformed a policy that first gated whether to recall; exact scores, ranking and uncertainty were not supplied. Compare these choices on outcomes and cost rather than assuming either policy always wins. When all evidence already fits in context, retrieval may add overhead without benefit; availability of the right memory does not ensure the model uses it correctly. [Source 18](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-18) [Source 19](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-19)

Use structured queries, rather than vector similarity alone, for counts, relationships and time constraints. An *illustrative* request for “my merged pull requests last week” requires a caller identity, a time window and an executable filter; discover relevant fields and types, resolve names to system IDs and validate the query under the caller's permissions. Sampling a schemaless database can miss uncommon shapes, and unresolved identity ambiguity should not silently become a guess. A bounded retry can repair an execution error, but a syntactically valid query may still answer the wrong question. [Source 20](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-20) [Source 21](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-21) [Source 22](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-22) [Source 23](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-23) [Source 24](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-24)

Large tool catalogs present a separate selection problem: retrieve a small shortlist from tool descriptions before presenting schemas to the agent, then test whether the needed tool remains available. A synthetic travel demonstration used 90 queries, 29 tools and a top-three shortlist; it does not establish production accuracy or a reproducible improvement. [Source 25](#retrieval-and-query-optimization-source-25)

## Model selection and runtime efficiency

Covers runtime selection and acceleration, not training model specialization.

Efficiency is not a single model score. A useful candidate must complete the intended work at acceptable quality, cost and latency in the actual harness and serving environment. Lower precision, less reasoning and a faster kernel affect different parts of that system; each needs its own acceptance evidence.

## Allocate precision to sensitivity, then test it

Quantization represents model values at reduced numerical precision. It can shrink weights, freeing memory for key–value (KV) cache and potentially more concurrent requests; reducing weight movement can also speed decoding. Those are distinct outcomes: increased capacity does not prove faster single-request decoding, and neither proves quality retention. A format that loads on a device may lack accelerated arithmetic and run slower than a higher-precision alternative. Test the actual format, implementation, device and workload. [Source 1](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-1) [Source 2](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-2)

Start with representative calibration inputs, including the context lengths, languages and modalities users need. Run them through the model and inspect layer-level changes; keep sensitive components at higher precision while compressing more tolerant ones. Testing individual layers and combinations, or using sensitivity analysis to guide allocation, is more informative than assuming one bit width fits every tensor. Attention projections, long-context linear-attention pathways and vision or audio components are reported sensitivities, not proof that those components cannot be quantized. Their importance depends on architecture and the calibration evidence provided. [Source 3](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-3) [Source 4](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-4) [Source 5](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-5)

Record the format's scaling arrangement as well as its nominal bit width: shared scales and the grouping of values change the representation. The source discussion contains an elements-versus-bits inconsistency, so it does not establish a format comparison or hardware support matrix. Small models may need higher precision or quantization-aware distillation to recover quality; model-size cutoffs are practitioner heuristics, not laws. Recovery data must reflect the capabilities being preserved: a panelist warns that mismatched distillation data can damage a reasoning model, without presenting a controlled dataset comparison. [Source 6](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-6) [Source 7](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-7)

Compare the original and quantized model at several levels. Reference-output distribution divergence on calibration inputs indicates fidelity to the original, but not whether the original or compressed model solves the application. Benchmark retention tests a defined suite; application-harness trials expose behavior that suite may miss. A panelist's stated benchmark degradation target is a release goal, not a guarantee for every checkpoint. Separately assess KV-cache compression and sparsity: success with weight quantization does not establish their quality. [Source 8](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-8) [Source 9](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-9) [Source 10](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-10) [Source 11](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-11)

## Budget reasoning and action together

Treat reasoning effort, timeouts, memory and CPU as recorded experimental settings. A quick draft and a review-ready answer may justify different budgets. Fewer output tokens do not establish better efficiency if they lose useful work: one reported coding comparison fell from 80% accuracy at maximum effort to 68% at high effort. Those are coding results, not evidence of the same change on financial research. [Source 12](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-12)

More thinking is not always better either. In two reported agent harnesses, maximum thinking scored worse; the speaker interpreted traces as long deliberation consuming a one-hour budget that could otherwise have supported commands, feedback and repairs. That explanation was not a controlled causal ablation, and other model comparisons behaved differently. Examine task completion, tool interactions, time and spend together; inspect repetitive reasoning and resource exhaustion rather than attributing every failure to model intelligence. [Source 13](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-13) [Source 14](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-14)

## Measure the whole system, not the attractive local win

Profile real execution to identify expensive work, then compare a proposed change against both correctness and the full workload. A kernel can look faster in isolation while disabling CUDA graphs makes end-to-end inference slower; the cited example's dramatic slowdown is speaker-reported without a disclosed benchmark configuration. Keep relevant production accelerations enabled and preserve a fallback where a kernel wins only for particular workload regimes. Combining individually useful changes also requires a combined-system test: gains need not compose indefinitely. [Source 15](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-15) [Source 16](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-16) [Source 17](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-17)

The same principle applies above the model. In a synthetic, spot-checked demonstration, a system answered aggregate questions correctly but spent many paginated API calls. Adding read-only SQL and prompting its use for counts and grouping was evaluated using task reward, tool calls and turns. The reported directional improvement was efficiency with preserved success, not a correctness rescue; the small database did not establish production-scale savings. [Source 18](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-18)

Targeted investigations can look for sleeps, excess queries, missing indexes or repeated allocation in observed hot paths. One account searched other services after finding repeated counter allocation; the proposed savings were conditional estimates, not measured fleet-wide results. Reusable diagnostic procedures can improve consistency, but the vendor account did not quantify that improvement. Verify each candidate in its actual service before deployment. [Source 19](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-19) [Source 20](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-20) [Source 21](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-21)

## Choose and combine acceleration mechanisms

Identify what actually changed. Component-specific quantization changes numerical representation; pruning removes components; compiler fusion and hardware-aware execution can instead reduce overhead in the serving path. In image or video diffusion, distillation or caching may reduce repeated denoising work, but the cited description gives neither a cache-validity rule nor a quality curve. A vendor's claim that a speedup came from execution rather than compression is a useful distinction, not itself a controlled proof of quality equivalence. [Source 22](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-22) [Source 23](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-23) [Source 24](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-24)

A proposed inference-native stack combines graph compilation, fusion and eager execution for debugging; portable abstractions still need low-level tuning access when hardware-specific bottlenecks matter. Neither portability nor a transformed checkpoint guarantees compatibility with a particular compiler, attention implementation and quantization combination. Test that combination and its quality on the target workload. [Source 25](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-25) [Source 26](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-26) [Source 27](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-27)

One clinical voice team describes treating output quality as a constraint while using quantization, speculative decoding and cache compression to reduce latency, then spending recovered time on additional intelligence. That is an engineering objective, not proof that its quantization is lossless or its safety gains measured. For serving measurements and interaction deadlines, see [Measuring inference serving performance](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/inference-serving.html) and [Interactive latency](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/interactive-latency.html); for deployment allocation, see [Allocating models and deployment resources](https://flaviusapop.github.io/ai-engineer-evals/wiki/articles/routing-and-deployment.html). [Source 28](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-28) [Source 29](#model-selection-and-runtime-efficiency-source-29)
